## Audit Summary
The report is **not fully trustworthy as written**. It contains substantial citation-bibliography linkage problems, many unsupported or unverifiable statistics, and several instances where study design labels are overstated relative to the source material. The overall narrative is broadly consistent with the source set, but the final report overclaims precision in places where the iteration history and pre-scored source list do not provide it. The most critical issues are: (1) bibliography numbering is largely disconnected from inline citations, (2) many numerical/statistical claims are not traceable to the iteration history, and (3) several studies are described as RCTs/QEDs without source-backed confirmation.

## Check 1 — Citation-Bibliography Linkage
Issues found:
- **Inline citations do not match the Bibliography numbering scheme.** The report body cites numbers like `[165]`, `[69]`, `[121]`, etc., but the Bibliography table is numbered **1–30 only**. Therefore, most or all inline citations are **missing from the Bibliography**.
- **Bibliography entries 1–30 are orphaned relative to the body citation system.** The body does not cite `[1]`–`[30]` inline in the report text, so the Bibliography table entries are not linked to the body citations.
- **Title/URL matching cannot be validated for the inline citations** because the cited numbers do not correspond to the Bibliography entries.
- **The Bibliography includes source names that are not present in the pre-numbered source list** as cited report numbers; however, the main auditable issue is numbering mismatch rather than specific title mismatch.

### Specific problems
- Inline citations cited in the body: `[165] [69] [121] [121] [71] [166] [73] [83] [116] [181] [79] [128] [59] [57] [54] [149] [136] [118] [182] [87] [167] [70] [74] [77] [88] [51] [53] [91] [56] [145] [165] [121] [166]` and many others.
- Bibliography entries present only for `1–30`, with no correspondence to those inline citation numbers.
- **Result:** citation-bibliography linkage is effectively broken.

## Check 2 — Statistic Provenance

| Statistic | Source Citation | Status | Notes |
|-----------|----------------|--------|-------|
| “grades 9–12 is still limited, heterogeneous, and often indirect” | [165][69][121][121] / narrative claim | UNVERIFIED | General synthesis claim; not a specific statistic. Not found verbatim in iteration history as a numeric statistic. |
| “The most defensible conclusion is that AI tools are most likely to help with revision, mechanics, and immediate writing performance…” | [165][69][121] | UNVERIFIED | Directional synthesis, not a specific statistic. |
| “The retrieved source records do not report the effect sizes or pooled coefficients…” | [165][121][166] | VERIFIED | Matches iteration history’s repeated note that exact effect sizes were not retrieved. |
| “The RCT titled Artificial Intelligence, Teacher Tasks and Individualized Pedagogy studied automated writing evaluation in high school” | [121] | VERIFIED | Study exists in source list; however the claim about exact study framing is broad and not numeric. |
| “the retrieved record does not provide the exact sample size or effect estimate” | [121] | VERIFIED | Iteration history explicitly says exact statistics were not provided. |
| “The quasi-experimental study The Role of AI Assisted Writing Feedback in Developing Secondary Students Writing Skills compared AI-assisted feedback with traditional teacher feedback” | [83] | VERIFIED | Source list confirms QED, but exact outcome stats absent. |
| “The pilot study Learning to Prompt in the Classroom to Understand AI Limits indicates that a short classroom AI-literacy workshop can help…” | [87] | UNVERIFIED | The iteration history supports a pilot workshop but does not provide the claimed directional outcome verbatim. |
| “many are small, preliminary, or not fully reported” | [73][79][116][128][181] | UNVERIFIED | General characterization, not a checkable statistic. |
| “The meta-analysis of automated feedback and writing reports positive pooled effects on writing performance, though heterogeneous” | [165] | VERIFIED | Iteration history supports positive overall pooled effects with heterogeneity. |
| “The school-setting systematic review reaches a broadly similar conclusion…” | [121] | VERIFIED | Consistent with iteration history. |
| “The direct high-school studies are more mixed.” | [121][83][87] | UNVERIFIED | Synthesis statement; not a statistic. |
| “The study on AI-generated feedback for ELL writers highlights coherence and cohesion…” | [116] | VERIFIED | Source title indicates coherence and cohesion focus. |
| “students may accept, modify, or rework machine-produced text in different ways” | [79] | VERIFIED | Matches the study description in source list. |
| “benefit may depend on prior proficiency” | [128] | UNVERIFIED | Plausible from source summary but not a precise statistic. |
| “The evidence is stronger for automated writing evaluation and hybrid feedback systems than for generative chatbot use alone” | [165][121][71][166] | UNVERIFIED | Comparative synthesis, not a statistic. |
| “confidence is moderate” / “confidence is low” | various | UNVERIFIED | No formal quantitative confidence metric in source material. |
| “one clear high-school RCT record and at least one direct high-school comparison” | [121][83] | VERIFIED | This matches the iteration history and source list. |
| “The evidence base contains one clear high-school RCT record and at least one direct high-school comparison…” | [121][83] | VERIFIED | Supported by source list/iteration history. |

### FABRICATED statistics
No clear numeric value was found to be explicitly fabricated, but the report contains **many numerically styled claims without provenance**:
- “grades 9–12”
- “11th-grade ELA”
- “8-week high-school comparison” (not substantiated in provided source history)
- “short classroom AI-literacy workshop” (duration not sourced)
- any implied pooled-effect magnitude beyond “positive pooled effects”

### UNVERIFIED statistics / quantitative claims needing removal or sourcing
- Any claim of **exact sample size**
- Any claim of **effect estimate / effect size**
- Any claim of **pooled coefficient**
- Any claim of **percentages** or **durations** not explicitly stated in the iteration history
- Any claim of **moderate/low confidence** if intended as a formal evidence-grade statistic

## Check 3 — Study Design Accuracy
Issues found:
- **Potential overstatement of RCT/QED labels** in the narrative:
  - **Artificial Intelligence, Teacher Tasks and Individualized Pedagogy** is labeled as an RCT in the Bibliography and source list, so the report’s RCT label is supported.
  - **The Role of AI Assisted Writing Feedback in Developing Secondary Students Writing Skills** is labeled QED in the source list, so the report’s QED label is supported.
- **However, several studies are described as causal-comparison designs in ways not supported by the source material**, especially when the report implies experimental strength beyond the metadata:
  - **Learning to Prompt in the Classroom to Understand AI Limits** is a **Mixed-Methods pilot** in the source list, not an RCT/QED.
  - **The high-school case study on the CGScholar AI Helper Project** is qualitative, not causal.
  - **The study of secondary students’ prompt engineering pathways** is qualitative, not experimental.
- **No explicit false RCT/QED labels were identified for the two named studies above**, but the report repeatedly uses causal-sounding wording for non-causal studies.

### Specific design-risk issue
- “The pilot study Learning to Prompt in the Classroom to Understand AI Limits indicates that a short classroom AI-literacy workshop can help…” is **not an RCT/QED claim**, but the wording implies intervention efficacy beyond a pilot design.

## Check 4 — Sub-question Coverage

| Tier | Sub-question | Coverage | Key Citations |
|------|-------------|----------|--------------|

| Tier 1 | For which populations/settings has AI-supported writing been studied? | Covered with cited evidence | [121][83][69][73][128] |
| Tier 2 | How do students develop writing outcomes without AI writing assistants? | Covered with cited evidence | [69][74][121][165] |
| Tier 2 | What alternative digital approaches have been used as comparison conditions? | Covered with cited evidence | [69][121][165] |
| Tier 2 | What is the baseline level of literacy growth or writing performance under standard instruction? | Partially covered | [69][121][165] |
| Tier 3 | How are AI writing assistants integrated into instruction? | Covered with cited evidence | [73][79][83][118][182][87] |
| Tier 3 | What implementation features matter most? | Covered with cited evidence | [83][118][167][73][87][121] |
| Tier 3 | What mechanisms explain impact? | Covered with cited evidence | [165][121][79][73][87] |
| Tier 4 | Do AI writing assistants improve outcomes more than standard instruction/teacher feedback/non-AI tools? | Covered with cited evidence | [165][121][83] |
| Tier 4 | Which implementation conditions are associated with stronger or weaker effects? | Covered with cited evidence | [83][118][167][121] |
| Tier 4 | Are effects different for specific subgroups? | Covered with cited evidence | [54][116][128][149] |
| Tier 4 | What tradeoffs, risks, or unintended consequences are reported? | Covered with cited evidence | [57][59][79][116][88][51][53][91][56][145][203] |

### Missing tier support
- **No tier is entirely unsupported**, but **Tier 2 “baseline level of literacy growth”** is only partially answered because the report does not provide a concrete baseline estimate or clearly sourced comparator statistics.

## Check 5 — URL Integrity
Issues found:
- The Bibliography URLs are mostly **not auditable against the report body** because the body citations are not mapped to the Bibliography numbering.
- The source list contains many entries with **not_reported** URLs or placeholder/invalid URLs; those are not necessarily invented by the report, but they complicate verification.
- No report-invented URL string was introduced in the Bibliography table itself beyond what appears in the source list, but several URLs are placeholder-like.

### MISMATCH / INVENTED
- **No definitive MISMATCH or INVENTED URLs in the Bibliography table can be confirmed from the supplied material**, because the Bibliography table uses the same titles as the source list items for the included studies, and most URLs are “not available” placeholders.
- However, because the report’s inline citation numbers do not match the Bibliography numbering, **URL integrity is effectively uncheckable for the body citations**.

## Recommended Fixes
1. **Rebuild the citation system so inline citations match Bibliography numbers exactly.**  
   This is the most serious issue. The body should cite `[1]`, `[2]`, etc., matching the Bibliography, or the Bibliography should be renumbered to match the inline citations.

2. **Remove or qualify all unsupported numeric/statistical claims.**  
   Any sample size, effect size, p-value, percentage, or duration not directly present in the iteration history should be deleted or clearly labeled as unavailable.

3. **Stop implying causal strength for non-causal studies.**  
   Keep “pilot,” “case study,” “qualitative,” and “observational” studies framed as implementation or descriptive evidence, not efficacy evidence.

4. **Align design labels with the source list exactly.**  
   Verify each RCT/QED claim against the pre-numbered source list; do not upgrade qualitative or mixed-method studies into quasi-experimental evidence.

5. **Clarify which evidence is direct high-school evidence versus indirect higher-education or EFL evidence.**  
   The current report blends these too freely and overstates applicability to grades 9–12.

6. **Tighten the Bibliography to only sources actually used in the report body.**  
   Remove orphan entries or add missing in-text citations so every bibliography item is linked.

7. **Replace confidence language with explicit evidence grades if available.**  
   “Moderate confidence” and “low confidence” are not substantiated as formal metrics in the source material.

8. **Audit the URL field for each bibliography entry.**  
   Ensure every URL exactly matches the source list entry; if a URL is unavailable in the source list, mark it as unavailable rather than implying a stable link.

paper_profiles.title: Language learning and study abroad
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This state-of-the-art review synthesizes empirical research on undergraduate language learners’ study-abroad experiences lasting a year or less. Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper surveys mixed-method, quantitative, and qualitative studies to explain how study abroad affects language learning, learner identity, motivation, agency, and intercultural development.

The review organizes the literature around research design (quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods) and around learning outcomes across reading, writing, listening, speaking, and communicative competence. It emphasizes that study-abroad outcomes are highly variable, shaped by individual differences, context, and the quality of interaction and engagement abroad. Across studies, the authors report that study abroad often supports gains in listening, speaking, and some aspects of writing and reading, but effects are inconsistent and sometimes not significantly different from at-home or intensive domestic comparison conditions.

A major conclusion is that research should move beyond treating study abroad as a simple categorical treatment and instead examine the social ecosystem, learner trajectories, and the alignment between abroad and at-home curricula. The review also argues for more mixed-method and longitudinal work, since quantitative gains alone do not capture the complexity of learner experiences or the reasons some learners benefit more than others.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds mixed evidence for literacy gains in study abroad. Reading comprehension often improves relative to at-home learners in some studies, but other comparisons show no significant differences (e.g., Huebner 1995; Dewey 2004). Writing shows similarly mixed results: some studies report gains in fluency, lexical diversity/richness, accuracy, and cohesion during or after SA, while others find no advantage over at-home instruction.
finding.measure: Standardized reading comprehension tests; writing fluency/quality measures; lexical diversity, accuracy, syntactic complexity, cohesion

finding.finding_summary: Study abroad is associated with more consistent gains in listening and speaking than in literacy, but the pattern is still mixed. Many studies report significant listening gains over time and sometimes relative to at-home learners, yet other studies find only modest gains or no significant differences; speaking proficiency often improves, but holistic oral measures can remain unchanged even when fluency, pronunciation, or pragmatic subskills improve.
finding.measure: Listening comprehension tests; oral proficiency interviews; speech rate, turn length, hesitancy, pronunciation, pragmatic comprehension

finding.finding_summary: The review documents consistent positive changes in several affective and motivational outcomes, including reduced anxiety, increased self-confidence, stronger intended effort, and more positive motivational stances after study abroad. These changes are reported in longitudinal and pre/post studies, including a 4-wave design showing that formal instruction plus SA triggered positive motivational change that persisted after return.
finding.measure: Motivation, anxiety, self-confidence, intended effort, attitudes, willingness to communicate

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights development of learner agency, self-regulation, strategy use, and reflective practices as important outcomes of study abroad. Intervention studies and qualitative work suggest that activities such as blogs/journals, ethnographic projects, and conversation-partner supports can strengthen learners’ ability to monitor comprehension, reflect on learning, and engage independently in the target culture.
finding.measure: Learner agency, self-regulation, strategy use, reflective journals/logs, ethnographic projects

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that study abroad has institutional importance for aligning abroad curricula with at-home curricula and broader internationalization goals. It concludes that SA programs should better coordinate learning objectives with home-campus courses and consider broader policy and program design issues related to internationalization and mobility.
finding.measure: Curriculum alignment, program design, internationalization framing, policy discussions

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Project Based Learning with Virtual Media Assistance on Student’s Creativity in Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether project-based learning supported by virtual media can improve students’ creativity in physics. The paper situates creativity as an important educational outcome and argues that traditional instruction often does not sufficiently develop divergent thinking, especially when assessment is limited to routine problem solving.

The authors conducted a pretest-posttest control group quasi-experiment in one senior high school in Mataram, Indonesia. Two intact classes were selected by cluster random sampling and assigned to an experiment group (project-based learning with virtual media) and a control group (direct instruction), with 30 students in each class. Creativity was measured with validated essay tests covering verbal and figural creativity, and gains were analyzed using N-gain and t-tests.

Results showed that both groups improved from pretest to posttest, but the experiment group improved more than the control group. The paper reports an average N-gain of 40.8% for the experiment class and 31.1% for the control class, both in the average category, and a significant between-group difference (tcount > ttable, 3.21 > 2.00). Verbal creativity increased more than figural creativity in both groups, suggesting that the intervention was more effective for verbal divergent thinking than for pictorial/shape-based creativity.

finding.finding_summary: Project-based learning with virtual media produced a statistically significant gain in students’ creativity compared with direct instruction. The experiment class (n=30) had an average N-gain of 40.8% versus 31.1% in the control class (n=30), and the authors report a significant t-test result (tcount > ttable, 3.21 > 2.00).
finding.measure: Verbal and figural creativity test; N-gain from pretest-posttest scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper specifically frames creativity in physics learning as a valued academic capability and reports that the intervention improved students’ ability to express and elaborate ideas in the physics context. Both verbal and figural creativity increased from pretest to posttest, with the experimental group outperforming the control group.
finding.measure: Physics-learning creativity test (verbal and figural items)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention appeared to increase students’ enthusiasm and active participation during learning, according to the discussion of classroom observations and the authors’ interpretation of the virtual-media project environment. However, these outcomes were not measured with a dedicated motivation or engagement scale, so the evidence is indirect.
finding.measure: Classroom participation/enthusiasm as discussed by authors

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Cooperative Learning on Developing Speaking Ability and Motivation Toward Learning English
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether cooperative learning improves English speaking performance and learning motivation compared with traditional whole-class instruction in an Iranian university EFL context. The authors frame the problem as a persistent reliance on teacher-centered methods that limit student speaking practice and motivation, and they argue that cooperative learning may provide a more student-centered alternative.

The intervention used adapted cooperative learning structures, especially STAD and Numbered-Heads-Together, in which students worked in small groups, shared responsibilities, presented work to the class, and received feedback and grades from both peers and the teacher. The comparison condition was conventional instruction dominated by teacher talk, emphasis on grammar/vocabulary accuracy, and limited peer interaction. Ninety male TEFL students at Islamic Azad University were assigned to one experimental and one control group in a non-equivalent pre-test/post-test design.

Results showed that the cooperative learning group improved significantly more than the control group on speaking performance, with a large effect size (d=0.81). On motivation, the experimental group improved significantly in intrinsic motivation and identified regulation, while no meaningful differences emerged for the other motivation subscales. Overall, the paper concludes that cooperative learning was more effective than traditional instruction for developing speaking ability and some aspects of motivation in this university EFL setting.

finding.finding_summary: The cooperative learning group showed significantly greater gains in speaking performance than the control group receiving traditional instruction. The experimental group increased from M=59.13 (SD=2.94) to M=63.48 (SD=7.63), while the control group changed only from M=58.46 (SD=2.61) to M=58.91 (SD=2.32); the post-test difference was significant, t=3.84, p=.000, with a large effect size of d=0.81.
finding.measure: English speaking test with tasks on picture differences, reading aloud, and expressing an opinion; scored on pronunciation, grammatical accuracy, vocabulary, fluency, and interactive communication
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post-test SD=7.63; Control post-test SD=2.32

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved some motivation outcomes but not all. The experimental group showed significant pre-post gains in intrinsic motivation (M=35.86 to 40.68; effect size=0.49) and identified regulation, while the control group did not show comparable improvement; ANCOVA found a significant group difference only for intrinsic motivation after adjusting for pre-test scores (p=.05).
finding.measure: Language Learning Orientations Scale (LLOS) motivation subscales: intrinsic motivation, integrated regulation, identified regulation, introjected regulation, external regulation, amotivation
finding.effect_size: 0.49 for intrinsic motivation; 0.18 for identified regulation; others below average/not meaningful
finding.std_deviation: Intrinsic motivation SDs: experimental pre=8.98, post=10.89; control pre=11.02, post=10.26

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that cooperative learning improved collaboration and peer interaction as part of the instructional process, but these were not the primary measured outcomes. Evidence is indirect and embedded in the design rationale rather than reported as a separate quantitative result, so the finding is only moderately central to this outcome category.
finding.measure: Observed cooperative group work, peer discussion, shared presentation, and team assessment processes

paper_profiles.title: Preparing teachers to integrate Web 2.0 in school practice: Toward a framework for Pedagogy 2.0
paper_profiles.population: Primary and secondary teachers (including secondary/high school context)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how to prepare teachers to integrate Web 2.0 tools into classroom practice through a professional development program grounded in TPACK and authentic learning. The central problem is that teachers often use ICT in limited, add-on ways and need support to move toward more purposeful, pedagogically meaningful uses of participatory web tools such as blogs, wikis, e-portfolios, social bookmarking, and WebQuests.

The study reports the design and implementation of a blended training course ('Web 2.0 tools in Practice') delivered to 86 primary and secondary teachers in Greece. The program combined face-to-face workshops, online collaboration, hands-on design tasks, and reflective discussion. Data came from an anonymous post-course questionnaire with Likert-scale items and open-ended responses administered six weeks after the course.

Findings suggest that participants were generally positive about Web 2.0 and felt the course increased their knowledge, confidence, and readiness to use these tools. Teachers especially valued blogs and wikis and believed well-designed Web 2.0 activities could improve student participation, collaboration, creativity, critical thinking, and connections between school and home. Reported barriers included lack of time, infrastructure, curriculum constraints, and the need for more pedagogical support. The paper concludes that a coherent pedagogical framework and authentic professional development can help teachers move beyond treating Web 2.0 as an add-on technology.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that properly designed Web 2.0 learning activities could enhance students' creativity (M=4.63), critical thinking (M=4.39), and collaboration (M=4.66), and they believed these tools would promote active participation (M=4.68). These are perception data from 86 primary and secondary teachers rather than direct student outcome measures, but they indicate strong anticipated benefits for durable skills.
finding.measure: Teacher perception survey items about expected student creativity, critical thinking, active participation, and collaborative learning

finding.finding_summary: The participating teachers believed Web 2.0 would make instruction more interesting for students (M=4.53) and support active participation (M=4.68), and open-ended responses described students as more engaged in blogging and other Web 2.0 activities. The evidence is based on teacher perceptions after training, not on direct measurement of student engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perception survey and open-ended responses about anticipated student interest/engagement

finding.finding_summary: The program improved teachers' reported readiness to integrate Web 2.0 into instruction and highlighted institutional barriers such as infrastructure, time, and curriculum constraints. Teachers indicated the training had a positive impact on their professional development and their intention to adopt Web 2.0 practices, suggesting potential school-level implementation effects.
finding.measure: Teacher readiness, intentions, and reported barriers to implementation

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the course increased their knowledge and skills to integrate Web 2.0, and they viewed some tools (blogs, wikis, GoogleDocs, forums) as practical for classroom use. However, the study did not quantify changes in productivity or workload; it only captured perceived preparedness and implementation feasibility.
finding.measure: Teacher self-reported preparedness and perceived feasibility of implementing Web 2.0 learning activities

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; discusses primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional education broadly)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks how large language models, especially ChatGPT/GPT-3-class systems, might be used in education and what risks their adoption introduces. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the authors synthesize emerging applications and policy concerns across learner, teacher, and institutional perspectives.

The paper argues that LLMs can support education by generating questions, summaries, explanations, feedback, lesson materials, and personalized practice across grade levels and subjects. It emphasizes potential benefits such as more efficient teacher workflows, adaptive feedback, and richer learner support, while also warning about bias, hallucinations, plagiarism, privacy, overreliance, and the need for human oversight, fact-checking, and curricular alignment.

The paper is not focused on a specific intervention, sample, or school level, and it does not present original outcome data. Its main contribution is a conceptual and practical framework for responsible integration: teachers and institutions should use LLMs as supplements rather than replacements, provide training and guidance, ensure transparency and fairness, and embed AI use within curricula, assessment, and ethical governance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by assisting with lesson planning, generating questions, providing feedback, and semi-automating grading and text review. No original empirical study is reported, but the authors cite prior examples such as grading effort reduction of up to 85% in related NLP feedback systems.
finding.measure: teacher workload, grading effort, content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and fact-checking when used as scaffolds for hypothesis generation, perspective-taking, and revision. At the same time, it warns that overreliance could weaken these skills by making answers too effortless and reducing students’ independent inquiry.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking, metacognitive support (conceptual proposals)

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies writing support as a major use case: LLMs can help with syntactic correction, grammar/style feedback, outlining, summaries, and drafting of essays and research papers. It does not report primary outcome data, but it explicitly frames these functions as supporting reading and writing development across school levels.
finding.measure: writing support, grammar/style assistance, summaries, outlines, essay generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that effective adoption of LLMs depends on institutional governance, privacy/security policies, training, curriculum alignment, transparency, and human oversight. It highlights risks such as bias, plagiarism, cost, and inequitable access, and proposes mitigation strategies rather than reporting measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: policy/governance, privacy/security, fairness, curricular integration

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs may improve student engagement, interaction, and curiosity, including through personalized guidance and curiosity-prompting cues. These claims are conceptual and based on cited prior work rather than original empirical measurement in this paper.
finding.measure: engagement, curiosity, interaction, willingness to participate

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education from 2007 to 2018. The authors ask how the field has developed, how AI is conceptualized, what ethical concerns are raised, and what kinds of AI applications have been studied in higher education settings. They screened 2,656 records, included 146 peer-reviewed journal articles, and coded them for journal distribution, geography, disciplinary affiliation, methods, and application type.

The review finds that AI in higher education research is dominated by computer science and STEM authors, quantitative methods, and learner-facing applications such as profiling/prediction, assessment/evaluation, adaptive systems, and intelligent tutoring systems. Only a small number of papers explicitly define AI or critically discuss risks such as privacy and cost. Across the reviewed studies, AI systems were typically used for prediction, automated feedback, tutoring, and personalization; most studies reported preliminary positive results, but implementation was usually short-term and long-term effectiveness evidence was limited.

The paper also argues that educators are underrepresented in the literature and that the field has weak connections to pedagogical theory. Overall, the review suggests that AI tools can support assessment, feedback, and student support in higher education, but it highlights substantial gaps in educational framing, ethical reflection, and rigorous longitudinal evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: Across 146 reviewed higher-education studies, AI applications were most often used for assessment and evaluation tasks, including automated essay scoring, feedback, and evaluation of student understanding. The review reports that these systems often achieved high classification accuracy and could reduce cost and time in large-scale assessments, but the evidence base is heterogeneous and mostly short-term.
finding.measure: Automated grading / feedback accuracy; agreement between machine and human ratings; evaluation of student understanding
finding.study_size: n=146 studies reviewed; individual studies ranged from small pilots to large datasets

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies used AI to predict or monitor student engagement, motivation, and dropout risk. The review notes that AI-based engagement prediction and early warning systems can identify at-risk students and prompt intervention, but it also reports at least one negative finding where support was not well matched to more advanced learners.
finding.measure: Student engagement, academic motivation, dropout/attrition prediction

finding.finding_summary: The review includes studies on AI-supported writing, collaborative writing, and automated feedback that were intended to support revision, self-regulation, and collaborative problem solving. The authors also note that some AI feedback systems helped reduce cognitive overload and encouraged more revisions, suggesting support for metacognitive and self-regulatory processes.
finding.measure: Writing revision behavior, collaborative writing processes, cognitive overload/self-regulation proxies

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the review is that AI tools can reduce teacher and administrative workload by automating grading, feedback, admissions screening, course scheduling, and other routine tasks. The review states that these systems can improve efficiency and free staff to focus on more complex cases, especially in large-enrollment settings.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, administrative efficiency, assessment automation, prediction/classification accuracy
finding.study_size: n=146 studies reviewed; individual studies varied widely

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies substantial use of AI for institutional applications such as profiling and prediction, drop-out and retention monitoring, admissions decisions, course scheduling, and alignment of students with programs or competencies. These applications were frequently reported as useful for institutional decision-making and student support, though the paper also emphasizes privacy, governance, and cost concerns.
finding.measure: Institutional decision support, retention prediction, admissions and scheduling outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper examines how ChatGPT responds to a set of science-education prompts and considers what those responses imply for educators. The author asks three questions: how ChatGPT answers science education questions, how educators might use it to design science pedagogy and resources, and how it can function as a research tool. The study uses a self-study methodology in which the author prompts ChatGPT and compares the outputs with established science education literature.

The paper is not an intervention study with students; it is primarily a reflective analysis of generated text and its possible educational uses. Prompts asked ChatGPT to describe effective science teaching, compare teacher-centered and student-centered pedagogy, respond to a struggling student, design a Year 7 5Es unit on renewable and non-renewable energy, generate a student self-assessment rubric, and create a quiz with answer key. The author argues that ChatGPT can be useful for generating ideas, scaffolding planning, and supporting writing, especially for early-career teachers or pre-service teachers, but its outputs are often generic and require strong teacher judgment and contextual adaptation.

Main conclusions are that ChatGPT’s responses often align with accepted science education themes such as inquiry, real-world connections, differentiation, and formative assessment, but the tool frequently lacks evidence, nuance, and attention to context. The paper emphasizes concerns about factual unreliability, bias, and ethics, including false references, epistemic authority, and responsible use. It also suggests ChatGPT may help with editing, unit design, rubric creation, quiz drafting, and idea generation, provided educators critically evaluate and adapt outputs to their curriculum, students, and teaching goals.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test student achievement directly, but it analyzes ChatGPT outputs related to science pedagogy and content. ChatGPT’s answers often aligned with established science education themes such as inquiry-based learning, real-world connections, assessment, and differentiation, but the author notes the outputs were sometimes generic and insufficiently evidence-based.
finding.measure: Quality and content alignment of ChatGPT-generated science education responses against cited science education literature

finding.finding_summary: The paper examines ChatGPT-generated teaching materials for Year 7 science, including a 5Es unit on renewable and non-renewable energy, a self-assessment rubric, and a quiz. The outputs were judged useful as starting points for planning and resource creation, but often too vague or generic to use without substantial refinement.
finding.measure: ChatGPT-generated unit plan, rubric, and quiz content for Year 7 renewable/non-renewable energy

finding.finding_summary: The author proposes that ChatGPT could support students who are struggling, including helping with writer’s block and offering a learning scaffold before engaging with more traditional resources. These claims are presented as plausible uses rather than tested effects, and the paper emphasizes that use should be paired with responsible guidance and clear expectations.
finding.measure: Proposed support uses of ChatGPT for struggling students and writers

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally discusses critical thinking, metacognition, and teacher judgment in relation to ChatGPT use. The author argues that ChatGPT can prompt idea generation and scaffold writing, but it also risks encouraging uncritical acceptance of outputs; educators and students should evaluate, adapt, and question AI-generated content.
finding.measure: Interpretive analysis of ChatGPT’s implications for critical thinking, contextual judgment, and responsible use

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can improve efficiency for educators by helping draft science units, rubrics, quizzes, and edited prose. The author reports using ChatGPT mainly for editing assistance, phrasing, flow, and word choice, describing it as a helpful tool for moving beyond a blank page and clarifying text.
finding.measure: Author-reported utility of ChatGPT for editing and generating instructional resources

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the concerns and perceived opportunities of using ChatGPT in education among early adopters. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors use ChatGPT as a case study to explore public discourse, stakeholder perspectives, and hands-on user experiences, focusing on issues such as cheating, response quality, ethics, privacy, fairness, and manipulation.

The study uses a three-stage qualitative instrumental case study: (1) social network analysis and sentiment analysis of 2,330 tweets from 1,530 Twitter users, (2) content analysis of 19 publicly posting interviewees from mixed roles including educators, students, developers, and AI freelancers, and (3) a one-week user experience exercise with three educators across ten educational scenarios. Across all stages, the paper argues that ChatGPT is viewed as potentially transformative and useful, but also risky because its outputs can be inaccurate, inconsistent, misleading, and ethically problematic.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT should not simply be banned; instead, education systems should develop guidance, new teaching philosophies, and responsible-use practices that emphasize critical thinking, prompt skill, teacher oversight, fairness, privacy, and human–machine collaboration. The paper is primarily conceptual and exploratory, offering implications for policy and future research rather than measured learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Participants frequently described ChatGPT as useful for reducing teacher workload and speeding up preparation of educational materials. The paper reports perceived gains such as generating outlines, creating quizzes, and producing teaching resources in about a minute, but it does not provide quantitative workload measures.
finding.measure: Perceived teacher workload reduction; creation of teaching materials and quizzes
finding.study_size: n=19 interviewees; 3 educators in user experience stage

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses substantially on writing-related uses of ChatGPT, including essay writing, thesis drafting, and writing assistance, but the findings are cautionary rather than outcome-based. Users reported that ChatGPT can help generate essays and provide immediate feedback, yet it may also facilitate cheating, encourage laziness, and produce inaccurate or overly generic writing content.
finding.measure: Writing support, essay generation, thesis-writing assistance, and immediate feedback
finding.study_size: n=19 interviewees; 3 educators in user experience stage

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that ChatGPT may support critical thinking and metacognitive support when used well, but may also weaken these skills if students rely on it too heavily. The paper repeatedly argues that users need prompt skill development, critical questioning, and judgment to obtain useful outputs and avoid overreliance on plausible but inaccurate responses.
finding.measure: Perceived critical thinking, prompt skill development, and metacognitive judgment in interacting with ChatGPT
finding.study_size: n=19 interviewees; 3 educators in user experience stage

finding.finding_summary: The study strongly emphasizes institutional concerns and policy implications, including cheating, privacy, fairness, regulation, and the need for guidelines for responsible adoption. It argues that schools and universities should not simply ban ChatGPT, but should instead establish policies, curricula, and teaching philosophies for safe and equitable use.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy, fairness, and institutional adoption concerns

paper_profiles.title: Potentials of ChatGPT in Computer Programming: Insights from Programming Instructors
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Information Technology Education: Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines programming instructors’ perceptions of ChatGPT as a support tool in programming instruction. The study asks what benefits, drawbacks, and implementation strategies instructors see for integrating ChatGPT into teaching and learning, especially in relation to students’ coding practice and instructors’ workload.

The author conducted 26 in-depth interviews with 12 programming instructors from the School of Information Technology at AL al-Bayt University in Jordan. Using qualitative thematic analysis, the study found that instructors viewed ChatGPT as useful for code generation, debugging, personalized learning, interactive practice, immediate feedback, and helping students compare solutions and test code. Instructors also believed it could save time by helping with assessment, lesson planning, examples, and individualized guidance.

At the same time, participants raised concerns about inaccurate or undesired outputs, contradictory responses, limited coverage of some programming topics, technical constraints, unstructured learning, cheating, over-reliance, privacy, and reduced human interaction. Overall, instructors favored a complementary model in which ChatGPT augments rather than replaces traditional teaching, with careful guidance, ethical use, and assignment design that requires critical thinking rather than trivial prompt-to-answer tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Programming instructors reported that ChatGPT can save time and effort by supporting assessment, generating lesson plans and teaching strategies, preparing examples and quizzes, and helping identify student difficulties. The study is qualitative and does not report effect sizes, but the consistent perception across participants was that ChatGPT improves instructor efficiency and reduces workload.
finding.measure: Instructor perceptions from in-depth interviews about assessment, lesson planning, examples, quizzes, and instructional support

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed ChatGPT could support students’ problem-solving, critical thinking, and programming proficiency by offering immediate feedback, multiple solutions, and opportunities to modify code and test outputs. However, they also worried that over-reliance and ready-made solutions could weaken critical thinking and problem-solving development, so the net effect was seen as conditional on careful use.
finding.measure: Instructor perceptions of critical thinking, problem-solving, and programming skill development

finding.finding_summary: Instructors repeatedly described ChatGPT as increasing student motivation, engagement, confidence, and interactive participation in programming tasks. They argued that immediate conversational responses and the ability to iterate on code can make programming practice more dynamic and accessible, although misuse and over-reliance were also noted as risks.
finding.measure: Instructor perceptions of motivation, engagement, confidence, and interactive participation

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in higher education: Benefits, challenges, and future research directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the potential benefits and challenges of ChatGPT in higher education through the lens of constructivist learning theory. Rather than reporting results from a primary empirical study, it offers a perspective-based synthesis of likely uses, risks, and design implications for teaching, learning, assessment, research support, and administration.

The article argues that ChatGPT may support adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research and writing assistance, administrative automation, and innovative assessment design. It also highlights major concerns, including academic integrity, biased or falsified outputs, equity of access, and the inability of ChatGPT to fully assess or develop graduate skills and learning outcomes. The authors conclude that institutions should prioritize AI literacy, ethical use, new assessment strategies, and human oversight when integrating generative AI into higher education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support academic writing by generating drafts, helping with language barriers, and providing writing assistance, but it also raises concerns about hallucinations, fabricated references, and academic integrity. No primary data are reported; the claims are theoretical and based on literature and author perspective.
finding.measure: Writing support, text generation, draft creation, language translation, academic writing tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, metacognition, and self-regulation, arguing that ChatGPT may support some of these through scaffolding, prompts, and revision opportunities while potentially weakening them if used as a shortcut. No empirical effect sizes or sample sizes are reported because this is a perspective article.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, self-regulated learning, metacognitive abilities

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims ChatGPT can reduce administrative burden, automate parts of feedback, and speed up tasks such as email summarization and response drafting. It also notes that automated or augmented feedback could save educator time, but these are conceptual assertions rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Administrative support, feedback automation, grading efficiency, email summarization, response templates

finding.finding_summary: The article focuses strongly on institutional implications, including academic integrity policy, AI literacy, assessment redesign, equity of access, and governance around ethical use of ChatGPT. It proposes that institutions should create new policies and training structures, but it does not evaluate these empirically.
finding.measure: Academic integrity policy, AI literacy, assessment design, equitable access, institutional governance

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual paper argues that the rapid rise of generative AI in education requires a shift in how institutions prepare students and teachers to use these tools responsibly. The paper is not an intervention study; rather, it combines informal case-based observations from a Swiss University of Applied Sciences with a narrative literature review to discuss the challenges posed by ChatGPT-style systems, including hallucinations, overreliance, academic integrity concerns, and uncertainty about appropriate use.

The article centers on three capabilities the author sees as essential for AI-era education: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It describes how one institution developed internal AI guidelines for student writing that require transparency about model use, critical evaluation of outputs, and documentation in appendices, while still permitting generative AI under restrictions. It also proposes broader supports such as workshops, curriculum integration, AI literacy courses, and teacher training to build a campus-wide “culture of AI.”

The paper further reviews prompt engineering as a pedagogical tool, summarizing prompting methods such as zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, expert prompting, self-consistency, automatic prompt engineering, generated knowledge prompting, and tree-of-thought prompting. The main conclusion is that AI should be treated as a sparring partner rather than a tutor or ghostwriter, with strong emphasis on human oversight, explicit boundaries, and student training to promote responsible, critical, and effective use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy and prompt engineering can strengthen students’ critical thinking and metacognition by requiring them to evaluate AI outputs, compare alternatives, and revise prompts iteratively. This claim is supported conceptually rather than with direct outcome data; no sample size, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, AI literacy, prompt-engineering skill, reflective evaluation of AI outputs

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses generative AI as a support for academic writing, particularly paper drafting, brainstorming, and improving written work through prompt engineering and revision. However, it does not report empirical writing outcomes for students; it offers conceptual guidance and institutional policy examples rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Academic writing/paper production

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes institutional AI guidelines, workshops, curriculum integration, and governance recommendations intended to shape responsible AI use across a university. These are presented as institutional responses and implementation proposals, but no quantitative outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: Institutional AI policy, guidelines, training structures, and governance practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI tools can reduce workload and help teachers create curricula, case studies, and classroom materials more efficiently. This is a conceptual claim based on observed use cases and discussion, not a measured productivity effect, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / curriculum and material creation efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular focus on chatbots and ChatGPT. It asks how AI technologies may be incorporated into educational settings, what benefits they may offer, and what ethical and practical challenges they raise. The paper is not an intervention study; rather, it synthesizes existing literature to argue that AI can support teaching and learning when used responsibly and in alignment with pedagogy.

The authors discuss AI applications across education, including personalized learning, instant feedback, automated assessment, student support, and teacher workload reduction. For writing-related use, the paper briefly mentions tools such as Grammarly, InstaText, QuillBot, and Microsoft 365 Copilot as examples of AI systems that can provide feedback and guidance on written work, but it does not evaluate a specific writing intervention, assignment type, or implementation model in high school writing instruction.

The paper’s main conclusion is that AI and chatbots hold substantial promise for improving engagement, learning outcomes, and efficiency, but successful use depends on teacher training, careful supervision, ethical safeguards, and curriculum alignment. It also stresses risks such as bias, privacy, over-reliance, and threats to academic integrity, arguing that further research is needed to understand effective and responsible educational implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can reduce repetitive work and teacher workload by automating grading, scoring, and feedback provision. It cites examples such as chatbots, AutoGradr, and Repl.it as systems that can save teachers many hours and free time for lesson planning, student support, and professional development, but it does not present original empirical estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / administrative efficiency discussed in narrative review

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that AI can support writing through personalized and instant feedback, and specifically names Grammarly, InstaText, and QuillBot as examples of tools that provide tailored feedback on written assignments. This is presented as a literature-based claim rather than a direct evaluation; no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Written assignments / writing feedback

finding.finding_summary: The review claims that AI-supported environments can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce learning anxiety by providing personalized learning and timely feedback. These claims are synthesized from prior studies and examples, not measured in this paper.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, confidence, and anxiety discussed in literature review

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that AI can foster self-reflection, self-directed learning, self-regulation, critical thinking, and creativity, especially when learners receive individualized guidance and timely feedback. The paper does not test these mechanisms empirically, but it explicitly frames them as important learning benefits of AI tools.
finding.measure: Self-regulation, self-reflection, critical thinking, creativity discussed in review

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that successful institutional adoption of AI requires teacher preparation, support, ethical oversight, privacy protections, and policy/curriculum alignment. At the same time, it warns that AI may exacerbate inequities, bias, and academic integrity concerns, so the institutional impact is presented as both promising and risky.
finding.measure: Institutional adoption, ethics, privacy, academic integrity, policy alignment discussed in review

paper_profiles.title: A Critical Review of Research on Student Self-Assessment
paper_profiles.population: K-20 (with examples from elementary through higher education); not limited to a single grade band
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper critically reviews research on student self-assessment, with a focus on how the construct is defined, how it is operationalized, and what the empirical literature says about its relationship to learning and performance. Rather than treating self-assessment as a single activity, the review distinguishes formative versus summative uses and also separates assessments of competence, processes, and products.

The paper synthesizes 76 empirical studies published largely between 2013 and 2018, along with two meta-analyses, and organizes the evidence around consistency with external judgments, achievement, student perceptions, and self-regulated learning. Across the review, the author argues that formative self-assessment is more useful than summative self-assessment, especially when students use clear criteria, rubrics, checklists, feedback, and opportunities to revise.

Most of the evidence reviewed comes from K-20 instructional contexts, including writing, science reports, vocational tasks, dart throwing, speaking English, and exam preparation. The central conclusion is that self-assessment tends to improve achievement and self-regulated learning when it is formative, criteria-referenced, and scaffolded; however, the field still lacks strong evidence on the internal cognitive and affective mechanisms through which self-assessment affects learning, as well as on precisely which forms and conditions are most effective.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that formative self-assessment is associated with improved writing quality and other literacy outcomes. It cites a meta-analysis of 10 studies by Graham et al. (2015) reporting an average weighted effect size of 0.62 on writing quality, and notes that the included studies generally found that rubric- or script-based self-assessment helped students produce more effective writing.
finding.measure: Writing quality; scores on written assignments; revision outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that self-assessment is generally associated with stronger self-regulated learning, motivation, and related student perceptions when it is used formatively. Across the studies summarized, students who used self-assessment tended to report greater self-regulation, goal setting, monitoring, and reflection than comparison groups, with several studies showing statistically significant but small-to-moderate effects.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning questionnaires; think-aloud protocols; student perceptions surveys

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the relationship between self-assessment and metacognition/self-regulated learning, which the author frames as durable skills. The review reports that students using rubric- or script-referenced self-assessment were more self-regulated than controls, and one study found associations across all three SRL phases (forethought, performance, reflection).
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning measures; metacognitive judgments; think-aloud protocols

finding.finding_summary: Beyond writing, the review reports positive achievement effects across a range of academic tasks and disciplines, including exams, map-making, speaking English, and other school tasks. The evidence summarized in the review suggests that formative self-assessment can improve task performance when learners use explicit criteria and have opportunities to revise or re-learn.
finding.measure: Task performance; exam scores; disciplinary performance tasks

paper_profiles.title: The effect of ChatGPT on students’ learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis examines whether ChatGPT improves student learning outcomes and under what conditions its effects are stronger or weaker. The authors note that prior studies on ChatGPT in education have reported mixed findings, so they synthesized experimental and quasi-experimental evidence to estimate overall effects on learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking.

The review included 51 studies published between November 2022 and February 2025, yielding 72 independent effect sizes. Across studies, ChatGPT produced a large positive effect on learning performance (g=0.867, 95% CI [0.683, 1.052], k=44), and moderate positive effects on learning perception (g=0.456, 95% CI [0.287, 0.625], k=19) and higher-order thinking (g=0.457, 95% CI [0.255, 0.650], k=9). The authors also found moderation by course type, learning model, duration, and ChatGPT role for some outcomes; for example, learning performance was strongest in problem-based learning and in 4–8 week interventions, while learning perception was strongest in interventions lasting more than 8 weeks.

Most included studies were college-level, with some secondary-school studies and very limited primary-school evidence. The paper does not specifically focus on writing-assistant comparisons against teacher feedback or non-AI tools in K-12 writing contexts; rather, it evaluates ChatGPT broadly across STEM, language/writing, and skills-development courses. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support learning, especially when integrated with appropriate scaffolds and used continuously over several weeks, but they also caution that evidence is heterogeneous and that some moderator categories contain limited studies.

finding.finding_summary: Across language learning and academic writing studies, ChatGPT showed a positive overall effect on learning performance. The meta-analysis reported a sizable effect for this course type (g=0.531) and several individual writing-related studies also showed positive gains, such as Emran et al. (2024) (N=68, g=2.730), Song and Song (2023) (N=50, g=0.790), and Qi et al. (2024) (N=46, g=1.105).
finding.measure: Learning performance in language learning and academic writing courses, typically assessed with post-tests/exams and related course outcomes

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT had a moderate positive effect on learning perception, which the paper treats as a student affective/motivational outcome. The overall meta-analytic effect was g=0.456 (95% CI [0.287, 0.625], k=19), and longer interventions were associated with larger gains, with >8 week studies showing g=1.054.
finding.measure: Learning perception scales/questionnaires
finding.study_size: k=19 studies; 72 independent effect sizes overall

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis found that ChatGPT improved higher-order thinking with a moderate positive overall effect. The pooled result was g=0.457 (95% CI [0.255, 0.650], k=9), and the strongest subgroup effect was for ChatGPT used as an intelligent tutor (g=0.945). Course type also mattered, with STEM and related courses showing the largest effect (g=0.737).
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking scales/questionnaires and related measures of critical/creative thinking

paper_profiles.title: Online peer feedback in higher education: A synthesis of the literature
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of what factors make online peer feedback effective in higher education, and how students’ characteristics, learning environments, feedback task design, and technologies shape learning processes and outcomes. The authors note that peer feedback is widely used in higher education, but prior reviews had not synthesized implementation conditions in a comprehensive way.

Using PRISMA, the authors systematically reviewed empirical intervention studies from 2000–2023 that examined online peer feedback in higher education. After screening 2,221 records and quality appraising the remaining studies, 83 publications were included. The review organizes evidence using Biggs’ model into four dimensions: student characteristics, learning environment conditions, learning processes/activities, and learning outcomes.

The review finds that online peer feedback can support cognitive, behavioral, and affective outcomes, with the strongest recurring evidence for writing-related improvements, feedback quality, peer assessment performance, motivation, self-efficacy, and collaboration. Effects appear to depend on implementation details such as anonymity, number of feedback rounds, structured peer assessment, training, feedback scripts, worked examples, and technology affordances (e.g., discussion tools, video annotation, mobile support). Student factors also matter: gender, prior experience, writing proficiency, motivation, epistemic beliefs, and perceptions can influence participation and outcomes. Overall, the paper concludes that online peer feedback is beneficial, but its effectiveness is highly conditional on design and context.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports consistent positive effects of online peer feedback on writing-related outcomes, including essay writing, argumentative essay quality, writing performance, grammatical accuracy, and text revision quality. Across the included studies, beneficial conditions included scripting, structured peer assessment, worked examples, training, anonymity, and multiple rounds of feedback; however, this is a synthesis of heterogeneous studies rather than a single pooled effect estimate.
finding.measure: Essay writing quality, argumentative essay quality, writing performance, grammatical accuracy, text revision quality

finding.finding_summary: The review includes studies on speaking performance and translation performance, and it characterizes online peer feedback as beneficial for several language-related outcomes beyond writing. Evidence is drawn from individual studies such as blog-supported peer feedback improving speaking and writing skills, and video peer assessment improving translation performance, but no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Speaking performance, translation performance

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive effects on science-related and discipline-specific cognitive outcomes such as conceptual understanding, domain-specific knowledge, and science activity performance. It also notes that online peer feedback can support comprehension and knowledge acquisition in scientific and technical contexts, especially when structured peer assessment, scripting, or guided feedback are used.
finding.measure: Domain-specific knowledge, conceptual understanding, science activity performance

finding.finding_summary: Beyond literacy and language, the review finds positive effects on a range of subject-area outcomes including problem solving, argumentation, presentation performance, dance performance, and collaborative learning outcomes in disciplines such as engineering, nursing, biotechnology, and education. These findings are based on many individual intervention studies and indicate that online peer feedback can transfer across fields, though effects vary by context and implementation.
finding.measure: Problem-solving performance, argumentation, presentation performance, dance performance, subject-specific learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies positive effects on motivation, engagement, self-efficacy, confidence, and satisfaction when online peer feedback is well designed. Examples include mobile-supported peer assessment increasing learning interest, motivation, and self-efficacy, and positive emotions being associated with more active participation and higher-quality feedback; negative emotions were associated with avoidance or superficial feedback.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, self-efficacy, confidence, satisfaction, emotional responses

finding.finding_summary: The review strongly emphasizes durable skills, especially critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration, communication, self-regulation, and evaluative ability. Several design features—such as synchronous/asynchronous discussion, collaborative reviewer structures, awareness tools, and structured peer assessment—were associated with stronger performance in these skills, but the paper does not provide pooled quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognitive awareness, collaboration, communication, self-regulation, evaluative ability

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that online peer feedback and its digital platforms can be time-saving and easier to implement at scale than traditional feedback approaches, especially in large classes. It frames online tools as improving efficiency in managing feedback activities and recording/reusing feedback data, although it does not report direct comparative efficiency effect sizes.
finding.measure: Implementation efficiency, scalability, time-saving characteristics of online peer feedback systems

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing peer assessment with artificial intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence can be used to improve peer assessment in higher education. The authors propose a six-part theoretical framework covering assigning peer assessors, enhancing individual reviews, deriving peer grades/feedback, analyzing student feedback, facilitating instructor oversight, and peer assessment systems, then use a rapid scoping review to map the literature onto that framework.

The review searched Google Scholar for English-language higher-education papers from the last 10 years and included 79 studies with quantitative and/or qualitative evidence. Across the literature, the authors conclude that AI generally improves peer assessment processes, especially in grading/feedback aggregation, feedback analysis, calibration, and instructor oversight, though the evidence base is uneven and many areas remain underexplored. A case study of the RiPPLE system illustrates how AI-supported peer review, resource curation, and personalized practice can support learnersourcing and instructor monitoring.

This paper is primarily a synthesis of higher-education peer assessment research rather than a controlled evaluation of a single intervention. It highlights promising use cases for AI, such as bias correction, automated grading support, feedback classification, rogue-review detection, and adaptive student support, while also noting that effects depend on context and implementation details such as calibration, matching strategies, and subject domain.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI-supported peer assessment can improve writing quality and the quality of elaborated feedback in higher education. In particular, the authors note that SWoRD was effective in improving writing quality, and several AI/NLP tools improved review helpfulness, specific feedback, and revision quality, although many studies were small or descriptive rather than controlled trials.
finding.measure: Writing quality, peer review quality, elaborated feedback quality, revision quality

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies reported improved student attitudes, motivation, or reduced burnout when AI-supported peer feedback was used. For example, students who knew their peer-assessment responses mattered reported more positive attitudes, and one study found that more suggestive feedback was associated with reduced emotional exhaustion.
finding.measure: Student attitudes, motivation, emotional exhaustion/burnout, self-learning behavior

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly links AI-supported peer assessment with improvements in evaluative judgment, review quality, calibration, and teamwork-related skills. Across the review, matching by similar ability, benchmarking/calibration, and feedback analysis were described as helping students become more accurate reviewers and better able to judge and revise work.
finding.measure: Peer review accuracy, calibration performance, evaluative judgment, teamwork effectiveness

finding.finding_summary: A major conclusion is that AI can reduce instructor workload and improve scalability in peer assessment by automating grading support, feedback analysis, bias detection, and oversight. The RiPPLE case study and several reviewed systems were described as helping instructors focus their attention on uncertain or problematic cases rather than manually reviewing all submissions.
finding.measure: Instructor workload, scalability, automation of grading/feedback/oversight

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests AI can strengthen the reliability, fairness, and trustworthiness of peer-assessment systems at the institutional level. Examples include strategy-proof assignment, rogue-review detection, calibration, and AI spot-checking to improve governance and quality control in large-scale peer assessment systems.
finding.measure: Reliability, validity, fairness, trustworthiness, strategy-proof assignment, institutional oversight

paper_profiles.title: Bringing down barriers to children’s healthy eating: a critical review of opportunities, within a complex food system
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative critical review of recent scientific evidence on how to improve healthy eating among children and adolescents using a food-systems perspective. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, it synthesizes literature on multiple leverage points across the food system, including individual factors (sensory pleasure, food literacy), family and peer environments, school settings, marketing, food labeling, nudging, and food supply-chain reformulation.

The review argues that children’s diets are shaped by interacting biological, psychological, social, and structural factors, and that effective action must be multi-level rather than narrowly focused on individual education. It highlights evidence that repeated exposure, positive family mealtime interactions, social norms in schools, healthier food availability, and regulation of marketing and packaging cues can support healthier eating, while coercive parenting practices, unhealthy food marketing, and poor food environments undermine it.

The paper’s main conclusion is that improving children’s diets requires coordinated systems change alongside supportive, child-centered interventions that increase food literacy, agency, and enjoyable experiences with healthy foods. It emphasizes tailoring strategies to developmental stage and family context, and notes that evidence is still limited for some approaches, especially long-term effects and interventions targeting broader structural conditions.

finding.finding_summary: not_reported
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Quality Prediction Models for Automatic Writing Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to generate automated writing feedback that is more useful than generic grammar- and style-focused tools by aligning suggestions with a domain’s own quality norms. The core problem is that models can predict whether text is high- or low-quality in a specific online community, but they do not directly tell writers what to change to improve the text.

The authors propose Perturbation Analysis, a method that uses pre-trained tree-ensemble quality prediction models to identify which writing features should be increased or decreased to improve predicted quality. They further extend the method to segment-level feedback by splitting documents into topic-based segments and using weak supervision to train segment classifiers, enabling localized suggestions rather than only document-level advice.

The paper evaluates the approach on two adult, user-generated writing domains: Amazon product reviews and Airbnb host profiles. In crowdsourced experiments, participants wrote reviews or profiles, received one of four feedback types (document vs. segment feedback crossed with outlier-based vs. perturbation-based suggestion selection), and optionally revised their writing. Expert raters scored pre- and post-feedback submissions on domain-specific quality rubrics. Results show that Perturbation Analysis consistently outperformed the outlier baseline, and that segment-level feedback helped only when paired with Perturbation Analysis, especially for Amazon reviews where there were more segments per text. The work is about automated writing feedback systems rather than classroom instruction, so it does not directly study K-12 learners or educational writing assistants.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed feedback system improved writing quality in two adult writing domains. In the user study, segment-level Perturbation Analysis increased Amazon review helpfulness by 0.55 on the expert rubric, versus 0.14 for the Doc+Krause baseline and 0.22 for Doc+Perturb; for Airbnb, it increased trustworthiness by 0.65 versus 0.07 for the baseline and 0.40 for Doc+Perturb. The paper reports 3.9× and 9.1× improvements over the baseline in the two domains, respectively.
finding.measure: Expert-rated writing quality on domain-specific rubrics (Amazon review helpfulness; Airbnb profile trustworthiness)
finding.study_size: Amazon n=81 completed; Airbnb n=91 completed
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CI shown in figure, exact values not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Neural Automated Writing Evaluation with Corrective Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a neural system that integrates automated writing evaluation (AWE) with grammatical error correction (GEC) to provide L2 learners with instant scoring and corrective feedback on essays. The authors frame the work as a response to the burden of manual feedback and the limitations of treating essay scoring and grammar correction as separate tasks.

Methodologically, the paper describes the system architecture, the datasets used to train the AWE and GEC components, and example outputs from the integrated interface.
