For AWE, the authors use ASAP/ASAP++ data and a RoBERTa-based regression model after text denoising; for GEC, they build seq2seq models using fairseq with pretrained LLMs such as BERT and BART, trained on BEA 2019 shared-task data. The paper also discusses extensions to multilingual settings (Chinese and Korean), rubric design, and potential instructor-facing workflows.

The paper does not report a controlled evaluation of student writing outcomes from classroom use of the integrated tool. Instead, it argues that the system could improve learning by simulating examination conditions, delivering immediate feedback, and reducing teacher workload. It mentions planned perception experiments with students and instructors, but these are future work rather than reported empirical results.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that integrating AWE and GEC would reduce the burden of manually correcting large numbers of essays and provide instantaneous scoring and feedback. This claimed efficiency benefit is presented as a system-level advantage of the tool, but no classroom trial or measured workload outcome is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload / feedback efficiency (claimed, not empirically measured)

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Writing Style Development in High School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how writing style develops over time among Danish high school students. The authors ask whether students’ writing becomes more similar or more different as they progress through school, and whether different developmental trajectories are associated with writing-quality indicators.

Rather than testing an instructional intervention, the study uses a large corpus of more than 131,000 Danish essays from 10,095 students collected through the Lectio learning management system. The authors train a Siamese neural network to measure similarity between pairs of texts, then construct writing-style development profiles for 3,688 students in an analysis subset. These profiles are clustered to identify typical developmental patterns, and clusters are compared using proxy quality measures including SMOG readability, noun phrases per sentence, verb phrases per sentence, and average text length.

The main finding is that students’ writing styles tend to diverge over the course of high school, with average similarity decreasing over time. Five clusters of developmental trajectories were identified: two clusters showed relatively strong improvement in the quality indicators alongside substantial writing-style change, while three clusters showed weaker development, including one cluster that briefly reverted toward earlier writing style after the first-year summer vacation. The paper concludes that writing development is heterogeneous, that some students appear at risk of stagnation or regression, and that teachers might use style-development profiles to identify students who may need additional support. However, the study does not evaluate an AI writing assistant or compare AI feedback with teacher feedback or other instructional conditions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test an intervention, but it does find substantial heterogeneity in writing development across 3,688 students. Two clusters (C1, C2) showed stronger improvement in proxy writing-quality indicators such as SMOG grade, noun phrases per sentence, verb phrases per sentence, and text length, while three clusters (C3, C4, C5) showed weaker or more limited improvement; one cluster briefly reverted toward earlier writing style after the first-year summer vacation. The strongest developmental gains were observed in C1 and C2, but no causal effect sizes for instruction or tools were reported.
finding.measure: Writing-style similarity over time; SMOG grade; noun phrases per sentence; verb phrases per sentence; average text length
finding.study_size: n=3688 analyzed students; 131,095 essays in the full corpus

paper_profiles.title: The Agency Gap: How Generative AI Literacy Shapes Independent Writing after AI Support
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether students’ generative AI (GenAI) literacy helps them perform better when they must write independently after AI support has been removed, and whether that relationship depends on the style of chatbot support. The authors frame this as an “agency gap”: the extent to which GenAI literacy predicts later writing performance in situations that require self-initiation and self-regulation rather than ongoing scaffolding.

The study involved 79 medical and nursing students and graduates recruited online. Participants completed multimodal academic writing tasks based on visual data and were randomly assigned to either a reactive chatbot, which only responded to student questions, or a proactive chatbot, which actively scaffolded the task through structured questioning and feedback. Students first wrote with AI support and then completed a parallel writing task without AI support. Writing was scored on insightfulness, visual data integration, organisation and coherence, linguistic quality, critical thinking, and a composite score, while GenAI literacy and visualisation literacy were also measured.

The main finding is that GenAI literacy predicted stronger independent writing performance after AI support was removed, especially in the reactive condition. In that condition, higher GenAI literacy was associated with better post-support performance across several writing dimensions, and the relationship remained after controlling for visualisation literacy. In contrast, proactive scaffolding largely equalised outcomes across literacy levels, and GenAI literacy did not significantly predict performance there. The authors conclude that GenAI literacy matters most when learners must self-direct their use of AI, while proactive scaffolds can reduce dependence on such literacy and help equalise performance.

finding.finding_summary: GenAI literacy was positively associated with independent academic writing performance after AI support was removed. In the reactive condition (n=39), higher GenAI literacy correlated with better scores for insightfulness (rs=.41, p=.010), visual data integration (rs=.40, p=.013), organisation and coherence (rs=.44, p=.005), linguistic quality (rs=.32, p=.045), critical thinking (rs=.37, p=.019), and the composite score (rs=.44, p=.005). These associations remained significant after controlling for visualisation literacy, with partial correlations ranging from rs=.35 to rs=.45.
finding.measure: Academic writing rubric scores (insightfulness, visual data integration, organisation and coherence, linguistic quality, critical thinking, composite score) after AI removal
finding.effect_size: rs=.32 to .45; OR=1.11 to 1.15 in regression for selected outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines GenAI literacy as a transferable competence and links it to later independent performance, which is most closely related to durable skills such as metacognition and self-regulation. The study found that GenAI literacy predicted independent writing after AI support was withdrawn, but the mediated pathway through AI-supported performance was not significant in either condition (indirect effect reactive=0.032, 95% CI [-0.022, 0.108]; proactive=0.022, 95% CI [-0.055, 0.102]). This suggests GenAI literacy operates as a direct, task-general competence rather than merely producing temporary performance gains.
finding.measure: Correlation, partial correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and mediation models using GenAI literacy and independent writing scores
finding.effect_size: Indirect effect=0.032 (reactive), 0.022 (proactive); regression OR=1.11 to 1.15 for selected outcomes
finding.confidence_interval: Indirect effect reactive 95% CI [-0.022, 0.108]; proactive 95% CI [-0.055, 0.102]

finding.finding_summary: The study discusses learner agency, self-initiation, and self-regulation as central mechanisms, but it does not directly measure motivation or engagement with a dedicated scale. Results indicate that proactive scaffolding reduced reliance on student literacy/agency, while reactive support required students to actively formulate prompts and mobilize their own strategies. Because these constructs are discussed conceptually rather than measured as outcomes, the evidence for this category is indirect and limited.
finding.measure: Not directly measured; inferred from task condition and writing outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Help Me Write a Story: Evaluating LLMs’ Ability to Generate Writing Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can serve as useful writing-feedback tools for story writing. The authors frame the task as generating open-ended, constructive feedback on short English stories, rather than directly rewriting text. They ask whether model feedback is well-formed, specific, correct, and focused on the most salient writing issues.

To study this, the authors create STORYFEEDBACK, a dataset of 1,300 short stories, including 326 original stories and corrupted versions created by backtranslation, sentence swapping, or sentence deletion. They prompt eight commonly used LLMs (Bloomz, Gemma, Gemini, and GPT variants) under four prompt styles and both zero-shot and two-shot settings, then evaluate outputs with automatic metrics and human annotations. Human raters score feedback on sanity, feedback type, agreement that the story is perfect-as-is, correctness, error detection, specificity, and relevance, and also write their own feedback for comparison.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs can produce plausible, specific, and often helpful feedback, but they frequently miss the biggest writing problem and are inconsistent about when to give positive encouragement. Performance varies by model family and prompt design: larger proprietary models generally outperform smaller open-source ones, bulleted-list prompts do best, and two-shot prompting does not consistently help. Because the study uses synthetic short-story corruptions and evaluates model feedback rather than student learning outcomes, it is best understood as an assessment of feedback quality and model capability, not an intervention study on educational gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM-generated feedback for story writing and finds that models can often produce plausible and specific suggestions, but they frequently miss the most salient writing problem and sometimes incorrectly say corrupted stories are "perfect as-is." In human evaluation, the best models reached correctness scores around 0.7-0.8, but error-detection and relevance were notably weaker, indicating that feedback may help some aspects of writing while still failing on the most important revisions.
finding.measure: Human ratings of feedback correctness, error-detection, specificity, relevance, and perfect-agree; automatic precision of "perfect-as-is" and trigram repetition
finding.study_size: n=1,920 feedback examples for human evaluation; 83,456 story-feedback pairs in the dataset

paper_profiles.title: Celestial mechanics, from high-school to Newton's Principia
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper uses a classic high-school physics contest problem about a spacecraft transitioning from a circular orbit to an elliptical orbit around a planet to illustrate different ways of reasoning about planetary motion. The author’s goal is not to evaluate an educational intervention, but to show how the same problem can be solved with multiple levels of sophistication, ranging from Kepler’s laws and conservation principles to the Runge-Lenz vector, hodographs, Frenet formulas, Maxwell’s geometric method, and a result from Newton’s Principia.

The context is a high-school physics exercise, specifically an Eötvös contest problem, and the paper situates it within the Hungarian tradition of challenging secondary-school physics contests. It argues that such problems can promote creative thinking and even lead to research-level insights, while also serving as bridges from secondary-school reasoning to university and historical mechanics.

The main conclusion is mathematical/physical rather than empirical: the relative loss of kinetic energy when the spacecraft is slowed at aphelium equals the numerical eccentricity of the new orbit, with the sample values giving a loss of 1/19. The paper does not report any student outcome data, comparison groups, or educational effects, so it provides no evidence about writing, revision, AI tools, or instructional effectiveness beyond illustrating the pedagogical value of rich physics problems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is a theoretical exposition of a physics problem and its multiple analytic solutions, not an evaluation of instruction or learning outcomes. It demonstrates that the spacecraft-orbit problem can be solved using Kepler’s laws, conservation laws, the energy formula for planetary motion, the radial equation, Frenet formulas, the Runge-Lenz vector, hodographs, Maxwell’s geometry, and Newton’s Principia, but it reports no student performance data (n=not_reported).
finding.measure: Theoretical derivations / solution methods for an orbital mechanics problem

paper_profiles.title: eRevise+RF: A Writing Evaluation System for Assessing Student Essay Revisions and Providing Formative Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents eRevise+RF, an automated writing evaluation system designed to assess and give formative feedback on student revisions in argumentative writing. The motivation is that many AWE systems can score drafts, but fewer can evaluate whether students’ revisions actually respond to prior feedback and improve essay quality. The system adds a revision-feedback layer to an existing evidence-use feedback system, with the goal of helping young writers better revise in response to text-based argumentative prompts.

The system combines essay-level scoring indicators for evidence use (number of evidence topics and specificity) with sentence-level revision classifiers that identify whether revisions are surface or content changes, whether they are evidence or reasoning revisions, and whether they are successful in improving the essay. It was deployed in three sessions over 3–5 days with 6 teachers and 406 students in grades 4–8 across three schools in Pennsylvania and Louisiana, using two response-to-text articles (MVP and SPACE). Students wrote three drafts per prompt and received automated feedback between drafts.

The paper reports mainly technical validation and descriptive pre-post comparisons rather than a controlled causal impact study. The NLP components showed moderate-to-strong agreement with human annotations (e.g., QWK=0.67 for NPE, 0.82 for SPC; F1=0.96 for revision-content classification, 0.66 for evidence-vs-reasoning, 0.70 for success classification). Student essays improved across drafts on word count, evidence breadth, specificity, and predicted essay score, and the authors argue that both evidence-use feedback and revision feedback were aligned with subsequent student revisions. However, there was no control group, so the study does not isolate the system’s causal effect relative to standard instruction or non-AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: Across the deployed sessions, student argumentative essays improved from draft 1 to draft 3 on multiple writing metrics. For MVP essays (n=516 total drafts from 172 essays) predicted word count increased from 293 to 405, evidence score from 2.45 to 2.91, NPE from 2.56 to 3.34, and SPC from 8.81 to 13.98; SPACE essays (n=450 total drafts from 150 essays) showed similar gains, with word count increasing from 228 to 338, evidence score from 2.09 to 2.85, NPE from 3.02 to 4.09, and SPC from 6.07 to 8.84. The authors also report that annotated NPE and SPC increased across drafts, and that improvements were especially visible after evidence-use feedback and again after revision feedback.
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality: word count, evidence score (ES), number of pieces of evidence (NPE), and specificity (SPC)
finding.study_size: n=172 MVP essays and n=150 SPACE essays (3 drafts each; 516 and 450 draft instances respectively)

paper_profiles.title: Investigating High School and Pre-High School Teachers’ Perceptions and Experiences Introducing Quantum Concepts: A Survey of QuanTime and other Quantum-related Activities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-high school and high school teachers perceive and implement QuanTime and other quantum-related activities intended to introduce foundational quantum concepts and build early quantum literacy in K-12 classrooms. The authors frame the work around the need for accessible, standards-compatible quantum education materials and use teacher survey data to understand classroom fit, teacher confidence, student engagement, and implementation burden.

The study used a survey with 12 Likert-scale items and 14 open-ended prompts, administered to a self-selected sample of 36 educators and one after-school outreach coordinator who had expressed interest through the National Q-12 partnership. Teachers represented a range of STEM subjects, with 12 pre-high school and 23 high school respondents, and many implemented QuanTime activities such as Wave-Particle Duality, Electron Transitions, and Art & Polarization. About two-thirds used QuanTime materials, while the rest used other quantum-related activities.

Overall, teachers reported positive experiences: they felt the activities fit curricula reasonably well, were easy to implement, and did not require substantial extra preparation or support. Teachers also reported that students enjoyed the activities and were often engaged, though reported interest in quantum-related careers was more mixed. The authors conclude that QuanTime and related activities appear to be teacher-friendly tools for early quantum education, with especially strong promise for sparking curiosity and supporting integration into existing science instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that quantum-related activities helped students learn foundational quantum concepts and make sense of core ideas such as wave-particle duality, electron transitions, and entanglement. Across 36 survey respondents, Likert responses were generally favorable (most averages >4 on a 7-point scale), and open-ended comments described students using graphs, visuals, and discussion to build understanding of the concepts.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings and open-ended teacher reports of student understanding of quantum concepts
finding.study_size: n=36 teachers (12 pre-high school, 23 high school, 1 after-school coordinator)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently reported that students enjoyed and were engaged by QuanTime and other quantum-related activities. On the 7-point Likert items, mean ratings for enjoyment were 5.8 overall and engagement 5.7 overall, with high school teachers reporting slightly higher enjoyment/engagement than pre-high school teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated student enjoyment and engagement on Likert survey items

finding.finding_summary: Open-ended responses suggest the activities supported curiosity, discussion, group work, and critical thinking about quantum phenomena. Teachers described students collecting results, plotting graphs, and asking higher-level questions about waves, particles, and entanglement, indicating gains in collaborative and analytical engagement rather than only content recall.
finding.measure: Teacher open-ended descriptions of student interaction and reasoning during activities

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that QuanTime and other quantum-related activities were easy to integrate into existing curricula and did not require substantial extra preparation or support. Mean ratings were 4.0 for needing more preparation time and 3.6 for wanting more implementation support (where lower values indicate less need), suggesting the materials were manageable and teacher-friendly.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings on preparation time, implementation support, and curriculum fit

finding.finding_summary: Teachers generally reported administrative support and strong willingness to reuse the activities in future years, suggesting institutional feasibility for broader adoption. Mean ratings indicated supportive school environments (5.6 overall for administrator flexibility/support), and 87% of high school teachers and 82% of pre-high school teachers said they would like to do the activities again next year.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings on administrator support and willingness to reuse the activities

paper_profiles.title: Cosmic rays studied with a hybrid high school detector array
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Cosmic Ray Conference (ICRC)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the LORUN/NAHSA hybrid detector setup as a pathfinder for cosmic-ray research and educational outreach in high schools. The project combines radio antennae and particle detectors on school and university buildings, with the system largely assembled by students, to test whether coincident radio and particle measurements can detect extensive air showers from high-energy cosmic rays.

The paper is not an education intervention study in the usual sense; rather, it reports the technical implementation and first physics results from the hybrid array. High school students are involved in building and extending the detector network through the HiSPARC project, gaining hands-on experience with detector construction and scientific instrumentation. The main conclusions are that the prototype worked as intended, three candidate cosmic-ray events were identified over the study period, and the hybrid radio-plus-particle approach appears promising for both cosmic-ray science and future school-based outreach, but no student learning or writing outcomes are measured.

Overall, the paper argues that a hybrid high-school detector array can be successfully deployed and could expand access to astro-particle physics for students. It suggests that additional development would be needed before a full high-school-ready implementation is available, but provides proof-of-concept evidence for the scientific feasibility of the setup.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that the hybrid LORUN/NAHSA system successfully detected cosmic-ray air-shower candidates, confirming that the prototype functioned as intended for scientific investigation. Three candidate events were identified between 2005-01-01 and 2005-08-01, with estimated primary energies above 0.2 EeV for all three and >0.3 EeV for one event, supporting the feasibility of using the array for scientific measurement and inference.
finding.measure: Detection of coincident cosmic-ray air-shower events; estimated primary energy from HiSPARC/LORUN measurements

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and their teachers perceive a generative AI system designed to support creative mathematical writing. The core question is not whether the system improves test scores, but what educational benefits and challenges emerge when 5th-grade students use GenAI to co-create math stories, represent math ideas visually, and revise AI-generated story drafts.

The study was conducted in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and six teachers. The intervention followed an Ask–Represent–Transform sequence in which students first analyzed a math story, then represented their thinking with visual tools, and finally used GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to generate and revise culturally relevant math stories. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations, analyzed thematically.

The findings suggest that students and teachers perceived multiple benefits: increased creativity in math writing, stronger mathematical understanding, growth in AI literacy, and improved affective engagement such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. At the same time, they identified important challenges, including weak critical evaluation of AI output, difficulty generating coherent stories, limited pedagogical feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connection, and accessibility limitations. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI can support mathematical creative writing, but only when intentionally designed to preserve room for student thinking, feedback, and collaboration.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that the GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing process strengthened mathematical understanding. The Ask and Represent steps helped students break down word problems, represent quantities and relationships visually, and uncover misconceptions; however, these are qualitative perceptions rather than measured achievement gains. No effect size or standard deviation was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of mathematical understanding, problem decomposition, and mathematical knowledge representation from interviews, surveys, and observations
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=6 teachers (10 student interviewees)

finding.finding_summary: The study focused substantially on creative writing processes, showing that GenAI was perceived to support students’ story drafting, revision, originality, and narrative development in math writing. Students reported that AI helped them create and improve stories more quickly and with more detail, but the paper does not report quantitative writing-quality scores or revision metrics.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creative mathematical writing, story drafting, revision, and narrative quality
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=6 teachers (10 student interviewees)

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived clear gains in interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning during the GenAI-supported activity. The paper reports that students found math more fun, felt more curious about solutions, and experienced stronger responsibility for their work as authors, but these outcomes were not measured with standardized scales.
finding.measure: Perceptions of interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning from interviews, surveys, and observations
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=6 teachers (10 student interviewees)

finding.finding_summary: A major theme was the development of AI literacy and related higher-order skills, especially prompt engineering and critical evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses. Students reportedly learned through trial and error how to make prompts more specific and recognized that AI output must be revised and judged critically, but no direct performance metric was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI output
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=6 teachers (10 student interviewees)

paper_profiles.title: A Comparative Study of Technical Writing Feedback Quality: Evaluating LLMs, SLMs, and Humans in Computer Science Topics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students perceive the quality of technical writing feedback generated by large language models (LLMs), small language models (SLMs), and human graders in computing courses. The authors ask whether AI-generated feedback can match or exceed human feedback in readability, specificity, actionability, helpfulness, and overall quality, and whether students can tell whether feedback was produced by AI or a human.

The study was conducted at a North American research university in three undergraduate courses: an introductory computer science course (CS2, n=176 valid survey responses), an upper-year operating systems course (n=80 valid responses), and a smaller upper-year writing-intensive AI-topics course (n=7 valid responses). Students were shown three anonymized feedback responses on their own technical writing assignment—one from GPT-4, one from LLaMA 3.1 8B, and one from a human TA or instructor—and then rated them on multiple dimensions and explained their preferences in open-ended responses.

Overall, students often preferred the SLM or human feedback depending on context. In the larger and more technical courses, AI feedback was frequently judged as clearer, more structured, and more actionable, with SLM feedback receiving the strongest ratings in the operating systems course and being preferred by a majority in CS2. In the smaller writing-intensive course, instructor feedback was clearly preferred and rated highest on all dimensions, reflecting the value of personalized, context-aware human comments. The paper concludes that AI feedback can be effective for scalable first-pass support in large, rubric-driven technical courses, but human feedback remains superior where nuance, personalization, and context are essential; the authors recommend hybrid human-in-the-loop workflows.

finding.finding_summary: Students generally rated AI-generated feedback, especially SLM output, as clearer, more structured, and more actionable than human feedback in the larger technical-writing contexts (operating systems n=80; CS2 n=176). However, in the smaller writing-intensive AI-topics course (n=7), instructor feedback was preferred by all respondents and scored best on readability, detail, specificity, actionability, helpfulness, and overall quality, indicating that AI did not outperform human feedback when personalization and context were central.
finding.measure: Student ratings of feedback readability, detail, specificity, actionability, helpfulness, and overall quality on a 1–7 Likert scale; student preference choice among three feedback sources

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial efficiency advantages for AI-generated feedback over human marking. The authors report that the SLM pipeline generated feedback for 143 operating-systems students in about 1.8 hours and for 13 writing-course students in about 10 minutes, while human feedback required roughly 35 hours of writing plus training time in the operating-systems course and about 4.5 hours of instructor marking in the writing course.
finding.measure: Time required to generate feedback and estimated labor hours for humans versus AI pipelines

finding.finding_summary: Students’ qualitative responses emphasized that AI feedback supported revision-oriented judgment by providing structured, rubric-aligned next steps, but they also reported that it was often too generic, overly verbose, or insufficiently context-aware. This suggests a positive effect on students’ ability to identify what to change, but a negative effect when deeper interpretation of intent and nuanced revision decisions were needed.
finding.measure: Open-ended student comments about clarity, specificity, actionability, and contextual relevance of feedback

finding.finding_summary: Students frequently described AI feedback as quick, helpful, and friendlier for low-stakes revision, but also as cold, distant, or less empathetic than human feedback. The paper therefore suggests that AI may support engagement with feedback for some students, while reducing motivation or trust for others when tone and relational support matter.
finding.measure: Open-ended student responses describing helpfulness, tone, trust, and openness to AI feedback

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Applications of Generative AI in High School STEM Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can improve high school students’ learning outcomes in STEM, with physics as the focal subject. The author frames the study as a response to uncertainty about how tools like ChatGPT and Bing AI affect student performance, engagement, and responsible use, arguing that schools need empirical evidence rather than speculation.

The study used a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design in Tomball Memorial High School with 171 participants across AP Physics 1 and on-level physics. Students were assigned to one of four conditions: control (peer discussion only), search engine use, generative AI use (Bing AI), or generative AI plus a literacy program. All groups received a teacher lecture first, then a 20-minute study period using the assigned tool, followed by a post-test and survey.

Results were mixed. In AP Physics, there were statistically significant differences among groups on score gains (ANOVA p=0.011), and the generative AI-only group performed worse than both the search engine group and the generative AI plus literacy program group; the literacy program appears to mitigate negative effects of unguided AI use. In on-level physics, however, there were no statistically significant differences across groups (p=0.619). Survey results did not show statistically significant differences in perceived understanding, engagement, or enjoyment, suggesting that the short intervention had limited observable effects on self-reported experience even where test-score differences emerged.

finding.finding_summary: The study’s primary objective outcomes were pre-test/post-test score changes on physics topics, making scientific reasoning the central academic outcome. In AP Physics, group differences were statistically significant (ANOVA p=0.011): the generative AI-only group had the lowest mean gain (M=-0.857, SD=1.791, n=14), while the search engine group (M=0.484, SD=1.387, n=31) and the generative AI plus literacy program group (M=0.500, SD=1.225, n=14) performed better. In on-level physics, no significant differences were found (p=0.619), indicating mixed effects overall.
finding.measure: Physics pre-test/post-test score differences on unit assessments (momentum/impulse for AP Physics 1; electricity/circuits for on-level physics)
finding.study_size: n=171 total; AP Physics n=91, on-level physics n=80
finding.std_deviation: AP control SD=1.355; SE SD=1.387; GAI-LP SD=1.225; GAI SD=1.791. On-level control SD=1.700; SE SD=2.250; GAI SD=2.199; GAI-LP SD=1.569

finding.finding_summary: The survey measured student-reported engagement, confidence/understanding, and enjoyment during the learning process. Despite descriptive differences, the MANOVA found no statistically significant differences across experimental groups (Pillai’s Trace p=0.115), and the confidence intervals overlapped substantially. This suggests that the treatments did not reliably change students’ self-reported engagement or enjoyment over the short intervention window.
finding.measure: Post-survey ratings of understanding, confidence, engagement, and enjoyment
finding.study_size: n=43 survey cases in MANOVA (as reported in Table 5 residual df=42), with 60 total survey responses overall
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CIs overlapped substantially; exact intervals not reported

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examines whether ChatGPT-supported language learning improves academic writing and writing motivation among Chinese EFL undergraduates. The authors frame the work around the need for more effective, timely feedback in writing instruction and the potential for AI tools to provide personalized scaffolding, immediate correction, and increased practice opportunities.

Fifty undergraduate students at a Chinese university were randomly assigned to an experimental group using ChatGPT for writing instruction or a control group receiving traditional teacher-led instruction over 12 weeks. Quantitatively, the AI-assisted group outperformed the control group on overall writing performance, writing organization, language use, and writing motivation; the reported effect sizes were large for overall writing (d=0.76), organization (d=0.84), and language use (d=0.88), and medium for motivation (d=0.52) and content (d=0.65).

Qualitative interviews with nine students showed broadly positive perceptions of ChatGPT as an innovative, accessible, and personalized writing support tool that increased engagement and confidence. At the same time, students raised concerns about contextual accuracy, over-reliance, and the risk that frequent dependence on generated text could weaken their own writing development over time. The study therefore concludes that ChatGPT can be beneficial when used as a scaffold rather than a substitute for independent writing, and it emphasizes the need for guidance on ethical use and careful implementation safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The AI-assisted group showed significantly better academic writing outcomes than the control group after 12 weeks. Overall writing improved more in the experimental condition (post-test M=59.12, SD=14.23) than in the control group (M=45.18, SD=15.62), with a large effect size (d=0.76) and ANCOVA showing a significant group effect [F(1,47)=19.01, p=0.00, partial eta squared=0.27].
finding.measure: IELTS academic writing tasks 1 and 2; overall writing performance

finding.finding_summary: Writing motivation increased more in the ChatGPT group than in the traditional instruction group. The experimental group’s motivation scores rose from M=17.36 (SD=3.12) to M=20.06 (SD=3.33), compared with the control group from M=17.71 (SD=3.09) to M=18.21 (SD=3.58); the between-group effect was medium (d=0.52) and significant [F(1,47)=29.62, p=0.00, partial eta squared=0.38].
finding.measure: Writing Motivation Scale (WMS)
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post SD=3.33; Control post SD=3.58

finding.finding_summary: The study’s qualitative findings suggest that ChatGPT supported learners’ self-regulation and perceived ability to improve their writing through feedback use and revision. Participants reported that immediate feedback helped them identify errors, revise more effectively, and work more independently over time, although the paper also noted concerns about over-reliance on AI feedback.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on self-regulation, revision, and independent writing

paper_profiles.title: Impact of ChatGPT on ESL students’ academic writing skills: a mixed methods intervention study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed methods intervention study examines whether ChatGPT can function as a formative feedback tool to improve undergraduate ESL students’ academic writing. The paper is motivated by the difficulty of providing timely, individualized feedback in large writing classes and asks whether a generative AI tool can support self-assessment and peer assessment more effectively than traditional feedback approaches.

The study was conducted in a first-year science and engineering course at a private university in India. An intact class was split into an experimental group and a comparison group; the experimental group received a short training session on using ChatGPT for self- and peer-assessment, then used it during six hours of instruction on process, comparison, and cause-effect writing. Data came from pre-, post-, and delayed post-writing tests plus three focus group discussions with five students.

Quantitative results showed large gains for the ChatGPT group: repeated-measures ANOVA found a strong time effect (F[2,72]=330.704, p=5.146e-37, η²=0.902), and the experimental group outperformed the comparison group on both the post-test and delayed post-test. Qualitative feedback was overwhelmingly positive, with students reporting better idea generation, clearer organization, improved grammar accuracy, and more confidence using feedback. The paper also notes some concerns, including reduced independent thinking, increased machine dependence, and the possibility that ChatGPT may impose a formulaic pattern on writing, but concludes that training and guided use can make ChatGPT a useful feedback tool in large ESL writing classes.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT used as a formative feedback tool significantly improved undergraduate ESL students’ academic writing performance. The experimental group’s writing scores increased from M=12.581 (SD=0.833, n=37) at pre-test to M=19.216 (SD=2.485) at post-test and M=20.419 (SD=2.575) at delayed post-test; the repeated-measures ANOVA showed a strong effect over time (F[2,72]=330.704, p=5.146e-37, η²=0.902). The experimental group also scored significantly higher than the comparison group at post-test (t(70)=-5.643, p=3.297e-7) and delayed post-test (t(70)=-9.371, p=5.544e-14).
finding.measure: Academic writing test scores across process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraph tasks; rubric criteria included content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary
finding.study_size: n=72 analyzed; EG n=37, CG n=35
finding.std_deviation: pre SD=0.833; post SD=2.485; delayed post SD=2.575

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT increased confidence, reduced anxiety about asking questions, and made writing feel more manageable through instant support. Qualitative data also indicated some negative affective concerns, including fear of becoming dependent and losing motivation to think independently, but the overall student perception was strongly positive.
finding.measure: Focus group discussion themes on motivation, autonomy, confidence, anxiety, and dependence

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was perceived to support collaboration, self-regulation, and idea organization during writing, helping students stay focused on the topic and work together more effectively. At the same time, students noted risks such as reduced independent thinking, more machine dependence, and a tendency to follow a preset pattern, suggesting both skill support and possible erosion of autonomous thinking.
finding.measure: Focus group discussion themes on learner autonomy, peer collaboration, focus, and creativity in organization

finding.finding_summary: Students said ChatGPT made brainstorming and writing faster and saved time by providing immediate, tailored feedback. Reported benefits included faster task completion, reduced brainstorming time, and easier correction of grammar and organization, although the paper did not provide a direct time-on-task metric.
finding.measure: Focus group discussion themes on faster writing speed, time-saving in brainstorming, and efficiency of feedback use

paper_profiles.title: Utilization of Writing Assistance Tools in Research in Selected Higher Learning Institutions in the Philippines: A Text Mining Analysis
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how faculty researchers in selected higher learning institutions in the Philippines perceive and use AI-powered writing assistance tools in research writing. The authors were interested in both the perceived usefulness of these tools and the concerns associated with their use, including overreliance, reduced independent thinking and writing development, plagiarism, and context/culture mismatch in Filipino academic writing.

Using descriptive text mining, k-means clustering, and sentiment analysis, the study analyzed open-ended responses from 327 faculty respondents across 11 public and private higher education institutions. Respondents reported using or intending to use tools such as Grammarly, Quillbot, ChatGPT, and other grammar/checking applications. The analysis found that respondents generally viewed writing assistance tools positively for speeding up writing, improving clarity, and reducing grammatical errors, but they also recognized risks such as dependency, weakened critical thinking, possible inaccuracies in tool suggestions, academic integrity concerns, privacy/data issues, and potential plagiarism.

The paper concludes that AI writing assistance tools can support research productivity and writing quality when used responsibly, but they should not replace human judgment or core research work. The authors recommend institutional guidance, clear ethical policies, plagiarism controls, educational campaigns, and multi-pronged safeguards to promote responsible use and reduce misuse. They also emphasize the need to consider context, user skill level, and linguistic/cultural fit when implementing such tools in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: Faculty respondents generally reported that writing assistance tools improve writing quality, clarity, grammar, and speed, helping them proofread, paraphrase, translate, format, and correct spelling and punctuation. At the same time, respondents warned that overreliance can reduce independent writing development, weaken originality, and sometimes introduce incorrect or context-mismatched suggestions; the study does not report a quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Open-ended faculty responses analyzed via text mining and sentiment analysis; reported themes about writing quality, clarity, grammar, and plagiarism

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly reports concerns that AI writing tools may reduce critical thinking, analytical thinking, creativity, and the ability to write independently if users overrely on them. Respondents also noted that users should critically evaluate outputs and not simply accept tool suggestions, indicating that the main finding is a tradeoff between efficiency and durable-skill development rather than a measured causal effect.
finding.measure: Open-ended faculty responses about critical thinking, creativity, independent analysis, and skill development

finding.finding_summary: Respondents overwhelmingly described writing assistance tools as saving time and effort by expediting proofreading, editing, formatting, and other repetitive writing tasks. The paper reports that the tools help faculty complete work faster, improve efficiency, and free time for other research activities, but no numerical productivity effect is provided.
finding.measure: Open-ended faculty responses on usefulness, speed, and workflow efficiency; sentiment analysis of positive implications

finding.finding_summary: The study highlights institutional concerns around academic integrity, plagiarism, privacy, cultural/language fit, and the need for policy and governance when adopting AI writing tools in higher education. The authors recommend clear guidelines, strict plagiarism policies, detection tools, prevention measures, and educational campaigns to support responsible implementation, but they do not evaluate a policy intervention quantitatively.
finding.measure: Reported institutional concerns and recommended safeguards from faculty responses and discussion/conclusion sections

paper_profiles.title: Advancing Students’ Academic Excellence in Distance Education: Exploring the Potential of Generative AI Integration to Improve Academic Writing Skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines how generative AI tools, especially ChatGPT, might support academic writing in a South African open and distance e-learning (ODeL) university. The paper responds to growing concerns that students are increasingly using AI writing tools in academic work, while lecturers are uncertain about how to respond. It asks how lecturers, students, and markers perceive generative AI in the Academic Writing module and whether it can improve writing skills and motivate students.

The study is situated in an undergraduate Academic Writing module (WRI124) at a large distance-learning university. Data were collected in late 2023 using email interviews with 12 lecturers, a focus group discussion with 12 students, and a WhatsApp discussion with 10 markers. The authors interpret the data through socio-cultural theory and a human-AI collaboration framework, emphasizing AI as scaffolding rather than a replacement for human effort.

Across stakeholder groups, the paper finds cautious optimism: participants generally see generative AI as a useful supplementary tool for brainstorming, correction, and feedback, but not as a substitute for independent writing. At the same time, the paper repeatedly identifies risks and unintended consequences including overreliance, reduced independent effort, plagiarism/academic misconduct, threats to authenticity and creativity, privacy concerns, and the possibility that AI may encourage shortcuts. The authors recommend safeguards such as clear usage rules, transparent communication about AI’s limits, training for lecturers and students, human oversight, and assignments that emphasize responsible use and comparison of original versus AI-corrected writing.

finding.finding_summary: Participants generally viewed generative AI as helpful for academic writing, especially for correcting grammar, structure, and refining text. However, the paper also reports strong concerns that excessive use could undermine independent writing, authenticity, and real writing-skill development, so the overall finding is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Perceptions of academic writing support; self-reported writing improvement, grammar/structure help, and authenticity concerns from interviews and focus groups

finding.finding_summary: Students and markers reported that generative AI could increase motivation, reduce stress, and save time, which may support engagement with writing tasks. At the same time, several participants worried that heavy reliance on AI could make students lazy, complacent, or less motivated to improve on their own.
finding.measure: Perceptions of motivation, stress reduction, engagement, and laziness/complacency in discussions

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames AI as a scaffold for learning rather than a substitute for effort, and several participants recommended using AI to compare original and corrected text or as a brainstorming aid. However, concerns about overreliance, verbatim copying, and reduced active engagement suggest potential negative effects on self-regulation and independent problem solving.
finding.measure: Stakeholder perceptions of independence, active engagement, responsibility, brainstorming, and avoiding plagiarism/copying

finding.finding_summary: Participants described generative AI as a time-saving tool that could reduce stress and support faster drafting and editing. The study reports perceived efficiency benefits, but these are based on qualitative judgments rather than measured productivity outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived time savings, reduced stress, and workflow support in academic writing and marking contexts

finding.finding_summary: The study highlights institutional concerns around academic misconduct, plagiarism detection limits, privacy, and the need for clear governance of AI use in distance education. It also proposes safeguards such as transparent reporting, usage rules, lecturer guidance, and assignment redesign, indicating that institutional policy and implementation choices are central to the paper.
finding.measure: Stakeholder perceptions of academic integrity, AI governance, and implementation safeguards; discussion of institutional responses

paper_profiles.title: The Influence of AI Writing Tools on the Content and Organization of Students’ Writing: A Focus on EFL Instructors' Perceptions
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Current Debates in Social Sciences
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative case study examines how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instructors perceive the use of AI writing tools in writing instruction, with particular attention to students’ content development and organization. The paper responds to a gap in the literature by moving beyond grammar-focused AI writing research to consider higher-level writing dimensions such as idea generation, coherence, and logical flow.

Data were collected through interviews with 12 instructors at the School of Foreign Languages in a state university. Participants reported using a range of AI tools, especially ChatGPT and Quillbot, along with Paperpal, Jenni, Wordtune, DeepL, Copy.ai, Perplexity, Elicit, and Essay Writer, to support brainstorming, paraphrasing, translation, grammar/style feedback, and essay structuring. The instructors generally perceived AI writing tools as helpful for content generation and organization because they provided prompts, suggestions, and real-time feedback that improved coherence and sentence flow.

At the same time, instructors expressed concerns that these tools could promote overreliance, weaken critical thinking, reduce originality, and dampen students’ personal creativity and independent idea generation. The paper’s main conclusion is that AI writing tools can support writing development when used in a balanced way, but educators should be cautious about overdependence and preserve opportunities for students to think and write independently.

finding.finding_summary: Across interviews with 12 EFL instructors, AI writing tools were perceived to improve students’ writing quality by supporting idea generation, paraphrasing, vocabulary use, coherence, and logical organization. However, instructors also reported risks such as overreliance, reduced originality, and possible weakening of students’ independent writing and critical thinking, so the overall effect was described as beneficial but conditional on balanced use.
finding.measure: EFL instructors’ interview perceptions of student writing content and organization

finding.finding_summary: Instructors repeatedly linked AI writing tool use with both support and risk for durable skills, especially critical thinking and independent problem-solving. While tools helped students organize thoughts and identify logical gaps, participants warned that excessive dependence could hinder the development of original idea generation and critical thinking.
finding.measure: EFL instructors’ reported perceptions of students’ critical thinking, problem-solving, and originality

finding.finding_summary: Instructors stated that AI writing tools helped students feel more confident while writing by providing real-time guidance, phrasing suggestions, and organizational support. This confidence boost was reported qualitatively rather than measured with a scale, and no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported student confidence during writing

finding.finding_summary: Participants described AI writing tools as efficient supports for writing instruction because they generated sample texts, outlines, paraphrases, and immediate feedback that saved time in drafting and revising. The paper did not quantify workload or time savings, but the qualitative evidence suggests improved drafting/revision efficiency.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported usefulness of AI tools for drafting, revising, outlining, and feedback

paper_profiles.title: Examining the user experience of artificial intelligence tools in academic writing: The perceptions lecturers practices
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study explores lecturers’ perceptions and practices regarding artificial intelligence writing tools in academic writing, with a particular focus on how instructors understand the benefits, risks, and classroom implications of these tools. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the authors interviewed 10 lecturers from three universities in Malang, Indonesia to understand perceived usefulness, ease of use, attitudes toward AI writing tools, behavioral intentions, and actual usage.

The paper reports that lecturers commonly use tools such as Grammarly, QuillBot, Wordtune, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Consensus AI for grammar checking, paraphrasing, translation, reference searching, idea generation, and improving coherence. Instructors generally viewed AI writing tools as helpful supplements that can improve efficiency and writing quality, but they also expressed strong concerns about overreliance, reduced creativity and critical thinking, difficulty distinguishing student-authored from AI-generated text, academic integrity violations, possible misinformation and inaccurate citations, and the need for clear institutional policies. The study concludes that AI writing tools should be used cautiously as aids rather than substitutes for learning, and that transparency, accountability, and guidance are needed for responsible classroom integration.

finding.finding_summary: Lecturers reported that AI writing tools improved grammar, spelling, sentence flow, coherence, readability, vocabulary, and translation, supporting academic writing quality. At the same time, they cautioned that using AI to generate entire papers could weaken originality and writing development, and some still preferred professional proofreaders to validate outputs.
finding.measure: Instructor interviews about observed effects on student/lecturer writing; reported use for grammar, spelling, coherence, translation, paraphrasing, and text organization

finding.finding_summary: A major concern was that overdependence on AI could reduce creativity, critical thinking, reasoning, and problem-solving. Lecturers repeatedly stated that AI should support, not replace, independent thinking and that students may become less able to develop ideas on their own if they rely too heavily on chatbots.
finding.measure: Instructor perceptions of effects on creativity, critical thinking, reasoning, and problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: Participants consistently described AI writing tools as making writing and teaching tasks faster and easier, increasing productivity and reducing effort for grammar correction, translation, reference searching, and drafting support. Grammarly was especially valued because the institution subscribed to it, though some instructors still relied on human proofreaders for final validation.
finding.measure: Instructor reports of usefulness, ease of use, productivity, and workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The study found strong concern about academic integrity, institutional policy gaps, transparency, and detection of AI-generated text. Lecturers argued for clear usage limits, guidelines from higher education authorities, proper citation/acknowledgment, fact-checking of outputs, and tools such as Turnitin to detect AI-generated writing; they also emphasized that AI should not be listed as an author.
finding.measure: Instructor perceptions of academic integrity, policy, transparency, and enforcement practices

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Role of AI-Driven Dynamic Writing Platforms in Improving EFL Learners' Writing Skills and Fostering Their Motivation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examines whether an AI-driven interactive writing platform can improve English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners’ writing performance and motivation relative to traditional classroom-based writing instruction. The paper asks whether AI-supported writing activities improve fluency, lexical use, grammatical accuracy, coherence, task completion, and willingness to write, and how students perceive the platform’s strengths and limitations.

The study was conducted with 65 intermediate TEFL undergraduates at Islamic Azad University, Varamin-Pishva branch, who were randomly assigned to an AI group (n=33) or a classroom-based group (n=32). Over 12 weeks, the AI group used an interactive writing platform that provided real-time, personalized feedback, grammar and vocabulary exercises, and additional practice tasks, while the control group received traditional instruction with similar content and duration. Quantitative results from IELTS-style pre/post writing assessments and a motivation scale showed statistically significant gains favoring the AI group across writing dimensions and willingness to write, with medium-to-large ANCOVA effects (e.g., fluency ηp²=0.15, lexicon ηp²=0.41, accuracy ηp²=0.61, total writing ηp²=0.46, WTW ηp²=0.42).

finding.finding_summary: The AI-supported group outperformed the classroom-based group on multiple writing outcomes after 12 weeks. ANCOVA results showed significant advantages for fluency (F(1,62)=7.43, p=0.01, ηp²=0.15), lexicon (F(1,62)=29.46, p<0.01, ηp²=0.41), accuracy (F(1,62)=76.12, p<0.01, ηp²=0.61), and total writing performance (F(1,62)=29.07, p<0.001, ηp²=0.46) for the AI group, using IELTS-style writing scores.
finding.measure: IELTS-style writing tasks assessing fluency/coherence, lexical resource, grammatical accuracy, and total writing performance
finding.std_deviation: AI posttest SDs: fluency=1.14, lexicon=0.79, accuracy=0.94, total writing=0.64; classroom posttest SDs: fluency=0.79, lexicon=0.84, accuracy=0.90, total writing=0.82

finding.finding_summary: The AI group showed a significant increase in willingness to write compared with the classroom-based group. Descriptively, mean WTW rose from 3.57 (SD=0.71) to 4.16 (SD=0.81) in the AI group, versus 3.26 (SD=0.61) to 3.58 (SD=0.61) in the classroom group; the ANCOVA found a significant group effect (F(1,62)=29.16, p<0.001, ηp²=0.42).
finding.measure: Willingness to Write (WTW) scale
finding.study_size: n=45 for WTW analysis (AI n=23; classroom-based n=22)
finding.std_deviation: Pre-WTW SDs: AI=0.71, classroom=0.61; Post-WTW SDs: AI=0.81, classroom=0.61

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports qualitative and literature-based claims that AI-supported writing helped learners with self-regulation and autonomy, and the motivation scale included independence as one dimension. However, the empirical evidence here is indirect and not isolated as a standalone durable-skills outcome. The strongest direct evidence is learners’ interview comments describing personalized feedback and self-directed practice as supporting autonomous writing development.
finding.measure: Interview themes; motivation scale items including independence

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI-assisted feedback and EFL writing: a study on proficiency, revision frequency and writing quality
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether AI-assisted writing feedback improves English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing development more than traditional teacher feedback, and whether students’ revision behavior changes when they use an AI tool. The author compares Grammarly Premium, used as an automated feedback and revision support tool, with standard written teacher feedback in a postgraduate EAP writing course.

The intervention ran for 6 weeks with 60 postgraduate EFL students at a public university in Egypt, randomly assigned to an experimental group using Grammarly Premium (n=30) or a control group receiving traditional teacher feedback (n=30). The study measured overall writing proficiency, analytic writing components (content, organization, language use), and revision frequency; it also interviewed 25 students from the experimental group about their experiences. Grammarly was introduced through a training session, and students were instructed to critically evaluate suggestions rather than accept them passively.

Quantitatively, the Grammarly group outperformed the control group on the post-test total score and on organization and language-use sub-scores, but not on content. Within the Grammarly group, more frequent use of AI features and more revisions were positively associated with better post-test scores, and generative feature use predicted post-test performance beyond prior assignment score. Qualitatively, students reported greater efficiency, confidence, and perceived accuracy gains, but also emphasized the need for critical thinking, warned against overreliance, and noted that the tool did not adequately support higher-order language needs such as natural fluency and broader writing development.

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group using Grammarly Premium scored significantly higher on the post-test writing assessment than the control group receiving traditional feedback. Total post-test scores were M=54.37 (SD=5.54) for the Grammarly group versus M=45.50 (SD=5.32) for control, Welch’s t(47.35)=10.89, p<0.001; Mann–Whitney U also confirmed the difference (U=16.50, z=6.42, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Timed argumentative essay writing scores (total and analytic rubric components: content, organization, language use)

finding.finding_summary: Interview data indicated that Grammarly use increased students’ confidence, reduced anxiety, and made the revision process feel less burdensome. In the thematic analysis (n=25), 80% reported boosted confidence and 72% said the tool streamlined revision, helping them focus on ideas rather than surface errors.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on confidence, anxiety reduction, and engagement with revision

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests Grammarly use supported critical engagement and metacognitive checking, but also raised concerns about overreliance. Quantitatively, more frequent use of generative AI features correlated with better post-test scores (r=0.346 to 0.373) and with more revisions (r=0.398 to 0.421), while qualitatively 56% of interviewees emphasized the need to critically evaluate suggestions and avoid passively accepting them.
finding.measure: Correlations between AI feature use, revisions, and post-test scores; interview themes on critical thinking and avoiding overreliance

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that Grammarly made revision faster and more efficient, reducing the time and effort needed to correct surface-level errors. In interviews, 72% said the revision process was streamlined and 68% described the editing experience as smoother and less overwhelming, indicating improved task efficiency rather than a measured time-on-task outcome.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on revision efficiency and workflow

paper_profiles.title: Voices of the Future: Exploring Students’ Views on the Use of GenAI in Academic and Professional PR Writing
paper_profiles.venue: LEARN Journal: Language Education and Acquisition Research Network
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines how Thai public relations majors view generative AI (GenAI) for academic and professional PR writing. The authors situate the work in the context of new GenAI policies in Thai higher education and ask what students know about GenAI, how they use it, what benefits and drawbacks they perceive, and whether they intend to adopt it in future writing tasks.

The study used three semi-structured focus group sessions with 22 native Thai PR major students at Chulalongkorn University. Before discussion, participants completed a hands-on workshop using GenAI tools for Thai and English PR writing, including drafting prompts and trying tasks such as press releases, promotion writing, translation, grammar checking, paraphrasing, and information search. The analysis was qualitative and framed by Diffusion of Innovations and the Technology Acceptance Model.

Findings showed that all students were aware of GenAI, and most had already used it for daily and academic purposes, but none had used it for professional PR writing before the workshop. Students generally saw GenAI as useful for idea generation, information gathering, language support, and time savings, especially in English writing, but they also raised concerns about inaccurate or outdated output, weak Thai-language performance, limited creativity, plagiarism/copyright risk, reduced critical thinking, overdependence, academic integrity, and possible job displacement. The paper concludes that GenAI may be adopted cautiously as an assistant rather than a full replacement for human writing, and recommends adequate resources, practical guidelines, and ethics-focused training for students and instructors.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that GenAI helped with academic and professional writing tasks by providing ideas, summaries, translation, grammar checking, paraphrasing, and drafting support, especially in English. However, they also said the output was sometimes inaccurate, uncreative, contextually inappropriate in Thai, and required rechecking and rewriting before use; no numerical effect sizes were reported from this qualitative study.
finding.measure: Focus group reflections on writing support, draft generation, language quality, and revision needs

finding.finding_summary: Participants described both positive and negative motivational effects of GenAI. Some felt it could reduce frustration, save time, and help weaker students perform better, while others worried it would reduce enjoyment of writing and undermine their confidence, creativity, and sense of competence.
finding.measure: Focus group reflections on motivation, confidence, and enjoyment in writing tasks

finding.finding_summary: A central concern was that overreliance on GenAI could weaken students’ critical thinking, creativity, and ability to produce original work independently. Participants said excessive dependence might make them less able to think outside the box and less prepared for professional work that requires hands-on judgment and originality.
finding.measure: Focus group reflections on critical thinking, creativity, originality, and independent work

finding.finding_summary: Students viewed GenAI as a productivity aid that could shorten the writing process, generate starting points, and help with routine tasks such as summarizing information or drafting structured texts. They specifically highlighted time savings as important in fast-paced PR work, though they noted the outputs still needed human checking and editing.
finding.measure: Focus group reflections on efficiency, time savings, and workflow support

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports concerns about academic integrity, plagiarism/copyright, and social stigma around using AI, alongside a call for institutional safeguards. The authors recommend adequate resources, training, and practical guidelines for ethical and appropriate GenAI use in higher education and classroom settings.
finding.measure: Focus group concerns plus author recommendations on policy, training, and guidelines

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of AI Writing Tools on Academic Integrity: Unveiling English-Majored Students’ Perceptions and Practical Solutions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how English-majored university students perceive AI writing tools in relation to academic integrity, and what practical safeguards they believe are needed to use these tools responsibly. The authors focus on concerns that have emerged around AI writing assistants, including plagiarism, cheating, over-reliance, reduced independent writing, difficulty tracing sources, fairness in assessment, and the risk that students may submit AI-generated work as their own.

The paper uses a mixed-methods approach with survey and semi-structured interview data from 114 English-majored seniors at Ho Chi Minh City University of Foreign Languages and Information Technology (HUFLIT) in Vietnam, collected during a summer semester advanced writing course. Students reported frequent use of tools such as ChatGPT, QuillBot, and Grammarly for grammar/spelling checking, paraphrasing, idea generation, outlining, and information searching. While most students viewed AI tools as helpful for improving writing quality and saving time, they also expressed substantial concern about dependency, weakened critical thinking and creativity, plagiarism, and ethical ambiguity around when AI use becomes cheating.

The study concludes that AI writing tools are generally seen as useful supplements rather than replacements for student writing, but their impact on academic integrity depends heavily on how they are used. Students recommended mitigation strategies including explicit institutional guidelines, AI literacy and ethics training, integrating AI responsibly into instruction, limited and transparent use of AI, and the use of detection tools and assignment designs that reduce misconduct. Overall, the paper argues for balanced adoption supported by clear policy, education, and assessment safeguards rather than outright bans.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that AI writing tools improved writing quality, especially grammar, spelling, vocabulary, coherence, and coherence/organization, but they also worried that overuse could reduce their own writing competence and originality. In the survey, 87/114 students believed AI writing tools improve writing quality, while 68/114 (59.6%) feared plagiarism and 91/114 (79.8%) reported concern about over-reliance that could diminish writing skills.
finding.measure: Survey items and semi-structured interview responses about writing quality, grammar/spelling correction, paraphrasing, coherence, originality, and perceived risk of plagiarism/skill loss

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived AI writing tools as supporting idea generation and reducing time spent drafting, but they also believed excessive dependence could weaken critical thinking, independent work, and creativity. In the survey, 77/114 (67.5%) identified reduced learning and critical thinking as a concern, and 91/114 (79.8%) expressed concern about over-reliance on technology.
finding.measure: Survey items and interview responses on critical thinking, creativity, independence, and dependence on AI tools

finding.finding_summary: Students commonly used AI tools to save time on writing tasks, especially for grammar checking, outlining, paraphrasing, and generating starting points for unfamiliar or lengthy assignments. In the survey, 75/114 students identified time-saving as a benefit, and interviewees described using AI to speed up information search and produce drafts under deadline pressure.
finding.measure: Survey and interview responses about time-saving, drafting efficiency, and workflow support

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that students view AI writing tools as creating both institutional risks and governance needs, especially around academic integrity, fairness in evaluation, and policy clarity. Students recommended education/training on academic integrity (72.8%), clear institutional guidelines/policies (69.3%), responsible integration of AI into coursework, and detection tools such as Turnitin or institution-specific AI filters to reduce misuse.
finding.measure: Survey preferences and interview suggestions regarding institutional policies, training, detection tools, and academic integrity governance

paper_profiles.title: Compositional Sequence Labeling Models for Error Detection in Learner Writing
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates automated error detection in learner writing, asking whether neural sequence labeling models can identify grammatical and usage errors in context more effectively than prior approaches such as CRFs and error-correction systems. The authors treat error detection as a separate task from correction and compare several compositional architectures, including convolutional networks, bidirectional recurrent networks, and bidirectional LSTMs.

Experiments are conducted on learner-English essay data from the public FCE dataset and the CoNLL-14 shared task test set. The paper shows that a bidirectional LSTM sequence tagger achieves the best error-detection performance among the tested models, outperforming a CRF baseline and strong shared-task systems when trained with additional learner corpora. The authors also show that adding the model’s error probabilities as a feature improves an automated essay-scoring system deployed in a self-assessment/tutoring tool.

The work is situated in second-language writing assessment and feedback for learners, primarily upper-intermediate English learners and broader learner populations in the Cambridge Learner Corpus/CoNLL settings. The main conclusion is that token-level neural error detection is a scalable and effective approach, especially when trained on diverse learner data; however, performance depends strongly on training-data volume and domain match. The paper also suggests that error detection may be pedagogically preferable to fully automatic correction because it identifies likely errors without attempting to replace all learner text with corrected output.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies automated detection of grammatical and writing errors in learner essays. The best model, a bidirectional LSTM, achieved F0.5=41.1 on the FCE-public test set (n=2,720 test sentences) and F0.5=44.0 on the CoNLL-14 shared-task annotation when trained on all available datasets, outperforming the CRF baseline and all compared shared-task systems on error detection.
finding.measure: Token-level error detection in learner writing; F0.5 on FCE-public and CoNLL-14 test annotations
finding.study_size: n=2,720 test sentences on FCE-public; CoNLL-14 test set with 25 students writing 2 essays each (exact sentence count not reported)

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the use ChatGPT in improving students' paragraph compositions skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative case study examines how undergraduate English Language Education students perceive the use of ChatGPT in a paragraph composition course. The paper asks what advantages students experience from using ChatGPT and what impediments they encounter, with particular attention to writing support, feedback, and limitations of AI-generated responses.

The study was conducted at Universitas Muhammadiyah Malang in Indonesia with five fourth-semester undergraduate students (ages 19–21) who had used ChatGPT for at least three months. Data were collected through individual face-to-face interviews and analyzed thematically. The authors report that students viewed ChatGPT as helpful for generating ideas, improving efficiency, refining paragraph structure, vocabulary, and grammar, and providing immediate feedback that supported better writing performance and even better grades.

At the same time, students reported several drawbacks: ChatGPT sometimes gave irrelevant, incomplete, or inaccurate responses; it lacked contextual understanding for complex or nuanced writing; and there was concern about dependency on AI assistance that could weaken independent writing skills. Connectivity problems were also identified as a practical barrier. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support paragraph writing if used as a supplementary tool rather than a replacement for human instruction, and it recommends critical evaluation of outputs, more specific prompting, and reliable internet access as safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students perceived ChatGPT as beneficial for paragraph writing, including generating ideas, refining structure, improving vocabulary and grammar, and receiving immediate feedback. However, students also reported that ChatGPT could provide irrelevant, incomplete, or inaccurate suggestions, especially for complex or nuanced writing, which limited its effectiveness as a writing aid.
finding.measure: Student interview reports about paragraph composition support, grammar, vocabulary, structure, and feedback quality

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT helped them write more efficiently and reduced the time needed for brainstorming and drafting.
