They also described the tool as helping them understand lecture material more quickly and participate more confidently in class, which the authors interpreted as supporting motivation and engagement in the writing course.
finding.measure: Student interview reports on writing efficiency, engagement, and perceived academic confidence

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was seen as supporting some higher-order writing processes, such as organizing thoughts and exploring alternative writing styles, but students and the discussion also raised concerns about reduced independent writing and overreliance. The paper explicitly notes the need to balance AI support with critical evaluation and independent skill development.
finding.measure: Student interview reports on dependence, independent writing, and critical evaluation of AI suggestions

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT improved writing efficiency by helping them quickly generate ideas and refine paragraphs without spending as much time on brainstorming or research. The tool was also described as free and easily accessible, although internet connectivity problems could limit usability.
finding.measure: Student interview reports on time savings, access, and usability

paper_profiles.title: It is like a friend to me: Critical usage of automated feedback systems by self-regulating English learners in higher education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate / Postgraduate / HDR students in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how international students in an Australian university used automated feedback systems (AFSs) for self-regulated English language learning. The authors were motivated by a persistent problem in their personalized autonomous English enhancement course (PELE): students often struggled to identify their own areas for improvement and set specific learning goals, so the study asked which AFS tools students adopted, how they perceived them, how they used them across the learning cycle, and what pedagogical supports were needed.

The study combined qualitative data from seven students’ e-portfolios and focus group interviews with a small survey of 32 students. Students used a range of tools, including Grammarly, ELSA, Write and Improve, vocabulary tests, and speaking apps, mainly for goal setting, progress monitoring, and practice. Overall, students found the tools helpful, motivating, and confidence-building, but they also identified important limitations such as invalid or inconsistent feedback, narrow feedback scope, lack of emotional nuance, and the risk of blindly accepting automated suggestions.

The main conclusion is that AFSs can support self-regulated English learning when they are scaffolded carefully and combined with human feedback. The paper argues for context-sensitive tool choice, explicit teacher guidance, emotional self-regulation support, and low-stakes formative use rather than high-stakes automated assessment. It also highlights broader implementation concerns relevant to AI writing assistants more generally, including inaccuracy, overreliance, and the need for learners to remain critical rather than dependent on automated feedback.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that writing-focused AFS tools such as Grammarly and Write and Improve helped them improve academic writing, identify errors, and measure progress. For example, one participant reported moving from IELTS 6.5/B2 to 7/C1 after five weeks of use, while the survey rated Grammarly highly (mean 4.2414/5, n=29) and the writing tools were among the most valued resources.
finding.measure: Writing quality, error detection/correction, IELTS-equivalent writing scores, perceived usefulness ratings
finding.study_size: n=7 qualitative; survey n=32, writing-tool ratings n=29 for Grammarly
finding.std_deviation: SE reported for some survey ratings only; not_reported for outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Speaking-oriented AFS tools such as ELSA, Speechace, Liulishuo, and Voice Analyst were reported to improve pronunciation, speaking confidence, and intelligibility. Participants described gains such as being able to pronounce their own name, and the survey rated ELSA highly (mean 4.0/5, n=18); however, the paper reports this as perceived improvement rather than a controlled effect size.
finding.measure: Pronunciation, speaking confidence, IELTS-speaking-equivalent scores, speech rate/intonation feedback, perceived usefulness ratings
finding.study_size: n=7 qualitative; survey n=32, ELSA rating n=18

finding.finding_summary: A central finding was that AFS use supported self-efficacy, confidence, emotional self-regulation, and reduced anxiety about communication. Participants described AFSs as a “safe” place to practice and said they became more comfortable interacting with humans after using the tools; the course also explicitly scaffolded emotional reflection and self-regulation.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy, confidence, emotional self-regulation, affective responses to feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied critical engagement, metacognition, and selective acceptance of automated feedback. Students learned to question AFS outputs, compare multiple tools, synthesize human and automated feedback, and adapt tool use to context, showing stronger critical thinking and self-assessment over time.
finding.measure: Critical engagement with feedback, self-assessment, contextual judgment, feedback synthesis

finding.finding_summary: Students valued AFSs for fast, always-available feedback that helped them track progress without waiting for human evaluation. The paper argues these tools can extend feedback availability and sustainability, though no formal workload or efficiency metrics were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived availability, immediacy, and sustainability of feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests institutional value in adopting AFSs for low-stakes, formative language support, but it also notes barriers such as unequal access to paid tools, device compatibility, and low digital literacy. The recommended implementation safeguards include teacher scaffolding, explicit introduction of strengths and limitations, and institutional support for learners who need technical or financial assistance.
finding.measure: Perceived accessibility, sustainability, and implementability of AFS-supported learning

paper_profiles.title: One Small Step for Generative AI, One Giant Leap for AGI: A Complete Survey on ChatGPT in AIGC Era
paper_profiles.venue: ACM (Manuscript submitted to ACM; arXiv preprint)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of ChatGPT and related generative AI systems, aiming to synthesize the model’s underlying technology, applications, limitations, and societal challenges. The authors review the Transformer and autoregressive foundations of GPT models, trace the progression from GPT-1 through GPT-4, and then organize discussion around applications in scientific writing, education, medicine, software development, and management.

In the education section, the paper describes how ChatGPT may be used by students and teachers for tutoring, assessment, course material generation, language translation, and writing support, while also noting risks such as plagiarism, overreliance, and the weakening of independent thinking. The survey is not an empirical study of a specific K-12 intervention; instead, it compiles findings from prior papers and examples across domains. Its main conclusions are that ChatGPT is highly capable and potentially useful, but its factual unreliability, inconsistency, and misuse risks mean it should be used as an assistant rather than a replacement for human judgment and learning.

finding.finding_summary: The survey reports that ChatGPT can support writing-related tasks such as brainstorming, literature review, content generation, and proofreading, but it also warns that generated academic text may contain incorrect references, missing details, and stylistic differences from human writing. In the education context, the authors note that over half of surveyed adult students reported using ChatGPT to write essays, but this is presented as descriptive usage rather than an effectiveness result.
finding.measure: Reported applications and concerns related to writing, essay generation, proofreading, and plagiarism risk

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may stimulate brainstorming and idea generation, but it also highlights a major risk of overreliance that could weaken critical thinking and independent thinking. As mitigation, the authors recommend more opportunities for discussion and explicit teaching of critical thinking so students do not simply outsource thinking to ChatGPT.
finding.measure: Reported concerns about independent thinking, critical thinking, and brainstorming support

finding.finding_summary: Within the education discussion, the survey notes that ChatGPT may support students through interactive dialogue and personalized assistance, but the paper does not present direct evidence of changes in motivation or engagement. The main educational concern tied to this area is that easy access to generated answers may reduce effortful persistence and encourage passive completion of assignments.
finding.measure: Reported student usage patterns and concerns about engagement/effort in learning

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Applications of Generative AI in High School STEM Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI (GAI), compared with a search engine and no external tools, affects high school students’ learning in physics. The study is framed around a central question in AI-in-education research: whether GAI can improve academic performance and engagement, and whether those benefits depend on students understanding how to use the tools responsibly.

The author conducted a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test study in Tomball Memorial High School with AP Physics 1 and on-level physics students. Students were assigned to one of four conditions: control, search engine access, generative AI access, or generative AI plus a generative AI literacy program (GAI-LP). The study used Bing AI for the GAI conditions, and the literacy program emphasized responsible, ethical, and effective use. Quantitative outcomes came from pre/post physics tests, and qualitative outcomes came from post-surveys about understanding, engagement, and enjoyment.

Results were mixed. In AP Physics, there were statistically significant differences between groups on the score changes; the GAI-only group performed worse than both the search-engine and GAI-LP groups, and the literacy-program group outperformed the GAI-only group. In on-level physics, however, group differences were not statistically significant. Survey responses showed no statistically significant differences across groups, although students using GAI reported slightly higher engagement. The paper concludes that generative AI can be detrimental when used without guidance, while a literacy program can improve academic outcomes and help students use the technology more responsibly.

finding.finding_summary: The study focused on physics test performance measured with pre-test/post-test score differences. In AP Physics, the one-way ANOVA showed a statistically significant difference across experimental groups (p=0.011), with the GAI-only group performing worse (M=-0.857, SD=1.791, n=14) than the search-engine group (M=0.484, SD=1.387, n=31) and the GAI-LP group (M=0.500, SD=1.225, n=14). In on-level physics, the ANOVA was not significant (p=0.619), and no treatment group differed meaningfully from control.
finding.measure: Physics pre-test/post-test score differences
finding.study_size: n=171 total quantitative participants; AP Physics n=91, on-level physics n=80
finding.std_deviation: AP Physics SDs: control 1.355, SE 1.387, GAI-LP 1.225, GAI 1.791; on-level physics SDs: control 1.700, SE 2.250, GAI 2.199, GAI-LP 1.569

finding.finding_summary: Student survey responses did not show statistically significant differences across experimental groups for understanding, confidence, engagement, or enjoyment. A MANOVA on the survey measures returned p=0.115, indicating no detectable overall treatment effect. Descriptively, the GAI group showed slightly higher engagement, but the confidence intervals overlapped substantially and the author concluded the differences were not significant.
finding.measure: Post-survey ratings of understanding, confidence, engagement, and enjoyment
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CIs reported for interval plots; exact values not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly argues that responsible GAI use and GAI literacy are linked to better student understanding of how to use the tools effectively and ethically. Empirically, the GAI-LP group outperformed the GAI-only group on AP Physics score changes (GAI-LP M=0.500 vs. GAI M=-0.857; t-test p=0.0256), suggesting that guidance improves students’ ability to apply the tool productively. However, the study did not directly measure critical thinking or metacognition with a dedicated instrument.
finding.measure: AP Physics score differences; GAI literacy program exposure
finding.study_size: AP Physics GAI-LP n=14; GAI n=14

finding.finding_summary: The paper is partly about implementation guidance for schools and districts, arguing that outright bans are less effective than clear policies, literacy programs, and safeguards for ethical use. It also reports that the literacy program appeared more effective objectively than students perceived, implying that institutional adoption should include training, not just access. The only empirical basis here is indirect: the GAI-LP condition improved AP Physics outcomes relative to GAI-only, supporting a school-level implementation safeguard.
finding.measure: Effect of a generative AI literacy program on AP Physics outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Latent Directions: A Simple Pathway to Bias Mitigation in Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses bias in generative AI, specifically text-to-image diffusion models, and asks whether bias can be mitigated without modifying prompts or embeddings. The authors argue that biased training data and limited transparency in generated outputs make responsible deployment difficult, and they introduce a new method that learns a “latent direction” in diffusion noise space to steer generations toward more inclusive outputs.

The proposed pipeline first uses pairs of prompts representing a neutral concept and a target debiased concept to generate images and save latent states at selected denoising steps. A linear SVM is then trained to separate these latent representations and produce a direction vector dZ. At inference time, the method adjusts only the initial Gaussian noise with zT = zT + ω·dZ, leaving the prompt embeddings untouched. The paper also introduces a developer-facing tool that uses cosine similarity, CLIP-based classification, and Kosmos-2 object descriptions to inspect apparent biases in generated images and help select mitigation concepts.

Experiments are conducted on Stable Diffusion XL and Stable Diffusion 2.1 across several bias scenarios: gender representation in professions, skin tone, waterbirds in spurious-correlation settings, and geographic/cultural representation in weddings and housing. The authors report successful debiasing in these settings and note that combining latent directions can further improve results. They also report an important tradeoff: very high latent weights can distort generations and move them out of distribution, so practical use requires balancing debiasing strength against output quality.

paper_profiles.title: Natural Language Query Engine for Relational Databases using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of making relational database querying accessible to non-technical users who do not know SQL. The author argues that existing natural-language-to-SQL systems often produce syntactically valid queries that are not semantically correct, do not incorporate domain-specific business rules, and leave users with raw SQL or unvalidated outputs that are hard to interpret.

To address these issues, the paper proposes a generative-AI-based natural language assistant that translates user queries into SQL, validates the SQL syntactically and semantically, and generates a natural-language response from the retrieved data. The system also stores database schema information and business rules in a vector database so relevant context can be retrieved during query processing. The prototype uses IBM watsonx.data, watsonx.ai, Milvus, and Llama 3/Mixtral models.

The paper evaluates a prototype on the BIRD-SQL benchmark and reports that over 50% of queries were translated correctly on the first attempt, with higher success on simpler queries and improved performance after iterative refinement. It also reports that a small set of nontechnical users found the generated natural-language responses coherent and easy to understand, with 90% of test cases rated excellent. The main conclusions are that iterative validation plus business-rule retrieval can improve query correctness and usability, though the prototype still struggles with ambiguous questions, specialized domain knowledge not captured in the rules, execution time, and scalability to larger databases.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed system is designed to reduce the effort required for non-technical users to query relational databases by automating natural-language-to-SQL translation, query validation, refinement, and response generation. In the prototype evaluation, over 50% of benchmark queries were translated correctly on the first attempt (more than 58% for simple queries), and iterative refinement improved success further; the paper frames this as improving productivity and reducing manual intervention.
finding.measure: SQL translation accuracy and iterative query success on the BIRD-SQL benchmark

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the approach can democratize access to data by allowing non-expert users to query enterprise databases without SQL knowledge, and it is explicitly positioned as a scalable interface for organizational data access. The prototype also integrates business rules and semantic validation to support institutional correctness in real-world database use, though the paper does not report formal policy or governance outcomes.
finding.measure: Prototype feasibility and benchmark performance for enterprise database access

paper_profiles.title: Exploring utilization of generative AI for research and education in data-driven materials science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports on AIMHack2024, a July 2024 hackathon organized to explore how generative AI can be used in research and education in data-driven materials science. The authors focus on three practical use cases: AI-assisted software trials, building an AI tutor for a scientific software package (PHYSBO), and using generative AI to help develop a Windows GUI application from Python scripts.

In the first example, participants used ChatGPT to learn ImageJ workflows for counting objects in images, including overlapping objects via watershed segmentation. In the second, the authors tested MyGPT as a tutor for PHYSBO and found that URL-only reference materials led to inaccurate responses, while uploading full documentation PDFs substantially improved correctness. In the third, they used ChatGPT iteratively to convert a PHYSBO-based Python script into an executable GUI tool, add user input dialogs, select input files, and generate a manual. The paper concludes that generative AI can substantially reduce effort for software learning, tutorial generation, and GUI development, but emphasizes that human verification is still necessary because AI can produce plausible but incorrect outputs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that generative AI reduced the effort required to learn unfamiliar software, generate tutorials, and build a GUI application. Examples include ChatGPT producing usable ImageJ instructions, accelerating PHYSBO tutorial creation, and helping create a Windows executable and manual; however, no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Task completion efficiency / reduced effort for software learning, tutorial generation, and GUI development

finding.finding_summary: The hackathon was explicitly designed to strengthen participants' ability to critically evaluate AI-generated content. Participants were encouraged to verify AI outputs against literature and domain knowledge, and the authors report that this process fostered critical thinking about reliability and applicability; no quantitative measure was reported.
finding.measure: Critical evaluation of AI-generated content / verification practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames generative AI as useful for education in materials science by supporting hands-on software learning and creation of instructional materials. It does not test a direct learning intervention with academic outcome measures, but it reports that several participants successfully used software they had not used before after AI-assisted guidance.
finding.measure: Successful use of unfamiliar scientific software in an educational hackathon context

paper_profiles.title: Using Scenario-Writing for Identifying and Mitigating Impacts of Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that conventional AI impact assessment methods are too dependent on expert judgment, fixed metrics, and already-known risks, and therefore miss contextual, lived, and emerging harms of generative AI. The authors critique common approaches to risk identification and mitigation and propose Scenario-based Sociotechnical Envisioning (SSE) as an alternative framework.

SSE is a scenario-writing method in which participants are introduced to a generative AI technology, its capabilities and limitations, and then asked to write narratives projecting future impacts and, optionally, mitigation strategies. The method is designed for survey or workshop settings and emphasizes inclusive sampling, sociotechnical context, and anticipation of unknown risks. The paper is primarily conceptual/provocation-oriented rather than reporting an empirical evaluation of SSE in a specific educational setting.

The paper's main conclusion is that qualitative, narrative-based approaches can complement existing quantitative impact assessment practices by surfacing overlooked impacts, especially those affecting marginalized groups or arising from human-AI interaction in context. The authors also discuss safeguards for using SSE, including equitable participatory design, involving multiple researchers with different backgrounds, careful instruction design, and allowing alternative solutions when working with marginalized communities. However, the paper does not present direct empirical evidence about AI writing assistants in high school settings or measure student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that scenario-based sociotechnical envisioning (SSE) can improve institutional AI impact assessment by surfacing overlooked and unknown risks, especially in generative AI governance. It proposes using participant-written narratives to identify impacts, support mitigation planning, and strengthen democratic accountability and inclusion, but it does not report empirical effect sizes or study outcomes.
finding.measure: Conceptual proposal of an AI impact assessment method; no empirical outcome measure reported

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Adoption in Postsecondary Education, AI Hype, and ChatGPT’s Launch
paper_profiles.venue: Open/Technology in Education, Society, and Scholarship Association Journal
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT’s launch in late 2022 shaped public and educational discourse about generative AI in postsecondary education during the first six months after release. Rather than testing an intervention, the article uses critical discourse analysis of mainstream news coverage and selected education-facing sources to understand how hype, fear, and expectations about AI influenced how educators and institutions interpreted the technology.

The study focuses on postsecondary education in Canada and broader English-language media discourse, analyzing a corpus drawn from The Globe and Mail and The Economist, narrowed to 55 articles that discussed education-related terms. It identifies four recurring themes: overwhelming capability, impending job loss, anthropomorphism, and vulnerability/fear/existential risk. These themes are used to argue that hype pushed education stakeholders toward reactive, uneven adoption and away from measured, value-based policymaking.

The paper’s main conclusion is that generative AI is simultaneously framed as a productivity tool and as a threat to education’s core practices, especially writing and assessment. The author argues for best practices, AI literacy, inclusive co-design, ethical guardrails, and stronger policy input from students, marginalized communities, and other stakeholders. It also notes concerns about cheating, bias, factual inaccuracy, and overreliance on automation, while recommending that AI systems in education be subject to strict oversight and monitoring.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can rapidly produce passable prose, but this convenience also reduces students’ independent composing work and shifts writing from composing to prompting, editing, and copy/pasting. The article does not report an experimental effect size; instead, it documents discursive concerns about reduced rhetorical engagement, cheating, and diminished writing process quality in postsecondary settings.
finding.measure: Critical discourse analysis of news articles and selected educational text discussing writing, composition, and academic misconduct

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT is described as highly efficient for drafting prose, brainstorming, and helping educators with lesson-plan materials, quiz questions, and grammatical or structural feedback. The paper frames this as a convenience gain for students and instructors, but emphasizes that efficiency comes with tradeoffs in reduced independent work and increased dependence on automated outputs.
finding.measure: Discursive references to productivity, efficiency, and time-saving use cases for ChatGPT in education
finding.study_size: n=55 education-subset articles plus OpenAI educator examples cited in the paper

finding.finding_summary: The article centers on how hype shapes institutional adoption, policy formation, academic integrity responses, and broader governance concerns around generative AI in education. It highlights uneven, ad hoc adoption, fears about job displacement, the need for regulatory frameworks, and recommendations for inclusive policy and co-design, but does not quantify institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Critical discourse analysis of media framing plus discussion of policy guidance and institutional responses

paper_profiles.title: How Close is ChatGPT to Human Experts? Comparison Corpus, Evaluation, and Detection
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how closely ChatGPT matches human experts in question-answering, what linguistic differences distinguish ChatGPT from humans, and whether automated methods can detect ChatGPT-generated text. The authors build the Human ChatGPT Comparison Corpus (HC3), a large bilingual dataset of nearly 40K questions paired with human and ChatGPT answers drawn from open-domain and domain-specific sources including finance, medicine, law, psychology, and computer science.

The paper combines human evaluation, linguistic analysis, and content-detection experiments. Volunteers compared human and ChatGPT answers in Turing-test-style settings and judged helpfulness; ChatGPT was often harder to distinguish when a human-answer comparison pair was available, and it was frequently rated as more helpful than human answers in many domains, but less helpful in medicine. Linguistic analysis found that ChatGPT answers were typically longer, more organized, more neutral, and less emotionally varied, but could also fabricate facts in expert domains, which the authors flag as a risk for professional consultation.

The second major contribution is a set of ChatGPT detectors, including GLTR-based logistic regression and RoBERTa classifiers for single-text and question-answer settings. The authors test how indicating words, sentence-level versus full-text inputs, mixed training data, and question-answer context affect detection. They conclude that RoBERTa-based detectors are more robust than GLTR, that sentence-level detection is harder than full-text detection, that mixed and sentence-level training data improve robustness, and that QA-style detectors generally outperform single-text detectors. The paper also notes limitations, including unbalanced data sources and the fact that all ChatGPT outputs were generated without special prompting.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is primarily about detecting AI-generated content and understanding ChatGPT’s differences from humans, with implications for online platform governance, content moderation, and academic integrity. The authors argue that detection tools are needed to flag machine-generated text and reduce societal risks, but they also note that ChatGPT can bypass detectors under some prompting conditions, so the institutional value is real but limited by robustness concerns.
finding.measure: Detector F1 scores and qualitative discussion of content moderation / platform safety implications

paper_profiles.title: MusicScaffold: Bridging Machine Efficiency and Human Growth in Adolescent Creative Education through Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a central tension in adolescent AI-assisted creative work: prompt-output generative AI can make creation fast and easy, but it may also leave learners dependent on the system and fail to build deeper expressive skill. The authors focus on music creation as a testbed, arguing that current tools such as Suno and Udio help students produce songs quickly but do not make the reasoning behind expressive choices visible or learnable.

To address this, the paper proposes MusicScaffold, a hybrid AI learning framework with three roles: guide, coach, and partner. The system translates vague intentions into symbolic musical attributes with explanations, prompts iterative reflection and refinement, and then generates final music while preserving learner autonomy. The paper describes a prototype implementation and evaluates it through a four-week exploratory study (n=60) and a comparative study (n=270 total; 90 per condition) with middle school students aged 12–14 in regular music classes.

Across both studies, the authors find that direct prompt-output systems produce efficient but shallow behavior: students mostly used emotional labels, relied on regeneration, showed high prompt homogeneity, and reported low confidence and motivation. By contrast, MusicScaffold improved prompt specificity, broader use of musical elements, strategic refinement, after-class engagement, and self-efficacy. The paper concludes that generative AI in adolescent creative education should be designed as a scaffold for growth rather than only as a generator of outputs, with transparency, iterative reflection, and autonomy-preserving co-creation as key safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: MusicScaffold improved students’ music-creation performance by increasing prompt specificity and the breadth of musical elements used. In the comparative study (n=270, 90 per group), the MusicScaffold group’s mean prompt specificity was 3.00 versus 1.53 and 1.80 in the two control groups, and 68.8% of its prompts used three or more musical dimensions compared with much narrower coverage in controls.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated prompt specificity and musical element coverage in music-creation tasks

finding.finding_summary: MusicScaffold strengthened self-efficacy, autonomy, and sustained motivation for creative expression. In the comparative study (n=270), the MusicScaffold group reported higher confidence in expressing emotions through music (M=3.60) than Control A (M=2.01) and Control B (M=2.37), and showed higher voluntary after-class participation that increased over four weeks.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy ratings and voluntary after-class participation/interactions

finding.finding_summary: The framework improved reflective strategy use and reduced reliance on homogeneous, trial-and-error behavior, indicating gains in metacognition and self-regulation. In the comparative study (n=270), MusicScaffold increased prompt modifications to 51.1% of adjustment behaviors and reduced regeneration-only responses to 28.9%, while teacher ratings showed reduced homogeneity by Week 4.
finding.measure: Adjustment behavior coding, prompt homogeneity, and reflective refinement patterns

paper_profiles.title: Will Code Remain a Relevant User Interface for End-User Programming with Generative AI Models?
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 ACM SIGPLAN International Symposium on New Ideas, New Paradigms, and Reflections on Programming and Software (Onward! '23)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This essay asks whether traditional programming languages and other formal systems will remain relevant for end-user programming in a world where generative AI can translate natural-language prompts into code. The paper frames this as the “generative shift hypothesis”: generative AI will expand the scope, frequency, and intensity of end-user programming by making code generation, debugging, reuse, and explanation much easier and more accessible.

Rather than presenting an empirical intervention, the paper develops a conceptual argument using examples from code generation, spreadsheets, prompting, and end-user software customization. It evaluates several reasons formal code may still matter: limited model abilities, the need for control and agency, awareness of what is possible, explanation and debugging, trust, and the fact that “informality” may be illusory because prompt engineering still requires skill.

The paper also identifies risks and limitations of generative AI for end-user programming, including errors, hallucinations, misinformation, bias, privacy/security concerns, accountability issues, and the possibility that novice learners may become over-reliant on AI assistance. It concludes with research implications for future end-user programming work, emphasizing new questions around tradeoffs, attention investment, learning barriers, self-efficacy, and how to design systems that preserve useful forms of control, verification, and transparency.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can improve coding task performance for end-user programmers, but it also warns that model failures, incorrect code generation, and abstraction mismatches can make code harder to understand and use reliably. Examples cited include incorrect generated programs for simple tasks such as averaging string lengths, selecting rows from a table, and spreadsheet-style data analysis, but these are illustrative rather than newly produced empirical results.
finding.measure: Code generation correctness, debugging, reuse, comprehension, and explanation quality in end-user programming tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that generative AI may reduce effort and increase convenience, but could also weaken self-sufficiency, metacognition, and confidence in one’s own programming ability if users become over-reliant on AI. It argues that self-efficacy may shift from authoring code directly to effectively using tools to solve problems, but it does not report a measured intervention effect.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy, motivation, and reliance on automated assistance in end-user programming

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that generative AI may change, rather than eliminate, the need for durable skills such as critical thinking, problem solving, and metacognitive understanding. The paper cautions that over-reliance on generative AI may hinder the development of novice programmers’ metacognition and ‘bad habits,’ while also noting that users may still need to reason about outputs, limitations, and tradeoffs when using AI-generated code.
finding.measure: Metacognition, critical thinking, problem solving, and self-sufficiency in programming-related tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can substantially increase the efficiency of authoring, debugging, reuse, comprehension, and one-off automation by reducing the cost of creating code from natural language. It cites benchmark and prior-study examples to support the claim that generative models can handle a broader range of programming tasks and speed up automation, but it also notes that efficiency gains may be offset by verification and correction work.
finding.measure: Programming task completion, automation effort, and code generation/debugging productivity

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights institutional and governance concerns around generative AI, including academic integrity, accountability, privacy/security, bias, attribution, and oversight. It proposes mitigation strategies such as ethical design, critical use, and governance, including output verification, bias mitigation, user feedback mechanisms, and independent monitoring, but these are recommendations rather than evaluated interventions.
finding.measure: Ethical risks, governance, oversight, and policy implications of generative AI use

paper_profiles.title: Will ChatGPT get you caught? Rethinking of Plagiarism Detection
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT-generated academic essays can evade standard plagiarism-detection tools, motivated by growing concern that students may use large language models to produce assignments with little or no effort. The authors frame the issue as one of academic honesty and institutional readiness in the face of increasingly capable AI writing systems.

The study is a descriptive quantitative analysis of 50 essays generated by ChatGPT on 50 topics, each prompted as a 500-word essay. The outputs were checked with Turnitin and iThenticate, and the authors also tested a reverse-engineering approach by asking ChatGPT itself to judge whether the essays were AI-generated. Across the 50 essays, similarity scores ranged from 0% to 64%, with most essays falling below 20% similarity; the average similarity score was 8.76% for iThenticate (n=25) and 13.72% for Turnitin (n=25). ChatGPT reportedly identified 46 of 50 essays as generated by itself (92% accuracy), suggesting that conventional plagiarism detection may miss AI-generated text.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can produce original-sounding essays that often bypass conventional plagiarism software, creating a significant academic integrity risk. The paper argues that institutions should reconsider plagiarism workflows, potentially shifting from similarity-based detection toward origin verification and AI-detection approaches. It also recommends safeguards such as clearer AI-use policies, student/instructor training, assignments that require critical thinking beyond basic essay production, and explicit guidance on ethical use of ChatGPT.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT poses a serious institutional challenge because conventional plagiarism systems (Turnitin and iThenticate) often failed to flag AI-generated essays as suspicious. In a sample of 50 essays, 40 were described as having a similarity score of 20% or less, and only 10 were identified as having critical similarity levels; the authors conclude that plagiarism workflows need to be revised toward content-origin verification and AI-specific detection.
finding.measure: Plagiarism/similarity scores from Turnitin and iThenticate; ChatGPT self-identification of AI-generated text

paper_profiles.title: Feedback sources in essay writing: peer-generated or AI-generated feedback?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether ChatGPT can function as a useful source of feedback for argumentative essay writing, and compares the quality of AI-generated feedback with peer-generated feedback. The authors situate the work in the broader problem that teachers in large or demanding classes may struggle to provide timely, detailed feedback, while peer feedback can also vary in quality because it requires cognitive processing, critical thinking, and domain knowledge.

The study was conducted in an online module at a Dutch university with 74 graduate students in food sciences. In week one, students wrote argumentative essays on controversial course-related prompts; in week two, they provided peer feedback, and the same essays were also passed to ChatGPT using a nearly identical feedback prompt. The researchers coded essay quality and feedback quality using established schemes and analyzed differences and correlations using MANCOVA and Spearman correlations.

Results showed that peer feedback was overall higher quality than ChatGPT feedback, mainly because peers were better at identifying specific problems in essays, while ChatGPT produced more descriptive summaries. There was no overall significant relationship between essay quality and feedback quality for either peers or ChatGPT. The authors interpret ChatGPT and peer feedback as potentially complementary, and suggest that AI could help reduce teacher workload in essay-feedback settings. The paper also notes that ChatGPT can produce inaccurate results in principle, although no major inaccuracies were observed in this study, and recommends prompt validation, blind assessment, and additional coder training in future work.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluated argumentative essay writing and feedback quality in a writing task. Essay quality was measured with an 8-element rubric based on argumentation structure, and feedback quality was coded for affective, cognitive, and constructive features. Peers produced higher-quality feedback than ChatGPT overall, especially on problem identification, while ChatGPT produced more descriptive feedback; no overall significant relationship was found between essay quality and feedback quality.
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality rubric; feedback quality coding scheme

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively addresses cognitive and critical-thinking dimensions of peer and AI feedback in essay writing, including identification of issues, justification, and constructive recommendations. Peers outperformed ChatGPT in identifying problems, which the authors attribute to human contextual knowledge and critical thinking, but ChatGPT provided stronger descriptive summaries. No overall relationship was found between essay quality and feedback quality.
finding.measure: Feedback coding dimensions: description, identification, justification, constructive feedback

finding.finding_summary: A central motivation and conclusion of the paper is that AI-generated feedback may help alleviate teacher workload in essay evaluation and scale feedback provision in large or online classes. The study itself did not directly measure workload reduction, but it explicitly argues that combining peer and ChatGPT feedback could reduce teachers’ time and effort while maintaining constructive feedback quality.
finding.measure: Teacher workload implications discussed from feedback-source comparison

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted academic writing: recommendations for ethical use
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This commentary addresses the rapid adoption of LLM-based generative AI tools, especially ChatGPT, in academic writing and the resulting concerns about plagiarism, hallucinations, fabricated references, and threats to academic integrity. The authors ask how such tools can be used legitimately and ethically in scholarly writing, with a particular emphasis on healthcare simulation researchers and academic authors rather than students in K-12 classrooms.

The paper is not an empirical intervention study; instead, it synthesizes journal and publisher guidance, reviews published examples of AI failure modes, and uses ChatGPT outputs as a starting point for reflection. The authors propose a tiered framework for ethical use: relatively acceptable uses include grammar/spelling refinement, readability improvement, and translation with human review; more contingent uses include outlining, summarizing, clarification, and brainstorming; and higher-risk uses include de novo drafting, literature review, data interpretation, ethical-compliance checking, and plagiarism checking.

The main conclusion is that generative AI can support writing only when humans remain responsible for originality, accuracy, interpretation, and final accountability. The paper emphasizes transparency in disclosure, human vetting, substantial human contribution, and safeguarding scholarly development by avoiding overreliance on AI for core intellectual tasks. It also warns that AI can reproduce copyrighted or biased content, generate fabricated references, and undermine critical thinking if used indiscriminately.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can help with writing-related tasks such as grammar, spelling, readability, translation, outlining, and summarizing, but only with strong human oversight. At the same time, it warns that AI-generated text can be plagiarized, factually inaccurate, or misleading, and that de novo drafting without human input can reduce authors’ deep engagement with the source material.
finding.measure: Not an empirical measure; conceptual assessment of writing-related uses and risks of LLM-generated text

finding.finding_summary: A central concern is that reliance on ChatGPT for ideation, primary drafting, and initial data interpretation could create dependency and arrest scholarly development. The authors explicitly caution that overuse may diminish critical thinking and prevent researchers from maintaining competence in core writing and reasoning skills.
finding.measure: Not an empirical measure; expert argument about impacts on critical thinking and scholarly development

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames generative AI as potentially improving efficiency by helping authors re-structure text, improve clarity, refine readability, and translate manuscripts. However, these efficiency gains are treated as conditional and limited by the need for careful human checking, especially because AI can generate inaccurate content and fabricated references.
finding.measure: Not an empirical measure; conceptual discussion of productivity and writing efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses strongly on publication ethics, journal policy, authorship norms, and disclosure standards for AI use in scholarly manuscripts. It argues for transparent reporting, clear non-author status for AI tools, and human accountability, while warning that weak governance could amplify plagiarism, hallucinations, bias, and integrity violations.
finding.measure: Not an empirical measure; policy and governance recommendations for academic publishing

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not explicitly studied; broad K-12, higher education, and teacher audiences
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT/GPT-3-class systems, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize emerging research and provide a conceptual review of how LLMs may support learning, teaching, assessment, lesson planning, writing, and educational technology design across schooling levels.

The paper discusses likely uses for elementary through higher education, with particular attention to reading, writing, question generation, feedback, tutoring, and teacher productivity. It argues that LLMs can enhance personalization, support creative and critical thinking when used appropriately, and improve efficiency for teachers. At the same time, the authors emphasize major risks: bias, copyright and plagiarism, privacy/security, inaccurate or unverified outputs, overreliance by learners and teachers, difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from student-generated work, and inequitable access.

To address these concerns, the paper recommends safeguards such as fact-checking, human oversight, transparency, professional training, curriculum design that promotes critical thinking, and policies for privacy, fairness, and responsible use. Overall, it frames LLMs as promising but requiring careful governance and instructional design to avoid unintended consequences in educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual position paper, not an empirical study, so it does not report quantified effects. It identifies multiple institutional risks and safeguards for adopting LLMs in education, including bias/fairness, privacy/security, copyright, plagiarism, integrity, cost, and access inequities, and recommends governance frameworks, human oversight, and policy controls.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.population: Junior High School (Gymnasium) students with migrant/refugee background learning German as a foreign language
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines whether ChatGPT can function as a feedback tool to improve foreign language writing for students with migrant/refugee backgrounds. The paper is motivated by the challenge of supporting socially vulnerable learners who face additional language barriers and by the growing interest in generative AI for language education.

The intervention took place in a junior high school in Patras, Greece, with 8 fifteen-year-old students enrolled in German as a foreign language. Students first wrote a personal email, then ChatGPT was prompted to improve the vocabulary and grammar of their texts, and finally students wrote a second, related email after reviewing the AI-enhanced version. The researchers compared pre- and post-writing outputs using text-based indicators such as total words, unique words, and average words per sentence.

Results showed increases in total word count, unique words, and average sentence length in most students’ revised writing, suggesting that ChatGPT-supported feedback may help learners enrich vocabulary and produce longer sentences. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support language learning in multilingual classrooms, especially for students with refugee/migrant backgrounds, but they emphasize that the study is small and exploratory. They also note important cautions from the broader literature, including risks of cheating, the need to verify accuracy, and the importance of human teacher supervision and digital literacy training.

finding.finding_summary: After ChatGPT was used to improve students’ German writing, most students showed gains in writing quantity and lexical variety. Across 8 junior high school students (n=8), total words increased by a mean of 38%, unique words increased on average by 19.1 per student, and average words per sentence increased by approximately 42% in the post-intervention texts.
finding.measure: Foreign language writing quality indicators: total words, unique words, average words per sentence

paper_profiles.title: Will ChatGPT get you caught? Rethinking of Plagiarism Detection
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT-generated essays can evade conventional plagiarism-detection systems, motivated by concerns that students may use large language models to complete writing assignments dishonestly. The authors focus on the originality of ChatGPT outputs and on whether standard similarity-based tools can identify them as plagiarized or machine-generated.

Using a descriptive quantitative approach, the authors prompted ChatGPT to write 50 short essays on diverse topics, then checked 25 with Turnitin and 25 with iThenticate. They also performed a reverse check by asking ChatGPT whether the essays were AI-generated. The study found that most essays were judged highly original by plagiarism software (average similarity 8.76% for iThenticate and 13.72% for Turnitin), while ChatGPT itself identified 46 of 50 essays as generated by itself. The paper concludes that traditional plagiarism detection may be insufficient for AI-written text and recommends institutional policies, clearer guidance, and assignments that emphasize critical thinking and originality as safeguards against misuse.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-generated writing often evaded standard plagiarism checks, suggesting that AI-assisted essay writing can undermine independent writing assessment. Across 50 essays, similarity scores ranged from 0% to 64%, with average similarity of 8.76% on iThenticate (n=25) and 13.72% on Turnitin (n=25); 40 of 50 essays had similarity scores of 20% or less. However, the study does not measure student writing quality directly—only detectability of AI-generated writing.
finding.measure: Plagiarism/similarity scores of ChatGPT-generated essays assessed by Turnitin and iThenticate

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-generated text creates a serious institutional challenge for academic integrity systems because conventional plagiarism software may miss chatbot-written essays. The reverse-engineering test found that ChatGPT identified 46 of 50 essays as AI-generated, leading the authors to recommend a two-step detection approach, updated institutional policies, clearer guidelines, and training on responsible AI use.
finding.measure: Effectiveness of plagiarism-detection tools and proposed institutional safeguards

paper_profiles.title: ‘Words are Flowing Out Like Endless Rain Into a Paper Cup’: ChatGPT & Law School Assessments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can answer a range of law school exam questions and what that implies for assessment design and academic integrity in higher education. The author’s core question is not whether ChatGPT is useful in general, but where it succeeds or fails when asked to complete common law-school assessment types, especially essays and problem questions.

The study uses a practical demonstration approach: past exams from the Chinese University of Hong Kong Faculty of Law were submitted to ChatGPT (GPT-3.5, January 9, 2023 version), and the outputs were then evaluated by instructors or expert assessors. The paper finds that ChatGPT performs better on short, broad, essay-based questions about non-local or internationally well-represented topics, but struggles with narrow, hyper-local legal issues, fictional fact patterns, and tasks requiring legal judgment, precise doctrinal application, or use of local authorities. It also emphasizes that the model sometimes fabricates cases, omits relevant law, and gives superficially plausible but incorrect answers.

A major theme is academic integrity. The paper argues that existing plagiarism detectors are poorly suited to AI-generated text because outputs are unique and detectors only provide probabilities, not proof. The author also notes equity and implementation concerns tied to jurisdictional training-data bias: ChatGPT is much better at English-language, Anglo-American legal material than at Hong Kong-specific law, which can disadvantage students and distort assessment validity. The paper concludes that generative AI is likely to force a rethink of law-school assessment and teaching, while recommending caution around overreliance on detection tools and highlighting the need for institutional safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT creates significant institutional challenges for higher education assessment, especially around academic integrity and assessment validity. It reports that AI-generated answers can be difficult to detect with plagiarism tools, that false positives are a risk, and that law schools may need to redesign assessments rather than rely on detection software alone.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of ChatGPT performance on law school exams and discussion of academic integrity/detection practices

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s performance on law assessments was highly variable. It performed best on broad essay questions and worst on narrow, local, or scenario-based legal problems; the paper reports no consistent ability to apply Hong Kong law accurately, and notes fabricated cases and missed issues in multiple exams.
finding.measure: Grades and expert-assessor evaluations of past law school exams answered by ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that reliance on ChatGPT may weaken students’ need to perform core legal reasoning tasks independently, such as issue spotting, applying law to facts, and making judgments under uncertainty. Although this is inferred from the model’s performance rather than directly measured as a student outcome, the author repeatedly frames these as competencies that the tool may replace or obscure in assessment contexts.
finding.measure: Interpretive analysis of assessment tasks requiring legal reasoning, issue spotting, and judgment

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT can rapidly generate complete answers to exam prompts, making it operationally efficient for users attempting to complete written tasks quickly. The paper notes that the system could produce responses in minutes and that this speed contributes to the risk of misuse in take-home assessments.
finding.measure: Author-observed time and ease of generating exam responses

paper_profiles.title: The Effectiveness of Software Designed to Detect AI-Generated Writing: A Comparison of 16 AI Text Detectors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a practical problem created by generative AI in academic writing: whether publicly available AI text detectors can reliably distinguish AI-generated writing from human student writing. The author frames the issue in terms of academic integrity and the risk that students may submit AI-generated work as their own, especially as ChatGPT-4 becomes harder to detect than earlier versions.

To test detector performance, the study evaluates 16 AI text detectors on 126 documents: 42 undergraduate essays generated by ChatGPT-3.5, 42 generated by ChatGPT-4, and 42 first-year composition essays written by students before ChatGPT was widely available. The detectors were assessed on overall accuracy, accuracy by document type, decisiveness, false positives, and false negatives. Copyleaks, TurnItIn, and Originality.ai performed best overall, correctly classifying almost all documents; most other tools handled GPT-3.5 reasonably well but struggled substantially with GPT-4.

The main implication is that AI text detection is uneven and should be used cautiously. The paper warns that false positives can lead to unjust academic misconduct allegations, while false negatives can allow cheating to go undetected. It recommends a moderate approach in which detector output is considered alongside other evidence, and it notes that a limited number of detectors appear viable for educational use, especially when examining student writing for possible AI involvement.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates how well 16 AI text detectors classify writing as AI-generated or human-written, which is directly tied to writing assessment. Copyleaks, TurnItIn, and Originality.ai achieved very high accuracy across 126 documents (42 GPT-3.5, 42 GPT-4, 42 human essays), while most other detectors were reasonably accurate for GPT-3.5 but much weaker for GPT-4.
finding.measure: AI-text detector classification accuracy on undergraduate essays (correct/incorrect/uncertain), false positives, and false negatives

finding.finding_summary: The study’s central concern is institutional use of AI-detection tools for academic integrity enforcement. It warns that false positives can produce unwarranted misconduct accusations, while false negatives can let violations go undetected; it also recommends that detector results be used cautiously and alongside other evidence rather than uncritically.
finding.measure: Detector false positives/false negatives and overall suitability for academic-environment use

paper_profiles.title: Will ChatGPT get you caught? Rethinking of Plagiarism Detection
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT-generated academic essays can evade standard plagiarism-detection systems, motivated by concerns that students may use AI tools to produce essays with minimal effort. The authors frame the study around academic honesty, cheating, and the limitations of similarity-based plagiarism tools in the context of rapidly improving large language models.

The study is a descriptive quantitative analysis of 50 ChatGPT-generated essays on 50 open-ended topics. Each essay was submitted to two plagiarism-detection tools, iThenticate and Turnitin, and the authors also tested a reverse-engineering approach by asking ChatGPT whether the texts were AI-generated. The paper finds that many outputs appeared highly original to the plagiarism tools: 40 of 50 essays had similarity scores of 20% or less, with average similarity scores of 8.76% for iThenticate and 13.72% for Turnitin, suggesting that AI-generated writing may bypass conventional plagiarism checks. In contrast, ChatGPT itself identified 46 of 50 essays as AI-generated, leading the authors to argue that plagiarism detection should shift from simple text matching toward AI-origin verification. The paper concludes with mitigation suggestions for teachers, students, and institutions, including more critical-thinking-oriented assignments, clear academic integrity guidance, and institutional policies and training on responsible AI use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT-generated essays can evade conventional plagiarism detection, creating a risk for institutional academic integrity systems. In the sample of 50 essays, 40 had similarity scores of 20% or less, and the authors conclude that plagiarism policies and detection workflows need revision; they also suggest a two-step process combining AI-origin verification with similarity checking.
finding.measure: Plagiarism/similarity scores from Turnitin and iThenticate; chatbot-origin detection by ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on written essay production and shows that ChatGPT can generate text that appears original to plagiarism software, raising concerns about writing assessment and academic integrity in essay-based literacy tasks. Across 50 essays, similarity scores ranged from 0% to 64%, with average similarity scores of 8.76% (iThenticate) and 13.72% (Turnitin), indicating that AI-assisted writing may undermine independent writing evaluation.
finding.measure: Originality/similarity of essay writing outputs

paper_profiles.title: Modifying AI, Enhancing Essays: How Active Engagement with Generative AI Boosts Writing Quality
paper_profiles.venue: ACM (manuscript submitted to ACM / arXiv preprint)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how different ways of interacting with generative AI during writing are related to the quality of the final essay product. The authors ask whether students’ writing behaviors—specifically, seeking AI suggestions but not accepting them, accepting AI suggestions without revision, or accepting and then revising them—are associated with better or worse writing outcomes, and whether these patterns relate to linguistic bias in the text.

The study uses the CoAuthor dataset, which contains 1,445 writing sessions from 63 crowd-sourced writers using GPT-3 across 20 writing topics. The authors apply causal modeling techniques (back-door adjustment and X-learner estimation) to estimate the effects of the three AI-writing behaviors on lexical sophistication, syntactic complexity, text cohesion, and gender bias, while controlling for genre, topic, language background, and GPT settings.

The main conclusion is that active engagement with AI-generated text matters: accepting AI text without revision is associated with lower essay quality, while accepting and revising AI suggestions is associated with higher quality across lexical sophistication, syntactic complexity, and cohesion. Using AI text in any form also tends to reduce gender bias in the final writing, though the paper argues that bias remains a concern, especially for non-native writers. The authors recommend process-aware assessment and explicit instruction to help writers critically refine AI suggestions rather than rely on them passively.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that AI-writing behavior strongly relates to writing quality. Across 1,445 writing sessions, accepting AI suggestions without revision (T2) reduced lexical sophistication (ATE = -0.086), syntactic complexity (ATE = -0.869), and text cohesion (ATE = -0.007), while accepting and revising suggestions (T3) improved all three measures (ATE = 0.102, 0.963, and 0.008, respectively).
finding.measure: Lexical sophistication (Advanced Guiraud), syntactic complexity (Mean Length of T-Unit), and text cohesion (Semantic Overlap)

finding.finding_summary: The paper also evaluates gender bias as a linguistic quality outcome. All three behaviors were associated with reduced gender bias, with the largest decrease for seeking suggestions but not accepting them (T1, ATE = -0.163), followed by accepting without revision (T2, ATE = -0.012) and accepting with revision (T3, ATE = -0.013).
finding.measure: Gender bias measured with Genbit Score

finding.finding_summary: The study’s core interpretation is that active revision of AI output reflects deeper cognitive engagement and critical evaluation, whereas direct acceptance reflects lower-order engagement. The results show a strong positive pattern for revising AI output (T3) and negative patterns for passively accepting it (T2), which the authors frame as evidence that meaningful cognitive engagement during writing is linked to better products.
finding.measure: Process behavior patterns interpreted as cognitive engagement/critical revision in relation to essay quality outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Embracing AI in Education: Understanding the Surge in Large Language Model Use by Secondary Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how widely large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are being used by secondary students, what they are using them for, and how students perceive their usefulness and risks. The authors aim to inform educators and developers about student adoption patterns in the face of school restrictions and concerns about cheating, inaccurate answers, and unequal access to AI tools.

The study uses a survey of 306 middle and high school students in the United States, with respondents spanning grades 6 through 12 and representing 43 states. The paper reports that 71% of respondents had used an LLM at least once and 9% used one daily; usage was roughly consistent across grades 7–12. Students reported using LLMs across subjects, including writing/language arts, history, foreign languages, math, and STEM, but their feedback was mixed because models sometimes hallucinated in historical contexts and produced incorrect answers, especially where rigorous reasoning was needed.

The paper also examines school policy strictness, ethical concern ratings, and demographic differences in access. It finds that students in more technologically advanced states and private-school students reported higher usage, and that students with paid versions of models used them more frequently, suggesting an access gap tied to resources. In response, the authors propose mitigation and implementation ideas such as subject-specific models, training models on textbooks and teacher input, personalized learning, AI tutors, and AI classrooms, along with safeguards to reduce harmful content and protect privacy.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs for writing text and language arts, and 57% of LLM users said the tools were useful for writing. However, the paper also reports student concern that increased reliance on such tools may lower fundamental skills, and some respondents noted inaccuracies, indicating both perceived support for writing and possible risks to independent writing development.
finding.measure: Survey responses on LLM use for writing/language arts and perceived usefulness for writing

finding.finding_summary: The survey found that 28% of students used LLMs for math, and 43% of LLM users found them useful for math and STEM questions. At the same time, the paper notes that students expressed dissatisfaction with incorrect answers and that prior research shows weaker mathematical capability, suggesting mixed utility for math learning and homework support.
finding.measure: Survey responses on LLM use for math and perceived usefulness for math/STEM questions

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs across multiple non-literacy subjects, including history and foreign languages, and the paper notes that students sometimes observed hallucinations in historical contexts. The survey indicates broad academic use beyond writing and math, but also concerns about factual accuracy in subject-specific tasks.
finding.measure: Survey responses on subject areas of LLM use and open-ended feedback on usefulness/accuracy

finding.finding_summary: Open-ended responses included concerns that increased reliance on LLMs may lower fundamental skills, and the authors interpret some feedback as suggesting students should be prompted to explore topics more deeply rather than simply receive answers. The paper does not measure critical thinking directly, but it documents perceived risks of overreliance and motivation to preserve deeper reasoning.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about academic impact and proposed model improvements

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports students’ ratings of ethical concern and school-policy strictness, showing that LLM use persisted despite restrictive policies and moderate ethical concern. This suggests users may experience tension between convenience and concern, but the study does not directly measure engagement or self-regulation outcomes.
finding.measure: Ratings of school policy strictness and ethical concern about LLM use

finding.finding_summary: The study finds widespread student adoption despite school restrictions: 71% of respondents had used LLMs at least once, and students rated school policy strictness at an average of 3.48/5. It also finds equity gaps, with higher usage in more technologically advanced states (80.2% vs. 64.3%) and among private-school students (76.7% vs. 71.3%), plus a pay-to-access advantage for students with paid models.
finding.measure: Survey responses on LLM usage, school policy strictness, ethical concern, state technology rankings, school type, and paid-model ownership

paper_profiles.title: Exploring EFL Secondary Students’ AI-generated Text Editing While Composition Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how Hong Kong secondary school EFL students actually edit and revise text generated by generative AI while completing an expository writing task. The authors ask what kinds of edits students make to AI-generated text and what overall editing patterns emerge during machine-in-the-loop writing, a process in which students collaborate with chatbots and digital writing tools while composing.

The researchers ran an exploratory mixed-methods workshop with 29 students aged 12 to 18 from seven secondary schools. Students reviewed prompt engineering and either process-writing or genre-based writing instruction, then completed a 500-word expository article task on Google Docs using POE chatbots and any combination of self-written and AI-generated content while screen recordings captured their writing processes. Twenty-five recordings showed AI-generated text edits and were analyzed through hierarchical content analysis and thematic case study analysis.

The paper identifies 15 distinct edit types across seven categories, including insertion, deletion, replacement, pre-edit formatting, and acceptance of predictive text from Apple iOS and Google Docs. A key finding is that students were not passively pasting AI text; they frequently inserted, deleted, and replaced AI output, suggesting active evaluation and modification. The study also found four editing patterns combining planning vs. no planning with top-down vs. bottom-up drafting, showing that many students maintained a more traditional writing process, while others pasted full AI-generated drafts and revised them directly.

The paper’s main caution is that AI-generated writing now includes semi-autonomous suggestions from tools like iOS and Google Docs, which can reduce student control and complicate agency in machine-in-the-loop writing. The authors recommend explicit instruction in prompt engineering, AI-text editing strategies, and ways to preserve authorial voice and agency, as well as formative assessment of the writing process rather than only the final product.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that EFL secondary students made 266 edits across 25 screen recordings, including insertions (n=68), deletions (n=58), and replacements of AI-generated text (e.g., Replacement AI:Human n=44). This suggests students actively evaluated and revised AI-generated writing rather than passively accepting it, but the paper does not report direct outcome measures of writing quality or achievement.
finding.measure: Screen-recorded AI-generated text edits during expository writing; counts of edit types and editing patterns
finding.study_size: n=25 analyzed screen recordings (from n=29 participants)

finding.finding_summary: The paper analyzes planning, revising, and prompt-engineering behaviors in machine-in-the-loop writing and concludes that students engaged in more complex cognitive processes than simple text insertion. Four patterns emerged (e.g., planning with top-down drafting, planning with bottom-up drafting), indicating variation in metacognitive control and strategy use, but no quantitative effect on metacognitive outcomes was reported.
finding.measure: Planning vs. no planning; top-down vs. bottom-up drafting and revising patterns derived from screen recordings and thematic analysis

finding.finding_summary: The study highlights implementation concerns for classroom use of generative AI, especially that Apple iOS and Google Docs produced unanticipated AI-generated text suggestions that could reduce student agency. The authors recommend instructional safeguards such as explicit teaching of AI-generated text editing strategies, prompt engineering, and formative assessment of process, but no institutional-level outcome data were measured.
finding.measure: Observed AI-initiated edits from writing software and authors’ pedagogical implications

paper_profiles.title: The Digital Divide in Generative AI: Evidence from Large Language Model Use in College Admissions Essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI is changing high-stakes essay writing in U.S. college admissions, with a focus on whether the benefits and risks of LLM-assisted writing are distributed evenly across socioeconomic groups. The authors argue that LLMs may expand access to writing support for students with fewer resources, but they may also standardize student voice, encourage overreliance, and create new inequities in how writing is evaluated.

Using a de-identified longitudinal dataset of 81,663 applications to a selective U.S. university from 2020 through 2024, the study estimates essay-level LLM use with a distribution-based detector trained on synthetic and historical essays. It then tracks changes in linguistic features, adoption rates, and admissions outcomes before and after ChatGPT's release, using fee-waiver status as a proxy for lower socioeconomic status.

The results show substantial post-2023 convergence in surface-level writing features across groups, sharp increases in estimated LLM use in 2024, and higher adoption among lower-SES applicants. However, LLM use is associated with larger admissions penalties for lower-SES applicants than for higher-SES applicants, even after controlling for academic credentials and stylometric features. The paper concludes that generative AI may reduce disparities in access to writing support while worsening disparities in returns, raising concerns about equity, authenticity, and the validity of essay-based evaluation in admissions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds substantial post-2023 convergence in surface-level writing features, with essays becoming more similar across socioeconomic and admissions groups. At the same time, among essays with detectable LLM use, lower-SES applicants produced slightly shorter, less lexically diverse text than higher-SES LLM users (e.g., MTLD 90.88 vs. 95.78; d=0.15 for overall LLM use differences), suggesting uneven benefits from AI-assisted writing.
finding.measure: Essay linguistic features including lexical diversity (TTR, MTLD, HDD, Yule's K), average word length, sentence length, readability/complexity, token and word counts, and estimated LLM usage (\u03b1)
finding.study_size: n=81,663 overall; post-GPT LLM-use subgroup n=17,654; stylometric comparison n=7,377 higher SES and n=3,249 lower SES
finding.std_deviation: SDs reported in tables vary by metric; not_reported for a single summary value

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that lower-SES applicants adopted LLMs at higher rates but experienced larger negative associations between estimated LLM use and admission probability. In the post-GPT era, the SES admissions gap widened (DiD b2=-0.170, OR=0.844, p=.025), and the penalty associated with LLM use was about twice as large for lower-SES applicants as for higher-SES applicants (interaction b2=-1.028, OR=0.358, p=0.023).
finding.measure: Admission decision / predicted admission probability from logistic regression, difference-in-differences, stratified models, and interaction models
finding.study_size: n=30,488 for DiD; n=17,654 for post-GPT LLM-usage models
finding.effect_size: OR=0.844 (DiD interaction); OR=0.358 (LLM use �d7 lower SES interaction)

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing AI in Secondary Education to Enhance Writing Competence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT may affect writing instruction and writing development in secondary education.
