The authors frame the central tension as one between technological augmentation and risks such as dependency, plagiarism, reduced ownership of writing, and weakened development of a personal writing voice.

Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the article synthesizes prior research, examples from practice, and logical arguments to propose how AI might be integrated into writing instruction without undermining learning. The authors argue that AI is potentially useful in pre-writing and revision, especially for brainstorming, counterargument generation, and feedback, but is less appropriate during the actual drafting phase where students should formulate their own text.

The paper focuses on high school/secondary students and emphasizes safeguards such as process-based assessment, tightly specified prompts, authentic and personal writing tasks, controlled exam conditions, teacher oversight, and limited or supplementary use of AI. It also notes that AI-generated text may hallucinate or contain inaccuracies, that plagiarism is a concern when students copy unaltered AI output, and that AI detection tools are not yet reliable enough to serve as the sole integrity safeguard.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI may support aspects of writing development in secondary education, especially brainstorming, revision, and feedback, but it may also weaken the development of writing competence and a personal writing voice if students rely on it for drafting. No original effect estimate is reported; the discussion is based on prior studies and illustrative examples rather than a new empirical test.
finding.measure: writing competence, writing voice, quality of drafts, feedback use

finding.finding_summary: The article repeatedly highlights tradeoffs for critical thinking, creativity, and independent judgment. It suggests AI can help students generate ideas and counterarguments, but warns that overuse may reduce depth of thinking, ownership of ideas, and the development of independent problem-solving in writing tasks.
finding.measure: critical thinking, creativity, independent judgment, counterargument generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI can lighten teacher workload by providing instant feedback, answering routine questions, and semi-automating some assessment-related tasks. It does not provide a quantitative estimate, but argues that these efficiencies could free teacher time for more individualized pedagogical support.
finding.measure: teacher workload, feedback turnaround, routine question handling, assessment support

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses institutional concerns about academic integrity, exam security, and the limitations of AI detection tools. It argues that schools should adopt process-based assessment, controlled testing environments, and clearer guidance on acceptable AI use because current detection tools are unreliable and national regulations are unclear.
finding.measure: assessment policy, exam design, plagiarism control, AI detection reliability

paper_profiles.title: Approaches to Generative Artificial Intelligence, A Social Justice Perspective
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines generative artificial intelligence through a social justice lens, with a strong emphasis on the risks and ethical concerns raised by tools such as ChatGPT, Bard, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, and AI detectors. The central question is not whether AI improves a measured educational outcome, but how generative AI may affect academic integrity, bias, privacy, copyright, and equity in schooling.

The paper is primarily a conceptual and argumentative essay rather than an empirical study. It argues that AI writing assistants make plagiarism and other forms of academic dishonesty more accessible and less detectable, while also creating broader concerns about biased training data, stereotyping, and the potential for false accusations when AI detection tools are used against student writing. Examples from image generation and AI detection are used to illustrate how model training practices and detection systems may disproportionately harm marginalized groups, especially non-native English writers and ELL students.

The author concludes that schools should not rely on an escalating arms race of AI tools and detectors. Instead, educators should remain central in instructional decision-making and reconsider how teaching and assessment should adapt to generative AI. The paper also notes mitigation-oriented practices in the broader AI ecosystem, such as guardrails, human feedback, filtering/reweighting training data, public-domain training sets, and watermarking, but these are discussed as examples of design safeguards rather than as evaluated interventions in schools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI creates major institutional risks for schools, especially around academic integrity, equity, and governance. It does not report a school-based intervention effect, but it warns that AI writing assistants make plagiarism more accessible and less detectable and that AI detectors can produce harmful false positives, especially for non-native English writers and ELL students.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of academic integrity, equity, and AI detection risks

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Quality Prediction Models for Automatic Writing Feedback
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of generating useful automated writing feedback for user-generated multi-paragraph text in online communities. The authors argue that existing tools often focus on grammar and surface-level correctness, while many platforms judge writing by community-specific quality norms such as helpfulness, trustworthiness, informativeness, or topic relevance.

To tackle this, the paper proposes Perturbation Analysis, which uses pre-trained quality prediction models and model explanations to identify which writing features should be changed to improve predicted quality. It also introduces segment-based feedback: documents are split into topic-cohesive segments using TopicTiling, and weak supervision is used to train a segment-level model so feedback can be localized. The approach is evaluated with crowdsourced experiments on Amazon reviews and Airbnb host profiles, comparing document-level versus segment-level feedback and the proposed method versus an outlier-based baseline.

The study finds that Perturbation Analysis substantially outperforms the baseline feedback method, and that localized segment feedback helps most when paired with Perturbation Analysis, especially for Amazon reviews. The authors also report user concerns about trust in automated feedback and the possibility that repeated feedback may not change after revisions, and they discuss safeguards and limitations such as using only non-sensitive writing features, improving personalization, and integrating specialized tools like Grammarly for grammar-focused feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies writing quality feedback and finds that Perturbation Analysis plus segment-level feedback improved post-feedback writing quality on two writing tasks. For Amazon reviews, the best condition (Seg+Perturb) improved overall helpfulness by 0.55 on the rubric versus 0.14 for the baseline Doc+Krause; for Airbnb profiles it improved trustworthiness by 0.65 versus 0.07. The authors report statistically significant effects for Perturbation Analysis in both domains and a significant interaction with segmentation for Amazon.
finding.measure: Expert-rated writing quality / helpfulness / trustworthiness of multi-paragraph writing submissions
finding.study_size: n=81 Amazon participants; n=91 Airbnb participants
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CI reported in figure, exact values not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to automate writing feedback generation at scale, replacing slower and costlier human feedback approaches. The paper reports that feedback generation runs in approximately 1/10 second, suggesting high practical efficiency for deployment in large online communities. However, this outcome is secondary to the paper’s main focus on writing-quality improvement.
finding.measure: Feedback generation latency / scalability of automated feedback system

paper_profiles.title: FEANEL: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Error Analysis in K-12 English Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of fine-grained error analysis for K-12 English writing, motivated by the limited ability of current large language models (LLMs) to provide detailed, pedagogically useful feedback on student essays. The authors argue that existing systems typically focus on surface-level grammatical correction or holistic scoring, but do not adequately capture the multiple, intertwined error types that appear in real student writing.

To study this, the paper introduces FEANEL, a benchmark of 1,000 anonymized essays written by elementary and secondary students, annotated by English education experts with error type, severity, and explanatory feedback. The benchmark uses a 29-class error taxonomy and evaluates a range of state-of-the-art LLMs under zero-shot and one-shot prompting settings. Results show that current LLMs still struggle with complex error classification, nuanced severity judgment, and high-quality explanations, especially when edits contain multiple overlapping issues.

The study is primarily an evaluation benchmark rather than an intervention study, so it does not test student learning gains directly. Its main contribution is demonstrating that prompt detail, reasoning style, and model scale affect performance, while human teachers still outperform LLMs on nuanced pedagogical feedback. The paper also highlights implementation considerations such as the importance of standardized taxonomies, careful annotation procedures, and output formatting for reliable educational use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates LLM performance on fine-grained English writing error analysis for K-12 essays. Across 1,000 essays (n=1,000; 8,676 error analyses), models achieved moderate-to-strong error classification accuracy but substantially weaker explanation quality, with no single model consistently outperforming others across classification, severity, and explanation tasks. Human teachers outperformed all evaluated LLMs on the nuanced feedback tasks.
finding.measure: Error classification accuracy/Macro-F1, severity Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and explanation BLEU/METEOR/ROUGE-L on K-12 English writing errors

paper_profiles.title: Exposía: Academic Writing Assessment of Exposés and Peer Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces Exposía, a new public dataset for studying academic writing assessment and peer feedback in higher education. The dataset captures a full writing workflow in a computer science course: students draft a research exposé, receive peer and instructor feedback via inline comments and free-text reviews, revise their work, and submit a final exposé. The authors also create fine-grained, pedagogically grounded rubrics for grading exposés and feedback quality.

The paper uses Exposía to benchmark open-source large language models on two automated scoring tasks: criterion-based exposé scoring and criterion-based review scoring. The study is set in a Bachelor-level course, Introduction to Scientific Work, at a technical university, with 193 enrolled students and a released subset of 55 consented exposés, 306 reviews, and 2,253 inline comments. The main finding is that LLMs can align reasonably well with human raters on criteria requiring limited domain knowledge, but performance drops on content-heavy criteria such as motivation, approach, and methodology.

The paper also analyzes how exposés change from draft to final version after feedback. Revisions improve mainly on content-related rubrics, especially approach, motivation, language/quality, and methodology. For classroom use, the authors conclude that combined prompting across multiple criteria is more effective and more efficient than scoring one criterion at a time, and they recommend using LLMs only as decision-support tools with human oversight rather than for fully automated grading.

finding.finding_summary: Students' exposé drafts improved from draft to final version after peer/instructor feedback, with the largest gains in content-related and writing-related rubrics. Average final drafts were longer (528 to 649 words), and rubric scores improved most on Approach, Motivation, Language/Quality, and Methodology, indicating better academic writing quality after revision.
finding.measure: Criterion-based exposé rubric scores and draft-to-final word count
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CIs reported for rubric score changes in Figure 3, but not numerically specified in the text

finding.finding_summary: The strongest draft-to-final gains were on scientific-writing dimensions tied to reasoning about a research proposal, especially Motivation, Approach, and Methodology. These results suggest that feedback helped students strengthen problem formulation, state-of-the-art discussion, and methodological planning in their research exposés.
finding.measure: Exposé rubric scores for Motivation, Approach, and Methodology
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CIs reported for rubric score changes in Figure 3, but not numerically specified in the text

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that combined prompting over multiple criteria is more effective and more computationally efficient than single-criterion prompting for LLM-based scoring, with one exception (Qwen3 on exposé scoring). The authors explicitly recommend combined prompting for classroom deployment because student activity is deadline-driven and efficiency matters for practical use.
finding.measure: Quadratic weighted agreement (QWA) and computational efficiency of prompting variants
finding.study_size: 4 open-source LLMs; evaluation on 55 exposé drafts and 110 student reviews

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that automated scoring can reduce instructional workload, but it also warns against fully automated grading because models may miss substantive issues and could incentivize strategic gaming. As a mitigation, the authors recommend a human-in-the-loop decision-support workflow with human oversight, especially for assessment-oriented uses.
finding.measure: Author analysis and deployment recommendations based on model behavior and rubric-level agreement

paper_profiles.title: Assisting in Writing Wikipedia-like Articles From Scratch with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies how to use large language models (LLMs) to generate grounded, organized long-form articles from scratch, using Wikipedia-like articles as the target task. The authors argue that the difficult part of expository writing is often the pre-writing stage—researching a topic, gathering references, and creating an outline—so they propose STORM (Synthesis of Topic Outlines through Retrieval and Multi-perspective Question Asking) to automate that stage.

STORM works by first identifying multiple perspectives on a topic, then simulating multi-turn question-asking conversations grounded in trusted internet sources, and finally synthesizing the gathered information into an outline that can be expanded into a full article. The study evaluates the approach on the FreshWiki dataset of recent, high-quality Wikipedia articles, using both automatic metrics and human judgment from experienced Wikipedia editors. Compared with retrieval-based baselines, STORM improves outline quality, organization, breadth, and coverage.

The paper is not a K-12 educational intervention study; it is a system/evaluation paper about AI-assisted writing for Wikipedia-style expository writing. The main substantive takeaways are that question-asking plus outline planning helps produce more comprehensive grounded writing, but the generated articles still lag behind well-revised human work in neutrality and verifiability. The human evaluators also identify risks such as bias transfer from web sources and unverifiable or over-speculative connections between facts.

finding.finding_summary: STORM is designed to reduce the effort required to research and outline long-form articles. The paper reports that the system can help initiate in-depth topic research and may greatly reduce expensive expert hours needed for expository writing, with human Wikipedia editors saying it is helpful for the pre-writing stage and could support editing on new topics.
finding.measure: Human editor usefulness judgments; system capability to collect references and produce outlines
finding.study_size: n=10 editors for usefulness survey; n=20 topics for human evaluation

finding.finding_summary: Although not a K-12 study, the paper directly examines writing support for Wikipedia-like expository writing, which is an academic writing task. STORM produced more organized and broader outlines than baseline methods, including a 25% absolute increase in articles judged organized and a 10% increase in breadth/coverage relative to an outline-driven RAG baseline in expert review.
finding.measure: Outline quality and article organization/coverage ratings
finding.study_size: n=100 article samples for automatic evaluation; n=20 topics with expert human evaluation
finding.effect_size: 25% absolute increase in organized articles; 10% absolute increase in broad coverage

finding.finding_summary: The system is explicitly built around perspective-taking, iterative research, and question formulation, which are durable skills related to inquiry and metacognition. Compared with direct prompting and retrieval-only baselines, STORM’s multi-perspective question asking produced higher-quality outlines and more unique sources, suggesting improved research planning and sensemaking.
finding.measure: Heading soft recall, heading entity recall, number of unique references collected
finding.effect_size: Heading soft recall improved to 86.26% vs 73.59%/74.40% baselines; entity recall 40.52% vs 33.85%

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated Essays: Characteristics and Implications on Automated Scoring and Academic Integrity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines essays generated by multiple large language models (LLMs) in the context of the GRE Analytical Writing task, with a focus on two issues central to assessment in the AI era: automated essay scoring and academic integrity. The authors ask how AI-generated essays differ from human-written essays, where current scoring engines succeed or fail, and whether detectors can identify AI-generated writing across models.

Using 2,000 AI-generated essays from 10 LLMs plus 200 human-written GRE essays, the study compares essay length, semantic and verbatim similarity, e-rater® language features, perplexity, human rater scores, automated scores, and classifier performance. The authors find that newer proprietary models generally produce essays that are more coherent and higher-scoring than older open-source models, while still showing lower perplexity than human essays and some differences in length and similarity patterns. However, e-rater® systematically over-scores AI-generated essays relative to trained human raters, suggesting that feature sets calibrated on human writing do not fully capture deeper reasoning and originality in AI-generated text.

For academic integrity, the paper reports that classifiers using language and perplexity features can detect AI-generated essays with high accuracy, including across different LLMs, although detection becomes harder when human edits or mixed human-AI writing are involved. The study concludes that AI-assisted writing raises concerns about academic integrity, the validity of existing automated scoring systems, and the need for improved scoring features and recalibrated weights that better assess depth of thought rather than surface fluency.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that AI-generated essays are often linguistically strong but can lack deeper substance. Compared with 200 human essays, essays from newer proprietary LLMs generally received higher GRE scores from human raters (e.g., GPT-4o mean 4.67, Gemini 4.78) and even higher scores from e-rater® (GPT-4o mean 5.32, Gemini 5.08), despite e-rater® missing weaknesses in deeper reasoning and over-scoring AI text relative to human raters.
finding.measure: GRE Analytical Writing essay quality; human rater scores; e-rater® scores; language features (grammar, mechanics, usage, style, organization, development, word complexity); essay length; semantic/verbatim similarity; perplexity
finding.study_size: n=2,000 AI-generated essays and n=200 human-written essays

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that widespread AI-generated writing creates serious academic integrity and test security concerns while also showing that detection remains feasible in practice. Detectors trained on one model often generalized well to others, with XGBoost classifiers achieving very high accuracy in within-model and many cross-model settings (often around 0.95-0.997 accuracy), but performance is expected to drop when human revision or human-AI coauthoring is present.
finding.measure: Detection accuracy for AI-generated essays using language-feature and perplexity-feature classifiers; cross-model and within-model classification performance
finding.study_size: n=2,000 AI-generated essays and n=200 human-written essays

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly raises concern that over-reliance on AI writing tools may reduce independent writing proficiency and critical thinking, because users may bypass the cognitive processes involved in generating and organizing ideas. This concern is discussed as a long-term implication of LLM-assisted writing, though it is not directly tested with outcome measures.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Machine-Assisted Grading of Nationwide School-Leaving Essay Exams with LLMs and Statistical NLP
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) and statistical NLP tools can support grading of high-stakes national essay exams in Estonia. The authors are motivated by the need to score large volumes of essays consistently and quickly, especially as Estonia moves toward nationwide computer-based graduation exams and considers AI-assisted assessment within a regulated, human-in-the-loop framework.

The study uses two datasets of digitally produced trial exam essays from full national cohorts: 781 essays from 9th grade and 764 from 12th grade, each scored by two human assessors. The authors compare zero-shot LLM scoring (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, o4-mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash) against human consensus scores, and also build supervised statistical NLP regression models for selected rubric dimensions. They evaluate performance with mean absolute error, range agreement, and bias, and additionally probe prompt-injection vulnerability and whether an LLM can itself produce essays that score highly on the rubric.

Results suggest that automated scoring can approximate human grading reasonably well, especially for some rubric components and in the 9th-grade set. The LLMs generally fell within the human scoring range more often than not, though they showed modest systematic biases and did not perfectly match human consensus; statistical NLP sometimes performed better on lower-level language features. The paper emphasizes that automated grading is viable only under clear rubric design, human oversight, and safeguards against prompt injection and overreliance on the model, and it argues for hybrid, rubric-driven workflows rather than fully automated grading.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLMs and statistical NLP can grade high-school essay writing with near-human performance on several rubric dimensions. On total scores (0–27 scale), MAE ranged from 2.66 to 4.97 for LLMs, and the best supervised pipelines achieved similar or slightly better performance on some language-accuracy categories; predictions often fell within the human min-max range (e.g., 67% for GPT-4o on 9th grade, 55% for Gemini 2 Flash on 12th grade).
finding.measure: Essay rubric scores for writing quality, including content, vocabulary, syntax, punctuation, orthography/morphology, and structuring/formatting

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that machine-assisted grading can reduce assessor workload and enable faster, scalable scoring of national exams. They note that LLM-based scoring could process a full annual cohort and support automated feedback generation, while also being cheaper and more efficient than fully manual grading, though they do not report a direct workload effect size.
finding.measure: Feasibility, scalability, and potential workload reduction for exam grading workflows
finding.study_size: n=1,545 essays total used in grading experiments (781 + 764)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central institutional claim is that a rubric-driven, human-in-the-loop AI grading pipeline is viable for high-stakes national assessment under emerging EU and national regulatory constraints. The authors frame the system as compatible with human oversight, data governance, transparency, and national-scale e-exam modernization, while also showing concrete risks such as prompt injection and model bias that must be managed.
finding.measure: Policy and implementation viability of national-scale AI-assisted exam grading, plus prompt-injection vulnerability and bias checks
finding.study_size: n=100 essays in the prompt-injection probe; n=1,545 essays in the main grading study

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluates writing-related higher-order skills embedded in the rubric, especially content quality, argumentation, and structure, which the authors treat as proxies for advanced written reasoning. LLMs performed reasonably well on these dimensions when the rubric was explicit, but the paper also notes that models can reward surface fluency and that deeper reasoning remains harder to score reliably than lower-level mechanics.
finding.measure: Rubric-based essay dimensions capturing argumentation, content, and structure

paper_profiles.title: The Death of the Short-Form Physics Essay in the Coming AI Revolution
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether modern AI text-completion systems, especially davinci-003 and ChatGPT, can produce short-form Physics essays that would earn high marks in a university assessment. The authors focus on a Durham University undergraduate module, Physics in Society, which uses five short essay questions (300 words each) and a rubric-based marking scheme.

The study generated 10 AI-written submissions from 50 AI outputs, had them independently graded by five markers, and compared the resulting marks to historical module averages. The AI essays averaged 71 ± 2%, essentially matching the module average of 71 ± 5%, and plagiarism software scored them as low-plagiarism (Grammarly 2 ± 1%; TurnItIn 7 ± 2%). The authors argue that short-form essay assessments are highly vulnerable to current AI writing tools, that plagiarism detection is insufficient for identifying AI-generated work, and that non-invigilated essay assessments may no longer be fit for purpose.

The paper also discusses implications for teaching and assessment beyond Physics. It suggests that AI could be used both as a student cheating tool and as a legitimate support tool in workshops or tutoring contexts, but emphasizes that institutions may need to redesign assessment conditions or use invigilated settings to preserve authenticity. It additionally demonstrates that ChatGPT can provide plausible AI-generated feedback on AI-written essays, hinting at future automated marking applications.

finding.finding_summary: AI-generated short-form Physics essays achieved marks comparable to human student work on an undergraduate assessment. Ten AI submissions were independently marked by five markers and averaged 71 ± 2%, matching the module average of 71 ± 5% for the current cohort; this indicates current AI can produce creditable essay responses in Physics history/philosophy contexts.
finding.measure: Independent marker scores on 5-question short-form Physics essays

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that current AI text-completion systems threaten the validity and fidelity of short-form essay assessment and can evade standard plagiarism checks. AI essays scored only 2 ± 1% on Grammarly and 7 ± 2% on TurnItIn, while still earning first-class-equivalent marks, suggesting that non-invigilated assessments are vulnerable and may need redesign or invigilation as a safeguard.
finding.measure: Plagiarism detection scores and assessment fidelity implications

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that AI can generate high-quality essay answers very quickly and cheaply, implying strong efficiency gains for producing text and feedback. It notes that AI can create essays within seconds and that ChatGPT can also generate plausible rubric-based feedback, which could support future automated feedback or marking workflows.
finding.measure: Time and ease of generating AI essays and AI feedback
finding.study_size: n=50 AI answers generated; n=1 example of AI feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper raises concerns that students could use AI as a co-pilot or substitute for their own writing, reducing the authenticity of independently produced work. It explicitly warns that students in the lower third of the cohort would have incentive to submit AI-generated work instead of original writing, and that the ease of prompt-based generation could undermine independent essay production.
finding.measure: Assessment authenticity / likelihood of AI substitution for student writing

paper_profiles.title: Loquacity and Visible Emotion: ChatGPT as a Policy Advisor
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a qualitative experiment examining how ChatGPT performs on a complex policy-writing task for a central bank audience. The authors prompt ChatGPT 4 to draft a policy brief for the Board of the Bank of Italy on the benefits, risks, and unintended consequences of using ChatGPT and similar applications in economics and finance, then iteratively refine the prompts and inspect the output for strengths, weaknesses, and failure modes.

The intervention is not an educational program but a human-AI writing workflow: the authors test outlining, drafting, rewriting, and prompt engineering, while annotating where the model produces useful structure versus superficial, inaccurate, or off-target content. The context is a high-level policy setting, with the intended readers described as economists and lawyers at a central bank and international policy fora. The paper emphasizes that the model can produce fluent, rapid drafts and useful brainstorming outputs, but only with substantial expert supervision.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT can accelerate writing workflows, especially for outlining and first drafts, but it is prone to superficiality, factual errors, prompt sensitivity, outdated knowledge, and overgeneralization. The authors also highlight risks of naive use, including incorrect or irrelevant output, hallucinated or inappropriate references, and failure to address cross-border or domain-specific concerns unless explicitly prompted. Suggested safeguards include careful prompt design, domain-expert review, and independent verification of claims and references.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT accelerated workflow by generating structured outlines and extensive linguistically correct draft text in seconds, reducing the time needed for brainstorming and drafting. However, the authors report that substantial expert supervision was required to reach an acceptable result, partially offsetting the productivity gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of drafting speed, outline generation, and revision burden in a policy-writing task

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses centrally on institutional and governance implications of adopting generative AI in central banking and finance, including cross-border regulation, concentration of power in technology providers, privacy, oversight, and labor-market disruption. The authors conclude that widespread adoption could create regulatory and coordination challenges and requires harmonized international responses, but also that it may improve institutional productivity if carefully supervised.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of policy risks, regulatory challenges, and cross-border implications in a central-bank policy brief context

paper_profiles.title: OverleafCopilot: Empowering Academic Writing in Overleaf with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This technical report presents OverleafCopilot, a browser extension that integrates large language models (LLMs) into Overleaf to support academic writing. The paper is primarily an engineering and system-design contribution rather than an evaluation study: it describes the motivation, architecture, agent system, prompt-sharing website (PromptGenius), and a template directive engine for customizing writing-assistant behaviors.

The authors frame three central implementation challenges: seamless interaction between Overleaf and LLMs, reliable communication with the model provider, and user privacy. To address these, they build a Chrome extension that routes user actions through a message-switch/event-bus architecture and supports customizable agents for paper polishing, grammar checking, translation, and writing advice. The system also includes shortcuts, interface customization, and a backend for licensing and updates.

The paper does not report a formal educational experiment, controlled study, or learner outcomes. Its main conclusion is that OverleafCopilot can accelerate and simplify academic writing workflows while preserving user control through customization and privacy-preserving request forwarding. The report claims the tool has already been adopted by thousands of researchers, but it provides no empirical evidence about writing quality, learning, dependency, or integrity effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that OverleafCopilot improves academic writing efficiency by reducing the effort required for paper polishing, grammar checking, translation, and revision. However, it does not report a controlled evaluation, so the claimed benefit is descriptive rather than empirically quantified.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The system is explicitly designed to support writing-related tasks such as paper polishing, grammar checking, translation, and writing suggestions in Overleaf. No outcome data are reported, but the paper positions these functions as tools for improving written academic text quality.
finding.measure: paper polishing quality, grammar correction, translation quality, writing suggestions

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant, can support K-12 students' writing by providing formative feedback aligned with teacher rubrics and classroom materials. The authors frame the work as an exploratory pilot of a tool designed to make feedback more detailed, more interactive, and more directly connected to instructional expectations than generic AI writing support.

The study was conducted in four public schools in the United States: three high schools and one middle school in diverse socioeconomic contexts. Across Grades 7, 8, 10, and 11, 121 students and 4 teachers participated in the pilot; data came from classroom observations, surveys, and interviews, with post-survey responses from 54 students and 3 teachers and interviews with 8 students and 1 teacher.

Findings were overwhelmingly positive. Students reported that CyberScholar gave specific, actionable feedback, helped them revise grammar, transitions, conclusions, and sentence structure, and supported them in understanding rubric criteria. The tool's interactive follow-up question feature was valued where available, and students appreciated the transparency of rubric-based ratings. At the same time, the paper notes limitations and concerns: some students found ratings inconsistent across repeated submissions, and the authors caution that AI should complement rather than replace teacher feedback. The discussion also highlights broader ethical issues in K-12 GenAI use, including unequal access, privacy, and the need to preserve critical thinking opportunities.

finding.finding_summary: Students generally perceived CyberScholar as helpful for writing development. Across the pilot (n=121 students; post-survey n=54), students reported that the tool provided detailed, specific, and rubric-aligned feedback that helped them revise grammar, transitions, conclusions, sentence structure, and clarity; some students also reported rubric score improvements after revision (e.g., one student improved a 'Compare/Contrast' rubric score from 0 to 2).
finding.measure: Student survey comments, interviews, classroom observations, and rubric-based writing revisions/scores
finding.study_size: n=121 students; post-survey n=54; interviews n=8 students

finding.finding_summary: Students described the tool as motivating and engaging, especially because they could ask follow-up questions and receive interactive responses. The post-survey showed that 36 students explicitly wanted to use CyberScholar again, while 11 were hesitant, suggesting generally favorable engagement with the tool and its feedback process.
finding.measure: Student post-survey willingness to reuse the tool; interview and observation evidence of engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that CyberScholar supported metacognition, self-regulation, and critical reflection by prompting students to revise drafts iteratively and ask clarification questions. Students used the feedback to compare drafts, locate problems, and refine writing, and the authors explicitly interpret the process as supporting metacognition and cyber-social learning.
finding.measure: Qualitative evidence from interviews, observations, and iterative draft revisions
finding.study_size: n=121 students; post-survey n=54; interviews n=8 students

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived the system as quicker and easier to use than peer review or self-analysis for identifying writing problems. The paper describes the tool as providing fast feedback and saving time by quickly locating areas for improvement, though no quantitative productivity metric was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of speed, ease of use, and time saved from surveys/interviews

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that aligning GenAI feedback with teacher rubrics, instructional materials, and student needs could help address resource disparities and improve equity of access to individualized feedback. However, they also acknowledge unresolved institutional concerns, including access inequities, privacy, and the risk that AI use could reduce opportunities for critical thinking if not carefully implemented.
finding.measure: Qualitative interpretation of implementation across four schools and discussion of equity/ethics implications
finding.study_size: n=4 schools; n=121 students; n=4 teachers

paper_profiles.title: Automated writing evaluation in an EFL setting: Lessons from China
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the classroom use of automated writing evaluation (AWE) software, Writing Roadmap, in Chinese EFL settings, with a focus on how an AWE-integrated teaching model affects writing performance and classroom processes. The study was motivated by concerns that students in China receive limited writing practice and feedback, especially in large classes, and by the need to understand not just whether AWE works, but how it is implemented alongside teacher and peer feedback.

The intervention was implemented over two semesters in six intact senior high school classes (n=268 across the full study; n=138 experimental and n=130 control for the high school analysis) and five universities (n=460; n=224 experimental and n=236 control). Students used Writing Roadmap for drafting and revision, received teacher feedback based on the system's six-trait rubric, and in the experimental condition also engaged in peer review and self-revision; control classes used more traditional instruction and/or paper-based peer revision. The study used a quasi-experimental pre-post design with questionnaires, interviews, and journals, and it reports that the experimental groups generally showed greater gains in writing scores than control groups, with especially strong effects in the university sample and statistically significant gains in the high school sample as well. Qualitative findings suggested that AWE increased revision frequency, supported grammar correction and self-assessment, reduced teacher marking workload, and shifted instruction toward a more process-oriented and autonomous writing model.

finding.finding_summary: The AWE-integrated intervention improved writing performance in both the university and senior high school samples. In the university sample (experimental n=224; control n=236), the experimental group showed a larger pre-post gain (0.52 vs. 0.11) and the overall group effect was significant (F=31.46, p=0.0001); reported effect sizes were 0.79 for the experimental group and 0.19 for the control group, with an especially large effect for English majors in the experimental condition (effect size 1.46). In the senior high school sample (experimental n=138; control n=130), the experimental group also outperformed the control group (gain 0.40 vs. 0.19; F=5.06, p=0.03), with experimental-class effect sizes of 0.71, 0.53, and 0.49 across the three teachers.
finding.measure: Pre- and post-test essay writing scores scored in Writing Roadmap and by human scorers; gain score analysis
finding.study_size: n=460 total across university sample; n=268 total across senior high school sample (writing outcomes reported separately for n=224 vs. n=236 university, and n=138 vs. n=130 high school)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased motivation, revision activity, and autonomy after using Writing Roadmap. In the post-questionnaire, 70% said they would be likely to write more and revise more after using the system; 62.3% reported revising 1–2 times and 27.9% reported revising 3–4 times. Interview and questionnaire comments also indicated improved self-assessment ability and a stronger sense of control over writing and revision.
finding.measure: Post-questionnaire responses and student interviews about motivation, revision frequency, and autonomy/self-assessment
finding.study_size: High school and university experimental-group respondents; questionnaire response counts reported as 71/138 high school experimental students and 185/224 university experimental students completed questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests gains in metacognitive and self-regulatory aspects of writing, especially students' ability to use assessment criteria to guide their own writing and revision. Students described learning to identify essay structure and strengths/weaknesses, and the authors argue that interaction with the six-trait assessment criteria helped students internalize standards and become more active co-assessors in the writing process.
finding.measure: Student interviews, questionnaires, and teacher journals about use of assessment criteria, self-assessment, and revision processes

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported reduced marking workload and more time for targeted instruction because the AWE system handled much of the language-level feedback. The paper describes a shift from extensive weekend essay marking to more focused teaching on content, rhetoric, and writing process, indicating improved instructional efficiency.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaires, interviews, and journals on workload and teaching practice

paper_profiles.title: ALEN App: Persuasive Writing Support To Foster English Language Learning
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 17th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2022)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents ALEN, a writing-support application that uses argumentation mining to provide adaptive feedback on persuasive essays written in English by secondary-school language learners. The core problem addressed is whether discourse-level feedback on claim-premise structure can help students write better persuasive texts and engage more deeply with English language learning, especially in contexts where standard grammar feedback alone may be insufficient.

The system highlights claims and premises in student text, shows a graph view of argument structure, and provides summarized scores for readability, coherence, and persuasiveness. The authors trained the underlying model on 1,000 student-written persuasive texts and then evaluated the tool in two field studies in a German high school with 28 12th-grade students. Students completed Cambridge English B2 persuasive writing tasks while using the app and then reported technology acceptance and self-efficacy; the study also collected open-ended feedback.

Results were primarily attitudinal rather than performance-based. Students rated ALEN positively on perceived ease of use, usefulness, and intention to use, and study 2 found relatively high self-efficacy for English language learning tasks. Qualitative feedback suggested that students liked the visual feedback and discourse-level support, but also wanted more grammar feedback and noted some incorrect highlighting. The paper concludes that ALEN shows promise as a proof-of-concept, but larger studies are needed to determine whether adaptive argumentation feedback improves actual writing quality or long-term language outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: In study 1 (n=10), students reported high technology acceptance of ALEN: perceived ease-of-use mean = 5.77 (SD=0.96), perceived usefulness mean = 5.60 (SD=0.69), and intention to use mean = 5.7 (SD=0.79) on a 7-point scale. In study 2 (n=18), self-efficacy for English language learning tasks was also relatively high (mean = 5.02, SD=1.24), suggesting the tool may support engagement and motivation during persuasive writing.
finding.measure: Perceived ease-of-use, perceived usefulness, intention to use, and self-efficacy Likert-scale surveys

finding.finding_summary: The tool was designed to support persuasive writing through discourse-level feedback on claim-premise structure, readability, coherence, and persuasiveness, but the paper does not report direct pre-post or comparison-group evidence of improved writing quality. The qualitative responses suggest students perceived the feedback as helpful for revising and evaluating essays, while also requesting more grammar support, indicating promising but unquantified effects on writing performance.
finding.measure: Qualitative feedback about persuasive writing support; tool-generated readability, coherence, and persuasiveness feedback

paper_profiles.title: Impact of ChatGPT on ESL students’ academic writing skills: a mixed methods intervention study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed methods intervention study examines whether ChatGPT can improve academic writing when used as a formative feedback tool in an intensive ESL writing course. The paper asks two questions: whether ChatGPT-based self- and peer-assessment improves writing performance when instructional time and tasks are held constant, and how students perceive the tool’s impact on their writing.

The study was conducted with first-year science and engineering undergraduates in India. An experimental group (n=35 analyzed) received a short training session and then used ChatGPT during six hours of instruction to support self-assessment and peer assessment while writing process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraphs; a comparison group (n=37 analyzed) received the same instruction without ChatGPT. Writing was measured through three tests (pre-test, post-test, delayed post-test) scored with rubrics covering content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary, and five students from the experimental group also participated in focus group discussions.

Quantitatively, the experimental group improved substantially over time and outperformed the comparison group at post-test and delayed post-test. The repeated-measures ANOVA showed a strong within-group effect across tests (F[2,72]=330.704, p=5.146e−37, η²=0.902), and post-hoc comparisons indicated large gains from pre-test to post-test and delayed post-test (d=-3.300 and d=-3.898). Between-group t-tests also favored the experimental group at post-test (t(70)=-5.643, p=3.297e−7) and delayed post-test (t(70)=-9.371, p=5.544e−14). Qualitative feedback was overwhelmingly positive, especially for content generation, organization, and grammar explanations, though students also noted possible overdependence and reduced independent thinking. The author concludes that ChatGPT can be an effective formative feedback tool in large ESL writing classes when students are trained to use it appropriately.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT used as formative feedback was associated with substantial improvement in academic writing performance. In the experimental group (n=35 analyzed), scores rose from M=12.581 (SD=0.833) on the pre-test to M=19.216 (SD=2.485) on the post-test and M=20.419 (SD=2.575) on the delayed post-test; the within-group effect was very large (RM ANOVA F[2,72]=330.704, p=5.146e−37, η²=0.902). Compared with the control group (n=37), the experimental group scored significantly higher on the post-test (t(70)=-5.643, p=3.297e−7) and delayed post-test (t(70)=-9.371, p=5.544e−14).
finding.measure: Rubric-scored writing tests assessing content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary
finding.effect_size: η²=0.902; d=-3.300 (pre vs post); d=-3.898 (pre vs delayed); d=-0.598 (post vs delayed)
finding.std_deviation: Pre-test SD=0.833; post-test SD=2.485; delayed post-test SD=2.575

finding.finding_summary: Students reported an overwhelmingly positive experience using ChatGPT for writing feedback, describing it as helpful, confidence-building, and supportive of independent work. Focus group data also identified a few negative concerns—such as reduced motivation to think and increased dependence on the machine—but the dominant pattern was positive perceptions of usefulness, autonomy, and reduced anxiety around feedback.
finding.measure: Focus group discussion themes and coded student perceptions

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative data suggested that ChatGPT supported several durable skills, especially collaboration and metacognitive monitoring of writing. Students said it helped them stay focused on the topic, connect main ideas and supporting details, discuss writing choices with peers, and make more deliberate organizational decisions, although a small number of comments noted that it could impose a pattern and hinder creativity.
finding.measure: Focus group discussion themes on organization, collaboration, and self/peer assessment processes

finding.finding_summary: Students frequently reported that ChatGPT made brainstorming and drafting faster and reduced the time needed to generate ideas and complete tasks. The coded focus group data explicitly identified faster writing speed and time-saving in brainstorming as positive effects, while some students worried about overdependence on the tool.
finding.measure: Focus group discussion themes on time-saving, brainstorming, and task completion

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education published from 2016 to 2022. The authors ask how AI has been studied across geography, academic departments, student level, subject domains, intended users, and use cases in higher education. Using PRISMA methods, they screened 371 records and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles for analysis.

The review does not evaluate a single AI writing assistant intervention or compare it against standard instruction. Instead, it synthesizes the field broadly and shows that most studies focused on undergraduate students, with language learning as the most common subject area. Within language learning, writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition were common, and the review notes that AI was often used for automated feedback of writing, though it does not report high-school-specific comparative outcomes or effect sizes for writing tools.

The main findings are descriptive: publications increased sharply in 2021–2022, China led publication counts, education departments became the most common author affiliation, and the dominant AI uses were assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The paper concludes that AI in higher education is growing quickly, but much of the work remains focused on traditional uses such as feedback, prediction, and personalization rather than novel pedagogical approaches. It also highlights gaps in research on graduate students, instructors, managers, and underexplored affordances of newer tools such as ChatGPT.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review found that language learning was the most common subject domain (17%), and within that area AI was frequently used for writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition. The paper describes several studies using automated feedback and AI-enriched tools for writing, but it does not aggregate writing outcomes or report a pooled effect size for literacy-related interventions.
finding.measure: Writing, reading, and vocabulary-related applications and outcomes reported across included studies
finding.study_size: n=138 studies total; literacy-related subset not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Across the included studies, AI was sometimes used to support students’ engagement, behavioral/cognitive/affective participation, and self-regulated learning. The review specifically notes that automatic assessment and feedback systems could help students engage behaviorally, cognitively, and affectively while improving writing, but the evidence is descriptive rather than comparative.
finding.measure: Engagement, affective participation, and self-regulated learning as reported in included studies

paper_profiles.title: Student engagement with teacher and automated feedback on L2 writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This naturalistic case study examines how two Chinese university students of English engaged with teacher-written feedback and automated writing evaluation (AWE) feedback over a 16-week semester. The paper asks how the feedback sources differ, how students cognitively, behaviorally, and affectively engage with them, and what individual and contextual factors shape that engagement.

The intervention/approach compared teacher feedback with automated feedback from the Pigai AWE system across two writing tasks: a 400-word essay in Advanced English and a 1,000-word essay in Tourism English. Data included student drafts, AWE logs and scores, teacher feedback, and retrospective interviews. The two focal students differed sharply: Flora showed high behavioral, affective, and cognitive engagement, resubmitted many times to AWE, and substantially improved her writing, while David showed more limited engagement, revised mainly at a surface level, and made fewer effective changes.

The main conclusion is that feedback alone is not sufficient; the extent and quality of student engagement mediates whether teacher or automated feedback leads to writing development. The authors argue that AWE can support timely, autonomous, multiple-draft revision, but teacher feedback remains stronger for content, organization, and broader corrective guidance. They recommend integrating both sources and emphasize that proficiency, motivation, and self-regulation strongly influence revision outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that both teacher and AWE feedback could support writing development, but improvement depended heavily on student engagement. Flora, who resubmitted her AWE essay 13 times, improved her AWE score from 79 to 90 and made broad revisions, while David resubmitted once and showed only minimal gains, with 21 of 35 AWE-identified errors left unaddressed.
finding.measure: Writing revisions, error correction, text organization, and AWE essay scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies affective engagement, including motivation, anxiety, frustration, embarrassment, and attitudes toward feedback. Flora reported feeling frustrated at first but became motivated by score gains, while David felt shocked, disappointed, and demoralized by the AWE score of 69.5 and was less willing to revise.
finding.measure: Interview-reported emotions and attitudes toward teacher/AWE feedback

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is cognitive engagement, including planning, evaluating, monitoring, and self-regulation during revision. Flora demonstrated strong self-regulation by spacing revisions across days, controlling pacing, and choosing which errors to address, whereas David showed limited metacognitive processing and mainly deleted uncertain text rather than deeply revising it.
finding.measure: Revision behaviors, metacognitive strategies, and self-regulation during drafting/revision

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AWE offers practical efficiency benefits through immediacy, convenience, and support for multiple drafting. Flora used the system repeatedly across 13 resubmissions, suggesting that instant feedback enabled iterative revision at her own pace, though the study does not quantify teacher workload or time savings beyond these descriptive observations.
finding.measure: Time-on-task, number of resubmissions, and descriptive comparison of feedback delivery

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary-school EFL students prompt ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots while completing a writing task. The authors are interested in the content, quantity, and sequencing of prompts, treating prompt engineering as a turn-by-turn process within a machine-in-the-loop writing framework.

Using a qualitative case-study design, the researchers observed four Hong Kong secondary students completing the same timed blog-entry task on iPads in class. Screen recordings captured prompt sequences, and the authors coded prompt types such as auto-complete, natural language instruction, questions, greetings, and search-engine-like prompts. The analysis identified different prompt engineering pathways and showed that students relied on trial-and-error, often revising prompts by making small wording changes or reusing prior prompts across different chatbots.

The study does not test whether ChatGPT improves the students’ final writing quality, grammar, or revision outcomes relative to standard instruction or other tools. Its main conclusion is that secondary students used a limited and uneven range of prompt strategies, suggesting that prompt engineering education may help them use AI chatbots more strategically in EFL writing classrooms. The authors also note that future research should examine the quality of resulting writing products and any associations with prompt pathways.

finding.finding_summary: The study does not evaluate writing quality, revision quality, grammar/mechanics, vocabulary, fluency, or any other literacy outcome as an intervention effect. It only documents how four secondary EFL students (n=4) engineered prompts while producing a blog entry, and the authors explicitly state that future research should examine the quality of students’ writing products.
finding.measure: prompt content and sequencing during a writing task; completed blog entries were collected but not analyzed for writing quality outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Secondary School Students’ Perceptions on the Use of Google+ towards Improving ESL Writing Skills
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines secondary school students’ and one teacher’s perceptions of using Google+ in ESL writing lessons in Malaysia. The study addresses whether a social media platform can make writing instruction more engaging, interactive, and supportive than conventional classroom writing lessons.

The intervention was not an AI writing assistant; it was Google+, a Web 2.0/social media tool used as the platform for writing activities, discussion, sharing videos and posts, and peer response. The researchers used a qualitative case-study approach with 12 upper secondary students aged 16–17 and one English teacher, collecting data through focus group interviews, an individual teacher interview, classroom observations, and field notes.

Findings were consistently positive at the level of perceptions and classroom experience. Participants reported that Google+ made lessons more enjoyable, less sleepy, and more interesting, and that it encouraged more confident interaction, idea generation, and peer feedback. Observations suggested students checked spelling, sentence structure, tenses, vocabulary, and ideas more actively during the Google+ writing activities, but the paper did not provide quantitative evidence of writing gains or compare student writing outcomes with a control group.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports positive perceptions that Google+ supported ESL writing activities, helped students generate ideas, check spelling, sentence structure, tenses, and vocabulary, and made writing feel more meaningful. However, this is qualitative evidence only; the paper does not report standardized writing scores, effect sizes, or a controlled comparison of writing quality.
finding.measure: Perceptions of ESL writing support; observed writing-related behaviors during Google+ lessons

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that Google+ made writing lessons more enjoyable, less boring, and less sleepy, and increased confidence in interacting and responding to peers and the teacher. The paper describes greater engagement and attention during lessons, but these outcomes were not measured with standardized instruments.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of enjoyment, engagement, confidence, and attentiveness

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests Google+ fostered collaboration and peer interaction: students exchanged ideas, responded to classmates, and learned from others’ posts. These collaborative and communicative behaviors were observed qualitatively, but no quantitative assessment of collaboration or metacognitive/self-regulatory skill was reported.
finding.measure: Observed peer interaction, idea exchange, and collaborative discussion in Google+ writing lessons

paper_profiles.title: The impact of expanding A Level students' awareness and use of metacognitive learning strategies on confidence and proficiency in foreign language speaking skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This small-scale action research study asks whether explicit instruction in metacognitive learning strategies can improve secondary students’ confidence and proficiency in foreign language speaking. The authors focus on A Level French learners in an English secondary school, where speaking was a relative weakness despite generally strong performance in reading, writing, and listening.

The intervention was a six-week strategy-based instruction (SBI) program embedded in normal lessons. Five Year 12 students (ages 16-17) completed pre/post questionnaires, interviews, strategy checklists, and two speaking presentations with transcription and self-assessment tasks. The instruction emphasized preparation, monitoring, and evaluation strategies such as planning vocabulary and structures, organizing ideas, paying attention to pronunciation and grammar while speaking, self-correcting, and using feedback to set targets.

Findings were broadly positive. Students generally reported greater confidence and more positive perceptions of speaking ability after the intervention, and all five improved their presentation-task scores from pre to post. The study also found increased reported value and use of metacognitive strategies, especially preparation strategies. The authors conclude that strategy instruction likely supported speaking development, but they caution that the small sample and action-research design limit generalizability and prevent strong causal claims.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that explicit metacognitive strategy instruction was associated with improved foreign language speaking performance. All five Year 12 French learners increased their presentation-task marks from the first to the second speaking task (scores out of 40), and the authors report that the most common self-identified improvements were fluency, better preparation, and reduced reliance on notes. The paper does not report a mean effect size, confidence interval, or standard deviation.
finding.measure: Foreign language speaking performance on presentation tasks scored out of 40; self-reported confidence and perceived ability in speaking

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported higher confidence in speaking after the six-week intervention. On the confidence questionnaire, two students increased their ratings, while three others described feeling more confident in post-intervention interviews; comments suggested that increased practice, preparation, and using feedback contributed to this change. No statistical effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Speaking confidence questionnaire ratings and semi-structured interview responses

finding.finding_summary: The intervention increased students’ reported awareness and use of metacognitive strategies, including preparation, monitoring, and evaluation. Average ratings increased most for preparation strategies (value: 2.61 to 2.8; use: 1.85 to 2.33), while monitoring use also rose slightly (2.29 to 2.42). The study provides descriptive evidence of improved metacognitive strategy use, but no inferential statistics or effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Strategy checklist ratings and interview data on metacognitive strategy use

finding.finding_summary: The paper also reports improvements in perceived speaking ability, including better pronunciation, accuracy, complexity, and participation in class, although these are based on self-report rather than independent proficiency metrics. Students described using more complex vocabulary, better grammatical planning, and more effective oral organization after the intervention.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceived ability in participation, fluency, pronunciation, accuracy, and complexity

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a structured ChatGPT prompt framework, called the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW), can improve second-language learners’ argumentative essay writing and critical thinking. The authors combine the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model with Tan’s argumentative writing framework and Hattie & Timperley’s feedback model to create structured prompts intended to help learners plan, develop, and revise essays with ChatGPT.

The study used a small experimental design with 10 university students from a state university, randomly assigned to an experimental group that used the CGCAW framework with ChatGPT and a control group that used ChatGPT without the structured guidelines. Participants wrote a short argumentative essay in 40 minutes on social media’s effects on society. Essays were scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor using different criteria. Results were mixed: Grammarly slightly favored the control group, ChatGPT favored the experimental group on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, and the instructor strongly favored the control group. The authors conclude that the CGCAW framework may support some aspects of argumentative writing and critical thinking, but it needs refinement and longer-term testing, especially because it may not yet improve grammar/mechanics or overall argumentative quality consistently.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined argumentative writing quality in 10 undergraduate second-language learners (n=10), comparing a CGCAW-guided ChatGPT condition with unguided ChatGPT use. Findings were mixed across raters: ChatGPT ratings favored the experimental group for clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, but Grammarly slightly favored the control group (mean 92.2 vs 90.6), and the course instructor strongly favored the control group (mean 56 vs 35).
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality ratings; sub-scores for clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness, and instructor rubric criteria
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT total SD=7.6 experimental, 5.5 control; ChatGPT clarity SD=2.4 vs 1.8; evidence SD=1.7 vs 1.2; coherence SD=1.9 vs 1.5

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the CGCAW framework may promote self-regulation through structured prompting and iterative feedback, but it does not provide a separate validated outcome measure for engagement or self-regulation. Evidence is indirect and based on the authors’ interpretation of how ChatGPT feedback may support monitoring, reflection, and revision rather than on a direct pre/post measure.
finding.measure: Observed use of ChatGPT-guided prompts and qualitative interpretation of feedback/self-regulation support

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantially focuses on critical thinking as a central outcome, framing the CGCAW framework as a way to improve analysis, inference, evaluation, and argument construction. In the experiment, the ChatGPT evaluation favored the experimental group on clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use, but the instructor and Grammarly results were unfavorable or mixed, so the overall effect on critical thinking-related writing performance is inconsistent.
finding.measure: Critical-thinking-oriented argumentative writing indicators (clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness) and rubric-based instructor scoring

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Summarization: Designing AI Support for Real-World Expository Writing Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper that argues for treating expository writing as a distinct and understudied problem for AI-assisted writing systems. The authors define expository writing as evidence-based and knowledge-generating writing, where the writer must read source documents, extract and organize evidence, and then synthesize that evidence into new knowledge or insights rather than simply summarize source text.

The paper does not evaluate a specific intervention with users; instead, it sketches a design framework for future AI support across three stages of expository writing: reading and collecting evidence, synthesizing information, and composing text. The authors emphasize that LLMs can support discovery, grouping, and drafting, but that systems should also preserve author control, reduce hallucination risk, and help users verify evidence against source documents.

The intended context is real-world expert writing such as literature reviews, medical notes, legal writing, and other professional expository tasks. The main conclusion is that AI support should be modular and stage-sensitive rather than generating entire long-form documents end-to-end, because expository writing depends on reading comprehension, sensemaking, and faithful integration of evidence into new writing.

paper_profiles.title: Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students’ essays.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT-3 improves students’ essay writing performance when used as a writing assistant. The authors compare a control group that wrote traditionally with an experimental group that used ChatGPT-3, focusing on essay grades, writing time, text authenticity, and essay similarity.

Eighteen second-year master’s students at the University of Split participated (n=9 control, n=9 ChatGPT-assisted). Students wrote an 800–1000 word essay in Croatian on a forensic science topic under identical time and formatting constraints. Essays were graded by two teachers using a rubric covering mechanics, style, content, and format; the study also measured writing time, plagiarism/unauthenticity, pairwise essay similarity, and AI-classifier judgments.

The main finding was that ChatGPT did not improve essay quality. Average essay scores were slightly higher in the control group (2.39 ± 0.71) than in the ChatGPT group (2.00 ± 0.73), and none of the predictors in the regression model significantly affected essay score (group p=0.184, duration p=0.669, module p=0.388, GPA p=0.532). Writing time was also similar across groups, and the experimental group showed slightly higher text unauthenticity. The authors conclude that, in this small first-use sample, ChatGPT did not enhance writing performance and may have introduced some distractive or authenticity-related issues.

finding.finding_summary: In this small comparative study, using ChatGPT-3 as a writing assistant did not improve essay quality. Mean essay grade was slightly lower in the ChatGPT group (2.00 ± 0.73) than in the control group (2.39 ± 0.71), and group status was not a significant predictor of overall essay score (p=0.184).
finding.measure: Essay quality score/grade based on rubric criteria (mechanics, style, content, format; converted A-D to 4-1)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT assistance did not reduce writing time. The experimental group took 172.22 ± 31.59 minutes versus 179.11 ± 31.93 minutes for the control group, and writing duration was not a significant predictor of essay score (p=0.669).
finding.measure: Essay writing duration (minutes)

finding.finding_summary: The paper examined whether ChatGPT increased plagiarism/authenticity problems in submitted essays. The ChatGPT group showed slightly higher text unauthenticity (11.87% ± 13.45) than the control group (9.96% ± 9.81), but pairwise essay similarity was very low overall (median Jaccard similarity index 0.002; range 0–0.054), suggesting limited evidence of broader institutional integrity harm in this sample.
finding.measure: Text unauthenticity/plagiarism checks, pairwise essay similarity (Jaccard index), AI text classifier outputs

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing AI in Secondary Education to Enhance Writing Competence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT might affect writing instruction in secondary education, especially the development of writing competence and a personal writing voice. The authors frame AI as a potentially useful supplement for brainstorming, drafting support, revision feedback, and self-/peer-assessment, but they also emphasize risks such as plagiarism, overreliance, reduced originality, and weakened learning if AI replaces students’ own writing processes.

The article is primarily a conceptual and argumentative discussion rather than an empirical evaluation. It reviews prior work and illustrates possible classroom uses of AI across pre-writing, writing, revision, and feedback phases, including examples of prompts and a sample student text. It argues that AI should be used in a balanced, teacher-guided way, with clear task criteria, process-based assessment, and safeguards that preserve student ownership and critical thinking.

The paper cites a small number of studies involving upper secondary students and teachers, including work on student uses of ChatGPT and one study comparing feedback quality from generative AI versus well-trained educators. However, the paper itself does not report original quantitative results on writing outcomes. Its main conclusion is that AI may support writing instruction in secondary school, but the current evidence base is still limited and teacher mediation remains essential.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI may support aspects of secondary students’ writing development, especially brainstorming, revision, and feedback, but that it can also weaken writing competence if it replaces students’ own composing. The article cites prior studies such as Steiss et al. (2024), which found human feedback to be better than AI feedback, but no original effect sizes are reported in this paper.
finding.measure: writing competence, writing voice, drafting/revision quality, grammar/structure feedback

finding.finding_summary: The discussion suggests AI may increase student engagement and reduce frustration during writing, particularly by helping stuck writers generate ideas and receive instant feedback. At the same time, the authors warn that overreliance on AI may reduce authentic engagement and ownership of the writing task. No direct quantitative engagement or self-regulation data are reported in the paper.
finding.measure: student engagement, motivation, perceived usefulness, self-regulated writing support

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes AI’s possible role in supporting higher-order writing processes such as planning, organizing arguments, considering counterarguments, and revising for coherence, which are framed as critical thinking and metacognitive activities. It also cautions that AI can undermine these skills if students skip the thinking and drafting work themselves. No direct empirical estimates are provided.
finding.measure: critical thinking, metacognitive revision, organization of arguments, counterargument generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly states that AI can lighten teachers’ workload by providing instant feedback, answering routine questions, and supporting formative assessment. This is presented as a practical benefit for large secondary classes, but the article does not quantify time savings or efficiency gains.
finding.measure: teacher workload, feedback efficiency, responsiveness

paper_profiles.title: eRevise+RF: A Writing Evaluation System for Assessing Student Essay Revisions and Providing Formative Feedback
paper_profiles.population: Middle School / High School (grades 4-8; only grades 7-8 are secondary-level)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents eRevise+RF, an automated writing evaluation (AWE) system that assesses students’ argumentative essay revisions and provides formative feedback on both evidence use and revision success.
