The core problem is that many student writers can add evidence after feedback but still fail to make substantive, text-based improvements; the authors aim to go beyond single-draft scoring by evaluating whether revisions actually respond to prior feedback.

The system combines essay-level scoring indicators for text evidence use (Number of Pieces of Evidence, NPE; Specificity, SPC) with sentence-level revision classifiers that label revisions as surface vs. content, evidence vs. reasoning, and successful vs. unsuccessful. It then generates expert-crafted feedback at multiple levels for three drafts (first, second, third), with evidence feedback after draft 1 and revision feedback after draft 2. The paper reports a deployment in Spring 2024 and Fall 2024 with 6 teachers and 406 students across one Pennsylvania school and two Louisiana schools; usable analyses include 172 MVP essays and 150 SPACE essays from students who completed all three sessions.

The paper’s main evidence is validation and descriptive pre/post analysis rather than a causal comparison against a control group. NLP evaluation shows substantial agreement for the scoring indicators and reasonably strong classification performance, and essay quality metrics generally increase across drafts (e.g., predicted NPE and SPC rise from draft 1 to draft 3). The authors conclude that students’ revisions were largely responsive to the feedback messages and that the system shows promise for scaffolding young students’ argumentative writing, but they also note important limitations: no control group, pilot-scale deployment, and a focus on text evidence rather than broader dimensions of writing quality.

finding.finding_summary: Across drafts, students’ argumentative writing improved on evidence-based measures after receiving automated feedback. In the MVP dataset (n=516 essay drafts; 172 students with all three drafts), predicted NPE increased from 2.56 to 3.34 and predicted SPC increased from 8.81 to 13.98 from draft 1 to draft 3; similarly, annotated NPE rose from 2.20 to 2.93 and annotated SPC from 9.00 to 13.59. The authors interpret this as evidence that the system helped students improve text-based evidence use and revision quality, though there was no control group.
finding.measure: Argumentative writing quality via Word Count (WC), Evidence Score (ES), Number of Pieces of Evidence (NPE), and Specificity (SPC) across essay drafts
finding.study_size: n=172 students for draft-to-draft analyses; n=516 essay drafts (MVP) and n=450 essay drafts (SPACE)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students responded to feedback in ways consistent with the system’s prompts, suggesting some support for self-regulated revision behavior. For example, after EF1 (need more evidence), annotated NPE increased by 128% from draft 1 to draft 2 (N=74), and after EF2 (need more specific details), annotated SPC increased by 55.0% (N=11); similar patterns were reported for revision feedback between drafts 2 and 3, though the study did not directly measure motivation or engagement with surveys.
finding.measure: Responsiveness to automated evidence and revision feedback; draft-to-draft changes in NPE/SPC as indicators of self-regulated revision
finding.study_size: n=74 (EF1), n=11 (EF2), n=87 (EF3) for MVP feedback analyses

finding.finding_summary: The system is explicitly designed to support revision quality, evidence use, and reasoning in argumentative writing, which are durable skills related to metacognition and critical thinking. Sentence-level revision classifiers and draft-to-draft analyses showed that students’ revisions were largely aligned with prior feedback, and the paper reports increased evidence use and specificity over successive drafts. However, these outcomes were measured indirectly through writing revisions rather than through separate metacognitive or transfer instruments.
finding.measure: Revision quality and alignment with prior feedback, including revision labels (surface/content, evidence/reasoning, successful/unsuccessful) and changes in NPE/SPC
finding.study_size: n=172 student essay triplets (MVP) for revision analyses

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s system-level purpose is to automate essay scoring and formative feedback, thereby reducing the need for fully manual assessment of evidence use and revision success. The backend achieved substantial performance on validation tasks (e.g., NPE QWK=0.67, SPC QWK=0.82, RC-Content F1=0.96), suggesting the system can operationalize feedback generation at scale, but the study does not report teacher workload reductions or time savings directly.
finding.measure: Automated scoring/classification performance for feedback generation (QWK and F1)
finding.study_size: n=516 MVP essays for scoring-indicator validation; n=1,525 revision pairs for RC-Content; n=1,046 for RC-Evidence; n=1,024 for RC-Success

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports a pilot deployment of a web-based AWE system across 6 teachers and 3 schools in two states, demonstrating feasibility for classroom use and district/school implementation contexts. The main institutional finding is deployment success and cross-school usability rather than measured policy or governance effects.
finding.measure: Classroom deployment feasibility across schools and teachers

paper_profiles.title: Product versus Process: Exploring EFL Students’ Editing of AI-generated Text for Expository Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how Hong Kong secondary school EFL students edit AI-generated text when composing expository writing and whether those editing behaviors predict human-rated writing quality. The authors focus on both the writing process (screen recordings of AI-text edits during drafting) and the final product (the completed compositions), with an emphasis on content, organization, language, and total scores.

Thirty-nine secondary students participated in a workshop where they learned about expository writing, prompt engineering, and using POE chatbots to generate text. Students then wrote an article of up to 500 words using a mix of their own words and AI-generated words; 25 screen recordings were available for process analysis, while all 39 compositions were analyzed for product-level patterns. The study used qualitative coding, descriptive statistics, temporal sequence analysis, human scoring, and multiple linear regression.

The main finding is that students made many edits, but these edits were mostly short, localized changes rather than broad, unit-level revisions. Two editing patterns emerged: one more introduction-oriented and another more body-oriented. In regression analyses, most editing variables had little unique predictive power for writing quality; however, the number of AI-generated words in the final compositions positively predicted all score dimensions, while some specific process variables (e.g., heading edits) were associated with better language and total scores and concluding-paragraph edits with lower scores. Overall, the paper concludes that extensive effort editing AI text does not automatically translate into better writing quality, highlighting a gap between engagement with AI and actual composition performance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on expository writing quality in a secondary-school EFL context. In the product-level regressions (n=39), the number of AI words positively predicted content, language, organization, and total scores, with partial correlations ranging from 0.375 to 0.457 and model R-squared values from 0.463 to 0.538. However, most process-level editing variables showed minimal or inconsistent effects, indicating that extensive editing effort did not reliably improve writing quality.
finding.measure: Human-rated expository writing scores for content, language, organization, and total quality; composition features based on AI words, human words, and editing units
finding.study_size: n=39 for product analyses; n=25 for process analyses

paper_profiles.title: Exploring EFL Secondary Students’ AI-generated Text Editing While Composition Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks how Hong Kong EFL secondary students edit AI-generated text while composing an expository article, and what patterns characterize their editing process. The authors are interested not in whether AI improves writing scores, but in the micro-processes of machine-in-the-loop writing: how students insert, delete, replace, and revise AI-generated material while drafting with chatbots and other AI-supported writing tools.

The study used an exploratory mixed-methods design, but the evidence reported here is qualitative/process-oriented. Twenty-nine students from seven Hong Kong secondary schools attended an AI-assisted writing workshop, received brief instruction on process writing or genre-based writing plus prompt engineering, and then completed a 500-word article task in Google Docs while using POE chatbots and other generative AI tools. Screen recordings were collected and analyzed via hierarchical content analysis and thematic multiple-case analysis. 

Results identified 15 edit types across seven categories, including insertions, deletions, replacements, and edits initiated by Apple iOS predictive text and Google Docs grammar/spelling/next-word suggestions. The authors also identified four editing patterns: planning with top-down drafting/revising, top-down drafting/revising without planning, planning with bottom-up drafting/revising, and bottom-up drafting/revising without planning. The paper concludes that students’ interactions with AI-generated text are cognitively complex and involve active evaluation and modification rather than passive copying. It argues for explicit instruction in AI-generated text editing and for pedagogies that help students maintain agency and authorial voice when writing with generative AI.

finding.finding_summary: The study does not measure final writing quality scores, but it provides detailed process evidence that secondary EFL students actively edited AI-generated text in complex ways. Across 25 analyzed screen recordings (10 hours total), researchers coded 266 edits, including 68 insertions, 58 deletions, 44 AI-to-human replacements, and several AI-assisted grammar/spelling/next-word suggestions from Google Docs and Apple iOS. The findings suggest students engaged in substantive writing revision and text development rather than simply pasting complete AI-generated essays.
finding.measure: Screen-recorded writing-process edits during an expository writing task

finding.finding_summary: The paper infers student agency, evaluation, and self-directed decision-making from the editing patterns, but it does not directly measure motivation, engagement, or self-regulation with a survey or scale. The authors interpret the prevalence of insertions, deletions, replacements, and planning behaviors as evidence that students were actively managing the writing process and maintaining agency in machine-in-the-loop writing.
finding.measure: Observed planning/editing behaviors in screen recordings and case studies

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines planning, drafting, revising, and evaluation as writing-process behaviors, making it substantively about metacognitive and strategic writing processes. Four patterns emerged: planning with top-down drafting/revising (n=1), top-down without planning (n=6), planning with bottom-up drafting/revising (n=13), and bottom-up without planning (n=3). These patterns show that students used different levels of planning and revision strategy when composing with AI, but no comparative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Planning, drafting, revising, and AI-text editing patterns

finding.finding_summary: The paper comments on the intensity and time involved in machine-in-the-loop writing, noting that the 25 recordings totaled 10 hours and 34 seconds with an average length of 24 minutes. However, it does not evaluate productivity, time savings, or workload against a comparison condition. The evidence suggests AI-assisted composing can involve extensive editing work, but no efficiency advantage or disadvantage was quantified.
finding.measure: Screen-recording runtime and editing volume during writing task

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of AI and Peer Feedback on Research Writing Skills: A Study Using the CGScholar Platform Among Kazakhstani Scholars
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether familiarity with AI tools and experience with peer feedback are associated with scholars’ openness to revising research writing on the CGScholar platform. The central question is not whether AI feedback improves writing scores directly, but whether participants’ prior exposure to AI and peer review relates to their receptiveness to feedback and expectations about revision support.

The study was conducted with 36 Kazakhstani female scholars enrolled in a scientific internship at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Over a semester-long course, participants experienced AI-generated feedback and peer feedback on research drafts within CGScholar, but the reported data come from a preliminary bilingual survey (English/Russian) administered before full engagement with the feedback cycles. The survey measured familiarity with AI, familiarity with peer feedback, openness to feedback, and research writing experience; the analysis used descriptive statistics and correlations.

Findings showed low familiarity with AI tools (mean 1.92/5) and moderate familiarity with peer feedback (mean 3.67/5), while openness to feedback was relatively high (mean 3.83/5). The main inferential results were correlations: familiarity with AI tools was moderately positively correlated with openness to making changes based on feedback (r=0.35), research writing experience was strongly positively correlated with expectations for peer feedback (r=0.68), and familiarity with AI tools was very strongly positively correlated with expectations for peer feedback on research methodology (r=0.82). The paper concludes that AI and peer feedback may be complementary in academic writing, but it does not provide post-intervention writing outcome data or causal evidence of writing improvement.

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on research writing processes and attitudes toward revising academic text rather than direct writing-performance gains. Among 36 Kazakhstani scholars, familiarity with AI tools was moderately positively correlated with openness to making changes based on feedback (r=0.35), and familiarity with AI tools was very strongly correlated with expectations for peer feedback on research methodology (r=0.82). No post-feedback writing-quality scores, revision-quality scores, or pre/post writing comparisons were reported.
finding.measure: Survey measures of familiarity with AI, openness to feedback, and expectations for peer feedback in research writing

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported generally high openness to feedback (mean=3.83 on a 5-point scale), suggesting receptiveness to incorporating suggestions into their research writing. The only reported inferential result tied to this outcome was a moderate positive correlation between AI familiarity and openness to making changes based on feedback (r=0.35), indicating that greater AI familiarity was associated with greater willingness to revise.
finding.measure: Openness to feedback survey scale; correlation with AI familiarity

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively discusses collaborative feedback processes and how scholars value peer input, especially for research methodology and higher-order revision. Research writing experience was strongly positively correlated with expectations for peer feedback (r=0.68), and AI familiarity was very strongly correlated with expectations for peer feedback on methodology (r=0.82), implying recognition of peer review as a support for analytical and revision-oriented skills.
finding.measure: Survey measures of research writing experience and expectations for peer feedback

paper_profiles.title: From Crafting Text to Crafting Thought: Grounding AI Writing Support to Writing Center Pedagogy
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how AI writing tools can be designed to support writing processes without replacing writers’ voices or agency. The authors ground their approach in writing center pedagogy, which emphasizes writer-centered, process-oriented, and collaborative support rather than direct text production.

The paper has two main empirical components. First, the authors conducted semi-structured interviews with 10 writing center tutors to translate writing-center practices into seven design guidelines for AI writing support. Second, they built Writor, a prototype LLM-based writing assistant that provides non-directive, goal-oriented feedback instead of copyable text, and evaluated it with 30 expert reviewers (writing instructors, tutors, and AI researchers) through surveys and follow-up interviews. The expert review found that participants generally saw Writor as aligned with writing center pedagogy, especially for positive tone, confidence-building praise, and encouraging reflection through questions.

Overall, the study concludes that AI writing assistants can be designed to support revision, reflection, and dialogue rather than direct generation. However, the evidence is limited to expert perceptions and internal audits rather than student learning outcomes, so the paper does not test whether the system improves writing quality in high school or other learner populations. Its main contribution is a pedagogical framework and prototype design, not an efficacy trial.

finding.finding_summary: Experts generally rated Writor’s feedback as pedagogically sound and aligned with writing improvement goals, especially for positive tone, confidence-building praise, and prompting reflection. In the internal audit, critique feedback was judged accurate, non-directive, and appropriately mapped to higher-order concerns at very high rates (generally >=96%), but this was not a student outcome study and did not measure actual writing gains.
finding.measure: Expert survey ratings; internal audit of generated goals, critiques, and praise
finding.study_size: n=30 expert reviewers; internal audit across 4 texts (24 goals, 24 topic identifications, 60 critiques, 36 praises)

finding.finding_summary: Participants consistently perceived the tool’s feedback as encouraging and confidence-building. The paper reports that high agreement ratings were observed for positive tone and boosted confidence, and interviewees frequently said the praise and balanced critique helped writers feel more confident and less reliant on shortcuts.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey items on feedback tone/helpfulness/confidence; interview themes on encouragement

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed and perceived to support reflection, critical thinking, and metacognitive revision rather than direct copying. Experts endorsed the question-based, non-directive feedback as prompting deeper thinking about how to revise, and several noted that it could discourage shortcuts while encouraging rhetorical thinking.
finding.measure: Expert survey responses and interviews on reflection, critical thinking, and revision process

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests Writor could help with organization, planning, outlining, and getting started on revisions, which experts viewed as useful process support. However, no direct productivity or time-saving outcome was measured; the evidence is limited to perceptions that the tool could be helpful in tutoring contexts and revision workflows.
finding.measure: Expert perceptions of usefulness for planning, outlining, and revision support

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Effects of Generative AI Assistance on Writing Self-efficacy
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study asks whether different configurations of generative AI assistance affect students’ writing self-efficacy during argumentative writing. The authors motivate the study with concerns that while AI tools such as ChatGPT may support writing performance and efficiency, they may also reduce learner agency, ownership, and independent effort depending on how they are used.

Using a 2 × 2 between-subjects experimental design, the study compared four conditions: no AI, ideation-only AI, sentence-level AI, and full-process AI. Korean undergraduates (final analytic sample n=13) completed two argumentative writing tasks and rated their writing self-efficacy after each task on a 0–100 scale. The study focused on whether AI support at idea generation, sentence construction, or both would shape self-efficacy levels and change over time.

Results were exploratory rather than confirmatory because of the small sample. Full AI showed the highest average self-efficacy (M=82.2, SD=6.4), ideation AI also performed well (M=80.1, SD=16.1), sentence AI was moderate (M=76.6, SD=7.2), and no AI was lowest (M=61.8, SD=24.0). Pairwise standardized effects favored AI over no AI (e.g., full AI vs no AI g=1.23, 95% CI [-0.60, 3.07]), but confidence intervals all crossed zero. Over time, ideation AI showed the largest positive change (ΔM=+11.1), full AI was stable (ΔM=+0.5), no AI slightly increased (ΔM=+1.3), and sentence AI declined for all five participants (ΔM=-5.7), suggesting that sentence-level feedback may undermine confidence. The authors conclude that where AI intervenes in the writing process matters more than whether AI is used, and that ideation support may better preserve agency than sentence-level or full-process assistance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central outcome was writing self-efficacy, measured with a 0–100 scale administered after each of two writing tasks. Across n=13 undergraduates, mean self-efficacy was highest in the Full AI condition (M=82.2, SD=6.4) and Ideation AI (M=80.1, SD=16.1), intermediate in Sentence AI (M=76.6, SD=7.2), and lowest in No AI (M=61.8, SD=24.0). Trajectories differed by condition: Ideation AI increased most (ΔM=+11.1), Sentence AI declined for all five participants (ΔM=-5.7), Full AI stayed nearly flat (ΔM=+0.5), and No AI rose slightly (ΔM=+1.3).
finding.measure: Writing self-efficacy ratings (0–100 scale)
finding.std_deviation: Full AI SD=6.4; Ideation AI SD=16.1; Sentence AI SD=7.2; No AI SD=24.0

finding.finding_summary: Although not the primary endpoint, the study repeatedly interprets results in terms of learner agency, ownership, and self-regulated control over the writing process. Qualitative observations suggested Ideation AI preserved independent language use and process ownership, while Full AI was associated with reduced attachment and sense of ownership, and Sentence AI may have induced downward comparison and diminished confidence over repeated exposure. These findings are exploratory and based on brief reflections rather than formal coding.
finding.measure: Post-task reflections, interaction logs, and self-efficacy items related to independent resolution, personal writing style, and process management

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how four secondary-school EFL students in Hong Kong used ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots to complete a blog-writing task for the first time. Rather than evaluating writing outcomes directly, the study focuses on the content, sequencing, and variety of prompts students entered, using iPad screen recordings and the students’ completed Google Docs writing as supporting context.

The authors identify six distinct prompt types, including auto-complete, natural language instruction, search-engine style prompts, greetings, questions, and chatbot-suggested follow-ups, plus several more sophisticated combinations of these elements. Across the four cases, students used different prompt-engineering pathways and mostly learned through trial and error, often making small modifications to prompts or repeating prompts across chatbots. The paper concludes that secondary EFL students are inexperienced prompt engineers and would likely benefit from explicit prompt-engineering instruction to better leverage chatbots for writing support.

The study does not compare ChatGPT against standard instruction, teacher feedback, peer review, or non-AI digital tools on writing quality or other performance outcomes. It is a qualitative case study about prompting behavior and machine-in-the-loop writing processes, with a small sample of four students and no reported statistical effects.

finding.finding_summary: The central finding is that the four secondary students developed different prompt-engineering pathways through a trial-and-error process, showing some learning in how to craft prompts but also clear limits in sophistication. Across 36 coded turns, students used six prompt types and occasionally refined prompts by making minor word changes or combining input exemplars with instructions and questions; however, no student used all prompt types, and several prompt types appeared only once, indicating uneven development of this durable skill.
finding.measure: Content analysis of prompt types, prompt sequencing, and prompt-pathway patterns from screen recordings

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests students engaged in exploratory, trial-and-error use of chatbots, which is consistent with active engagement and persistence while completing the writing task. At the same time, the authors note that students did not receive prompt-engineering instruction and often appeared to be experimenting without a clear strategy, so the evidence is descriptive rather than a measured improvement in engagement or self-regulation.
finding.measure: Observed prompting behavior during a timed writing task

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on writing a blog entry, but it does not directly measure writing quality, grammar, vocabulary, organization, or revision quality with a rubric or comparison condition. The completed texts show students used AI-generated content to support composition, yet the paper only reports that students were able to finish the writing task and discusses the potential for chatbot use to support higher-quality writing in principle.
finding.measure: Completed blog entries and their relation to prompt pathways; no formal writing-quality scoring reported

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Tools on Student Writing Development: A Case Study From The CGScholar AI Helper Project
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This case study examines whether a newly developed AI writing feedback tool, CGScholar AI Helper, can support high school students’ writing development in English Language Arts. The paper addresses a practical implementation question: how customized, rubric-aligned AI feedback might help struggling writers revise a short comparative writing assignment based on assigned readings.

The intervention was a mediated AI feedback workflow embedded in the CGScholar platform. Six 11th-grade students in one U.S. public high school wrote an initial 200-word response, received real-time AI feedback aligned to the teacher’s rubric and reading materials, revised, and then received a second round of AI feedback before final teacher evaluation. The study used qualitative evidence from student drafts, focus group comments, teacher post-survey responses, and researcher observations.

Findings indicate that the AI Helper generally supported revision and writing development. Five of six students improved on at least one rubric criterion, and one student improved on three criteria. Improvements were seen most clearly in compare/contrast, composing defensible claims, analyzing text, and introducing/connecting evidence. Students and the teacher described the feedback as helpful, direct, specific, actionable, and encouraging, though they also noted that some AI feedback was too long and linguistically complex. Because the study is a small qualitative case study without a comparison group, it provides suggestive evidence of positive writing-support effects rather than causal estimates.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative case study of six 11th-grade students, CGScholar AI Helper was associated with improved writing performance on rubric-based criteria after revision. Five of six students improved in at least one criterion, and one student improved in three criteria; gains were observed in compare/contrast, composing defensible claims, analyze, and introduce/connect evidence, with several rubric scores rising from 0 or 1 to 2, or from 2 to 3.
finding.measure: Teacher-aligned rubric scores on a 0-4 scale for a comparative writing assignment (compare/contrast, identify, compose, introduce/connect, support evidence, analyze)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the AI feedback was helpful and motivating, and the teacher said it encouraged revision, which is often difficult for students. Focus group comments indicated that students valued having actionable guidance to revisit and fix their work, suggesting improved engagement with the revision process rather than just the final product.
finding.measure: Student focus group feedback and teacher post-survey perceptions of revision motivation/engagement

paper_profiles.title: Exploring AI-Generated Text in Student Writing: How Does AI Help?
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school students (Hong Kong EFL students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary school students use AI-generated text when composing stories and whether different patterns of AI use relate to writing quality. The authors are motivated by a gap in the literature on machine-in-the-loop writing, especially for K-12 learners, and ask how AI-generated text is embedded into compositions and how it contributes to human-rated writing outcomes.

The study was conducted with 23 Hong Kong secondary school students from two schools. Students attended workshops on building and using open-source AI-NLG tools (e.g., GPT2/Hugging Face models) and then wrote short stories in a 45-minute machine-in-the-loop task, with both their own words and AI-generated text appearing in the final compositions. The researchers manually coded the amount and type of AI-generated text, scored stories on content, language, organization, and AI-word usage, and then used multiple linear regression and clustering analyses to examine associations between AI-use patterns and story quality.

The main finding is that writing quality was positively associated with both the amount of human-written text and the amount of AI-generated text, with stronger associations for human words but significant contributions from AI words as well. The study also found substantial variation in students’ AI-use strategies: more proficient writers tended to use less AI text overall while editing it more effectively, whereas less proficient writers sometimes used more AI text but did not necessarily achieve higher writing quality. The authors conclude that AI-generated text can support writing, especially language quality for weaker writers, but it does not reliably improve all students’ writing and depends on students’ editing skill and writing competence.

finding.finding_summary: This correlational study found that both human words and AI-generated words significantly contributed to story quality in 23 Hong Kong secondary school EFL students’ stories. In multiple linear regression, the grand total writing score and the C/L/O sub-scores were strongly positively related to human words (partial correlations 0.907-0.951) and moderately positively related to AI words (partial correlations 0.49-0.586), suggesting that AI text could support higher-quality writing but did not uniformly improve all compositions.
finding.measure: Expert ratings of story content, language, organization, CLO score, AI-words score, and grand total score; counts of AI chunks/words and human words
finding.std_deviation: C=1.8; L=1.42; O=1.6; CLO=4.74; AI words=1.84; grand total=5.94

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure motivation or self-regulation with a scale, but it does infer variation in students’ strategic use of AI-generated text and editing behaviors. Cluster analyses and descriptive results suggest that more proficient students were better able to regulate and strategically edit AI output, whereas less competent students often lacked effective strategies for using AI text productively.
finding.measure: Observed patterns of AI-text selection, editing, and integration into stories; cluster membership based on AI-use and scoring patterns

paper_profiles.title: Annotation and Classification of Evidence and Reasoning Revisions in Argumentative Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core problem in automated writing evaluation (AWE): whether students actually revise in response to feedback in ways that improve writing quality. The authors argue that prior revision research has focused on broad edit types (e.g., surface vs. content) rather than on whether revisions are desirable in relation to the feedback students receive.

To address this, they develop the RER (Revision of Evidence use and Reasoning) annotation scheme for sentence-level analysis of revision quality in argumentative writing. The scheme distinguishes desirable and undesirable revisions of evidence use (e.g., relevant, irrelevant, repeat evidence, non-text-based, minimal) and reasoning (e.g., linked claim-evidence, not linked, paraphrase, generic, commentary, minimal). They apply it to 143 first- and second-draft argumentative essays written by 5th- and 6th-grade students using the eRevise AWE system, which provides feedback about using evidence and explaining reasoning.

The study is primarily a descriptive and correlational analysis of revision behavior, reliability of the annotation scheme, and prediction of a holistic improvement score that reflects whether Draft 2 improved in line with feedback. The authors find substantial to excellent inter-rater reliability, and they report that desirable revisions such as adding relevant evidence and especially adding reasoning that links evidence to the claim are positively associated with improvement scores. They also show a simple logistic regression classifier can identify relevant evidence revisions above a majority baseline, suggesting the scheme could support future automated feedback on revision quality.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies revision quality in argumentative writing, using a holistic improvement score for how much Draft 2 improved in evidence use and reasoning in response to AWE feedback. In the 143-essay corpus, the total number of reasoning revisions correlated with improvement score (r=.30), and the total number of evidence-related revisions was weaker and not significant overall (r=.15), but adding relevant evidence (r=.25) and adding reasoning that linked evidence to the claim (LCE; r=.45) were positively associated with higher improvement scores.
finding.measure: Holistic essay improvement score for alignment with feedback on evidence use and reasoning; sentence-level revision categories in argumentative essays
finding.effect_size: r=.30 (reasoning total), r=.15 (evidence total), r=.25 (add relevant evidence), r=.45 (add LCE)

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively examines reasoning quality and argumentative revision quality, which overlap with higher-order writing-related durable skills such as analysis and metacognitive revision. Desirable reasoning revisions—especially adding explanations that linked evidence to claims—were associated with stronger improvement scores, while generic or not-linked reasoning was not meaningfully related.
finding.measure: Sentence-level reasoning revision categories (linked claim-evidence, paraphrase, generic, not-LCE, commentary) and holistic improvement score
finding.effect_size: r=.41 for total LCE revisions; r=.22 for add paraphrase; ANOVA showed LCE differed by improvement score level

finding.finding_summary: Although not an educator-workload study, the paper directly evaluates an automated classifier intended to support efficient AWE feedback by detecting relevant evidence revisions. In 10-fold cross-validation on 386 evidence revisions, logistic regression outperformed a majority baseline on precision, recall, and F1 (precision=.615, recall=.622, F1=.594), indicating the scheme is feasible for automating sentence-level revision detection.
finding.measure: Binary classification performance for identifying 'Relevant' evidence revisions in AWE feedback analysis

paper_profiles.title: eRevise: Using Natural Language Processing to Provide Formative Feedback on Text Evidence Usage in Student Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents eRevise, a web-based automated writing evaluation (AWE) system that uses NLP and rubric-based automated essay scoring to provide formative feedback on students’ use of text evidence in response-to-text writing. The system analyzes a first draft, selects two feedback messages from a small set of prewritten prompts, and then supports revision in a second class period.

The evaluation was a first classroom deployment in seven grade 5–6 classrooms in rural Louisiana, with 143 students completing the full workflow. The authors tested whether students improved on the Evidence dimension of an analytic writing rubric and on related NLP features that approximate evidence quantity and evidence specificity/relevance. Results showed small positive gains from first to second drafts on the human-scored Evidence rubric and significant improvements on the NLP evidence features, but no significant gains on the other RTA dimensions.

Overall, the study suggests that adaptive automated feedback can help upper-elementary students revise their writing to include more and better text evidence, especially for students whose drafts initially show weaker evidence use. The paper also frames eRevise as a formative tool aimed at reducing teacher workload while improving students’ evidence-based writing.

finding.finding_summary: In a deployment with 143 grade 5-6 students across 7 classrooms, human-scored Evidence rubric scores improved from the first draft (M=2.62, SD=0.95) to the second draft (M=2.72, SD=0.92) after students received eRevise formative feedback and revised their essays. The paired t-test was trending toward significance (p≤0.08), indicating a small positive effect on writing quality for the evidence dimension.
finding.measure: Human-scored RTA Evidence rubric score; NLP-based evidence quantity/relevance features (NPE, SPC Total Merged)
finding.std_deviation: First draft SD=0.95; second draft SD=0.92

finding.finding_summary: The system is explicitly designed to automate formative feedback selection and reduce teacher burden by using NLP to score drafts and deliver targeted revision feedback without requiring individualized human feedback. However, the paper does not report direct empirical measures of teacher time, workload, or productivity gains in this deployment, so the evidence is conceptual rather than outcome-based.
finding.measure: System design / intended teacher workload reduction; no direct efficiency metric reported

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Primary to professional development (broad education populations, including secondary/high school)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention experimentally, the authors synthesize early literature and provide a conceptual overview of how LLMs might be used by students and teachers for content generation, feedback, assessment, tutoring, writing support, and administrative tasks.

The paper discusses applications across educational levels, including primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning, with specific examples for middle and high school writing, language learning, and teacher feedback. It argues that LLMs could support personalized learning and teacher efficiency, but emphasizes that educational use must be paired with human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, and domain-appropriate pedagogy.

A major contribution of the paper is its discussion of risks and mitigation strategies. The authors highlight concerns about bias, plagiarism, misuse, overreliance by students and teachers, difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from student-generated work, data privacy, and unfair access. They recommend safeguards such as explicit policies, transparency, human review, verification with authoritative sources, training for educators and students, and curricula that promote critical evaluation rather than substitution of independent work.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support reading and writing development by suggesting grammatical corrections, generating summaries, outlines, and feedback, and helping with research and writing tasks for students and teachers. At the same time, it warns that reliance on generated text can contribute to plagiarism, weaker independent writing, and difficulty distinguishing student-authored from machine-authored work; no empirical effect size is reported because this is a position paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally discusses critical thinking, fact-checking, problem-solving, and independent inquiry as skills that may be strengthened or undermined by LLM use. It warns that learners may over-rely on the model, which could reduce their motivation to investigate, question, and reason independently, and recommends integrating critical thinking and verification activities into curricula.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by helping with lesson planning, generating materials, giving feedback, and semi-automating grading and plagiarism checking. It cites examples such as automated feedback and grading-effort reduction of up to 85% in prior studies, but does not present new original empirical data of its own.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / grading effort / feedback generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on governance, policy, and institutional safeguards for responsible educational use of LLMs. It discusses copyright, privacy, fairness, access, bans on ChatGPT in schools, and the need for curricula, institutional guidelines, oversight, and fact-checking protocols to prevent misuse and inequity.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks what it means for higher education, especially assessment, learning, and teaching. The authors provide a descriptive history of OpenAI and ChatGPT, review early academic and practitioner commentary, and conduct their own hands-on experimentation with the tool to probe its strengths, limitations, and risks.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it is a conceptual and exploratory analysis of a new AI writing assistant in the context of higher education. The authors test ChatGPT on explanation, statistics, essay generation, and Chinese composition prompts, and they argue that the system can produce fluent text quickly but remains unreliable, especially for higher-order thinking, accurate referencing, and non-English writing. They also discuss broader risks such as plagiarism, academic integrity, weak factual accuracy, and the possibility that students may outsource writing tasks to AI.

A major contribution of the paper is its discussion of how institutions and instructors might respond. The authors recommend moving away from traditional essay-only assessment, using more in-class or oral tasks, designing assessments that emphasize critical thinking and creativity, and adapting policies and pedagogy to account for AI-generated text. They also situate ChatGPT within the broader AIEd ecosystem, comparing it with existing automated writing evaluation and feedback tools such as Grammarly and Wordtune.

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that ChatGPT can generate fluent prose quickly and can help with basic explanatory writing, but it performs poorly on higher-order writing tasks. In the authors’ prompt tests, ChatGPT produced an essay of about 500 words instead of the requested 2000 words, lacked in-text citations and credible references, and generated a weak Chinese composition that was grammatically poor and illogical.
finding.measure: Quality of AI-generated writing outputs, including essay length, coherence, citation use, and language quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT threatens writing-related higher-order skills by making it easy for students to outsource writing and by reducing the need for independent drafting, critical analysis, and creativity. The authors explicitly frame the tool as less competent on tasks requiring critical and analytical thinking, and recommend assessment redesign to preserve these skills.
finding.measure: Observed performance on critical/analytical essay prompts and discussion of implications for independent writing and thinking

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that ChatGPT can improve efficiency by producing text rapidly and potentially supporting drafting, brainstorming, and routine writing tasks. However, this efficiency is offset by substantial reliability problems, including generic outputs, factual inaccuracies, and failure to produce complete requested essays or references.
finding.measure: Time-to-response and ease of generating draft text in prompt experiments

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that ChatGPT may disrupt conventional assessment systems and force institutions to reconsider plagiarism policy, assessment design, and guidance for AI use. The authors note that plagiarism detectors were unable to flag ChatGPT text in their tests and recommend policy and instructional changes such as altered assessment formats, more in-class work, and explicit adaptation to AI-generated writing.
finding.measure: Policy and assessment implications discussed alongside plagiarism-checking tests and institutional recommendations

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Prompt in the Classroom to Understand AI Limits: A Pilot Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines whether a short classroom AI literacy workshop can help secondary students better understand the limitations of ChatGPT and learn basic prompting strategies. The authors argue that many users, including adolescents, overestimate what large language models can do and may trust them too readily, despite issues such as hallucinations, limited instruction-following, and reasoning constraints.

The intervention was delivered in a high school in Palermo, Italy with 21 students ages 16-18 during a two-hour workshop. Students first received a short presentation on AI, LLMs, and human vs. machine intelligence, then completed a ChatGPT activity in which they tried to get the model to act as a personal teacher on democracy using a structured set of instructions. After discussing ChatGPT’s limitations, they were introduced to prompting techniques and repeated the task with a second prompt, allowing comparison of interactions before and after prompting guidance.

Results from pre/post questionnaires and open-ended responses suggest that the workshop reduced students’ perceived realistic and identity threat from AI, improved their evaluations of ChatGPT interactions, and increased awareness of the model’s limitations. Students still noted weaknesses such as repetitiveness, limited human-likeness, and the need to refine prompts repeatedly, but they also reported that prompting made the interaction clearer and better. The paper concludes that hands-on AI literacy activities can help adolescents develop more critical and informed attitudes toward generative AI, while also showing the need for larger studies and more refined measures of LLM interaction.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention reduced students’ negative feelings toward AI and increased positive emotions after interacting with ChatGPT. In the post-intervention survey, participants (n=21) reported significantly higher positive than negative emotions (mPositive=3.48, SD=1.79 vs. mNegative=1.35, SD=0.91, p<0.05), and the workshop also reduced perceived realistic and identity threat from AI (n=20; realistic threat mPre=4.17 to mPost=3.73; identity threat mPre=4.08 to mPost=3.57).
finding.measure: Self-reported discrete emotions; perceived realistic threat; perceived identity threat

finding.finding_summary: The workshop improved students’ understanding of AI limits and their ability to refine prompts, but it also revealed repeated difficulties in getting ChatGPT to follow complex instructions. Students reported that the second interaction after prompting instruction was better, clearer, and more natural (means: better 2.45, SD=1.19; clearer 5.25, SD=1.11; more natural 4.55, SD=1.61), yet open-ended responses described repetitiveness and the need to restate requests multiple times.
finding.measure: Perceived interaction quality, perceived improvement after prompting, open-ended reflections on prompt refinement and model limitations

finding.finding_summary: The classroom activity used ChatGPT to teach a history/civics topic (democracy) and showed that students could use the system to generate educational explanations, but they also encountered limitations in accuracy, repetition, and instruction-following. The paper reports an internal trial to verify outputs for accuracy and notes that students often had to repeat or rephrase prompts to get acceptable answers, with some describing the outputs as overly encyclopedic or not what they wanted.
finding.measure: ChatGPT-supported educational conversation task on democracy; qualitative feedback on content quality and usefulness

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived ChatGPT as useful for saving time and helping with tasks, suggesting potential productivity benefits in classroom use. In open-ended responses, one theme emphasized practicality and timing, and a participant noted that the tool could be useful for “practicality and timing”; however, the study does not report objective efficiency gains or task completion times.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness/practicality in open-ended responses

paper_profiles.title: From Guidelines to Governance: A Study of AI Policies in Education
paper_profiles.population: High School and Higher Education Administrators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the current policy landscape for generative AI in education, with a focus on how high school principals and higher education provosts in the United States are responding to tools such as ChatGPT. The authors ask what policies currently exist, what those policies cover, and what administrators think future AI governance should address. The study is motivated by concerns that schools are adopting generative AI faster than they are developing ethical and practical guidance for its use.

The authors surveyed 102 complete responses from educational administrators across five U.S. states (Arkansas, Massachusetts, New Mexico, Utah, and Washington). The survey included closed-ended questions on policy existence, adequacy, and policy components, as well as free-response items about needed policy features and concerns. The results show a substantial policy gap: many institutions, especially high schools, either have no AI policy or are not working on one. Where policies exist, they most often mention plagiarism, but less often address student privacy, bias mitigation, or algorithmic transparency.

Administrators overwhelmingly agreed that AI policies are necessary, mainly to support ethical use, student safety, and plagiarism prevention. They also favored flexible, iterative, and collaborative policy development involving school administrators, teachers, students, and other stakeholders. The paper concludes that generative AI governance in education is still nascent and that existing policies are often too generic to handle the specific risks of LLMs. The authors recommend adaptable policy frameworks, professional development, and model guidelines from successful schools or districts, while also noting caution about AI-detection tools and their reliability.

finding.finding_summary: Among 102 complete survey responses from high school principals and higher education provosts, the study found a substantial governance gap around generative AI. Over 80% of higher education institutions reported active policy development, while only about 50% of high schools were working on policies and about 45% of high schools had no policy and no plans to develop one; current policies were often judged inadequate and rarely named specific tools like ChatGPT or Bard.
finding.measure: Survey responses on AI policy status, adequacy, and policy coverage

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency was not a central outcome, but the paper reports that administrators saw policy support needs including professional development, consultation, and model guidelines, rather than a demonstrated productivity change. The study did not measure time savings or workload outcomes directly; it only notes that some policy focus areas included reducing teacher workload as a lower-priority concern.
finding.measure: Survey responses on policy support/resources and policy focus areas

paper_profiles.title: Who wrote this? Detecting artificial intelligence-generated text from human-written text
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether human evaluators can distinguish between human-written text and AI-generated text, motivated by concerns about academic integrity in postsecondary education. The authors frame GenAI as a growing challenge for authorship detection, plagiarism prevention, and assessment validity, especially as AI-written prose becomes more human-like.

The study used a survey-based detection task with 135 participants affiliated with an Ontario university’s faculty of education. Participants were shown short passages drawn from three sources: researcher-written, GPT-2-generated, and internet-copied text, and asked to identify each passage’s authorship, rate its writing quality, and indicate whether it was internet-sourced. The core finding was that participants identified human-written passages much better than AI-generated ones: human text was correctly identified 63%-66.7% of the time, while AI text was correctly identified only 24%-27% of the time. The authors argue that this low detection accuracy, combined with the limitations of automated tools and the growth of GenAI, creates serious risks for academic integrity and calls for improved AI literacy, assessment redesign, and broader institutional responses.

The paper is primarily concerned with postsecondary academic integrity rather than direct classroom intervention. It recommends several safeguards, including training for educators and markers, stronger AI literacy for educators/administrators/students, ongoing academic integrity workshops, and rethinking assessments so that AI output may be used only as an intermediary step rather than the final student artifact. It also cautions against relying solely on either human judgment or current automated detectors, noting false positives/negatives, privacy concerns, and the need for further larger-scale research.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that GenAI text is difficult for humans to detect, with participants correctly identifying AI-generated passages only 24% of the time (sensitivity/TPR=0.24; n=228 passage-level judgments) and correctly identifying human-written passages 63%-66.7% of the time. The authors argue this creates major institutional risks for academic integrity, authorship verification, assessment validity, and policy enforcement, and they recommend reassessing assessment design, training educators, and improving AI literacy rather than relying on detection alone.
finding.measure: Human ability to identify authorship of passages; diagnostic metrics for AI detection and human detection

finding.finding_summary: Although writing quality itself was not experimentally improved or compared as a student learning outcome, the paper directly studies written composition detection and argues that GenAI can produce human-like prose that challenges writing assessment. Participants were asked to judge writing level and authorship of short compositions, and the study found AI-written passages were often mistaken for human writing (24% correct AI detection), implying that writing products generated by AI can mask authorship and complicate evaluation of student writing development.
finding.measure: Passage authorship detection; writing-level ratings of short compositions
finding.study_size: n=135 participants; 6 passages total (2 AI, 4 human)

paper_profiles.title: Editorial: Generative AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial introduces a Frontiers Research Topic on generative AI in education and summarizes the 11 papers included in the volume. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it frames the broader research landscape around generative AI uses such as personalized feedback, AI tutors, assessment generation, emotional support, career mentoring, and integrity-oriented integration in education.

Across the summarized papers, the editorial highlights both opportunities and risks. It notes potential benefits such as individualized content, dynamic feedback, engagement, and support for learner needs, while also flagging key challenges including answer accuracy, interpretability, ethical use, privacy, fairness, algorithmic bias, and concerns about AI deceiving students. The piece is especially relevant as a synthesis of early work on responsible integration of generative AI in education, but it does not present original data of its own.

For the sub-question on risks and unintended consequences, the editorial explicitly points to concerns about the accuracy of AI answers, the possibility of deceptive behavior in AI-enhanced robots, and issues such as academic integrity, data privacy, and algorithmic bias. It also mentions the need for human-in-the-loop approaches, ethical guidelines, transparency, and thoughtful implementation as safeguards. However, because this is an editorial summarizing other studies, it offers no direct empirical evidence on dependency, weakened writing development, or writing-assistant-specific outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The editorial argues that generative AI can enrich education and support personalized, responsible learning, but it also emphasizes institutional risks including ethical concerns, privacy, fairness, and algorithmic bias. It recommends safeguards such as ethical guidelines, transparency, human-in-the-loop approaches, and thoughtful implementation, but reports no direct effect sizes or original institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Editorial synthesis of policy, ethics, and implementation considerations across the Research Topic

finding.finding_summary: The editorial summarizes prior papers suggesting generative AI may increase student engagement and support emotional needs, including immediate doubt clarification and more individualized assistance. It also notes that further research is needed on the emotional content of AI responses and on how well AI supports learners' socioemotional needs.
finding.measure: Engagement, emotional content, and socioemotional support discussed across included papers

finding.finding_summary: The editorial highlights generative AI's potential to foster critical thinking and strategic use of AI tools, but also notes limitations such as insufficient accuracy and the need for responsible use. It frames critical thinking as a central instructional goal, especially in the opinion pieces it summarizes, but provides no direct empirical estimate of effect.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and strategic use of AI tools discussed in the summarized opinion papers

finding.finding_summary: Although the editorial is not a primary writing study, it broadly discusses AI support for schoolwork, assessment, and mathematical reasoning. In the schoolwork-related adolescent studies it summarizes, older students used generative AI more frequently and students with greater executive-function challenges found it more useful, while no significant relationship with academic achievement was found.
finding.measure: Use frequency, perceived usefulness for schoolwork, and academic achievement in adolescents

paper_profiles.title: From Guidelines to Governance: A Study of AI Policies in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the current landscape of institutional policies governing generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in education, with a focus on how educational administrators perceive policy needs, coverage, and governance. The authors survey 102 U.S. administrators, including high school principals and higher education provosts, using a mixed-methods instrument with closed-ended questions and free-text responses.

The study finds a pronounced policy gap: most institutions either lack AI-specific guidelines or are still developing them, and high schools are less likely than higher education institutions to have policy work underway. Where policies exist, they commonly address plagiarism but less often cover student privacy, bias mitigation, or algorithmic transparency. Administrators overwhelmingly view AI policies as necessary, mainly to protect student safety and reduce plagiarism risk, and they favor flexible, iterative, multi-stakeholder policy frameworks. The paper also notes caution around AI-detection tools, with many administrators preferring them only as a screening aid rather than as the sole basis for punishment.

finding.finding_summary: The study documents a substantial institutional policy gap around generative AI in education. Among 102 administrators (81 high school, 21 higher education), over 80% of higher education institutions reported active policy development, 5% already had a policy, and 15% had no plans to enact one; in contrast, about 50% of high schools were working on policy and about 45% had no policy and no plan to develop one. Administrators overwhelmingly believed AI policies were necessary, but current policies were often seen as inadequate and insufficiently specific to LLMs like ChatGPT.
finding.measure: Survey responses on policy status, policy adequacy, policy content, and policy necessity

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure learning outcomes directly, but it reports that existing and proposed policies primarily aim to manage academic integrity issues in schoolwork, especially plagiarism. Administrators identified stopping plagiarism as one of the top policy priorities, and plagiarism was the most commonly covered element in current or in-progress AI policies.
finding.measure: Survey responses about policy focus areas and policy components covered

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-5 in Secondary Education: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Student Attitudes, AI Anxiety, and Hallucination-Aware Use
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examines how Greek secondary school students perceive and use ChatGPT-5 in a formal classroom setting, with particular attention to attitudes toward AI, AI-related anxiety, and responses to hallucinated outputs. The paper is explicitly motivated by concerns in the GenAI-in-education literature about inaccuracy, overreliance, academic integrity, and the need for critical AI literacy in K-12 settings.

The intervention involved 109 sixteen-year-old students from three high schools in rural metropolitan Athens participating in an eight-hour experience embedded in the national curriculum course "Technology." Students used ChatGPT-5 across several modalities and tasks, including information seeking, CV generation, document and video summarization, image generation, quiz creation, and age-adapted explanations. Importantly, the researcher also deliberately exposed students to hallucinated responses and asked them to verify incorrect answers, so the study could observe how learners respond to AI error.

Quantitative results showed moderately positive attitudes toward AI overall, but only modest behavioral intention to engage further with AI and moderate anxiety, especially about AI-driven job replacement. Qualitative interview data identified four affordances—knowledge expansion, immediate feedback, familiar interface, and perceived skill development—and three constraints: uncertainty about accuracy, anxiety about AI feedback, and privacy concerns. A key conclusion is that after encountering hallucinations, many students narrowed their use of the chatbot to topics they already knew well and could verify, which the author terms "epistemic safeguarding." The paper argues that exposing secondary students to AI limitations and teaching critical AI literacy can help prevent uncritical reliance on GenAI and support safer educational use.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported moderately positive attitudes toward AI but also non-trivial anxiety, especially about job replacement. On the AIAS (N=109), learning anxiety was modest (M=3.09, SD=1.37) while job-replacement anxiety was higher (M=4.07, SD=1.66); the latter was reflected in items such as fear that AI may make users dependent (M=4.03) or lazier (M=4.46).
finding.measure: SATAI attitudes scale; AIAS learning anxiety and job replacement anxiety scales

finding.finding_summary: The study found evidence that students developed and used critical evaluation and metacognitive strategies after being shown hallucinations. In interviews (n=36), 21 students expressed uncertainty about accuracy, and many said they would restrict future use to topics they already knew so they could verify answers and detect errors, a strategy the author labels epistemic safeguarding.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interviews on perceived affordances/constraints and responses to hallucinated outputs

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived ChatGPT-5 as saving time through immediate feedback and rapid response, particularly for writing-related feedback, document/video summaries, and generating quizzes. In interviews (n=36), 18 students cited immediate feedback as a pedagogical affordance and described it as motivating and time-efficient.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interviews on perceived affordances

finding.finding_summary: The intervention included academic tasks such as CV generation, document/video summarization, quiz generation, and age-adapted explanations, and students perceived ChatGPT-5 as helpful for knowledge expansion. However, the paper’s main academic finding is not subject mastery gains but students’ cautious use after observing hallucinations, with uncertainty about content accuracy identified as a major constraint (21 of 36 interviewees).
finding.measure: Task-based classroom intervention plus interviews on learning affordances and constraints

paper_profiles.title: “How can we learn and use AI at the same time?”: Participatory Design of GenAI with High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school students think about generative AI in education, with particular attention to both benefits and risks. The authors ask how GenAI tools and school policies, designed with students, can address the needs and challenges of high school settings, and what actionable design guidelines educators and developers should follow.

The study used a participatory design workshop with 17 high school students aged 14–17, many of whom had prior experience with text-generation tools such as ChatGPT. Students first brainstormed concerns about GenAI in schoolwork and then worked in small groups to design hypothetical GenAI tools and school policies. The workshop elicited concerns about hallucinations, bias, plagiarism, academic dishonesty, unreliable AI detectors, teacher AI literacy, privacy, equitable access, and over-reliance on AI. Students also proposed mitigations such as source citation and verification, incremental hints instead of direct answers, teacher training, parental consent, and data deletion/limited access rules.

The main conclusion is that students prefer system-level safeguards and transparent, consent-based design over placing the burden solely on users to detect AI errors or misuse. They wanted GenAI to support learning without replacing independent thinking, and they strongly rejected solutions that rely too heavily on detectors or punishment. The paper ends by proposing design guidelines for high-school GenAI EdTech that emphasize transparency, accessibility, academic integrity, and human oversight, while also urging schools and developers to include student voices in policy and product design.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop centered heavily on writing-related risks and uses of GenAI in schoolwork. Students worried that ChatGPT could be used to generate essays and other writing with better grades than work done independently, while also proposing mitigations such as banning GenAI as a legitimate source, requiring source citation, and using AI only for brainstorming or hints. Evidence is qualitative from 17 high school students (n=17); no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student workshop discussions and student-designed school policy proposals about writing assignments, plagiarism, and source use

finding.finding_summary: Students repeatedly raised concerns that overuse of GenAI could erode critical thinking, logic, creativity, and independent problem-solving. At the same time, they valued GenAI as a support for learning if it provided progressive hints, reflection prompts, and opportunities to think for themselves rather than direct answers. Evidence is qualitative from 17 students; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student discussions about balancing AI use with learning, critical thinking, and independence

finding.finding_summary: Students described stress, pressure, and a tendency to use AI as a 'last resort' under heavy workloads and tight deadlines, suggesting over-reliance may be partly driven by emotional strain. They also noted that workshop participation increased their understanding of GenAI and shifted their views, indicating improved AI confidence and awareness, but no quantitative learning gain was measured. Evidence is qualitative with survey reflections from n=17; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Workshop reflections and post-survey responses about feelings toward GenAI and workshop impact

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution of the paper is students’ policy and governance proposals for school and platform regulation. Students advocated for school AI policies, parental consent, teacher oversight, government or library regulation, data deletion rules, and limits on teacher over-reliance on AI detectors, showing strong interest in institutional safeguards. Evidence is qualitative from 17 students; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student-created school policies and discussions of governance, regulation, privacy, and institutional oversight

finding.finding_summary: Students discussed AI’s potential to speed up tasks and support personalized learning, but they also worried that more careful verification, teacher training, and policy constraints would make workflows more time-consuming. One proposed policy required teachers to spend minimum time on feedback and use standardized rubrics to reduce over-reliance on AI, indicating efficiency tradeoffs rather than a clear productivity gain. Evidence is qualitative from n=17; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student discussion of teacher feedback workflows, AI-assisted classroom tasks, and implementation constraints

paper_profiles.title: Approaches to Generative Artificial Intelligence, A Social Justice Perspective
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a social-justice-oriented commentary on the rise of generative AI in education, with a particular emphasis on risks to academic integrity, bias, and inequitable treatment. Rather than evaluating an instructional intervention, it argues that tools like ChatGPT lower barriers to plagiarism, make dishonest writing more accessible and harder to detect, and raise broader concerns about autonomy, privacy, copyright, and equity.

The paper surveys how large language models are built and why their outputs can be biased, highlighting training-data imbalances, harmful content generation, and stereotype reinforcement in AI image tools. It also discusses the risks of AI detectors, especially false positives that may unfairly penalize non-native English writers and ELL students. The author’s main conclusion is that schools should not rely on an arms race of AI detection; instead, educators should remain central in instructional decision-making and reconsider how teaching and assessment should adapt to generative AI in ways that preserve student learning and reduce injustice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI creates substantial institutional risks for schools, especially around academic integrity, equity, privacy, and policy. It does not report original empirical effects; instead, it synthesizes concerns that AI detectors can produce false positives and that schools need stronger guidance and more educator-centered approaches to assessment and regulation.
finding.measure: Not an empirical measure; discussion of academic integrity, AI detection, equity, and policy implications

paper_profiles.title: LLM Chatbots in High School Programming: Exploring Behaviors and Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 41st ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC '26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school students use an LLM chatbot integrated directly into a programming environment and whether a targeted pedagogical intervention can improve the quality of that use. The authors frame the central problem as unproductive help-seeking: students may ask executive, solution-seeking questions that promote dependency and shallow learning rather than instrumental questions that support understanding.

Using a design-based research cycle, the study analyzed interactions from an intervention group (IG, n=18) and a non-equivalent comparison group (CG, n=19) in elective Informatica classes at two Dutch high schools. Students used JELAI, a Jupyter Notebook environment with an embedded LLM tutor (Juno), during classroom programming tasks. The researchers logged all chatbot interactions, code executions, and errors, and related query patterns to midterm and final exam performance.

In the unguided baseline phase, higher overall LLM use correlated negatively with midterm performance, and executive queries were especially strongly associated with lower grades (e.g., ρ = -0.851, p < 0.001). The comparison group did not self-correct over time; engagement declined after initial novelty, and unproductive patterns persisted. After a mid-course intervention that explicitly taught instrumental versus executive help-seeking and prompted students to reflect on their own query patterns, executive queries decreased significantly (W = 15.0, p = 0.036, r = 0.560) and workflows became more productive, but exam scores did not improve significantly. The authors conclude that LLMs can support learning only when embedded in pedagogy that scaffolds productive help-seeking, and they recommend safeguards such as system prompts, adaptive scaffolding, metacognitive prompts, and learner-facing analytics.

finding.finding_summary: The study focused on introductory high school programming performance and found that, in an unguided baseline, higher overall LLM use was negatively correlated with midterm exam scores (ρ = -0.502, p = 0.034; IG n=18). After the intervention, behavior changed but final exam grades did not improve significantly (M=7.56 vs. 7.28, W = 34.0, p = 0.083), suggesting that changing help-seeking strategy alone was insufficient to raise achievement.
finding.measure: Programming exam scores (midterm and final)
finding.study_size: n=18 intervention group; n=19 comparison group

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation of ChatGPT and Microsoft Bing AI Chat Performances on Physics Exams of Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates how well ChatGPT and BingChat answer Vietnamese high school physics exam questions from the National High School Graduation Examination. The authors compare model performance on 200 multiple-choice questions drawn from five illustrative exams spanning 2019–2023, and they stratify questions by difficulty level (knowledge, comprehension, application, and high application). The goal is to assess whether these large language models can serve as useful supports for physics teaching and learning in a Vietnamese context.

The study reports that both models perform below Vietnamese students overall, with BingChat slightly more accurate and ChatGPT somewhat more stable across years. Both models answer knowledge- and comprehension-level questions relatively well but struggle with application and especially high-application problems. The authors conclude that LLMs may help students and teachers through immediate feedback and personalized learning, but they are not yet adequate replacements for human reasoning in physics instruction and require further domain-specific improvement.

Although the paper is centered on physics rather than writing, it explicitly discusses broader educational uses of LLMs, including individualized feedback and classroom support. It does not evaluate writing instruction risks such as dependency, academic integrity, or hallucinations in writing tasks, but it does note limitations in accuracy, reliability, and performance on advanced reasoning items.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT and BingChat answered easier physics items reasonably well but struggled on application and high-application questions. Across 200 multiple-choice questions, ChatGPT averaged 61% and BingChat 66%, both below Vietnamese students overall; performance was over 50% for questions 1–32 for ChatGPT and 1–31 for BingChat, then fell on harder items.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Vietnamese high school physics multiple-choice exam questions, stratified by difficulty level

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support teachers and students by providing immediate feedback, individualized learning experiences, and help with lesson preparation or grading-related tasks.
