However, this is a conceptual implication rather than a measured productivity outcome in the study itself.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Spontaneous Speech-Based Suicide Risk Detection Using Whisper and Large Language Models
paper_profiles.population: Adolescents (ages 10-18), primary and secondary school students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically detecting suicide risk from spontaneous speech in adolescents. The authors argue that early detection could support timely intervention, and they explore whether modern foundation models—Whisper for speech representation and large language models (Baichuan2 and Qwen1.5) for text representation—can improve classification performance on this task.

To study this, the authors collected a Mandarin speech dataset from 47 primary and secondary schools in Guangdong, China. The dataset includes recordings from 1,179 adolescents aged 10 to 18, with MINI-KID clinical assessment used to label suicide risk. The speech data came from self-introduction style interviews and related speaking tasks; the model pipeline transcribed speech, extracted acoustic and textual embeddings, and fused them using concatenation or in-context methods. They compared full-parameter finetuning, LoRA-based parameter-efficient finetuning, and different fusion strategies, as well as prompt variants for the LLMs.

The main finding is that foundation-model-based approaches substantially outperform simple baselines on this suicide-risk classification task. The best ensemble achieved 0.807 accuracy and 0.846 F1 on the test set of 119 students. The authors also find that prompt design and tuning strategy matter: brief task prompts helped finetuned LLMs, APFT often outperformed PEFT for Whisper and Baichuan2, and concatenation fusion generally worked better than in-context fusion. The paper concludes that speech and language foundation models show promising potential for real-world suicide risk detection in adolescent school settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies spontaneous speech processing for suicide-risk detection in adolescents, using speech recordings as the primary input and evaluating acoustic and textual representations. The best ensemble system reached 0.807 accuracy and 0.846 F1 on the 119-student test set, indicating strong classification performance for the speech-based task.
finding.measure: Suicide risk classification accuracy and F1-score from spontaneous speech recordings

paper_profiles.title: MathRobust-LV: Evaluation of Large Language Models’ Robustness to Linguistic Variations in Mathematical Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models remain reliable when high-school mathematics problems are rephrased without changing the underlying math. The authors argue that educational deployments such as tutoring, homework help, and automated assessment require robustness to surface-form variation, because instructors and students often phrase equivalent problems differently.

To test this, the paper introduces MathRobust-LV, a benchmark of 130 seed problems drawn from the MATH dataset and scraped AoPS competition problems at difficulty levels 4 and 5. The authors create 520 variants by preserving numerical structure, symbolic logic, and final answers while changing variables, context, and/or wording; they then evaluate 34 open- and closed-source LLMs in a zero-shot pass@1 setting.

The central finding is that accuracy usually drops under benign linguistic rewordings, especially for smaller models. The weakest models lose around 9-12 percentage points, while many larger models still show smaller but measurable degradation; frontier models such as Gemini-2.5-pro and GPT-5 are comparatively stable. The paper concludes that current benchmark performance alone is insufficient evidence of genuine mathematical reasoning, and that linguistic brittleness remains a practical risk for educational use.

finding.finding_summary: Across 34 models, accuracy generally declined when high-school math problems were minimally reworded while preserving the same numerical structure and answer. The paper reports drops of roughly 2-11 percentage points overall, with smaller models such as OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B dropping 11.52 points and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B dropping 9.59 points; a few models showed small positive changes (e.g., Qwen3-0.6B +3.16 points), but the authors interpret these as not evidence of robustness when baseline accuracy is low.
finding.measure: Pass@1 accuracy on baseline math problems vs. linguistically varied equivalent variants

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that linguistic brittleness poses a deployment risk for tutoring, homework-help, and automated assessment systems because models may fail on equivalent problems phrased differently by instructors or students. It does not evaluate policy interventions directly, but it explicitly recommends robustness testing, broader multilingual evaluation, and future fine-tuning on variant-rich datasets as safeguards.
finding.measure: Observed accuracy degradation under educationally realistic rephrasing; discussion of deployment implications
finding.study_size: n=34 models evaluated for educational deployment relevance

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models and Mathematical Reasoning Failures
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how several state-of-the-art large language models perform on a newly constructed set of 50 high-school-level mathematical word problems. The authors’ central question is not just whether the models get the final answer right, but whether they produce valid reasoning steps; they therefore manually inspect both answers and full solutions for eight models including Mixtral, Llama, Gemini, GPT-4o, o1-preview, o1, o3-mini, and deepseek-r1.

The benchmark problems cover high-school mathematics, especially spatial reasoning, strategy, arithmetic, number patterns, and set/logic tasks. Each problem was posed once to each model and evaluated manually by an experienced teacher. The paper finds that newer reasoning-tuned models generally score better, but all models still make substantial reasoning errors, including unwarranted assumptions, over-reliance on numerical patterns, and failure to respect constraints or physical intuition. In several cases, models produced correct answers with flawed explanations, showing that answer accuracy alone can overstate true reasoning competence.

The paper’s main conclusion is that LLMs can appear strong on mathematical tasks while still failing in important ways that are only visible when the full solution is examined. The authors caution against overestimating model problem-solving ability and argue for evaluating reasoning processes rather than only final outputs. They also note that their results are limited to one-shot prompting and a small, custom problem set focused on selected areas of high-school mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: Across 50 high-school-level math word problems, model performance varied widely: mixtral-8x7B solved 0/50, llama-3.3-70B-versatile 10/50, gpt-4o 14/50, o1-preview 30/50, o1 37/50, o3-mini 40/50, and deepseek-r1 36/50. The paper also reports 21 cases where models gave the correct answer but an incorrect solution, showing that surface accuracy often masked faulty reasoning.
finding.measure: Correct solutions/answers on a 50-item high-school math word-problem benchmark; manual checking of answer and solution quality
finding.study_size: n=50 problems; 8 models; 400 total model responses

paper_profiles.title: SMRC: Aligning Large Language Models with Student Reasoning for Mathematical Error Correction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of using large language models (LLMs) for educational error correction in mathematics, with a focus on aligning model corrections to students’ original reasoning rather than only producing the correct final answer. The authors argue that existing self-correction methods are insufficient for classroom use because they can overwrite students’ valid steps and fail to preserve pedagogically valuable reasoning paths.

To address this, the paper proposes SMRC (Student Mathematical Reasoning Correction), a framework that uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) plus a learned reward model to guide correction along student-like reasoning trajectories. The authors also build MSEB, a benchmark of 158 authentic high-school student solution records in algebra, geometry, matrices, and trigonometry, and define a new metric, Correct Step Retention Rate (CSRR), to measure how well a correction preserves valid student steps.

The paper evaluates SMRC against direct error correction, thought-preserving prompting, Self-Check, and Self-Refine on ProcessBench, MR-GSM8K, and MSEB. Results show that SMRC generally improves the balance between answer accuracy and step retention, especially on MR-GSM8K and MSEB, while highlighting a tradeoff: search-based methods like BFS/DFS can preserve more steps but often reduce answer accuracy. The paper concludes that student-centered correction requires both correctness and fidelity to learners’ reasoning, and it proposes instructional prompting strategies and search-based safeguards to reduce disruptive corrections.

finding.finding_summary: SMRC improved mathematical error correction performance on three benchmark datasets, with the strongest results on MR-GSM8K and MSEB. On MR-GSM8K, SMRC achieved ACC=91.4 and CSRR=94.5 (HM=92.9), and on MSEB it achieved ACC=40.1 and CSRR=73.7 (HM=51.8), outperforming the compared baselines in overall harmonic mean.
finding.measure: Math error-correction accuracy (ACC) and correct step retention rate (CSRR) on mathematical reasoning benchmarks
finding.study_size: n=158 for MSEB; public benchmark sizes not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Exploring EFL Secondary Students’ AI-generated Text Editing While Composition Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how Hong Kong secondary school EFL students edit AI-generated text while completing an expository writing task. The authors ask what kinds of edits students make to AI-generated output and what broader patterns characterize their drafting and revising behavior when writing with generative AI.

The study used an exploratory mixed-methods design centered on screen recordings from 29 students who attended an AI-assisted writing workshop; 25 recordings showed AI-generated text edits and were analyzed. Students were taught prompt engineering and practiced writing with POE chatbots in either a process-based or genre-based instructional approach, then completed a 500-word exam-style article writing task using any combination of self-written and AI-generated content in Google Docs.

The analysis identified 15 edit types across seven categories, including insertions, deletions, replacements, pre-edit formatting, and acceptances of Apple iOS and Google Docs suggestions. The study also found four broader editing patterns based on planning vs. no planning and top-down vs. bottom-up drafting/revising. The authors conclude that students’ interactions with AI-generated text are more cognitively complex than simple copy-paste behavior, but they also note that semi-autonomous suggestions from Google Docs and iOS can unexpectedly shape writing and complicate student agency. The paper argues for explicit instructional approaches to AI-text editing, planning, prompt engineering, and maintaining authorial voice and agency.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines secondary students’ writing processes with AI-generated text during an expository composition task. Among 25 analyzed screen recordings (10 hours total), the authors identified 266 edits across 15 edit types, showing that students frequently inserted, deleted, and replaced AI-generated text rather than simply pasting it unchanged. The paper does not report writing-quality scores or effect sizes, but it documents substantial variation in how students used AI during writing.
finding.measure: Screen-recorded writing edits during an expository article writing task

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that students engaged in planning, evaluation, and revision strategies while interacting with generative AI, indicating metacognitive and strategic writing behaviors. Four editing patterns were identified, combining planning/no planning with top-down/bottom-up drafting and revising, suggesting that students made deliberate process choices rather than using AI passively.
finding.measure: Observed planning and drafting/revising patterns in screen recordings

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure motivation or attitudes directly, but it does discuss student agency and authorial voice as important issues in AI-assisted writing. The authors argue that semi-autonomous AI suggestions can threaten students’ agency over the writing process, while many students in practice appeared to preserve their own control through bottom-up drafting and active editing.
finding.measure: Observed agency-related writing behaviors and authorial-voice concerns in screen recordings

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative case study examines how four secondary-school EFL students used ChatGPT and other proprietary chatbots while completing a timed blog-writing task for the first time. The paper is motivated by the idea that effective use of generative chatbots in writing requires prompt engineering skills, and it asks what kinds of prompt content students use and what patterns emerge across their prompt sequences.

The students, drawn from a Hong Kong secondary school, completed an in-class writing task on iPads using the POE app. Their screen activity was recorded and their prompts were coded into categories such as auto-complete, natural language instruction, questions, greetings, search-engine-like queries, and chatbot-suggested follow-up prompts. The authors then analyzed each student’s prompt engineering pathway as a sequence of turns, comparing differences in prompt type, repetition, and movement across chatbots.

The main finding is that students relied on trial-and-error rather than any formal prompting instruction, and each used a different mix of prompt types to complete the same task. The most common prompts were simple auto-complete prompts and one-shot prompts combining natural language instruction with questions; students often refined prompts by making small wording changes or reusing earlier wording, and some switched between chatbots to test outputs. The authors conclude that students were unsophisticated prompt users who would likely benefit from explicit prompt engineering education in EFL writing classrooms, especially instruction tailored to the task and to individual learner needs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test whether ChatGPT improved writing quality or writing development; instead it documents how four secondary EFL students used chatbot prompts to complete a blog-writing task. Across 36 coded turns (n=4 students), the study describes prompt types and sequencing, but it reports no outcome data on writing scores, writing quality, or independent writing performance.
finding.measure: Prompt content and sequencing during a blog-writing task; completed writing samples were collected but not analyzed for writing quality in the reported findings

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret students’ prompting behavior as evidence of trial-and-error learning, exploration, and some development of more sophisticated prompt engineering strategies. However, this is a descriptive interpretation based on prompt sequences rather than a direct measure of durable skills; the paper does not report effect sizes or standardized assessments of metacognition, critical thinking, or self-regulation.
finding.measure: Observed prompt engineering pathways and prompt-type variation

finding.finding_summary: The study does not evaluate whether chatbots made writing faster or more efficient, but it does report task completion behavior under a 45-minute limit. All four students completed the task, taking 5 to 12 turns each, and the authors describe chatbot use as a trial-and-error process rather than an efficiency gain with quantified productivity outcomes.
finding.measure: Number of prompt turns and task completion within a timed writing task

paper_profiles.title: SKYLENAGE Technical Report: Mathematical Reasoning and Contest-Innovation Benchmarks for Multi-Level Math Evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This technical report introduces SKYLENAGE, a pair of benchmark suites for evaluating large language models on mathematical reasoning. SKYLENAGE-REASONINGMATH is a 100-item structure-aware diagnostic set with metadata on length, numeric density, and symbolic complexity, while SKYLENAGE-MATH is a 150-item contest-style benchmark spanning four academic stages from high school through doctoral level and covering seven math subjects.

The paper’s main question is how well contemporary LLMs separate on harder mathematics tasks once existing benchmarks saturate. The authors evaluate 15 models under a unified prompting and grading protocol, finding that the strongest models separate clearly from mid-tier systems, especially on contest-style and hardest-slice items. Performance drops from high school to doctoral levels, and subject leadership rotates across models, suggesting specialization and the value of subject-aware routing or ensembles.

The report also emphasizes diagnostic limitations of answer-only scoring: some correct answers appear to come from shortcutting or inconsistent reasoning, especially on difficult, structure-heavy items. To address this, the authors propose future process-based scoring using minimal per-item hooks, step validity checks, and verifier agreement. They also describe anti-contamination procedures, canonical answer normalization, and plans for dynamic benchmark variants.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark evaluates mathematical problem solving across 100 reasoning items and 150 contest-style items. The strongest model reached 81% on SKYLENAGE-REASONINGMATH (n=100) and 44.0% on SKYLENAGE-MATH (n=150), while performance dropped from high school to doctoral-level items (26.3% HS vs. 14.1% PhD). The paper also reports strong variation by subject and difficulty, indicating that current LLMs are highly sensitive to numeric density, symbolic complexity, and grade-band difficulty.
finding.measure: Accuracy on mathematics benchmarks (overall, subject-wise, and difficulty-band accuracy)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines ChatGPT as an emerging AI text generator and its implications for higher education, especially assessment, learning, and teaching. The authors combine a desktop literature review with hands-on experimentation using ChatGPT to assess its capabilities, limitations, and likely effects on academic work. They situate ChatGPT within the broader history of educational technology and artificial intelligence in education (AIEd), arguing that the tool is both impressive and deeply limited.

A major focus of the paper is the risk ChatGPT poses to conventional written assessment. The authors report that ChatGPT can generate passable prose quickly, may evade plagiarism detectors, and can be used to rewrite text in ways that reduce originality scores. At the same time, their experiments show weaknesses in factual accuracy, depth, referencing, and performance on higher-order writing tasks, including generic or fabricated content and poor results in Chinese writing. The paper also discusses opportunities for instructional redesign, such as in-class work, oral presentations, flipped learning, and more robust assessment strategies that emphasize critical thinking and authentic performance.

The paper is primarily a conceptual and illustrative review rather than an empirical study of student outcomes. Its recommendations are aimed at teachers and institutions, including adapting assessment practices, educating students about appropriate use, and not relying on simplistic blacklist approaches. It concludes that while ChatGPT is unlikely to end education as we know it, it will require institutions to rethink writing instruction, academic integrity, and assessment design.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that ChatGPT can rapidly generate coherent text and draft essays, but its writing quality is uneven and often weak for higher-order academic writing. In the authors’ experiments, ChatGPT produced an approximately 500-word essay instead of the requested 2000 words, lacked breadth and depth, had no reliable in-text or end-of-text citations, and sometimes invented bogus references; it also produced a grammatically poor Chinese composition.
finding.measure: Quality of AI-generated writing output, including essay length, coherence, depth, citation accuracy, and language quality

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that ChatGPT may weaken students’ independent writing development by enabling outsourcing of assignments and reducing the need for sustained analytical effort. The authors specifically note concern that students could rely on ChatGPT to produce passable prose in seconds, potentially undermining critical and analytical thinking in writing tasks.
finding.measure: Observed limitations and educational implications of AI-assisted writing for critical/analytical writing tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that ChatGPT can improve task efficiency by generating text, explanations, and draft responses very quickly, often within 60-120 seconds. It is framed as potentially useful for brainstorming, quick drafting, and reducing time spent on some writing and feedback tasks, although the gains are offset by quality and reliability problems.
finding.measure: Speed and convenience of generating text and responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT creates serious institutional challenges for assessment design, plagiarism detection, and policy governance, while also prompting opportunities for assessment reform. The authors recommend that institutions avoid simple blacklisting and instead develop policies and instructional strategies that guide appropriate use, redesign assessments, and prepare for AI-influenced academic integrity issues.
finding.measure: Institutional implications for assessment policy, plagiarism control, and instructional redesign

paper_profiles.title: Who wrote this? Detecting artificial intelligence-generated text from human-written text
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines whether education-faculty participants can distinguish human-written passages from AI-generated passages and internet-copied passages. The paper is motivated by growing concerns that generative AI may make authorship harder to verify, undermining academic integrity and conventional writing-based assessment in higher education. The authors frame this as an emerging challenge for educators, markers, and institutions rather than as an intervention study.

Using a survey administered to 135 volunteers affiliated with an Ontario university faculty of education, participants reviewed two short passages and judged their source, writing level, and quality. The AI passages were generated with GPT-2 via InferKit using the prompt "How will technology change education?"; human passages were written by researchers; and a third set came from internet search. Participants identified human-generated passages correctly 63% of the time but AI-generated passages only 24% of the time, indicating that AI text was often mistaken for human text. The article argues this creates serious risks for academic integrity, suggests automated detection and human detection are both imperfect, and recommends stronger AI literacy, assessment redesign, and community/policy responses to mitigate misuse.

finding.finding_summary: Participants struggled to distinguish AI-generated from human-written text, with only 24% correct identification for AI passages and 63% for human passages (n=135 participants; 228 total passage judgments). The authors argue this creates institutional risks for academic integrity, assessment validity, and authorship verification, and may force universities to redesign assessments and policies.
finding.measure: Accuracy of judging passage authorship (AI vs human) and diagnostic classification rates

finding.finding_summary: The study directly tests whether participants can identify written compositions generated by AI versus humans. Accuracy was substantially lower for AI-generated passages (24%) than for human-written passages (63%), suggesting that AI text can pass as human writing and complicate writing assessment in education.
finding.measure: Authorship detection accuracy for short written passages

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in higher education: Considerations for academic integrity and student learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines how ChatGPT was being discussed in news media in relation to higher education in the first months after its release. The authors ask whether public and institutional discussions frame ChatGPT primarily as an academic integrity threat or as a tool that can support learning and access. They also look at whether the student voice is present in these discussions and what kinds of institutional responses are being proposed.

Rather than evaluating a classroom intervention, the paper conducts a content analysis of 100 English-language news articles from Australia, New Zealand, the United States, and the United Kingdom published between 2020 and February 2023. The corpus was coded for themes including academic integrity concerns, AI detection, assessment redesign, policy responses, learning uses, and equity considerations. The analysis shows that media coverage heavily emphasized cheating risks, detection limits, and assessment changes, while also noting some learning benefits such as feedback, brainstorming, and plain-language explanations.

The paper concludes that public discussion is highly mixed but tilted toward integrity concerns, with many articles recommending assessment redesign, explicit AI-use guidelines, and some institutional restrictions. At the same time, the authors argue that banning AI is not practical in the long term and that universities should instead develop ethical-use policies, teach critical AI literacy, and involve students more directly in policy and assessment conversations. The article also highlights under-discussed opportunities for equity and accessibility, while acknowledging that AI outputs can contain inaccuracies and biases.

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that media and university responses to ChatGPT were mixed, with heavy emphasis on academic integrity risks, policy uncertainty, and assessment redesign. In the 100-article corpus, 41 articles explicitly stated a university policy, 18 reported a ban, 10 allowed use, and 22 said institutions were undecided; many recommended revised policies, disclosure rules, or course-by-course guidance rather than outright prohibition.
finding.measure: Content analysis of news articles coding institutional policy responses, bans, allowances, and policy uncertainty

finding.finding_summary: The article repeatedly links ChatGPT to writing tasks, essay production, grammar feedback, drafting, and risks of students outsourcing essay writing. It also notes potential benefits for writing support, such as generating organization structures, exemplar texts, and grammatical feedback, but argues that overreliance may weaken the learning process by bypassing independent writing and revision.
finding.measure: Media-discussed writing-related uses and concerns, including essay writing, drafting, grammatical feedback, and plagiarism risk

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports concerns that ChatGPT could reduce students' critical thinking by making assignments too easy and by allowing them to skip the struggle that supports learning. At the same time, it argues that students need critical thinking and information literacy to evaluate outputs and use AI ethically, and some articles framed assessment redesign as a way to better cultivate those skills.
finding.measure: Media coverage of critical thinking, information literacy, and assessment redesign

finding.finding_summary: The article notes several proposed efficiency uses of ChatGPT, including generating first drafts, creating rubrics, editing student work, providing quick feedback, and helping with brainstorming or practice questions. These uses were discussed as ways to save time for teachers and students, although the paper does not empirically test workload reduction.
finding.measure: Media-discussed productivity and time-saving uses of ChatGPT for teaching and student work

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports some discussion that ChatGPT could reduce anxiety and shame around asking for help, especially for students with weaker academic backgrounds or less confidence seeking support. However, these equity and affective benefits were mentioned in only a small minority of articles, so the overall discussion of social-emotional outcomes was limited.
finding.measure: Media-discussed student anxiety, help-seeking comfort, and reduced shame

finding.finding_summary: The article identifies several safeguards and instructional strategies intended to mitigate risks of dependency, cheating, and inaccurate output, including authentic assessment redesign, more personalized reflective tasks, invigilated exams, explicit AI-use expectations, disclosure/acknowledgment rules, and student education about ethical use. It also emphasizes that detection tools are imperfect and that institutional policy development should involve staff and students, rather than relying only on bans or AI detectors.
finding.measure: Content analysis of proposed safeguards, assessment strategies, and policy guidance in news coverage

paper_profiles.title: A proposed methodology for investigating student-chatbot interaction patterns in giving peer feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This development article addresses a methodological problem in AI-in-education research: how to study what students actually do when interacting with an instructional chatbot, rather than only measuring end-of-activity outcomes. The authors argue that snapshot-style evaluations miss important process data, especially students’ judgments of their own understanding and how those judgments shape their decisions to accept or reject chatbot guidance.

To explore this, the paper describes and analyzes a purpose-built chatbot, DD, designed to support peer review in writing. DD taught four kinds of peer feedback, used comprehension-checking questions (CCQs), and then guided participants to revise fabricated peer-feedback examples on thesis statements and on arguments/counterarguments. The study involved 23 undergraduates in a first-year educational psychology course at a university in Western Canada. Students’ chat logs and revision choices were coded into interaction pathways.

The main conclusion is that many students were overconfident about their understanding: some answered CCQs correctly but still failed to revise feedback accurately later, while others rejected chatbot guidance and performed poorly. The authors conclude that CCQs alone are not enough to infer understanding, and they recommend more explicit task instructions, more robust comprehension checks, better natural-language understanding, and iterative refinement based on user interaction logs. The paper’s contribution is primarily methodological, aimed at helping researchers and designers trace learning trajectories in chatbot-supported writing instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The chatbot was designed to support peer-feedback skills for writing, and the paper reports that some students improved their ability to identify and revise fabricated feedback after interacting with DD, but many also misjudged their understanding and failed to transfer that learning to revision tasks. For thesis-statement feedback, 9/23 participants accepted guidance and 14/23 rejected it; for arguments/counterarguments, 10/23 accepted guidance and 13/23 rejected it. The paper does not report standardized writing effect sizes, but it documents that chatbot instruction could be effective for some participants while others remained incorrect or overconfident.
finding.measure: Correctness of revised fabricated peer feedback on thesis statements, arguments/counterarguments, and related feedback types

finding.finding_summary: A central finding was that students were often overconfident in judging their own understanding of how to give peer feedback. The paper repeatedly notes misjudgment of learning, overconfidence, and mismatch between self-judgment, CCQ performance, and later task success; for example, path E was interpreted as overconfidence, and 18 of 23 participants judged they knew how to pose questions for improvement but then failed to revise correctly without help in many cases.
finding.measure: Self-judgment of learning, CCQ responses, and acceptance/rejection of chatbot guidance

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively examines metacognitive judgment and decision-making during peer-feedback learning, which the authors frame as a learning-trajectory problem. Students often showed inaccurate judgments of learning: some answered CCQs correctly yet still did not successfully apply the skill later, and many rejected guidance despite needing it. The paper does not report a numeric effect size, but it emphasizes that chatbot interactions reveal learners’ metacognitive overconfidence and uneven self-regulation.
finding.measure: Judgments of learning, CCQ accuracy, and interaction pathways during peer-feedback tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions the chatbot as a way to supplement instructional support and mitigate teaching workload by coaching students during peer-feedback practice. Although it does not directly measure teacher workload or time savings, the design goal and discussion consistently frame the tool as a scalable support mechanism for large classes where instructors may not be available.
finding.measure: Instructor workload mitigation / conversational support for peer-feedback instruction

paper_profiles.title: Not quite eye to A.I.: student and teacher perspectives on the use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how students and teachers judge the appropriateness of generative AI use across stages of the writing process. The authors focus on six tasks: brainstorming, outlining, drafting/writing, revising, providing feedback, and evaluating writing. They are especially interested in where respondents draw the line between acceptable support (e.g., idea generation or modeling) and unacceptable substitution (e.g., submitting AI-generated text, especially without disclosure).

The study uses a cross-sectional questionnaire administered to 158 undergraduate students and 68 teachers, mostly higher education educators, with a small number of K-12 teachers included. Participants rated four scenarios for each writing task, ranging from AI use by someone already competent in the task to undisclosed submission of AI-generated output. The questionnaire also asked about general attitudes toward AI, perceived utility, concern, familiarity, and whether institutions had policies or training on AI use.

Findings show broad agreement that GenAI is acceptable for supportive uses such as brainstorming, outlining, and modeling, but largely unacceptable when used to complete writing assignments or when used without disclosure. Students were generally more accepting than teachers of some uses, especially submitting AI-generated work with or without disclosure, while teachers were more accepting of AI as a model for feedback and evaluation. The paper also highlights a major preparedness gap: most respondents reported little or no institutional policy or training on AI, leading the authors to call for explicit guidelines, transparency norms, and teacher professional development.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that respondents supported GenAI for supportive writing activities such as brainstorming, outlining, and revision modeling, but rejected its use as a substitute for independent writing. Across scenarios, means were higher for early-stage, idea-generating uses (e.g., brainstorming M=3.55 students, 3.53 teachers; outlining M=3.27 students, 2.96 teachers) and much lower for undisclosed submission of AI-written essays (writing D M=1.62 students, 1.22 teachers).
finding.measure: Survey ratings of appropriateness of GenAI use across writing-process tasks and disclosures

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames writing as a durable skill tied to rhetorical knowledge, critical thinking, persistence, and responsibility, and reports that participants largely believed GenAI should only be used when it supports rather than replaces the writer's own work. Respondents were most accepting of using GenAI as a model or for cognitive offloading of already-mastered tasks, but least accepting of uses that would weaken independent composing and judgment.
finding.measure: Survey ratings plus principal component analysis of acceptable-use judgments across writing-process tasks

finding.finding_summary: Participants generally viewed GenAI as potentially useful for reducing effort in limited writing tasks, especially for brainstorming, outlining, and teacher feedback/evaluation modeling. The paper reports relatively favorable ratings for using GenAI when the user already knows how to do the task (e.g., brainstorming A M=3.55 students, 3.53 teachers; feedback B M=3.23 students, 3.71 teachers), suggesting perceived efficiency gains for both students and teachers.
finding.measure: Survey ratings of acceptable AI use for task support and modeling in the writing process

finding.finding_summary: The strongest institutional finding was that respondents reported a major lack of preparedness for AI governance: 94.1% of teachers said their institution did not have an AI policy, 95.6% reported no AI training, and 89.7% had not taught students about appropriate AI use. The authors conclude that explicit guidelines, ethical-use statements, and teacher professional development are urgently needed to mitigate academic integrity risks.
finding.measure: Yes/no survey items on institutional AI policy, training, and instruction; policy discussion
finding.study_size: n=226 (policy items reported by students and/or teachers); teachers reporting teaching students n=68

paper_profiles.title: War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a rapid, critical обзор of the emerging landscape of large language model chatbots—especially ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Bard, and Ernie—and their implications for higher education. The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it surveys the corporate background of the major tools, summarizes early academic and media commentary, and then reports the authors’ own comparative testing of selected chatbots on multidisciplinary tasks relevant to university assessment.

A major focus is the risks and tradeoffs of using AI writing assistants and chatbot-based systems in education. The paper highlights concerns about hallucinations, inaccurate or outdated outputs, weak source reliability, plagiarism and academic integrity, and the ease of jailbreaking safety controls. It also notes that some AI tools are already being integrated into writing workflows (e.g., Microsoft Copilot in Word) while institutions respond with bans, assessment redesign, and renewed emphasis on in-class or pen-and-paper writing.

The article concludes that current chatbots are powerful but unreliable, and that their use in assessment should be treated cautiously. The authors recommend changes for faculty, students, and institutions, including updating integrity policies, redesigning assessments toward application and higher-order thinking, and using chatbots critically and with clearly defined instructional purposes rather than as unchecked substitutes for human writing and reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI writing assistants such as ChatGPT can generate essays, summaries, and other text quickly, but their outputs are often inaccurate, hallucinated, or weakly sourced. The authors cite comparative tests showing that GPT-4 outperformed earlier versions, yet still emphasize that these systems remain unreliable for independent writing and assessment, with risks of plagiarism and weakened writing development if used uncritically.
finding.measure: Chatbot-generated writing quality, accuracy, and suitability for essays/assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that AI tools can reduce writing and editing time, and explicitly cites Microsoft Copilot in Word as providing a 'first draft to edit and iterate on' that may save hours in writing, sourcing, and editing. At the same time, it cautions that these efficiency gains come with tradeoffs in reliability, integrity, and dependence on automated text generation.
finding.measure: Writing, sourcing, and editing time savings described in product and policy discussion

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers institutional responses to generative AI, including bans in schools and universities, revised academic integrity policies, and a shift toward closed-book or in-class assessment writing. It argues that institutions need governance and policy updates because detection is unreliable and chatbot use poses risks to academic integrity, plagiarism control, and assessment validity.
finding.measure: Policy and institutional response discussion; assessment redesign and integrity guidance

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents an exploratory, qualitative examination of an early version of GPT-4, framed by the authors as evidence that large language models may be approaching artificial general intelligence. The paper asks how far GPT-4 can generalize across domains and tasks, and it uses hand-crafted prompts and interactive demonstrations rather than a controlled benchmark study to probe capabilities in language, code, mathematics, vision-like tasks, tool use, theory of mind, and social reasoning.

The approach is intentionally informal and creative: the authors compare GPT-4 with ChatGPT on tasks such as writing rhymed proofs, generating code, composing interdisciplinary outputs, and evaluating hallucinations. The paper argues that GPT-4 shows striking breadth, but also notes important limitations, including hallucinations, arithmetic mistakes, weak planning, and biases. Because the work is primarily a qualitative showcase and not an educational intervention study, it does not directly examine schooling outcomes, but it does include a brief example of GPT-4 generating and evaluating a writing-related prompt and discusses the broader societal risks of erroneous generations and manipulation.

Overall, the paper concludes that GPT-4 represents a significant step toward more general AI, while still being incomplete and error-prone. It emphasizes that the model can appear highly capable across many domains, yet remains vulnerable to factual errors, biased outputs, and limited planning, suggesting the need for caution in deployment and further research on safety and reliability.

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes a writing-related demonstration in which GPT-4 generates a medical note from patient facts and then identifies hallucinated additions in that note. The example shows that GPT-4 can produce fluent text and can also be used to detect unsupported claims, but the paper does not evaluate student writing outcomes or writing instruction.
finding.measure: Quality of generated text and hallucination detection in a writing task

paper_profiles.title: Embracing AI in Education: Understanding the Surge in Large Language Model Use by Secondary Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how widely middle and high school students in the United States are using large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama, and Bing Copilot for schoolwork. The authors frame the study around growing concerns and uncertainty about student use of generative AI, including school restrictions, cheating concerns, and inaccurate answers, and seek to understand student behavior and attitudes so educators and developers can respond more effectively.

The study reports results from a survey of 306 students in grades 6-12 across 43 U.S. states. Students reported using LLMs across multiple subjects, with especially common use for writing, math/STEM, foreign languages, and history. The paper emphasizes both the perceived benefits and risks of LLM use: students valued help simplifying complex topics and writing text, but also noted inaccuracies, hallucinations in factual contexts, and concerns that reliance on such tools could weaken fundamental skills. The authors also document equity gaps by region and school type, finding greater use among students in more technologically advanced and higher-income contexts.

In response to these findings, the paper proposes mitigation strategies rather than restrictions: fine-tuning models for student use, incorporating textbooks and teacher inputs, adding safeguards against harmful or inappropriate content, developing personalized AI tutors, and creating AI classrooms that can promote critical thinking and support under-resourced students. The paper is primarily descriptive and policy-oriented, aiming to inform educators, policymakers, and AI developers about the prevalence, perceived usefulness, and equity implications of LLM use in secondary education.

finding.finding_summary: Survey respondents reported substantial use of LLMs for writing and language arts, and 57% of LLM users said the tools were useful for writing text. At the same time, open-ended responses raised concern that increased reliance on such tools may lower fundamental skills, and students also reported occasional inaccuracy/hallucination issues that could undermine writing support.
finding.measure: Student survey responses about LLM use and perceived usefulness for writing/language arts

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper notes that prior research finds LLMs have inferior mathematical abilities, 28% of students still reported using LLMs for math. Students reported that LLMs were useful for math and STEM questions, but concerns remained about incorrect answers and lack of rigorous reasoning.
finding.measure: Student survey responses about LLM use for math/STEM and perceived usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports student use of LLMs for STEM questions, but the main evidence here is concern about incorrect answers due to lack of rigorous reasoning rather than a direct test of scientific reasoning outcomes. The study does not measure learning gains; it mainly records student perceptions that LLMs can produce inaccurate STEM responses.
finding.measure: Student survey responses about STEM-question use and perceived answer quality

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs across multiple non-literacy subjects, including history and foreign languages. The paper highlights both convenience and risk: students found the tools helpful for schoolwork, but also reported occasional hallucinations in historical contexts and incorrect answers when reasoning was weak.
finding.measure: Student survey responses about cross-subject LLM use and perceived usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The survey suggests students use LLMs despite moderate school restrictions and moderate ethical concern, indicating that perceived utility can outweigh concern. Students also reported mixed satisfaction, with many asking for more coherent and accurate responses, which reflects attitudes but not measured changes in motivation or engagement.
finding.measure: Survey ratings of school-policy severity and ethical concern; open-ended student responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly raises concern that increased reliance on LLMs may lower fundamental skills and argues that fine-tuning models with teacher inputs should encourage critical thinking. However, the study does not directly measure critical thinking or metacognition; it reports student perceptions and author recommendations.
finding.measure: Open-ended student responses and discussion of potential skill erosion

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds widespread student use of LLMs despite restrictive school policies, with an average policy strictness rating of 3.48/5 and average ethical concern of 2.83/5. It also identifies equity gaps: 80.2% usage in the five most technologically advanced states versus 64.3% elsewhere, and 76.7% usage among private school students versus 71.3% in public schools; among the 17 paid-model users, nearly all used LLMs frequently, suggesting income-based advantage.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of school policy strictness and ethical concern; self-reported usage by state, school type, and paid-model access

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study asks whether ChatGPT can function as a feedback tool to improve second-language writing for secondary students with a refugee/migrant background. The authors are motivated by the need for language support in multilingual classrooms and focus specifically on writing challenges in grammar and vocabulary.

The study took place in a Greek junior high school (Gymnasium) and involved 8 students aged 15 in the third grade of junior high school who were learning German as a foreign language. Students first wrote a personal email, then ChatGPT was used to improve the texts’ grammar and vocabulary, and students reviewed the revised version before writing a second email on a similar topic. The paper reports pre/post descriptive changes in text length and lexical variety, including total words, unique words, and average words per sentence.

Results suggested increases in these descriptive measures after the ChatGPT-supported revision process, and the authors interpret this as promising evidence that ChatGPT can support foreign language writing. However, the study is explicitly framed as a small pilot with a very limited sample, short duration, no control/comparison group, and no delayed posttest or retention measure. The paper also notes that human teacher supervision is important and that further research is needed before generalizing the findings.

finding.finding_summary: In this small pilot with n=8 junior high school students learning German as a foreign language, ChatGPT-supported feedback was associated with descriptive improvements in writing outputs. The paper reports increases in total words (mean increase 38%), unique words (mean increase 19.1 per student), and average words per sentence (mean increase about 42%) from the first draft to the later writing attempt on a related topic.
finding.measure: Foreign language writing quality proxies: total words, unique words, average words per sentence, and most frequent words in student emails

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that ChatGPT may support students’ engagement with writing tasks by providing a supportive learning environment, but this is not measured with a formal engagement scale. The conclusion is based on the observed willingness of students to revise and produce a second related writing task after reviewing the AI-revised version.
finding.measure: Observed participation in the two-step writing/revision activity; no formal engagement or self-regulation instrument reported

paper_profiles.title: VNHSGE: VietNamese High School Graduation Examination Dataset for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces the VNHSGE dataset, a Vietnamese high-school graduation examination benchmark created to evaluate large language models on secondary-level academic content. The dataset includes 19,000 multiple-choice questions across eight subjects and 300 literature essays, all drawn from Vietnamese national high school graduation exams and comparable exams from 2019–2023. The literature portion is intended to assess reading comprehension and writing abilities, while the other subjects evaluate subject knowledge and reasoning across mathematics, English, science, history, geography, and civic education.

The authors also report baseline experiments using ChatGPT and BingChat on the dataset, standardizing model responses with a prompted answer format. They compare model performance with Vietnamese students using published exam score distributions, but the paper is a benchmark/dataset paper rather than an intervention study. For the literature dataset, the paper emphasizes that the exam covers reading comprehension and essay writing, and that answer keys and grading guidelines were used to support evaluation.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs show human-level performance in some subjects such as literature and English, but still struggle in areas requiring more complex reasoning, especially mathematics and the natural sciences. For the literature component, the paper frames the dataset as useful for training and evaluating LLMs on essay writing and writing proficiency, but it does not report a controlled experiment on student writing instruction, writing quality improvement, revision gains, or durable skill growth after AI use is removed.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test an instructional writing intervention; it introduces a high-school literature benchmark and reports LLM benchmark performance on essay and reading-comprehension items. The literature section is described as assessing reading comprehension and writing abilities, but no student outcome improvement, revision-quality gain, or delayed retention measure is reported (study_size=not_reported).
finding.measure: Literature exam performance / essay and reading-comprehension benchmark accuracy

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual and literature-review article about ChatGPT and its implications for higher education. The authors explain how ChatGPT works, situate it within the broader history of AI in education, and argue that generative AI will likely disrupt assessment practices, especially essay-based tasks. They also discuss strengths and limitations of ChatGPT through informal experimentation with prompts, including its ability to generate prose, answer questions, and produce text in English and Chinese.

The article does not study a K-12 or high-school population, nor does it evaluate a writing intervention with student outcome data. Instead, it synthesizes early post-ChatGPT scholarship, discusses risks such as plagiarism and hallucinated citations, and suggests that educators and institutions should adapt assessment and teaching practices rather than simply banning the tool. Its writing-focused discussion is limited to broad claims about AI-powered writing assistants and does not provide direct empirical evidence on writing quality, revision quality, grammar, fluency, engagement, self-regulation, or transfer in secondary students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is not an empirical study of academic outcomes; it is a conceptual review and informal demonstration paper about ChatGPT in higher education. It does not report student outcome data, effect sizes, or controlled comparisons on academic performance.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that ChatGPT and related AI tools may improve efficiency by generating text quickly, supporting drafting, and reducing some writing and assessment workload. These claims are based on informal examples and literature discussion rather than measured outcomes; no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: informal prompt-based demonstrations and literature review claims about drafting/assessment speed

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may disrupt assessment systems and force institutions to rethink plagiarism policies, essay-based assessment, and AI governance. This is a conceptual institutional-level discussion, not an empirical evaluation, and the paper reports no measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: conceptual analysis of assessment policy and institutional response

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a structured ChatGPT-use framework can improve second-language learners’ argumentative essay writing and critical thinking. The authors develop the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW) by combining the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model with Hattie and Timperley’s feedback model, then compare a CGCAW-guided ChatGPT condition against a ChatGPT-without-guidelines condition.

The study used a very small experiment with 10 university students from a state university, randomly assigned to two groups of five. All participants wrote a short argumentative essay in 40 minutes on the same topic about whether social media is beneficial or harmful to society. The experimental group received step-by-step prompts intended to structure idea generation, evidence use, and conclusion writing; the control group could use ChatGPT freely without the framework. Essays were evaluated by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor.

Results were mixed and depended strongly on the evaluator. Grammarly scored the control group slightly higher (M=92.2) than the experimental group (M=90.6), suggesting no advantage for the CGCAW framework on language-mechanics-oriented scoring. ChatGPT scored the experimental group slightly higher overall (M=74.0 vs 72.2) and specifically on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, but the course instructor scored the control group much higher (M=56 vs 35), especially on clear thesis and summary quality. The authors conclude that the framework may help with coherence and evidence integration, but likely needs refinement and more training; they also note that short duration, novice use of ChatGPT, and individual differences likely limited performance.

finding.finding_summary: The study assessed argumentative essay quality using three scoring sources. Grammarly slightly favored the control group over the CGCAW group (M=92.2 vs 90.6), while ChatGPT favored the CGCAW group (M=74.0 vs 72.2), and the course instructor strongly favored the control group (M=56 vs 35). This indicates mixed effects on writing quality, with gains in some dimensions (clarity, logical coherence, evidence) but losses in others (thesis quality, summary quality, and language mechanics).
finding.measure: Argumentative essay ratings of clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness, grammar/punctuation/clarity/engagement/delivery, and instructor rubric on thesis, evidence/reasoning, counterarguments, and summary
finding.std_deviation: Grammarly: not_reported; ChatGPT total SD G1=7.6, G2=5.5; instructor not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly frames the intervention as supporting critical thinking in argumentative writing and evaluates whether CGCAW improves clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use as proxies for critical reasoning. ChatGPT-based scoring suggested modest advantages for the CGCAW group on these dimensions, but instructor scoring and Grammarly did not consistently support improvement, so the evidence for durable critical-thinking growth is mixed rather than clearly positive. No delayed posttest or retention measure was reported, so the study does not show durable skill transfer after AI removal.
finding.measure: Critical-thinking-aligned argumentative writing dimensions (clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness; thesis/evidence/reasoning/counterarguments/summary)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT feedback can foster self-regulation and reflection, but it does not directly measure those constructs with a dedicated instrument. The only indirect evidence is that two participants in the CGCAW group could not complete the task within the 40-minute window because they were unfamiliar with the framework, suggesting the guided use may have increased cognitive/interactional demands rather than improving efficiency or persistence in this short task.
finding.measure: Task completion within 40 minutes; indirect discussion of self-regulation/reflection

paper_profiles.title: An Empirical Study to Understand How Students Use ChatGPT for Writing Essays
paper_profiles.venue: ACM (manuscript submitted to ACM / arXiv preprint)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students use ChatGPT during an essay-writing task and asks what kinds of writing support they seek, how those patterns vary by individual differences, and how those patterns shape their experience of the writing process. The motivation is to understand the real-world risks and opportunities of generative AI in writing education, especially concerns that students may outsource planning, drafting, and revising rather than actively engage in composing.

The authors built a custom writing platform with an embedded ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-turbo via OpenAI API) that logged queries, responses, and keystroke-level editing behavior. Seventy-seven U.S. college students completed an ACT-style argumentative essay prompt in about 30 minutes, with no encouragement or discouragement to use ChatGPT. The study is not an intervention comparison against teacher feedback, peer review, or tutoring; instead, it is a descriptive observational study of usage patterns. Participants’ queries were coded into planning, translating, reviewing, or all-phases assistance, and the authors also measured perceived ownership and perceived creativity support after writing.

The main finding is that students used ChatGPT in highly varied ways, from ideation and search-like fact seeking to direct generation of full essays and revision/polishing requests. More than half of participants issued at least one query spanning all writing phases, and 19.5% submitted essays that were 100% written by ChatGPT. Higher writing self-efficacy predicted less ChatGPT use, and students who used ChatGPT only for ideation or review reported perceived ownership comparable to non-users, raising concerns that some AI-supported writing may feel authentic to students even when it reflects substantial delegation. The paper provides rich descriptive evidence about student behavior and perceived experience, but it does not test whether ChatGPT improves writing quality, revision quality, grammar/mechanics, or durable writing skill growth in high school.

finding.finding_summary: This is a descriptive observational study of essay writing with ChatGPT rather than an outcome-evaluating trial, so it does not establish whether writing quality improved. The paper shows that students used ChatGPT for planning, drafting, and reviewing, and that 15 of 77 participants (19.5%) produced essays that were 100% written by ChatGPT; it also reports an average essay length of 382 words (sd=235) over 22.5 minutes (sd=15.1). No standardized writing-quality score, delayed posttest, or human-feedback comparison was reported.
finding.measure: Query types, essay composition traces, essay length, and qualitative analysis of writing use patterns
finding.std_deviation: sd=235 words (essay length); sd=15.1 minutes (time on task)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly measured post-task perceived ownership of the essay and the Creativity Support Index (CSI), both as reflections of students’ experience of writing with ChatGPT. The authors report that students who used ChatGPT only for ideation or review felt a comparable sense of ownership to students who did not use it at all, suggesting that some AI-supported workflows may preserve perceived authorship even when they involve substantial assistance. No inferential effect size or confidence interval for ownership/CSI is reported in the provided text.
finding.measure: Perceived ownership questionnaire; Creativity Support Index (CSI)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively discusses planning, translating, reviewing, and self-regulation-like prompting behavior as part of the writing process, but it does not measure durable skill growth such as transfer, retention, or delayed performance after AI removal. It reports that higher writing self-efficacy predicted less ChatGPT use, and that many students offloaded core composing activities to the system, including full-essay generation and iterative revision prompting. These results suggest potential concerns about reduced independent engagement, but they are process findings rather than evidence of skill gains or losses.
finding.measure: Self-Efficacy for Writing Scale (SEWS); ChatGPT query behavior categorized by writing-process phase

paper_profiles.title: Work-in-Progress: An empirical study to understand how students use ChatGPT for writing essays and how it affects their ownership
paper_profiles.venue: In2Writing '24 (ACM Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This work-in-progress paper proposes a user study to examine how students use ChatGPT while writing essays and how the tool affects their perceived ownership of the resulting text. The authors are primarily interested in the writing process itself: what prompts students ask, how they move between drafting and chatbot interaction, and how ChatGPT responses are incorporated into revisions.

The system being developed embeds a ChatGPT-like assistant directly into a writing interface that records keystrokes, cursor movement, insertions, deletions, cuts, and pastes, along with timestamps. Students will write an essay response to a prompt adapted from a junior-level university ethics course, and they will then complete an exit survey about ownership, perceived assistance, proofreading, and whether ChatGPT made their essay better.

The paper does not report completed empirical results; it mainly describes the planned instrumentation, study procedure, and intended analyses. Its main contribution is methodological: creating a way to study how LLM assistance is used during essay writing and to support future judgments about dependence, proofreading, and possible plagiarism. No direct evidence on writing quality or learning outcomes is yet available in the paper.

finding.finding_summary: No completed outcome data are reported. The paper describes a planned study of essay writing with ChatGPT and proposes tracking writing process features (e.g., pasted text, revisions, pace), but it does not present results on writing quality, grammar, organization, vocabulary, or retention. Because the study is still a work-in-progress, there is no empirical evidence yet that ChatGPT improves or harms literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: essay writing process traces and future essay quality outcomes

finding.finding_summary: No completed results are reported for engagement, motivation, self-regulation, or ownership. The study intends to measure students' perceived ownership and attitudes toward ChatGPT through an exit survey, but the paper only lists survey items and does not provide analyzed data. Therefore, there is no empirical finding yet on social-emotional outcomes.
finding.measure: exit survey on perceived ownership and attitudes toward ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes examining how students prompt ChatGPT and integrate its responses into drafting, which could inform metacognition or self-regulation, but no results are reported. It does not include measured effects on planning, revision strategy, or transfer beyond the immediate writing task.
finding.measure: prompt logs and writing revision traces

finding.finding_summary: The authors plan to analyze writing pace, pasted content, and other process indicators that may relate to productivity, but the paper provides no observed efficiency results. As a result, there is no direct evidence that ChatGPT increased or decreased task efficiency in this study.
finding.measure: pace of writing and process log metrics

paper_profiles.title: Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students’ essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether ChatGPT-3 can improve student essay writing when used as a writing assistant. The authors compare essays written traditionally versus essays written with ChatGPT-3 assistance, focusing on overall essay quality, authenticity/plagiarism-related indicators, similarity among essays, and time to completion.

Eighteen second-year master's students from the University of Split participated, with 9 in the control group and 9 in the ChatGPT-assisted group. Students were given the same essay prompt, 4 hours to complete the task, and were scored by two teachers using a rubric covering mechanics, style, content, and format. The experimental group received an introduction to ChatGPT; the control group wrote without it and was supervised to prevent its use.

Results showed no evidence that ChatGPT improved essay quality or reduced writing time. The control group slightly outperformed the ChatGPT group on average essay score (2.39 ± 0.71 vs. 2.00 ± 0.73), but the group difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.184). The authors also found slightly higher text unauthenticity in the ChatGPT group and no meaningful essay similarity overall. The study concludes that, in this small sample and first-use context, ChatGPT did not enhance writing performance and may have even slightly disadvantaged students.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-3 assistance did not improve essay quality in this small randomized comparison. The control group scored slightly higher on overall essay grade (2.39 ± 0.71) than the ChatGPT group (2.00 ± 0.73), and the group effect was not statistically significant (P = 0.184) in a sample of n=18.
finding.measure: Teacher-scored essay quality using a rubric covering mechanics, style, content, and format; overall average essay grade (A=4 to D=1)

finding.finding_summary: Using ChatGPT-3 did not reduce the time required to complete the essay. Mean writing duration was similar between groups: 172.22 ± 31.59 minutes for the ChatGPT group and 179.11 ± 31.93 minutes for controls, with no significant group effect (P = 0.669).
finding.measure: Essay writing duration (minutes)

finding.finding_summary: The study examined authenticity-related outcomes relevant to academic integrity. Text unauthenticity was slightly higher in the ChatGPT group (11.87% ± 13.45) than the control group (9.96% ± 9.81), but the difference was not tested as significant in the abstracted results and overall essay similarity remained very low (Jaccard index median 0.002, range 0–0.054).
finding.measure: Plagiarism/authenticity metrics from PlagScan, Jaccard similarity index, and AI-text-classifier labels

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary school EFL students prompt generative AI chatbots, especially ChatGPT, while completing a writing task. The authors are interested in the content, quantity, and sequence of prompts students use, framing the activity as a “machine-in-the-loop” writing process in which students iteratively prompt a chatbot, inspect its output, and revise prompts until the task is complete.

The study uses a qualitative case-study design with four high-achieving form-one students from a Hong Kong secondary school. Students completed a timed blog-entry writing task in an after-school lesson using iPads and the POE app, which provided access to ChatGPT and other proprietary chatbots (Sage and Dragonfly). Students had up to 45 minutes, received no explicit instruction on how to prompt chatbots, and were recorded via screen capture while writing.

The analysis is descriptive and focuses on prompt pathways rather than writing outcomes. Across 36 analyzed turns, the authors identify six distinct prompt types plus more complex combinations of prompt content. Students relied heavily on trial-and-error, often starting with simple auto-complete or natural-language prompts and gradually varying prompt content and sequence. The paper concludes that secondary students were unsophisticated prompt engineers and that prompt-engineering education could help learners use generative chatbots more strategically in EFL writing. The paper does not report direct evidence on writing quality, revision quality, grammar, vocabulary, fluency, engagement outcomes, self-regulation outcomes, or durable skill growth; it mainly provides process evidence about how students interacted with chatbots during writing.

finding.finding_summary: This study does not evaluate writing quality or any other literacy outcome with a pre/post or comparison design; instead, it documents how four secondary EFL students used prompts while completing a blog-writing task with chatbots. The writing task itself was completed by all students within 45 minutes (n=4), but no rubric-based writing scores, revision scores, grammar/mechanics measures, vocabulary measures, or delayed retention tests were reported.
finding.measure: Completed blog-entry writing task; prompt pathway analysis, not writing quality scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies prompt engineering as a skill/process, but only at the level of descriptive pathway patterns during a single task. It reports that students engaged in trial-and-error prompting and some prompt refinement, yet it provides no causal evidence of growth in metacognition, transfer, or durable prompt-engineering skill after instruction or AI removal.
finding.measure: Prompt content, sequencing, and prompt-type diversity during one writing session

finding.finding_summary: The paper mentions possible implications for confidence and learning-to-use chatbots, but it does not directly measure engagement, motivation, persistence, or self-regulation with a validated instrument. Observations are limited to students’ visible trial-and-error prompting behavior during the task, so no direct outcome evidence on social-emotional skills is reported.
finding.measure: Observed prompting behavior during a timed writing task

paper_profiles.title: Modifying AI, Enhancing Essays: How Active Engagement with Generative AI Boosts Writing Quality
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how different kinds of generative AI-assisted writing behavior relate to the quality of essay products. The authors ask whether students’ interaction patterns with GPT-3—especially whether they seek suggestions, accept them directly, or accept and then modify them—predict differences in writing quality and linguistic bias.

The study uses the CoAuthor dataset, consisting of 1,445 AI-assisted writing sessions from 63 crowd-sourced writers across 20 topics. Using causal modeling (X-learner with back-door adjustment) rather than an experiment, the authors estimate average and individual treatment effects for three behavioral patterns: seeking suggestions but not accepting them, accepting suggestions without revision, and accepting suggestions with revision. Outcomes are lexical sophistication, syntactic complexity, text cohesion, and gender bias.

The main conclusion is that active modification of AI suggestions is associated with better essay quality, while direct acceptance without revision is associated with worse quality on the main writing measures. Specifically, the modify-after-accepting pattern is associated with higher lexical sophistication, syntactic complexity, and cohesion, whereas blind acceptance shows the strongest negative associations. All three AI-use patterns reduce measured gender bias somewhat. The study argues that educators should pay attention not just to final products but to how students engage with AI during writing, and it suggests the need for in-process assessment and explicit student training on critical revision of AI-generated text.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines writing quality using 1,445 AI-assisted writing sessions (n=1,445). Active engagement with GAI by accepting and then revising suggestions (T3) was associated with higher lexical sophistication (ATE=0.102), syntactic complexity (ATE=0.963), and cohesion (ATE=0.008), while accepting suggestions without revision (T2) was associated with lower lexical sophistication (ATE=-0.086), syntactic complexity (ATE=-0.869), and cohesion (ATE=-0.007). Seeking suggestions without accepting them (T1) had smaller negative associations for lexical sophistication and syntactic complexity and a near-zero positive association for cohesion.
finding.measure: Lexical sophistication (Advanced Guiraud), syntactic complexity (Mean Length of T-Unit), text cohesion (Semantic Overlap)

finding.finding_summary: The paper also treats gender bias as a writing-quality outcome and finds that all three AI-use patterns were associated with lower gender bias scores (i.e., less bias). The largest reduction occurred when writers sought suggestions but did not accept them (T1 ATE=-0.163), with smaller reductions for accepting without revision (T2 ATE=-0.012) and accepting with revision (T3 ATE=-0.013).
finding.measure: Gender bias (Genbit Score)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT v Bard v Bing v Claude 2 v Aria v human-expert. How good are AI chatbots at scientific writing?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint/published article evaluates how well several generative AI chatbots can answer and write about complex scientific questions in the humanities. The authors compare ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Bard, Bing Chat, Aria, Claude 2, and two ChatGPT-4 plugins (Bing and ScholarAI) against human-expert responses on two one-shot prompts about the migration of South Slavs and the settlement of Alpine Slavs in the Early Middle Ages.

The study is not a classroom intervention; it is a benchmarking exercise using expert tagging of chatbot outputs for quantitative accuracy and qualitative precision. The prompts were designed to resemble a senior undergraduate-level humanities writing task, and the authors emphasize that the outputs were compared both to each other and to human-generated text.
