They also examined reasoning errors, hallucinations, and biases in references and content generation.

Main findings were that ChatGPT-4 performed best overall among the chatbots, but still fell far short of human expert writing and did not show substantial originality. Bing Chat and ChatGPT-4 with Bing produced some usable content but relied heavily on Wikipedia/search snippets and had citation problems; Bard was less stable; Aria, Claude 2, and ScholarAI performed worse. The paper concludes that current chatbots can generate plausible but limited scientific prose, are prone to errors and biased sourcing, and do not yet substitute for human scholarly reasoning or original contribution.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates AI-generated scientific writing in humanities/archaeology tasks, treating the outputs as a proxy for undergraduate-level written responses. ChatGPT-4 achieved the best quantitative accuracy, but the average score was still only -5 and all systems fell far below what would be expected of a senior undergraduate; human-written responses contained substantially more original contribution than any chatbot output.
finding.measure: Expert-tagged quantitative accuracy and qualitative precision of AI-generated scientific prose for two 500-word prompts
finding.study_size: n=8 chatbot systems; 2 prompts; human expert comparison not reported as a sample size

finding.finding_summary: The authors explicitly judge the chatbots' scientific reasoning to be weak, noting reasoning errors, failure to critically compare sources, hallucinated citations, and causal confusions. For example, several systems incorrectly linked Slavic migration to climate cooling or to the decline of the Western Roman Empire, and none attempted the kind of source comparison expected in scholarly reasoning.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of reasoning errors, hallucinations, and source use in generated answers

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats critical thinking and source comparison as central humanities skills and finds that the chatbots did not demonstrate them. The generated texts were one-sided, did not compare competing hypotheses, and often amplified the loudest or highest-ranking source rather than exercising metacognitive judgment or critical evaluation.
finding.measure: Qualitative evaluation of critical comparison of sources and original scientific contribution

finding.finding_summary: The systems sometimes produced quickly usable draft text, but the output quality was inconsistent and frequently required heavy correction because of inaccurate facts, fabricated references, and weak sourcing. Bing and ChatGPT-4 with Bing were somewhat useful as rapid starting points, but the study concludes they are not reliable substitutes for careful human research workflows.
finding.measure: Practical utility of chatbot-generated draft prose, reference generation, and search assistance

paper_profiles.title: Towards Explainable AI Writing Assistants for Non-native English Speakers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates why non-native English speakers struggle to use AI writing assistants for paraphrasing, especially when the tools generate multiple alternative rewrites without explaining why one suggestion may be better than another. The authors focus on the decision-making problem of selecting and trusting paraphrased outputs, rather than on measuring downstream writing gains.

The study uses semi-structured interviews and think-aloud writing sessions with 15 non-native English speakers who regularly write in English. Participants described difficulties judging whether AI-generated paraphrases preserved meaning, fit the context, and sounded natural or polite, and many relied on external evidence such as dictionary examples, search trends, or human feedback to evaluate suggestions. The paper then proposes design implications for explainable AI writing assistants, including confidence scores, example sentences from credible sources, usage trends, and textual explanations.

This is not an instructional efficacy study and does not test a classroom intervention, writing curriculum, or chatbot on student writing outcomes. Instead, it provides qualitative evidence about user needs and perceived limitations of current AI paraphrasing tools, with some participants noting that explanations might help learning and future use. The paper’s relevance to K-12 writing instruction is indirect, since the sample is adults and university-affiliated users rather than high school students.

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that AI writing assistants helped them paraphrase English text and improve surface-level wording, but they also struggled to judge whether the AI output preserved intended meaning, tone, and contextual appropriateness. In a qualitative sample of 15 non-native English speakers, the main issue was not measured writing improvement but uncertainty about the quality and correctness of paraphrased suggestions, including concerns about broken grammar and altered meaning.
finding.measure: Interview and think-aloud reports about paraphrase evaluation, meaning preservation, grammar, tone, and naturalness

finding.finding_summary: The interviews showed that participants experienced uncertainty, low trust, and caution when deciding whether to accept AI-generated paraphrases. Some participants appreciated explanatory features and believed they could help them learn to be more careful in future writing, but others gave up on perfecting sentences due to effort costs and confidence limits.
finding.measure: Interview themes on trust, uncertainty, confidence, and willingness to accept suggestions

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that explanations and real-world examples may support language learning, metacognitive evaluation, and better decision-making about paraphrased suggestions, but this is a design implication rather than a measured outcome. Participants reported using dictionaries, corpora, search results, and human feedback to reason about appropriateness, indicating active self-regulation in evaluating AI output.
finding.measure: Interview reports of strategy use and reflection during paraphrase selection

paper_profiles.title: Experimenting with Generative AI: Does ChatGPT Really Increase Everyone’s Productivity?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT improves student productivity on writing-analysis and math/data-analysis tasks, and whether gains differ by student ability and digital skills. The authors position the study as addressing a gap in evidence on generative AI in settings where the model may be less reliable, specifically Thai-language writing analysis and Stata-based quantitative tasks.

The experiment used 121 economics undergraduates from Chulalongkorn University and Thammasat University in Thailand. Students completed two writing-analysis sessions and two math/data-analysis sessions, with randomized order and counterbalanced task sets; each task was done once with ChatGPT and once without ChatGPT. Performance was scored out of 10 by three experts and measured by time to completion, with monetary incentives tied to both speed and quality.

The main findings were that ChatGPT improved average performance on both task types, but the gains were uneven. For writing-analysis tasks, mean score increased by 0.43 points (from 5.33 to 5.75; n=121) and mean time decreased by 1.73 minutes, yet 34% of students did not improve and higher-econometrics-grade students tended to do worse with ChatGPT. For math/data-analysis tasks, mean score increased by 1.65 points (from 3.09 to 4.74; n=121) and mean time decreased by 0.99 minutes, though 42% of students did not improve.

The paper concludes that generative AI can boost short-run task productivity, but benefits are heterogeneous and appear linked to user capability, especially digital skills. Because the study measures immediate task performance only and does not include delayed posttests or AI-removal retention checks, it provides evidence about output polish/productivity rather than durable skill growth.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT improved performance on Thai writing-analysis tasks. Mean expert-rated score increased by 0.43 points on a 10-point scale (5.33 without ChatGPT vs. 5.75 with ChatGPT; n=121), and completion time fell by 1.73 minutes. However, 34% of participants did not improve, and higher-econometrics-grade students tended to perform worse when using ChatGPT.
finding.measure: Expert-rated writing-analysis task score (0-10) and time to completion
finding.effect_size: 0.43 score-point increase; time reduced by 1.73 minutes

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT increased task efficiency on the writing-analysis tasks, with students finishing 1.73 minutes faster on average (19.19 minutes without ChatGPT vs. 17.46 with ChatGPT; n=121). The paper reports a similar productivity gain for the math/data-analysis tasks, where time fell by 0.99 minutes on average, indicating faster completion rather than durable learning.
finding.measure: Task completion time
finding.effect_size: 1.73 minutes faster for writing-analysis tasks; 0.99 minutes faster for math/data-analysis tasks
finding.std_deviation: 3.43 (writing time diff SD); 2.90 (math time diff SD)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT improved performance on math and data analysis tasks. Mean expert-rated score rose by 1.65 points on a 10-point scale (3.09 without ChatGPT vs. 4.74 with ChatGPT; n=121), and completion time decreased by 0.99 minutes. Despite this average gain, 42% of students did not improve, suggesting heterogeneous benefits rather than universal improvement.
finding.measure: Expert-rated math/data-analysis task score (0-10) and time to completion
finding.effect_size: 1.65 score-point increase; time reduced by 0.99 minutes

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines heterogeneity by prior ability and digital skills, which is relevant to self-regulation/adaptive use rather than direct durable-skill instruction. Higher digital skills predicted better performance with ChatGPT, while higher econometrics grades predicted worse performance on writing tasks; however, these are correlational moderation findings, not evidence of durable skill growth.
finding.measure: Regression of score difference on ChatGPT proficiency, econometrics grade, GPAX, and self-reported digital skills
finding.effect_size: Digital skills coefficient about 0.70-0.73 on math score diff; econometrics grade coefficient about -0.54 to -0.57 on writing score diff

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE), a high-stakes secondary-school exam spanning mathematics, literature, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education. The authors position the work as an exploration of generative AI’s potential to support learners in high-school exam preparation, rather than as an instructional intervention study.

Methodologically, the paper evaluates ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) in a zero-shot setting on the VNHSGE dataset and compares its generated answers to human-verified ground truth. For multiple-choice subjects, the model was prompted to output a choice plus explanation; for literature, the paper reports essay-related performance in the exam context. The study does not test classroom implementation, revision processes, teacher feedback, or writing instruction outcomes, and it does not include human baselines such as teacher conferencing, peer review, or tutoring.

Results show that ChatGPT achieved subject scores generally in the 4.8–7.92 range, with strongest performance in English and weaker performance in chemistry and mathematics. Using the Vietnamese graduation scoring formula, the model’s combined natural and social-science scores were reported as sufficient to pass in every year from 2019 to 2023. The paper concludes that ChatGPT has promise for answering high-school exam questions, but it also notes uneven performance and the need for further work on more complex questions and contexts. The evidence is about exam answering capability, not durable learning or writing-skill growth.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s performance on the high-school graduation exam varied by subject and year, with reported average subject scores ranging from 4.8 (chemistry) to 7.92 (English). The model was nevertheless reported to reach passing-level combined scores for the VNHSGE in all tested years (2019–2023), indicating strong but uneven exam-answering performance rather than uniformly high mastery.
finding.measure: VNHSGE subject scores and graduation combined scores
finding.study_size: n=1 AI model evaluated across exam years 2019–2023; question counts reported as 30 essays in literature and 1,700 multiple-choice questions overall
finding.std_deviation: reported in figures/tables but not numerically specified in text

finding.finding_summary: The literature and English components suggest comparatively stronger language performance than in math/science, with literature scores ranging from 5.63 to 7.5 (avg 6.8) and English from 7.6 to 8.6 (avg 7.92). The paper interprets these results as evidence that ChatGPT can produce well-structured text and handle language-heavy exam items, but the study does not evaluate writing instruction, revision quality, or durable writing-skill gains.
finding.measure: Literature and English exam scores on the VNHSGE
finding.study_size: n=1 AI model; literature test case included 30 essays; English subject evaluated across exam years 2019–2023
finding.std_deviation: reported in figures/tables but not numerically specified in text

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s mathematics performance was lower than its language-subject performance, with scores ranging from 5.2 to 6.6 (avg 5.88). The authors state that these scores were below the majority of Vietnamese students, suggesting limited reliability on the math portion of the high-school exam.
finding.measure: Mathematics exam score on the VNHSGE
finding.study_size: n=1 AI model evaluated across exam years 2019–2023
finding.std_deviation: reported in figures/tables but not numerically specified in text

finding.finding_summary: Performance on science subjects was uneven: physics averaged 6.1 and biology 5.8, while chemistry was the weakest subject at 4.8. The paper reports that ChatGPT generally scored below the majority of Vietnamese students in physics and chemistry, but did relatively better in biology, indicating subject-specific limitations in science reasoning.
finding.measure: Physics, chemistry, and biology exam scores on the VNHSGE
finding.study_size: n=1 AI model evaluated across exam years 2019–2023
finding.std_deviation: reported in figures/tables but not numerically specified in text

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, or self-regulation in students. It only infers that some exam items require higher-order thinking and that ChatGPT handles these inconsistently; no student-level durable-skill outcome or delayed retention measure is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: “It’s like a rubber duck that talks back”: Understanding Generative AI-Assisted Data Analysis Workflows through a Participatory Prompting Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHIWORK ’24 (Proceedings of the 3rd Annual Meeting of the Symposium on Human-Computer Interaction for Work)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how generative AI, specifically Bing Chat, can support end-user data-analysis workflows through a participatory prompting method. The authors ask how a researcher-mediated interaction with a real generative AI system can reveal opportunities and barriers in sensemaking work, especially for non-expert users working with spreadsheets and other data tasks.

The study used participatory prompting sessions with 15 adult spreadsheet users recruited from diverse backgrounds. Participants brought their own data-analysis scenarios, and a researcher relayed and adapted prompts to Bing Chat over 3-7 turns per task. The sessions focused on data-foraging and sensemaking activities such as finding data, generating hypotheses, choosing analysis strategies, and getting step-by-step help with spreadsheets, R, and related tools.

The main findings were qualitative: participants generally viewed generative AI as useful for brainstorming, getting unstuck, scaffolding analysis, and learning features or procedures, but they also encountered barriers in query formulation, context specification, long or vague responses, and verification of outputs. The paper argues that the participatory prompting method can expose both the benefits and limitations of generative AI in real workflows, while also noting that strong researcher mediation may shape the interaction and that reproducibility is a concern.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that generative AI was viewed as helpful for data-analysis and spreadsheet tasks, including generating hypotheses, suggesting analysis strategies, explaining spreadsheet functions, and drafting code. Participants also reported limitations: responses could be vague, too long, or hard to verify, and some tasks were too niche for the system to help effectively. No quantitative effect sizes were reported; evidence is based on qualitative reports from n=15 participants.
finding.measure: Qualitative interviews and think-aloud reflections about data-analysis workflow support

finding.finding_summary: Participants described generative AI as motivating, inspirational, and useful for getting unstuck during analysis, suggesting a positive effect on engagement and persistence in the workflow. Some participants also noted that the system could reduce frustration by providing a direct next step or a conversational partner-like experience ('a rubber duck that actually talks back'). This was assessed qualitatively in n=15 adults, with no effect size reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of inspiration, motivation, and getting unstuck

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines how generative AI supports sensemaking, hypothesis generation/testing, critical thinking, and learning new skills as part of analysis. Participants reported that the system helped them think through problems, consider alternative approaches, and learn unfamiliar spreadsheet or statistical procedures, but the study did not measure durable skill growth with delayed posttests or AI removal conditions. Findings are qualitative only from n=15 participants.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of sensemaking, hypothesis generation, and learning during analysis

finding.finding_summary: Participants consistently said generative AI made work easier, faster, and more efficient by streamlining information search, suggesting analysis paths, and providing step-by-step instructions. The paper reports perceived time-saving and reduced effort, but does not provide quantitative productivity measures or effect sizes. Evidence comes from think-aloud and interview data in a qualitative study with n=15 adults.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of workflow speed, effort reduction, and task support

paper_profiles.title: Voice Interaction With Conversational AI Could Facilitate Thoughtful Reflection and Substantive Revision in Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether voice-based interaction with an LLM-powered conversational agent could improve writers’ reflection and revision compared with text-based interaction. The motivation is that conversational, dialogic feedback from human tutors or writing centers often supports deeper reflection than static comments, and the authors hypothesize that spoken interaction may further reduce cognitive load and encourage more engagement with higher-order concerns.

The paper is a formative design/research proposal rather than a completed efficacy study. The authors describe a within-subjects experiment in which participants would write rough drafts of argumentative essays, interact with a conversational writing-support system in two conditions (typed input/output versus spoken input with written output), and then revise their drafts. Planned measures include counts and proportions of higher-order versus lower-order concerns in the dialogue, conversational turn rate, response latency as a proxy for cognitive processing, NASA-TLX cognitive load, and expert ratings of revised essays using an argumentative writing rubric.

The paper does not report empirical results from a conducted experiment; instead, it outlines the intended method and the expected contribution of examining speech versus text in AI-mediated reflection and revision. It positions the system as a writing-support tool that preserves user control by offering non-directive feedback and conversation starters, rather than directly rewriting the user’s text. Because the study is proposed and not yet completed, the paper offers no direct evidence on writing quality gains, revision quality, or durability of learning effects in high-school contexts.

finding.finding_summary: No empirical effect is reported because the paper is a formative study proposal rather than a completed evaluation. The authors state that participant revisions would be assessed with an argumentative essay rubric, but no sample size, effect size, or outcome results are available.
finding.measure: Argumentative essay rubric; revision quality

finding.finding_summary: No empirical effect is reported. The proposed study plans to measure engagement indirectly through conversational turns per minute and cognitive load using NASA-TLX, but results are not available in this paper.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX cognitive load; conversational turns per minute

finding.finding_summary: No empirical effect is reported. The paper frames reflection, higher-order concern use, and substantive revision as metacognitive/durable-skill processes, but it presents only a proposed design with no observed outcomes.
finding.measure: Frequency and proportion of higher-order concerns; revision depth

paper_profiles.title: Assisting Research Proposal Writing with Large Language Models: Evaluation and Refinement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models, specifically ChatGPT-4o, can generate and refine academic research proposals more effectively when given different prompting strategies. The authors focus on two evaluation dimensions: content quality and reference validity. They argue that prior assessments of AI-assisted academic writing are too subjective and propose a more quantitative framework based on AI grading systems plus manual reference fact-checking.

The study compares two proposal-generation strategies: GPT-only writing and GPT-assisted writing with human-provided references. Proposals were generated on three education topics related to agency and identity (all at the university level), then scored by three AI writing tools (Study Fetch, QuillBot, Grammarly) and checked for citation accuracy by the authors. The paper also tests an iterative prompting/refinement method in which score feedback and reference corrections are fed back into the model across multiple rounds. Results suggest that iterative prompting improves proposal content scores and reduces reference errors/fabrications, although the work does not evaluate human writing outcomes, classroom implementation, or durable writing-skill transfer.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies LLM-assisted academic proposal writing and finds that iterative prompting improved overall proposal content quality across three education topics. Average AI-graded scores were already above 80/100 in all conditions, and after refinement the largest reported gain was 11.02% for GPT-assisted Teacher Identity proposals (to an average score of 90.67), while the smallest gain was 3.84% for GPT-assisted Student Agency proposals (to 90).
finding.measure: AI-graded proposal content quality across Study Fetch, QuillBot, and Grammarly
finding.study_size: n=6 proposals total (3 topics × 2 writing strategies)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that its dual-metric evaluation and iterative prompting approach provides a more efficient and time-saving alternative to manual evaluation and revision. However, the study does not report direct time-on-task, workload, or productivity effect sizes; the claim is based on the authors' comparison of AI grading and iterative feedback workflows rather than measured human efficiency outcomes.
finding.measure: Author-reported evaluation workflow efficiency; AI grading versus traditional human evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on academic integrity and reliability concerns in AI-generated scholarly writing, especially fabricated or inaccurate references. It reports that iterative prompting improved citation correctness and in some cases raised reference accuracy from 40% to 80% (Teacher Agency, GPT-only) and from 80% to 100% (Student Agency, GPT-assisted), indicating potential institutional value for safer academic writing workflows.
finding.measure: Reference validity / citation correctness in generated research proposals

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Adoption in Postsecondary Education, AI Hype, and ChatGPT’s Launch
paper_profiles.venue: Open/Technology in Education, Society, and Scholarship Association Journal
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the early public discourse surrounding ChatGPT’s release and how that discourse shaped perceptions of generative AI in postsecondary education. Rather than evaluating learning outcomes, it uses critical discourse analysis to analyze 91 mainstream news articles from The Globe and Mail and The Economist published between November 2022 and May 2023, with a narrowed education subset of 55 articles.

The paper argues that media coverage framed generative AI through hype: emphasizing its overwhelming capabilities, anticipated job loss, anthropomorphic language, and existential risk. In the education context, ChatGPT was portrayed both as an alluring efficiency tool and as a threat to academic integrity and professional roles, which the author argues helped normalize rushed adoption and panic-driven reactions in higher education.

The paper does not report an empirical intervention, student outcome data, or any direct study of writing instruction outcomes. Its main contribution is conceptual and discursive: it calls for more measured, ethical, and policy-aware adoption of generative AI, including attention to student rights, marginalized communities, and institutional governance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that mainstream news discourse around ChatGPT contributed to hype-driven, panic-laden framing of generative AI in education, shaping how institutions and educators perceived adoption. Using critical discourse analysis of 55 education-related articles, it identifies four recurring themes—overwhelming scope of capabilities, impending job loss, anthropomorphism of AI, and vulnerability/fear/existential risk—but reports no direct institutional outcome measures or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Critical discourse analysis of mainstream news coverage about ChatGPT and education
finding.study_size: n=55 education-related articles (subset from 91 total articles)

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence (AI) research in higher education from 2016 to 2022. It asks where the research was conducted, what academic levels and subject domains were studied, who the intended users were, and how AI was used across studies. The review screened 371 records and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles after applying PRISMA-based inclusion criteria.

The paper does not evaluate a single intervention; instead, it maps the field and synthesizes patterns of use. Across the included studies, AI was most often used for assessment/evaluation, predicting student outcomes, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. Language learning was the most common subject domain, and the review notes that writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition were frequent contexts for AI use, but it does not report high-school-only evidence or isolate generative AI chatbots for grades 9-12.

The review concludes that AI research in higher education increased sharply in 2021–2022, with China overtaking the U.S. in publication volume. Most studies focused on undergraduates and students as the intended users. The authors identify gaps in the literature, especially in graduate education, institutional uses, and new tools such as ChatGPT, which they note did not appear in the reviewed corpus because it emerged at the end of 2022.

finding.finding_summary: This review reports that language learning was the most common subject domain (17%) and explicitly notes writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition as frequent uses of AI in higher education. However, it does not synthesize outcome effects for writing quality, revision quality, grammar, vocabulary, or reading-to-write performance, and it does not provide high-school-specific evidence or effect estimates.
finding.measure: Not an outcome study; field-level mapping of AI uses in language learning domains

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (review article; no direct participant population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and conceptual overview of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular focus on chatbots and ChatGPT. The authors describe what AI and chatbots are, summarize potential educational uses such as personalized learning, feedback, automated assessment, and student support, and discuss ethical and practical concerns including privacy, bias, accuracy, and academic integrity.

The article is not an empirical study and does not report a new intervention, sample, or experimental comparison. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature across education broadly, including some references to chatbot-supported learning and AI tools, and argues that AI may improve motivation, engagement, learning outcomes, and teacher efficiency when implemented responsibly and with adequate teacher support. It also emphasizes that AI should be integrated with pedagogical theory and that further research is needed to determine when and how tools like ChatGPT can meaningfully improve teaching and learning.

For the specific sub-question on high-school writing instruction, this paper does not provide direct secondary-school evidence on generative AI chatbots for writing outcomes. Any writing-related discussion is general and illustrative rather than based on high-school studies, delayed posttests, or comparisons against human-feedback baselines.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI chatbots may reduce teacher workload by automating grading, scoring, feedback, and routine student support, but this is presented as a conceptual claim rather than an evaluated result. No study sample, effect size, or implementation test is reported for workload reduction.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / assignment scoring and feedback automation (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI-supported learning may increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and self-regulation through individualized feedback and personalized learning experiences. These claims are synthesized from prior literature, but this article does not present original data, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, confidence, self-regulation (literature synthesis)

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (no human participants; model demonstrations only)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a descriptive, demonstration-style exploration of an early version of GPT-4. The authors ask the model to perform a wide range of tasks across language, coding, mathematics, vision, planning, tool use, and human interaction, with the aim of arguing that GPT-4 exhibits broad, general capabilities that look closer to early artificial general intelligence than prior language models.

The paper is not an education study and does not test students, teachers, or classrooms. Instead, it presents a series of prompted examples such as writing rhymed mathematical proofs, producing code, solving mathematical problems, generating dialogue in a Shakespearean style, and evaluating outputs as if acting like a teacher. The authors compare GPT-4 qualitatively against ChatGPT on selected tasks and emphasize that GPT-4 often produces more coherent, creative, and human-like outputs.

The main conclusion is that GPT-4 shows striking breadth and fluency across many domains, but the evidence is informal, subjective, and not based on controlled experiments. The paper also stresses important limitations, including hallucinations, planning weaknesses, and other errors, and argues that GPT-4 is an important step toward more general AI rather than a finished AGI system.

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes qualitative examples of GPT-4 generating fluent, coherent prose and poetry, including a rhyming proof of infinitely many primes and Shakespeare-style dialogue. However, these are demonstrations of output quality rather than evidence of improved writing instruction or durable writing skill growth, and no student outcomes, delayed posttests, or classroom comparisons are reported.
finding.measure: Quality of generated text / rhetorical style in prompted writing tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests GPT-4 can quickly generate useful artifacts such as code, explanations, and teacher-like evaluations of student work, implying potential productivity gains for writing-related or analytic tasks. But these are informal demonstrations only, with no measured time savings, workload outcomes, or comparison against human baselines in an educational setting.
finding.measure: Informal task completion speed and utility in prompted demonstrations

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of how AI should be integrated into education, with a focus on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It uses the author’s experience with AI adoption at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences (KFH) as a case study, followed by a narrative literature review, to argue that students and teachers need explicit guidance to use generative AI responsibly.

The paper is not an empirical study of student outcomes and does not test an intervention. Instead, it describes institutional AI guidelines developed at KFH, discusses risks such as hallucinations, overreliance, plagiarism, and lack of transparency, and proposes workshops, AI literacy courses, and prompt-engineering instruction as practical responses. It also sketches classroom uses of AI and argues that AI should be treated as a sparring partner rather than a tutor or ghostwriter.

Because the paper focuses on higher education and offers conceptual recommendations rather than direct evidence, it does not provide high-school-specific findings on writing instruction, revision quality, engagement, or durable writing gains. Its main contribution is a normative framework for educator and institutional policy around generative AI use, especially for academic writing and broader AI competence.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes and describes institutional AI guidelines, workshops, and AI-literacy initiatives at a Swiss university, but it does not evaluate their effects empirically. The discussion is policy-oriented and descriptive rather than outcome-based, so no measured institutional impact is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are important skills and repeatedly claims they may help students think more critically about AI outputs. However, it does not report any empirical measurement of critical thinking, metacognition, or other durable-skill gains.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Writing is discussed mainly as an application area for generative AI and AI literacy, including concerns about AI-generated papers and the ethics of using AI for academic writing. The paper does not present direct evidence on writing quality, revision quality, grammar, vocabulary, or reading-to-write performance.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Rankings and Reactivity: How Public Measures Recreate Social Worlds
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines how public quantitative measures reshape the behavior and institutions they are meant to describe, using U.S. News & World Report law school rankings as the central case. The authors ask how ranking systems become reactive—how being measured changes the measured object—and argue that rankings do not merely reflect law school quality but actively reorganize incentives, expectations, and organizational practices.

The study is based on 136 open-ended interviews with law school administrators, faculty, and staff, supplemented by analysis of admissions data, observed admissions events, and organizational materials. The paper identifies two mechanisms of reactivity: self-fulfilling prophecy and commensuration. Through these mechanisms, rankings influence prospective student behavior, reputation surveys, budgeting, admissions selectivity, resource allocation, marketing, and internal decision-making.

The main conclusion is that rankings create meaningful institutional effects by simplifying and standardizing complex organizational differences into a single hierarchy. This hierarchy then feeds back into the system through outside audiences, internal governance, and strategic behavior, producing both intended and unintended consequences such as intensified competition, resource redistribution, mission drift, and gaming strategies. The paper is theoretical and qualitative rather than an intervention study, but it offers a strong account of how public metrics can become consequential social forces.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that public rankings substantially reshape law school behavior and institutional structures, but the effects are mixed. Rankings influence admissions, resource allocation, reputation surveys, fundraising, marketing, and mission definitions, while also producing unintended consequences such as gaming and stratification; the evidence comes from 136 interviews plus supporting observational and archival data, but no causal effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Institutional responses to USN law school rankings (e.g., admissions decisions, budgeting, reputation surveys, marketing, mission change)
finding.study_size: n=136 interviews plus supporting data sources

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that rankings redirect administrative attention and resources toward managing rank rather than core educational goals, creating additional strategic work rather than efficiency gains. Administrators spend time tracking ranking indicators, adapting admissions and budgeting, and gaming criteria, but the paper does not provide a numeric effect size or workload estimate.
finding.measure: Administrative time, strategic planning, and resource allocation behaviors related to rankings

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a structured ChatGPT-guidance framework can improve second-language learners’ argumentative writing and critical thinking. The authors adapt the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model and Hattie & Timperley’s feedback model into a ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW), which prompts students to ask ChatGPT targeted questions about positions, explanations, evidence, and conclusions while composing an essay.

The study used a small randomized experiment with 10 university students split into an experimental group using the CGCAW framework and a control group using ChatGPT without specific guidelines. All participants wrote a short argumentative essay in 40 minutes on the same topic about social media; essays were then scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor using different criteria. Results were mixed: ChatGPT scoring suggested slightly better clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use for the guided group, but Grammarly and the instructor both rated the unguided control group higher overall, especially for language mechanics and thesis/summary quality.

The paper concludes that structured prompting may help some higher-order aspects of argumentative writing, but the framework in its current form may also distract from mechanics and overall argument articulation. The authors emphasize that the guidance needs refinement and that larger, longer-term studies are needed to test whether the approach supports durable writing improvement rather than only short-term output quality.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluated short argumentative essay quality after ChatGPT use. ChatGPT-rated scores slightly favored the guided group for clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence (mean total 74 vs 72.2; specific sub-scores: clarity 20.3 vs 19.4, evidence 17.7 vs 17.0, coherence 18.4 vs 18.0), but Grammarly and the course instructor rated the control group higher overall (Grammarly mean 92.2 vs 90.6; instructor mean 56 vs 35). This suggests the CGCAW prompt framework may improve some output features while reducing or failing to improve other aspects of writing quality such as mechanics, thesis strength, and summary quality.
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and course instructor on clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness, grammar/punctuation/clarity, thesis, reasoning, counterarguments, and summary
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT total SD=7.6 (Group 1) and 5.5 (Group 2); Grammarly and instructor SD not fully reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the structured ChatGPT guidance was intended to support self-regulation and that the authors discuss it as encouraging reflection and monitoring during writing, but the empirical evidence is limited. One practical indicator of struggle was that 2 participants in the guided group could not complete the essay within the 40-minute window because they were unfamiliar with the framework, suggesting added cognitive or procedural burden rather than clear engagement gains. No direct validated engagement or self-regulation scale was reported.
finding.measure: Task completion within a timed writing session; author interpretation of self-regulation/feedback use

finding.finding_summary: This study substantively targeted critical thinking as part of argumentative writing, using the Paul-Elder model to frame claims, evidence, inferences, and implications. On ChatGPT’s rubric, the guided group scored somewhat higher on clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use, which the authors interpret as improved critical-thinking-related writing performance; however, instructor and Grammarly ratings did not corroborate an overall improvement, and there was no delayed posttest or retention measure to show durable skill growth after AI removal.
finding.measure: Critical-thinking-aligned argumentative writing features (clarity, logical coherence, evidence use, thesis, counterarguments, summary)
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT group-level SDs reported as 7.6 and 5.5 for total score

finding.finding_summary: The guided framework did not improve task efficiency in this short implementation. Two of five participants in the experimental group failed to complete the essay within the allotted 40 minutes because they were unfamiliar with the CGCAW prompts, indicating that the additional structured workflow may have slowed writing rather than speeding it up. No formal time-on-task analysis beyond completion was reported.
finding.measure: Essay completion within a 40-minute timed task

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models for Automated Grading of Student Writing about Science
paper_profiles.venue: arXiv / conference-preprint cited as Golchin et al. 2024
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether GPT-4 can reliably grade short student writing assignments in science MOOCs and whether it can generate grading rubrics that produce scores comparable to an instructor’s. The motivating problem is the difficulty of assessing open-ended writing at scale in large online classes, where peer grading is commonly used but can be unreliable.

The authors sampled 120 learner responses across 12 writing questions from three Coursera MOOCs on astronomy, astrobiology, and the history and philosophy of astronomy. They compared three grading conditions: instructor grading, Coursera peer grading, and GPT-4 grading under different prompts (example answer only; example answer plus instructor rubric; example answer plus GPT-generated rubric). They also tested whether AI-generated rubrics could support grading accuracy.

Results showed that GPT-4’s grades were significantly different from instructor grades when only given an example answer, but not significantly different when paired with a rubric, whether instructor-created or GPT-created. GPT-4 was generally more aligned with the instructor than peer grading, and the reported ICC of 0.92 (95% CI 0.89–0.94) indicated excellent agreement among graders. However, performance varied by course and prompt, with weaker alignment on more open-ended, subjective questions in the history/philosophy course. The study is about automated assessment rather than student learning, so it provides evidence for operational scalability and grading reliability, not direct evidence that AI improves writing skill.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 substantially improved grading scalability by producing rubric-based grades that were not statistically different from instructor grades when given an example answer plus a rubric. Across 120 student responses to 12 questions, agreement was high (ICC=0.92, 95% CI 0.89–0.94), and the authors conclude the model could help automate grading of science writing in large online courses.
finding.measure: Agreement/reliability of grades; comparison of GPT-4, instructor, and peer scores on writing assignments

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies evaluation of science writing rather than student writing development: GPT-4 was able to grade short answers about astronomy/astrobiology at a level close to instructor scoring when provided with sufficient rubric information. The strongest alignment occurred with instructor answer + rubric prompts, while example-answer-only prompts were less accurate and sometimes significantly different from instructor grades.
finding.measure: Scores on science writing assignments in astronomy, astrobiology, and history/philosophy of astronomy MOOCs

paper_profiles.title: Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students’ essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT-3 improves students’ essay writing performance when used as a writing assistant. The authors compare a small control group that wrote traditionally with an experimental group that used ChatGPT-3 during a single essay-writing task. They evaluate overall essay quality using a rubric, along with writing time, authenticity/plagiarism-related indicators, essay similarity, and AI-generated text detection.

The study used 18 second-year master’s students in forensic sciences at the University of Split, Croatia (n=9 control, n=9 ChatGPT-assisted). Students wrote one 800–1000 word Croatian essay under a four-hour time limit; two teachers scored the essays on mechanics, style, content, and format, and the researchers also measured unauthentic text proportion, pairwise similarity, and classifier labels. The experimental group received an introduction to ChatGPT, but the paper does not report iterative teacher mediation, repeated prompt training, or delayed posttests after AI removal.

Results showed no statistically significant benefit from ChatGPT on essay score, writing duration, or authenticity measures. The control group slightly outperformed the ChatGPT group on mean essay score (2.39 ± 0.71 vs. 2.00 ± 0.73 on a 1–4 scale), and regression indicated no significant effect of group (P=0.184), writing duration, module, or GPA on essay score. The authors conclude that ChatGPT did not improve student essay quality in this setting and may have slightly underperformed compared with traditional writing.

finding.finding_summary: The study found no evidence that ChatGPT improved essay quality. Overall essay score was slightly higher in the control group than the ChatGPT group (2.39 ± 0.71 vs. 2.00 ± 0.73 on a 1–4 scale), and group status was not a significant predictor of score (P=0.184) in regression.
finding.measure: Teacher-scored essay rubric covering mechanics, style, content, and format; overall essay grade (A-D converted to 4-1)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT did not reduce writing time. The experimental group took 172.22 ± 31.59 minutes versus 179.11 ± 31.93 minutes in the control group, and writing duration was not a significant predictor of essay score (P=0.669).
finding.measure: Essay writing duration in minutes

finding.finding_summary: The paper examined whether ChatGPT increased text unauthenticity or detectable AI-like content, but found only a slight difference between groups. Mean text unauthenticity was 11.87% ± 13.45 in the ChatGPT group and 9.96% ± 9.81 in the control group, while essay similarity across students was generally low (median Jaccard similarity 0.002; range 0–0.054).
finding.measure: PlagScan-based authenticity/unauthenticity, Jaccard similarity, AI text classifier labels

paper_profiles.title: CodEv: An Automated Grading Framework Leveraging Large Language Models for Consistent and Constructive Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents CodEv, an automated grading framework for programming assignments that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate scores, reasoning steps, and constructive feedback. The authors focus on improving grading consistency and reducing educator workload by combining chain-of-thought prompting, ensemble voting, and agreement testing, then evaluating the framework against human grading benchmarks.

The experiments use introductory programming-course code submissions from a university information-technology context, with 30 randomly selected students per programming task and teaching assistants’ manual grading as the benchmark. The paper compares several models (Llama 3.1 8B/70B, Gemma2 9B, GPT-4o), showing that ensemble methods improve stability and reduce mean absolute error for smaller models, while large models remain closer to human scores overall. Intra-model and inter-model agreement is high, and generated comments receive moderate G-Eval quality scores, but the authors note that feedback quality still needs improvement and that models can be overly strict or hallucinate in edge cases.

This is not a study of student writing instruction or generative AI chatbots for high-school writing. It is an automated code-grading study in higher education, so it does not provide direct evidence for the requested K-12 writing outcomes. The paper does, however, offer evidence on operational efficiency and reliability of AI-assisted grading and feedback in programming education.

finding.finding_summary: CodEv reduces grading error for smaller models and aims to lower instructor workload by automating code scoring and feedback generation. With an ensemble size of 10, MAE improved from 17.22 to 12.66 for Llama3.1 8B and from 20.61 to 12.32 for Gemma2 9B compared with zero-shot prompting, suggesting more efficient and closer-to-human grading. The paper does not report time-on-task savings, but it explicitly frames the system as a way to reduce grading time and effort.
finding.measure: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between model scores and human TA scores; grading consistency (ICC)
finding.study_size: n=30 students per task across 3 programming tasks; 20 repeated queries per model for agreement tests
finding.confidence_interval: MAE/ICC CIs not reported for the efficiency outcome

finding.finding_summary: The framework is positioned as a scalable institutional tool for automated assessment in programming courses, with the goal of making large-scale grading more consistent and less labor-intensive. The paper reports high intra-model agreement (ICC(2,k)=0.971 to 0.998) and inter-model agreement (ICC(3,k)=0.840), supporting reliability for institutional use, but it does not evaluate policy, adoption, or broader organizational outcomes.
finding.measure: Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) for intra-model and inter-model agreement; comment quality via G-Eval
finding.study_size: 4 LLMs; 20 repeated queries per model; 20 sampled comments for G-Eval

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Generative AI assisted feedback writing for students’ written responses to a physics conceptual question with prompt engineering and few-shot learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether GPT-3.5 can act as a grading and feedback assistant for short student written responses to a physics conceptual question. The authors focus on prompt engineering and few-shot learning, using a small set of labeled response-feedback examples plus explicit physics preconceptions to improve the model’s feedback quality.

The study uses student responses from an introductory physics course taught in a studio format at the University of Central Florida (class enrollment n=99; 85 responses collected). In stage 1, the authors iteratively refined prompts using 20 responses and then generated feedback for 16 additional responses. In stage 2, four physics-education-research student raters compared GPT-generated feedback to author-written feedback on perceived correctness and usefulness and tried to identify which was AI-generated. In stage 3, four instructors rated 65 additional GPT-generated feedback statements by how much editing would be needed before using them.

The main findings are that GPT-generated and human-written feedback were perceived as similarly correct, while GPT-generated feedback was judged more useful by all student raters. Student raters identified AI-generated feedback at low rates overall, and instructors judged roughly 68%–78% of GPT outputs as needing only minor or no modification (average rating 2.06/3). The paper concludes that GPT-3.5 can feasibly assist with feedback generation for conceptual physics responses, potentially reducing instructor workload, but it is an exploratory study with a small sample and no direct measure of student learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-3.5 substantially reduced the amount of instructor editing needed for feedback generation in this exploratory study. Four instructors rated 68%–78% of 65 GPT-generated feedback statements as needing only minor or no modification, with an average rating of 2.06/3 on a 0–3 edit-needed scale.
finding.measure: Instructor ratings of how much modification/editing GPT-generated feedback needed before use
finding.study_size: n=65 feedback statements rated by 4 instructors

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on feedback for conceptual physics reasoning about Newton’s laws and whether force is 'transmitted' between boxes. GPT-generated feedback was judged similarly correct to human-written feedback by student raters, and the authors reported that all 65 outputs were largely usable with minor edits in most cases.
finding.measure: Perceived correctness and usefulness of feedback on physics conceptual written responses
finding.study_size: n=16 responses for student-rater comparison; n=65 responses for instructor edit ratings

paper_profiles.title: Grading Massive Open Online Courses Using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can replace peer grading for writing assignments in massive open online courses (MOOCs). The authors focus on grading and feedback quality rather than student learning: they compare GPT-4 and GPT-3.5, using zero-shot chain-of-thought prompts with three prompting variants—correct answers only, correct answers plus instructor rubrics, and correct answers plus LLM-generated rubrics.

The study uses data from three astronomy-related MOOCs: Introductory Astronomy, Astrobiology, and History and Philosophy of Astronomy. The authors evaluate 12 assignments from 10 students per course (120 question-level responses per prompt) and compare LLM-assigned grades against instructor grades and peer grades, using average scores, mean absolute error, and bootstrap resampling. Instructors serve as the ground truth, and peer grading is the baseline.

The main finding is that GPT-4, especially when given instructor-provided correct answers and rubrics, produces grades more closely aligned with instructor grades than peer grading does. LLM-generated rubrics perform comparably to instructor rubrics in many settings. The paper also reports that LLM feedback is more detailed and consistent than peer feedback. However, this is an automated grading study in adult MOOCs, not a study of K-12 writing instruction or student writing growth, so it does not provide direct high-school evidence for generative AI chatbots improving writing skills.

finding.finding_summary: Across three MOOCs and 120 question-level grading instances per prompt, GPT-4 with instructor-provided correct answers and rubrics produced scores more closely aligned with instructor grades than peer grading. The paper reports lower mean absolute error for GPT-4 than peer grades in many settings (overall MAE 1.01 vs. 1.35 for raw scores in Table 3; bootstrap overall MAE 1.92 vs. 2.09 for peer in Table 4), suggesting automated grading can reduce grading burden while preserving alignment with instructor judgments.
finding.measure: Agreement/alignment of LLM-assigned grades with instructor grades; mean absolute error (MAE); bootstrap resampled MAE; average grades
finding.study_size: n=10 students per course across 3 MOOCs; 120 question-level responses per prompt
finding.std_deviation: reported at the question level in tables (e.g., grades shown as mean±SD), but not aggregated as a single value

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies grading of open-ended astronomy and philosophy-of-astronomy writing assignments, not student learning gains. GPT-4 with rubrics generally matched instructor scoring better than peer grading, including on more imaginative or speculative prompts, and the authors conclude that LLMs can provide more accurate and consistent assignment scoring in these subject areas than peer graders.
finding.measure: Assignment grades on open-ended MOOC writing responses
finding.study_size: n=10 students per course across 3 MOOCs
finding.std_deviation: reported at the question level in tables (mean±SD)

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure student motivation or self-regulation directly, but it does compare the feedback quality produced by LLMs versus peers. The authors state that LLM feedback was more consistent and comprehensive than peer graders’ feedback and more likely to provide constructive explanations for point deductions, which may indirectly support student engagement, though no learner outcomes were tested.
finding.measure: Qualitative comparison of feedback consistency and completeness
finding.study_size: n=10 students per course across 3 MOOCs

paper_profiles.title: Can AI grade your essays? A comparative analysis of large language models and teacher ratings in multidimensional essay scoring
paper_profiles.venue: LAK '25 (Proceedings of the 15th International Conference on Learning Analytics and Knowledge)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably score student essays in a way that aligns with human teacher judgments. The motivation is practical: essay scoring is time-consuming for teachers, and the authors investigate whether generative AI could support assessment and reduce workload.

The study compares five LLMs—GPT-3.5, GPT-4, o1, LLaMA 3-70B, and Mixtral 8x7B—against ratings from 37 German teachers. The authors evaluate 20 real-world narrative essays written by Year 7 and Year 8 students from two secondary schools in Germany, using 10 predefined criteria covering content and language dimensions (e.g., plot logic, expression, spelling, overall judgment). Each model rated each essay 10 times with a zero-shot prompt framed as teacher-like evaluation, and the model outputs were compared to teacher averages.

Results show that the closed-source GPT models, especially o1, aligned much better with teacher judgments than the open-source models. o1 had the strongest overall correlation with teachers (Spearman r=.742 for overall score) and high correlations on language-related criteria such as spelling (r=.814), literal speech (r=.805), and verbal imagery (r=.738). However, the models tended to give higher scores than teachers, and the largest disagreements appeared on content-related criteria such as introduction, main part, and plot logic, where teacher judgment was more decisive. Open-source models performed poorly, with low or near-zero correlations and low internal consistency across repeated runs.

Overall, the paper concludes that current LLMs can be useful for assisting essay assessment, particularly for language-related surface features, but they are not yet reliable replacements for teachers—especially for deeper content evaluation. The study is about automated scoring rather than instruction or student learning, so it does not provide direct evidence on writing improvement, revision quality, or durable writing-skill growth.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLMs, especially o1, could reduce teacher workload by supporting essay scoring. The authors report strong agreement with teacher ratings for o1 on the overall score (Spearman r=.742) and moderate-to-high reliability across repeated runs for closed-source models (ICC=.73-.84), suggesting potential usefulness as an assistive assessment tool rather than a substitute for human grading.
finding.measure: Essay scoring reliability and agreement with teacher ratings; inter-rater correlation (Spearman r) and internal consistency (ICC)
finding.study_size: n=20 essays, 37 teachers, 5 LLMs, 10 repeated runs per essay per model

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies writing assessment across multidimensional essay criteria, including language-related aspects of written literacy. LLMs aligned best with teacher ratings on surface-language criteria such as spelling (o1 r=.814), expression (r=.675), and verbal imagery (r=.738), but performed less well on content-heavy writing dimensions like introduction and main part; open-source models showed weak or near-zero agreement with teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated essay quality across writing dimensions: spelling & punctuation, expression & sentence structure, verbal images & descriptive elements, literal speech & inner monologue, plot logic, headline, introduction, main part, conclusion, overall judgment

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative case study examines how four secondary-school EFL students in Hong Kong used ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots for the first time to complete a timed blog-writing task. The paper is focused on prompt engineering: what kinds of prompts students produced, how those prompts changed across turns, and how students combined prompt types while trying to get useful output from chatbots.

Students completed a familiar blog-entry writing task in class on iPads, with the first author teaching the lesson and screen recordings capturing their interactions. The paper code-mapped 36 usable prompt turns and identified six prompt types plus several more complex combinations, showing that students relied on trial-and-error rather than any prior prompt training. Students used chatbot output mainly for idea generation and text extension; the study does not measure writing quality, revision quality, grammar, fluency, engagement, or learning gains in the written products.

The main conclusion is that secondary students can experiment with generative chatbots in varied ways, but their prompt pathways are unsophisticated without instruction. The authors argue that prompt-engineering education may help students move beyond ad hoc trial-and-error and better exploit chatbot capabilities in EFL writing classrooms. Because the study is descriptive and does not compare writing outcomes against a control condition, it provides process evidence rather than evidence of impact on writing performance.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines student use of ChatGPT and other chatbots during a writing task, but it does not evaluate the quality of the resulting writing products against any baseline. The paper reports 36 coded prompt turns from 4 secondary students and describes prompt types and pathways, not changes in writing quality, revision quality, grammar/mechanics, vocabulary, or retention after AI removal.
finding.measure: prompt content and sequencing during a blog-writing task; completed writing samples collected but not analyzed for quality outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses student exploration, trial-and-error, and possible confidence/ignorance around chatbot use, but these are interpretive observations rather than measured effects. No engagement, motivation, self-regulation, or persistence scale was administered, so the study provides no direct evidence that chatbot use improved or harmed social-emotional skills.
finding.measure: observed prompting behavior and qualitative interpretation of trial-and-error pathways

finding.finding_summary: The central construct is prompt engineering, which the authors frame as an emergent skill involving strategy selection and refinement. However, the study only documents moment-to-moment prompting behavior in a single session and does not test durable growth in metacognition, transfer, or independent prompt-use after instruction or AI removal.
finding.measure: qualitative analysis of prompt pathways, prompt types, and sequencing

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how elementary students and teachers perceived a generative-AI-supported creative mathematical writing activity. The authors are interested in whether a GenAI-powered platform can support students in composing math stories and how students and teachers experience its benefits and challenges in authentic classroom use.

The intervention was a three-step sequence—Ask, Represent, Transform—implemented with 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers across two U.S. elementary schools. Students used a GenAI system built with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to draft, modify, and evaluate culturally relevant math stories based on fraction topics. The study collected focus-group interviews, teacher interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations; the analysis was thematic rather than outcome-based.

The main findings were perceptual rather than achievement-based. Students and teachers reported benefits related to creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, interest, curiosity, and ownership, but they also raised concerns about overreliance on AI, insufficient room for improvement, lack of adaptive feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connection, and accessibility limitations. The paper does not provide direct evidence on writing quality, revision quality, grammar/mechanics, fluency, or delayed retention, and it does not compare the GenAI approach against a human-feedback baseline.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived the GenAI-supported activity as helpful for creative mathematical story writing, mathematical understanding, and AI literacy, but the study did not measure writing performance directly. Across 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers, thematic analysis suggested the tool supported divergent/convergent thinking, originality, and story development, while also creating challenges such as overly polished AI output and limited room for student improvement.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions from interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that the GenAI activity increased interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning. Thematic evidence from 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers indicated that students felt more engaged and motivated when creating math stories with AI, though some also wanted more autonomy and less dependence on the system.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership from interviews/surveys/observations

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests GenAI use may support creativity-related durable skills, including divergent thinking, convergent thinking, flexibility, originality, and prompt engineering. These findings were based on qualitative perceptions rather than direct skill assessments, and no transfer or retention test was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived creativity, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI output

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that GenAI could speed up story generation and reduce the burden of starting from scratch, making the writing task feel easier and quicker. However, the study also noted that the system lacked adaptive feedback and could not replace teacher mediation, so the efficiency gains were partial and accompanied by new support needs.
finding.measure: Perceived task efficiency and ease of story drafting/revision

finding.finding_summary: The GenAI-supported creative math writing activity was perceived to strengthen students’ mathematical understanding, especially problem comprehension, representation of mathematical ideas, and identification of misconceptions. Across 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers, the Ask/Represent/Transform routine was described as helping students break down word problems and connect story elements to fraction concepts, but no quantitative achievement data were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding and representation in story-based math tasks

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation of ChatGPT feedback on ELL writers’ coherence and cohesion
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can generate useful writing feedback for English Language Learner (ELL) essays, focusing specifically on coherence and cohesion. The authors argue that while generative AI tools are increasingly used for writing support, there is little evidence that they provide accurate, actionable feedback on higher-order concerns such as organization, logical sequencing, and idea development.

Using 50 grade-12 essays from the ELLIPSE corpus, the authors prompted GPT-4 to generate a coherence/cohesion score and written feedback under several prompt variants (default vs. personalized prompts; with vs. without sample essays). They compared model scores to human rubric scores and performed a detailed linguistic analysis of the feedback, including sentence-type coding (positive reinforcement, problem statement, explicit example, indirect suggestion) and qualitative comparison against expert-written feedback.

Results showed that GPT-4’s numeric scores aligned reasonably well with human scores (quadratic weighted kappa around 0.78-0.82; Pearson correlation 0.81-0.86), especially with a personalized prompt, but the feedback itself was often generic, rubric-like, and insufficiently actionable. The model overfocused on surface features such as transitional words and repetitive phrases, sometimes misdiagnosing essays whose main issues were actually missing development, contradictions, or broader organization problems. The paper concludes that untrained ChatGPT is not effective for coherence/cohesion feedback and should not be relied on alone for high-school writing instruction without task-specific prompting or model tuning.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that GPT-4 could approximate human coherence scores for 50 grade-12 ELL essays (quadratic weighted kappa=0.78-0.82; Pearson r=0.81-0.86), but the generated feedback was often inaccurate, generic, and not actionable for revision. Human experts judged that the model overemphasized surface cohesion markers (especially transition words) and sometimes missed central organizational problems or idea development issues.
finding.measure: Human-vs-system coherence score agreement; qualitative accuracy/usability of coherence/cohesion feedback on essays

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides indirect evidence that the feedback had limited support for meaningful revision and self-regulated writing improvement, because it was too generic and focused on superficial cues rather than deeper organizational issues. The authors argue that students would not be able to make meaningful adjustments from this feedback alone, and that simply adding or removing transitions did not improve scores in four modified-essay trials.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of revision usefulness; score stability after minor connectives manipulation
finding.study_size: n=4 modified essays for robustness check; n=50 essays for feedback analysis

paper_profiles.title: AI-Mediated Feedback Improves Student Revisions: A Randomized Trial with FeedbackWriter in a Large Undergraduate Course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies whether large-language-model-assisted feedback provision improves student writing revisions compared with human-only feedback. The core question is not whether AI writes essays, but whether AI can help human evaluators produce better feedback that leads to better revisions and learning.

The authors built FeedbackWriter, a human-AI collaborative system that generates rubric-aligned feedback suggestions for teaching assistants (TAs) while preserving TA control to adopt, edit, or dismiss suggestions. The system was deployed in a large introductory economics course at a public R1 university, where 354 undergraduates completed two writing assignments with first drafts, formative feedback, and revised final drafts. TAs in the AI condition saw AI suggestions embedded in their workflow; the baseline condition used the same interface and rubrics but without AI suggestions.

Results show that AI-mediated feedback improved revision quality: students in the AI condition produced higher-quality final drafts than those receiving human-only feedback, with Cohen’s d = 0.50. The effect grew when TAs adopted more AI-generated constructive feedback. However, the post-test measuring learning after revision showed no statistically significant difference between conditions, suggesting the main benefit was stronger revisions rather than clearly detectable durable learning gains. TAs also rated the AI suggestions as useful for spotting missed issues and clarifying rubrics, but grading time did not decrease.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized trial with 354 undergraduates and 1,366 graded essays, AI-mediated feedback led to significantly higher-quality revised drafts than human-only feedback. The main revision-quality outcome improved by Cohen’s d = 0.50, with the authors describing this as roughly equivalent to moving a student from the 50th to the 70th percentile; the comparison was against human-only TA feedback using the same rubrics and workflow but without AI suggestions.
finding.measure: LLM-based rubric-scored final draft quality / revised essay quality

finding.finding_summary: The study focused on knowledge-intensive economics writing, where students had to apply course concepts in essays and then revise based on feedback. AI-mediated feedback improved the quality of these economics essays relative to human-only feedback, but the rubric emphasized conceptual accuracy and analysis rather than prose polish alone.
finding.measure: Rubric-scored economics essay revision quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper included a post-test after revision as a proxy for learning and reported no statistically significant difference between AI-mediated and human-only feedback conditions on post-test scores. Because the study did not directly measure motivation, engagement, or self-regulation as student outcomes, this is only a limited fit for this category and the central result here is null learning rather than socio-emotional change.
finding.measure: Post-test score following revision (optional extra-credit quiz)
finding.study_size: n=262 post-test completers for Assignment 1; n=305 for Assignment 2

finding.finding_summary: Despite AI assistance, TA grading time did not decrease; the authors explicitly report comparable time spent grading in both conditions. TAs found the AI suggestions useful and the system helped them spot overlooked errors and clarify rubrics, but the intervention did not yield measurable efficiency gains in the observed deployment.
finding.measure: Per-essay grading time from system logs; TA workflow observations/interviews

paper_profiles.title: AI as a Teaching Partner: Early Lessons from Classroom Codesign with Secondary Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report examines how secondary teachers integrated a generative AI classroom platform, Colleague AI, into instruction during a seven-week pilot in spring 2025. The project focused on whether AI could function as a “third agent” in classrooms by supporting teacher-designed student conversations, generating rubric-based formative feedback, aiding AI-assisted grading, and summarizing student growth patterns for teachers.

The pilot involved 21 in-service teachers across five Washington State sites and an independent school, with more than 600 students in grades 6-12 participating in teacher-directed activities. Teachers created 114 AI-assisted conversations and 58 assessment activities, and the report combines surveys, planning/reflection artifacts, group meetings, interviews, and platform logs.
