The evidence is exploratory and largely descriptive: teachers generally reported that AI was most useful when tightly scaffolded, aligned to clear instructional goals, and mediated by teacher oversight.

For writing-related use cases, the report indicates that high school English teachers used AI for prewriting and brainstorming and that this improved essay quality, but it does not provide direct quantitative evidence on writing quality, revision quality, grammar/mechanics, vocabulary, fluency, delayed retention, or comparisons against strong human-feedback baselines. Across assessment use, teachers valued AI-generated narrative feedback more than numeric scores, and they frequently used the tool as a first-pass feedback scaffold while retaining final grading authority. Overall, the report suggests promising but early-stage instructional uses of generative AI, with outcomes shaped heavily by teacher framing, prompt design, and implementation experience.

finding.finding_summary: The report offers direct but mostly qualitative evidence that generative AI supported some writing-related classroom tasks, especially prewriting and brainstorming in high school English, which teachers said improved essay quality. However, it does not report controlled comparisons, standardized writing scores, delayed posttests, or separate evidence on revision quality, grammar/mechanics, vocabulary, or transfer after AI removal; much of the writing evidence is based on teacher report rather than student artifact analysis.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of essay quality, prewriting/brainstorming usefulness, and AI-assisted written assessment feedback

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-supported conversations and feedback often increased student engagement, confidence, and willingness to participate, especially for students who were anxious, multilingual, or initially reluctant to speak. Engagement was strongest when teachers framed tasks clearly and tied AI use to meaningful classroom products; however, many classrooms showed mixed engagement and some students found feedback overwhelming or superficial.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated student engagement with Teaching Aide conversations; observations of student response to AI feedback
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers for Teaching Aide exit tickets; 13 teachers for assessment feedback survey; platform logs covered 33 classrooms and 936 submissions

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests potential gains in inquiry, evidence-based reasoning, and self-regulation when teachers scaffolded AI use, but the evidence is indirect and exploratory. Teachers described students revising work in response to narrative feedback, asking more focused questions, and engaging in deeper dialogue when prompts were well designed; at the same time, unstructured use often led to shallow exchanges or off-task behavior, and the study did not measure durable skill growth with delayed posttests.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on student inquiry, revision, and depth of dialogue; resubmission behavior in AI-assisted assessments

finding.finding_summary: The strongest and most directly supported finding concerns teacher workflow efficiency: AI grading and feedback reduced the burden of creating first-draft comments and surfaced class-wide patterns for reteaching. Platform logs show 58 assessments across 33 classrooms with mean submission rates of 54.8% and median AI grading coverage of 92.2%, and teachers reported that narrative feedback and Student Growth Insights saved time and streamlined formative assessment, even though numeric scores were sometimes inconsistent.
finding.measure: AI grading coverage, resubmission rates, teacher survey responses on rubric utility and feedback usefulness, and teacher reports of time savings
finding.study_size: 58 classroom-level assessment records; 33 classrooms; 19 teachers in assessment phase; 13 teacher survey respondents

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that successful classroom AI adoption depends on teacher AI competency, pedagogical framing, and oversight structures, implying institutional support needs rather than student-level treatment effects. Teachers generally preferred a collaborative model in which AI augmented instruction while teachers retained final authority, but this is presented as implementation insight rather than a measured school- or district-level outcome.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections on implementation conditions, trust, and classroom integration

paper_profiles.title: phyloseq: An R Package for Reproducible Interactive Analysis and Graphics of Microbiome Census Data
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces phyloseq, an open-source R/Bioconductor software package for importing, integrating, analyzing, and visualizing microbiome census data. The authors describe how the package helps researchers handle heterogeneous high-throughput sequencing outputs, perform ecological distance calculations and ordination, generate publication-quality graphics, and support reproducible research workflows.

The manuscript is primarily a software/ methods paper rather than an empirical evaluation of an intervention on human participants. Its central contribution is a framework for more reproducible and less error-prone microbiome data analysis, with examples showing how the package can process and visualize publicly available datasets. The paper does not study education, writing, or any K-12 intervention, and it contains no relevant evidence for high-school automated writing evaluation or feedback systems.

paper_profiles.title: Neural Automated Writing Evaluation with Corrective Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes an integrated neural system that combines automated writing evaluation (AWE) with grammatical error correction (GEC) for language learners. The system is designed to provide instantaneous holistic and rubric-based scoring together with inline corrective feedback, with the goal of supporting writing practice, simulating examination conditions, and reducing instructor workload.

The paper is primarily a system description and methods paper rather than a student outcome study. It describes the AWE component trained on ASAP/ASAP++ and the GEC component trained on several learner-language corpora, then reports a prompt-by-prompt evaluation of essay-scoring performance (QWK) on the denoised versus original ASAP data, with the denoised condition improving average QWK slightly (0.6047 to 0.6143). It also outlines a planned perception study with learner and instructor questionnaires about fairness, clarity, helpfulness, and mental effort, but no learner outcome results are reported in the paper. As a result, the paper offers technical evidence for system performance and implementation ideas, but not direct evidence of writing gains for grades 9-12 students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that integrating AWE and GEC can reduce teacher burden by providing instant scoring and corrective feedback and by automating correction of innumerable essays. This is a design/efficiency claim rather than a learner-outcome result; no classroom workload trial is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload / automated scoring and feedback workflow

paper_profiles.title: Annotation and Classification of Evidence and Reasoning Revisions in Argumentative Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core problem in automated writing evaluation (AWE): whether students actually use system feedback to make revisions that improve their writing, rather than merely changing text superficially. The authors argue that prior work on revision analysis in AWE has mostly tracked broad revision types such as addition, deletion, or surface vs. content changes, but has not assessed whether revisions specifically respond to feedback and improve the targeted aspect of writing.

To address this, the paper develops the Revision of Evidence and Reasoning (RER) annotation scheme for sentence-level analysis of argumentative essay revisions. The scheme was applied to 143 first- and second-draft essays from 5th- and 6th-grade students using the eRevise AWE system, which provided feedback on evidence use and reasoning in response-to-text argument writing. The study reports strong inter-rater reliability and shows that desirable revision types, especially adding relevant evidence and linking evidence to claims, are positively associated with a holistic improvement score aligned to the feedback students received.

The paper also tests a simple automatic classifier for identifying whether evidence revisions are relevant, using word-embedding features and logistic regression. The classifier outperforms a majority baseline intrinsically, but the extrinsic gains are limited and do not fully match human labels. Overall, the study concludes that revision quality can be meaningfully assessed at the sentence level and that such a scheme may support future automated feedback systems, though the current work is exploratory and limited to a small elementary-grade corpus rather than a high-school sample.

finding.finding_summary: In a corpus of 143 essays from 5th- and 6th-grade students using eRevise, desirable evidence/reasoning revisions were positively associated with a holistic improvement score for argumentative writing aligned to system feedback. Adding relevant evidence correlated with improvement (r = .20 overall; add relevant r = .25, p < .01), and adding reasoning that linked evidence to the claim showed the strongest relationship (r = .41 overall; add LCE r = .45, p < .01).
finding.measure: Holistic improvement score for evidence use and reasoning in argumentative essay revisions; revision category counts and correlations with improvement score

paper_profiles.title: Automated Topical Component Extraction Using Neural Network Attention Scores from Source-based Essay Scoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a technical problem in automated writing evaluation (AWE) for source-based essay writing: how to automatically extract Topical Components (TCs), the rubric-relevant evidence units used to score students’ use of source text evidence. The authors note that prior AWE systems required expert-created TCs, which is costly and limits scalability. Their goal is to use attention scores from a neural automated essay scoring model to recover TCs automatically, preserving the interpretability needed for downstream formative feedback.

The study evaluates a new method, TCattn, on two response-to-text assessment datasets (RTAMV P and RTASpace) containing essays written by students in grades 4-8. The method extracts sentence-level and phrase-level attention outputs from a neural AES model, clusters the resulting text spans, and constructs topic words and example phrases. They compare TCattn against human-made TCs (TCmanual) and two automated baselines (TClda and TCpr). On the downstream Evidence-scoring task, AESrubric using TCattn matches or slightly exceeds the human-created TC baseline in quadratic weighted kappa (e.g., 0.648 vs. 0.643 on RTAMV P; 0.622 vs. 0.609 on RTASpace), and the feature values derived from TCattn correlate strongly with human Evidence scores (e.g., r=0.639 for NPE on RTAMV P; r=0.625 on RTASpace).

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that automatically extracted Topical Components (TCattn) support source-based essay evidence scoring about as well as human-created TCs, and in some cases slightly better. Using TCattn in the AESrubric model produced QWK of 0.648 on RTAMV P and 0.622 on RTASpace, compared with 0.643 and 0.609 for TCmanual, respectively; feature-score correlations with human Evidence scores were also strong (e.g., NPE r=0.639 on RTAMV P and r=0.625 on RTASpace).
finding.measure: Quadratic weighted kappa for Evidence scoring; Pearson correlation between TC-derived features and human Evidence scores
finding.study_size: n=2970 essays (RTAMV P) and n=2076 essays (RTASpace)

finding.finding_summary: The main contribution is methodological efficiency: TCattn eliminates the need for manual expert creation of Topical Components while maintaining downstream scoring performance. The authors conclude that the approach can remove expert effort in TC extraction without degrading AESrubric performance or the underlying feature representations, suggesting a scalable route for building formative writing systems.
finding.measure: Need for manual expert TC creation; downstream AESrubric performance using automated versus manual TCs

paper_profiles.title: Human-AI Collaborative Essay Scoring: A Dual-Process Framework with LLMs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can support automated essay scoring (AES) and human grading in a high-school English writing context. The authors ask whether LLMs can produce accurate scores and useful feedback, how they compare with established AES baselines, and whether their outputs can improve human graders’ performance and efficiency.

The study evaluates GPT-4, GPT-3.5, and LLaMA3 on the ASAP benchmark and on a private Chinese high-school essay dataset (CSEE) drawn from 29 schools and 13,372 essays. The models are tested in zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned settings, with and without rubrics and explanations. The authors then propose a dual-process AES framework that separates a fast score-prediction module from a slower explanation-generating module, using confidence thresholds to decide when to escalate cases for deeper reasoning or human review.

Results show that prompting alone performs poorly, especially for GPT-4 in zero-shot settings, while fine-tuning substantially improves scoring accuracy but generally still does not beat strong traditional AES baselines. The proposed framework achieves competitive scoring and explanation quality, with performance on the high-school dataset around QWK=0.7162 on ASAP and QWK=0.7634 on CSEE for the integrated system. In a human-AI co-grading experiment with 10 novice teacher candidates and 5 experienced high-school English teachers, LLM feedback improved novice grading accuracy from QWK=0.5256 to 0.6609 and increased expert efficiency/consistency, suggesting value as a grader-support tool rather than as a fully autonomous writing tutor.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies high-school essay scoring and feedback quality. On the CSEE high-school dataset (n=13,372 essays), the integrated system achieved QWK=0.7634 overall (content 0.7347, language 0.7192, structure 0.6656), outperforming the BERT baseline (overall QWK=0.7674 on the same dataset was slightly higher than the integrated system, but the authors’ best LLM system was competitive and better than prompting-only variants). In the human-co-grading pilot (n=50 essays; 10 novice graders, 5 expert graders), LLM feedback improved novice grading accuracy from QWK=0.5256 to 0.6609 and expert grading from 0.7117 to 0.7734, indicating better writing-score judgments and rubric-aligned feedback rather than direct student-writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Essay scoring agreement (QWK) on overall/content/language/structure scores; human grader accuracy on scored essays
finding.study_size: n=13,372 essays (CSEE); n=50 essays in co-grading pilot; 10 novices; 5 experts
finding.effect_size: QWK=0.7634 (integrated system on CSEE); novice gain +0.1353 QWK; expert gain +0.0617 QWK

finding.finding_summary: The framework was designed to reduce grading workload by routing only low-confidence cases to slower reasoning or humans. The authors report that the fast module required less than 0.5 hours to train and about 0.2 hours for scoring, while the slow module required around 2 hours per epoch and about 10 GPU hours for inference; in the co-grading study, experts reported higher efficiency (4.4/5) and less time spent when supported by LLM feedback. The system therefore improves grading throughput and triage efficiency, especially for routine essays with high-confidence predictions.
finding.measure: Training/inference time; self-reported grading efficiency; workflow efficiency via confidence-based routing

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively evaluates human-AI collaboration, explanation use, and confidence-based self-reflection in grading, which are closest to metacognitive and decision-support skills rather than student writing skill growth. Low-confidence routing and explanation review improved graders’ ability to revise judgments, and novices with LLM support reached performance statistically indistinguishable from experts (p=0.2682). However, the study does not measure durable student metacognition or transfer over time; the evidence is limited to evaluator decision quality in the grading task.
finding.measure: Human-AI co-grading accuracy and revision of initial scores after receiving scores/confidence/explanations
finding.effect_size: Novice+LLM vs novice: +0.1353 QWK; Novice+LLM vs expert: -0.0508 QWK (ns)

finding.finding_summary: The study includes questionnaire evidence that graders found the system helpful and were willing to use it, suggesting improved engagement with the grading task. Experts rated the helpfulness of predicted scores at 4.6/5, confidence scores at 4.8/5, explanations at 4.7/5, and willingness to use the system at 4.3/5. These are self-reported perceptions rather than student motivation or persistence outcomes, so the evidence is indirect and task-specific.
finding.measure: 5-point Likert self-reports on helpfulness, efficiency, and willingness to use the AES system
finding.study_size: 5 expert evaluators (questionnaire); 10 novice evaluators participated in the co-grading task

paper_profiles.title: SpellMapper: A non-autoregressive neural spellchecker for ASR customization with candidate retrieval based on n-gram mappings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of customizing automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems so they better recognize user-specific vocabulary such as names, rare terms, and domain phrases. The authors argue that existing contextual spelling correction methods are limited by slow or weak candidate retrieval, especially when vocabularies are large, and propose a two-stage approach: retrieve likely candidate phrases using misspelled n-gram mappings, then score them with a non-autoregressive BERT-based model.

The method is trained on synthetic examples built from Wikipedia titles and evaluated on three public ASR personalization corpora: Spoken Wikipedia, SPGISpeech, and UserLibri. The system improves word error rate relative to baseline ASR models by 6.4-21.4% and achieves 49-68% of an estimated “ideal” improvement bound, but it also shows nontrivial false positives and a gap between candidate retrieval recall and final recall. The work is about post-processing ASR transcripts, not student writing instruction or generative AI, so it does not provide direct evidence on high-school writing outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence, Teacher Tasks and Individualized Pedagogy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies whether automated writing evaluation (AWE) systems can improve high school students’ writing outcomes, and whether adding human graders on top of AI feedback improves results further. The authors are motivated by a practical question in educational technology: can AI tools that score essays and provide instant feedback improve writing instruction, especially when teachers are time-constrained, and do human graders add value beyond the algorithm?

The study uses a randomized field experiment in 178 public high schools in Espírito Santo, Brazil, focused on high school seniors preparing for the ENEM college entrance exam. Schools were assigned to one of two writing-technology treatments: a “pure AWE” system that instantly returned an AI-generated score and feedback, or an “enhanced AWE” version that initially used the algorithm but then substituted a delayed human final grade and comments. Both programs were delivered through an online writing platform over the school year and were integrated into regular instruction at the discretion of teachers.

Main outcomes were ENEM essay scores, broken down into multiple writing competencies (syntactic, analytic, and policy proposal skills), along with mechanism measures such as number of practice essays written, feedback received, student perceptions of feedback quality, and teacher-student discussions about essays. The paper finds positive effects on essay performance for both treatment arms, with gains around 0.1 standard deviations, and no meaningful advantage from adding human graders. The technologies also increased writing practice, feedback exposure, and individualized teacher discussion, suggesting that the tools worked partly by shifting teacher effort toward higher-value, nonroutine feedback and discussion rather than by simply automating grading alone.

finding.finding_summary: Both AI-based writing interventions improved high school students’ essay performance on the ENEM argumentative essay. The paper reports intention-to-treat effects of roughly 0.1σ on overall essay score, with gains visible in syntactic skills (0.07σ), analytic skills (0.04σ), and policy proposal skills (0.16σ). The enhanced AWE arm and the pure AWE arm performed similarly, so adding human graders did not increase effectiveness.
finding.measure: ENEM essay score and component scores for syntactic skills, analytic skills, and policy proposal skills
finding.effect_size: approximately d=0.10 overall; 0.07σ syntactic; 0.04σ analytic; 0.16σ policy proposal

finding.finding_summary: The interventions increased student engagement with writing practice and feedback. The paper reports roughly a 30% increase in the number of practice essays written, greater uptake of feedback, and higher perceived usefulness/quality of comments, with the enhanced AWE arm showing somewhat stronger perceived feedback quality. No delayed or follow-up measure is reported for durability of these engagement gains.
finding.measure: Number of ENEM training essays written; number of essays receiving comments/annotations and grades; student perceptions of feedback usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds evidence that the technologies increased higher-order, nonroutine instructional interaction. Both treatments increased the number of essays that were personally discussed with teachers after grading by roughly one third, suggesting more individualized pedagogy and more teacher-student discussion about essay quality. The authors interpret this as a shift toward analytical and interactive tasks rather than mere short-term output polishing.
finding.measure: Number of ENEM training essays personally discussed with teachers after grading

finding.finding_summary: The interventions improved the efficiency of writing instruction by outsourcing routine grading and feedback tasks to the platform and reducing teacher time burden. The paper reports that teachers in the enhanced AWE arm reduced work-from-home hours and felt less time constrained, while both treatment arms supported higher feedback volume and similar teacher effort overall. These effects are consistent with time savings from automated grading and workflow support, though the paper does not report a single standardized effect size for workload outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported hours worked from home; perceived time constraints; platform logs on grading/feedback interactions

finding.finding_summary: The study provides evidence on how AI-enabled writing systems can be scaled within public school instruction and how they shift the composition of teacher tasks. Although this is not a policy evaluation per se, the paper’s central institutional finding is that both AWE models changed classroom pedagogy by moving teachers toward more individualized, nonroutine interactions without requiring human graders to improve student outcomes. No direct governance or system-level policy effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher task composition and classroom instructional patterns

paper_profiles.title: Confronting the Challenges of Participatory Culture: Media Education for the 21st Century
paper_profiles.venue: The MIT Press / MacArthur Foundation Reports on Digital Media and Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length report argues that young people’s participation in digital media culture creates important opportunities for learning, civic engagement, collaboration, and creative production, but that these benefits are unevenly distributed and require educational support. Rather than treating new media primarily as a technology access issue, the report frames participation in online communities, fan cultures, gaming, remixing, and other participatory practices as a set of cultural and social competencies that schools should help students develop.

The report’s central contribution is a conceptual and policy-oriented argument for media literacy education. It synthesizes examples and prior research to show how participatory environments can support informal learning, peer-to-peer mentorship, and skill development, while also raising problems of inequality, transparency, and ethics. It does not present a primary empirical study of an instructional intervention; instead, it draws on illustrative cases and citations to argue that schools, parents, and informal learning settings should more deliberately teach the new media literacies needed for full participation in contemporary culture.

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that participatory media environments can support durable skills such as collaboration, networking, judgment, and negotiation, and it cites illustrative cases where peer-to-peer communities help participants learn to give and receive feedback. However, these claims are not based on a single controlled evaluation in grades 9-12; they are synthesized from prior studies and examples, so no effect size or causal estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Illustrative reports of collaboration, peer feedback, networking, and judgment in participatory media environments

finding.finding_summary: The report claims that participation in digital media cultures may increase students’ self-confidence, sense of agency, and engagement, and that such environments can motivate deeper participation. These claims are descriptive and conceptual rather than experimentally tested in high-school writing contexts, so no quantitative impact estimate is provided.
finding.measure: Engagement, self-confidence, sense of agency, and participation in online communities

finding.finding_summary: The report discusses writing-related learning mainly through examples of fan fiction, online publishing, and beta-reading feedback, arguing that such practices can help young people improve reading and writing skills and understand narrative structure and sentence construction. These are illustrative claims rather than direct evidence from a grade 9-12 writing intervention, and the report does not report effect sizes, sample sizes, or delayed outcomes.
finding.measure: Writing skill development, editorial feedback, sentence construction, and narrative structure in online fan communities

finding.finding_summary: A major conclusion of the report is that schools, after-school programs, and families should adopt a systemic approach to media education so that all young people can gain access to participatory culture skills. The report frames this as a policy and institutional challenge rather than a measured program effect, and therefore does not provide quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Policy, schooling, after-school programming, and family support for media literacy and participatory culture

paper_profiles.title: EssayCBM: Rubric-Aligned Concept Bottleneck Models for Transparent Essay Grading
paper_profiles.venue: Conference'17 (ACM conference paper / proceedings placeholder in provided text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents EssayCBM, an interpretable automated essay scoring framework designed to make essay grading more transparent than standard black-box systems. The core idea is to predict eight rubric-aligned concepts—such as thesis clarity, evidence use, organization and coherence, grammar and mechanics, vocabulary appropriateness, sentence variety, critical thinking depth, and fluency—before aggregating those concept scores into a final essay grade. The authors position the system as a human-aligned alternative to opaque automated essay scoring, with the goal of making scoring decisions traceable and feedback more actionable.

The system is evaluated on an automated essay scoring dataset containing student essays with final grade labels, using encoder backbones including BERT-base, RoBERTa-base, GPT-2, and BiLSTM. The paper reports model-level grading performance comparisons between a baseline AES setup and EssayCBM, with BERT+EssayCBM showing a small improvement in accuracy and macro-F1, RoBERTa slightly worsening, and GPT-2/BiLSTM remaining unchanged. The work also includes a Streamlit web interface that surfaces concept-level scores and allows human-in-the-loop correction, but it does not report a student intervention study, user experiment, or delayed follow-up outcomes.

For K-12 relevance, the paper is only indirectly relevant to high-school writing support because it studies essay grading technology and feedback presentation, not classroom use with grades 9–12 learners. The evidence is limited to algorithmic performance on an essay scoring dataset rather than direct impacts on writing quality, revision quality, engagement, self-regulation, or transfer. Its main conclusion is that a concept-bottleneck design can preserve grading accuracy while improving interpretability and generating rubric-aligned feedback.

finding.finding_summary: On the essay scoring task, EssayCBM produced mixed results relative to the baseline automated essay scoring system. For BERT, accuracy increased from 80.70% to 81.14% and macro-F1 from 60.01 to 62.38, while RoBERTa declined from 80.70% to 79.39% accuracy and from 61.98 to 58.88 macro-F1; GPT-2 and LSTM were unchanged. The paper does not report effects on actual student writing quality, revision quality, grammar/mechanics, vocabulary use, or any delayed/durable writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Automated essay grading performance (accuracy, macro-F1) on student essays

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the system improves operational efficiency by providing real-time, transparent grading and human-in-the-loop correction in a web application. However, this is not evaluated with measured time savings or workload outcomes; the evidence is descriptive rather than causal. The reported classification results suggest the system can support practical deployment without major accuracy loss, but no teacher workload metric is reported.
finding.measure: Real-time grading / human-in-the-loop interface; no direct workload metric reported

finding.finding_summary: The system is explicitly framed as offering rubric-level feedback on concepts such as critical thinking depth and organization, but the paper does not measure any durable skill outcomes in students. No evidence is provided that the feedback improved critical thinking, metacognition, or transfer beyond the immediate grading task. Thus, there is no direct empirical finding of durable-skill change.
finding.measure: Concept-level rubric scores / feedback on critical thinking and organization; no student skill outcome measured

paper_profiles.title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how an LLM-based writing support tool (WriteAid) functions in real-time K-12 English-as-a-Foreign-Language classrooms. The authors address a practical question in AI-assisted writing instruction: whether step-by-step LLM scaffolding helps students compose better English text during normal class time, and how such support affects learners of different proficiency levels, teachers, and classroom dynamics.

The intervention was a chat-based system designed to support sentence construction, grammar revision, and vocabulary/grammar explanations. It was deployed over six weeks in a South Korean middle school English class with 157 eighth-grade students; 133 consented to analysis. Students used the tool during two in-class writing tasks, and the researchers combined system logs, qualitative coding of 1,386 sampled queries, a classroom observation study, and a delayed written assessment conducted 2–3 weeks later.

Results suggest that the LLM improved short-term grammatical correctness in students’ in-class sentence production, but benefits were uneven. Higher-proficiency students used the system more efficiently and tended to ask lower-level questions, while lower-proficiency students more often requested full sentence generation or repeated revisions, showed more confusion/annoyance, and became more dependent on the system. The delayed assessment indicated that many AI-generated sentences were copied into final essays, but transfer and retention were much stronger for higher-performing students than for middle- and lower-performing students. The paper concludes that real-time LLM scaffolding can scale support and reduce teacher workload for routine questions, but may also demotivate struggling learners, increase reliance, and complicate teacher oversight and peer interaction.

finding.finding_summary: In-class sentence construction with the LLM improved immediate grammatical correctness: among 632 assisted sentences in the fall semester, 82.3% of the 309 sentences later reused in final essays were grammatically correct. However, transfer to delayed writing was uneven by proficiency, with high-performing students correctly incorporating 65.8% of LLM-constructed sentences into the delayed assessment versus 37.8% for middle-performing and 14.0% for low-performing students. The study also found that step-by-step scaffolding sometimes produced awkward or incorrect sentences when Korean syntax and teacher-mandated structures did not align with English usage.
finding.measure: Grammatical correctness of LLM-constructed sentences and delayed written assessment essay quality (content, organization, vocabulary, language use/grammar/mechanics)
finding.study_size: n=133 consented; 632 assisted sentences; delayed assessment completed 2–3 weeks later

finding.finding_summary: The tool increased engagement for some students but demotivated others, especially lower-proficiency learners. High-performing students showed fewer negative affective reactions (3.8 times per session on average) than middle- and low-performing students (12.2 and 11.4 times per session, respectively), while lower-proficiency students were more likely to express confusion, annoyance, and dependence when the scaffolded interaction became too long or demanding.
finding.measure: Observed affective responses during LLM interaction (gratitude, annoyance, confusion, indifference) and engagement patterns in query logs
finding.study_size: n=133 consented; affective behavior summarized from sampled classroom interactions

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence about self-regulation and transfer rather than direct instruction of higher-order writing skills. High-performing students used the system to delegate lower-order tasks and then applied the feedback more efficiently, while lower-performing students more often outsourced core sentence generation and showed greater dependence on the system. The delayed assessment 2–3 weeks later suggests partial transfer of assisted sentences into independent writing, but durable learning was clearly stronger for higher-performing students than for lower-proficiency students.
finding.measure: Observed query strategies (e.g., validation seeking, sentence revision, full sentence generation) and delayed transfer into independent essay writing
finding.study_size: n=133 consented; 1,386 coded queries; delayed assessment 2–3 weeks later

finding.finding_summary: The LLM reduced teacher burden for routine language questions and allowed faster handling of low-level writing support. The teacher reported having more time to walk around the classroom and check student progress because the system handled many simple spelling, vocabulary, and grammar questions, although the tool also created new coordination challenges because students still directed some routine questions to the teacher.
finding.measure: Classroom observation and follow-up teacher interview on teacher workload and classroom orchestration
finding.study_size: n=1 teacher interview; observations across 3 class sessions

paper_profiles.title: CoCo Matrix: Taxonomy of Cognitive Contributions in Co-writing with Intelligent Agents
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Creativity and Cognition Conference (C&C ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem in research on AI-supported writing: existing evaluations of intelligent writing assistants tend to focus on the final written product and user self-reports, while largely missing what happens during the writing process itself. The authors argue that to understand human contributions in co-writing with intelligent agents, researchers need process-oriented measures that capture planning, translating, and reviewing rather than only polished output.

To address this, the paper proposes CoCo Matrix, a two-dimensional taxonomy based on entropy and information gain, inspired by Flower and Hayes’ cognitive process theory of writing. The authors conduct a structured literature review of 34 ACM papers on intelligent writing systems and classify them according to the kinds of cognitive contributions they enable across writing phases and interaction styles. The framework distinguishes four broad interaction patterns, including systems that support broad ideation, style variation, focused drafting, and low-entropy review/editing tasks such as grammar correction and feedback.

The main conclusion is that most reviewed systems emphasize high-entropy, high-information-gain co-writing, while low-entropy, high-information-gain systems are comparatively under-explored but promising. The paper does not present an empirical evaluation of writing outcomes for high-school students; instead, it offers a conceptual and taxonomic contribution for analyzing writing assistants and for designing future tools that better support human agency, revision, and reflection in co-writing contexts.

paper_profiles.title: FEANEL: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Error Analysis in K-12 English Writing
paper_profiles.population: Elementary and Secondary (K-12); includes secondary students aged 12-18, relevant to High School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces FEANEL, a benchmark for fine-grained error analysis in K-12 English writing. The authors argue that current automated writing tools and LLM-based systems often provide only coarse or surface-level feedback, and they propose a more detailed task that requires identifying an error type, rating its severity, and generating an explanation for each edit in student essays.

The benchmark contains 1,000 anonymized essays: 500 from elementary students and 500 from secondary students, with the secondary set drawn from essays by learners aged roughly 12-18. English education experts rewrote the essays to create minimal corrections, then annotated each edit with a 29-type error taxonomy, severity labels, and explanations. The paper evaluates multiple LLMs under zero-shot and one-shot prompting conditions and compares them to human English teachers on a subset of the data.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs remain substantially weaker than teachers at fine-grained error classification and pedagogically useful feedback, especially for complex edits containing multiple intertwined errors. Performance improves with richer prompts, in-context examples, larger model size, and chain-of-thought-style reasoning, but the gains are still limited and do not close the gap with humans. Because the paper is a benchmark and model evaluation study rather than an intervention with student outcomes, it does not provide direct evidence that these systems improve writing quality, revision quality, fluency, engagement, or durable writing skill growth for high-school students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates fine-grained error analysis quality on K-12 English writing, not student writing gains. On the benchmark, LLMs showed moderate-to-strong performance on error classification (e.g., zero-shot accuracy ranging from 35.33% to 72.06% across models; human teachers 79.90% on a subset) and weaker performance on explanation generation, with all models scoring low on BLEU/METEOR/ROUGE relative to human references. Richer prompts and one-shot examples improved classification and explanation metrics, but the study does not measure whether feedback improved actual writing quality or revision quality over time.
finding.measure: Error classification accuracy/Macro-F1, severity MAE, explanation BLEU/METEOR/ROUGE-L on the FEANEL benchmark
finding.study_size: n=1000 essays; 8676 error analyses; human subset n=1000 errors

paper_profiles.title: Two-qubit quantum photonic processor manufactured by femtosecond laser writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports the fabrication and characterization of a programmable two-qubit photonic quantum processor made with femtosecond laser writing (FLW) in fused silica. The work focuses on device engineering: low-loss waveguides, thermo-optic phase shifters, calibration of thermal cross-talk, and process tomography of a fixed CNOT gate. The authors also demonstrate a proof-of-principle variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) calculation of the H2 ground-state energy.

The experimental platform uses dual-rail photonic qubits, coherent and single-photon sources, and postselected coincidence measurements. The main reported results are high classical-circuit fidelity (99.18% vs. the ideal unitary matrix), mean single-qubit gate fidelities around 99.3%, and a two-qubit CNOT process fidelity of 94.4%. The paper concludes that FLW is a promising route for rapid prototyping of reconﬁgurable integrated photonic quantum processors, while noting that loss, thermal cross-talk, and photon indistinguishability remain important limitations.

This paper does not study education, writing, or any K-12 student outcomes. It is unrelated to automated writing evaluation or generative AI in education and provides no evidence for the requested school-writing sub-question.

paper_profiles.title: CorpusStudio: Surfacing Emergent Patterns in a Corpus of Prior Work while Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents CorpusStudio, a writing support environment designed to help authors notice and apply community-specific writing norms by surfacing patterns from a corpus of prior papers. The system combines two main supports: an ordered distribution of section titles from prior papers and contextual retrieval of many example sentences matched to a writer’s current draft position, with highlighting and note-taking tools to help users recognize commonalities, variation, and potential outliers.

The evaluation was a controlled within-subjects user study with N=16 participants, mostly students and researchers writing HCI manuscripts. Participants used CorpusStudio and a Google Docs baseline while drafting outlines and section text, then completed surveys, think-aloud tasks, and interviews. The study found that the tool helped participants overcome blank-page problems, compare structures more efficiently, identify possible section titles and phrasing, and gain confidence when their writing aligned with examples in the corpus. Participants also used the tool to find related work, fill content gaps, and inspect writing conventions, but the evidence is qualitative and does not report standardized performance gains or delayed follow-up measures.

finding.finding_summary: In a controlled within-subjects user study (n=16), participants reported that CorpusStudio helped them draft and revise outlines and manuscript sections by exposing section-title distributions and many contextually relevant example sentences. The tool supported structural decisions, terminology, phrasing, and content development; participants said it helped overcome blank-page problems, identify writing norms, and compare alternative ways of structuring sections. No quantitative writing-quality scores, effect sizes, or delayed transfer measures were reported.
finding.measure: Think-aloud observations, post-task surveys, and semi-structured interview reports about outline writing and section drafting/revision

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported improved confidence in aligning with or breaking norms, better awareness of variation across examples, and reflection on their own writing choices. The tool encouraged users to generalize from many examples, bookmark observations, and inspect structure and terminology, suggesting metacognitive support for writing strategy rather than just short-term text polishing. However, the paper provides qualitative evidence only and does not include follow-up measures demonstrating durable skill growth.
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence, reflection, and strategy use during think-aloud and interview

finding.finding_summary: Participants said the centralized interface was more efficient and less overwhelming than opening multiple papers separately to compare writing patterns. The tool helped them quickly find candidate section titles, retrieve analogous sentences, and locate related work, thereby reducing context switching during drafting. The study did not report timing outcomes, task-completion statistics, or formal productivity effect sizes.
finding.measure: Participant-reported efficiency and reduced context switching during outline and section drafting tasks

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Different Writing Tasks on Linguistic Style: A Case Study of the ROC Story Cloze Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether different writing prompts produce measurable differences in linguistic style, using the ROC Story Cloze dataset as a case study. The authors compare three task framings: writing an original five-sentence story, writing a coherent ending to a provided story context, and writing an incoherent ending. They then examine whether simple stylometric features can discriminate among these task types without using story context.

The approach is not an intervention study in schools; it analyzes text produced by Amazon Mechanical Turk annotators. The model uses length, word n-grams, and character n-grams to classify endings as right vs. wrong, original vs. new, or original vs. wrong. The main result is that style alone strongly separates task types: accuracy reaches 64.5% for right vs. wrong endings, 68.5% for original vs. right endings, and 75.6% for original vs. wrong endings, all above chance.

The paper also compares its style-only classifier to a neural language model and shows that combining both improves story-cloze accuracy to 75.2%, a new state-of-the-art at the time. The authors conclude that writing instructions can substantially affect the surface form of writing and that dataset/task design can introduce stylistic confounds. This is a machine-learning / NLP paper about writing-task effects, not a study of K-12 automated writing support, feedback, or student writing outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that different writing tasks produce clearly distinguishable writing styles, implying that prompt framing changes written output. Using only stylistic features and no story context, a logistic regression classifier achieved 64.5% accuracy for right vs. wrong endings, 68.5% for original vs. right endings, and 75.6% for original vs. wrong endings, all above the 50% chance baseline. This is evidence about text production style, not about writing instruction or durable writing-skill gains.
finding.measure: Stylometric classification of story endings using length, word n-grams, and character n-grams; task-type discrimination accuracy
finding.study_size: n=3,742 test endings (right vs. wrong experiment); additional training/dev counts reported as 3,366/374

paper_profiles.title: TEASPN: Framework and Protocol for Integrated Writing Assistance Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes TEASPN, a protocol and open-source framework intended to make a wide range of writing-assistance technologies easier to integrate into editors and word processors. The motivation is the “great divide” between NLP-based writing-assistance research systems and real-world writing software, which makes it difficult for writers to use tools such as grammatical error correction, completion, paraphrasing, dictionary lookup, and search within their normal writing environment.

The paper is primarily a systems/framework contribution rather than an educational intervention study. The authors build a demo TEASPN server and client, then run a small user experiment to see whether an integrated environment improves writing experience relative to a baseline editor with no built-in assistance (though participants could use external tools such as Grammarly and web dictionaries). The participants were 12 college students or researchers in NLP, so this is not a high-school study; the evidence is only indirectly relevant to K-12 writing support.

In the experiment, participants wrote short English texts under two conditions: integrated TEASPN versus baseline. Self-report results suggested that most participants preferred the integrated environment (10/12 rated the experience better), and 40% judged the integrated-condition text to be higher quality. The written texts in the integrated condition also had lower GPT-2 perplexity (26.4 vs. 37.8) and were shorter on average (335 ± 91 vs. 379 ± 116 characters), which the authors interpret as suggesting somewhat more fluent/typical English output. However, the study is small, short-term, and does not measure durable skill growth, delayed transfer, or K-12 outcomes; it mainly shows potential productivity and fluency benefits from combining multiple writing-assistance tools in one environment.

finding.finding_summary: In a small within-subject demonstration (n=12 adults), the integrated TEASPN environment was associated with text that the authors describe as more fluent/typical English. Objective text statistics showed lower GPT-2 perplexity in the integrated condition (26.4) than in the baseline condition (37.8), although the integrated texts were also shorter on average (335 ± 91 vs. 379 ± 116 characters).
finding.measure: Written text fluency/typicality proxy measured by GPT-2 perplexity; text length

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported a better writing experience in the integrated environment, with 10 of 12 participants (83.3%) favoring TEASPN on the experience question. This is a short-term self-report result from a small demonstration study rather than evidence of durable changes in motivation or self-regulation.
finding.measure: Post-task questionnaire on writing experience

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests potential workflow benefits from integrating multiple writing tools into a single editor, but it does not report a direct productivity or time-on-task effect size. The integrated-condition texts were shorter, and the authors speculate this may reflect participants spending time learning the tools rather than writing; thus the evidence is suggestive but mixed for efficiency.
finding.measure: Text length and user-reported use of multiple writing-assistance features

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines whether ChatGPT can serve as a feedback tool to improve foreign-language writing for students from refugee and migrant backgrounds in a multilingual, multicultural junior high school classroom in Greece. The authors frame the work as a response to the language-learning challenges faced by socially vulnerable learners who may need additional support in vocabulary and grammar development.

The intervention involved 8 students aged 15 in a German-as-a-foreign-language class. Students first wrote a personal email in German; ChatGPT then revised the drafts to improve vocabulary and grammar, and students reviewed the revised versions before writing a second, similar email on a related topic. The study compared pre- and post-intervention writing outputs using descriptive measures such as total words, unique words, and average words per sentence.

Results showed increases in the total number of words, unique words, and average words per sentence in the revised/post-intervention texts, suggesting improved writing productivity and linguistic elaboration. The paper concludes that ChatGPT may be a promising language-learning tool in multilingual classrooms, especially for students with a refugee/migrant background, but it emphasizes the very small sample size, short duration, and pilot nature of the study as limits to generalizability.

finding.finding_summary: In this pilot classroom study (n=8), ChatGPT-supported feedback was associated with improved L2 writing outputs in German. After revising their drafts with ChatGPT and writing a similar follow-up email, students showed increases in total words (mean increase 38%), unique words (average mean 19.1 more unique words per student), and average words per sentence (approximately 42% increase overall), indicating richer and longer written production.
finding.measure: Foreign-language writing quality/productivity proxies: total words, unique words, average words per sentence in German email writing

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the educational opportunities and risks of large language models, especially ChatGPT and related systems, across schooling and higher education. Rather than evaluating a single intervention experimentally, it synthesizes emerging uses of LLMs for learning content creation, tutoring, feedback, assessment, writing support, and teacher support, while also discussing ethical, pedagogical, and technical challenges such as bias, privacy, integrity, and overreliance.

For writing-related uses, the paper argues that LLMs can assist students and teachers by suggesting grammatical and stylistic improvements, generating outlines and summaries, and supporting feedback and assessment. It explicitly notes potential applications in middle and high school settings and for high school and university teachers, including help with research and writing tasks, but it does not report primary empirical results from a controlled study of grades 9-12 students. The paper’s conclusions are mainly normative: LLMs may improve personalization, efficiency, and access if used with human oversight, critical thinking, and strong safeguards.

Because this is a conceptual position paper, it does not provide direct outcome estimates for high-school writing interventions, subgroup effects, or comparator-based empirical findings. Its main contribution is a framework of opportunities, risks, and mitigation strategies for responsible adoption of LLMs in education, including concerns about multilingual access and fair access to AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by assisting with semi-automated grading, feedback generation, lesson planning, and creation of writing supports such as outlines, summaries, and grammar/style suggestions. These claims are not backed by a single controlled study in the paper, but they are presented as plausible efficiency gains for teachers and students in high school and university contexts.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes potential benefits for reading and writing, including syntactic and grammatical correction, style improvement, summarization, and outline generation. These are presented as opportunities for elementary through secondary students and for teachers supporting writing, but no direct empirical effect on writing quality or literacy outcomes is reported in the paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking when used as a complement to instruction, but also warns they may undermine these skills if learners rely on them too heavily. This is a conceptual discussion rather than an empirical test, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional issues such as responsible deployment, privacy/security, copyright, fairness, multilingual access, and governance for AI use in schools. It argues these conditions are necessary for trustworthy adoption, but does not evaluate policy or institutional outcomes empirically.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative case study examines how four EFL secondary school students in Hong Kong engineered prompts while using ChatGPT and other SOTA chatbots to complete a familiar blog-writing task. The paper is motivated by the question of how students, especially non-technical users, move beyond trial-and-error prompting when collaborating with generative AI in a writing classroom.

The intervention/approach is not an instructional treatment but an observation of students’ first-time use of chatbots during a timed in-class writing assignment. Students completed a blog entry using an iPad and the POE app, which gave them access to ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly. Screen recordings were transcribed and coded to classify prompt content (e.g., auto-complete, greeting, search-engine style questions, natural language instruction, one-shot prompts, question prompts, and chatbot-suggested “tell me more” prompts) and to trace each student’s prompt pathway across turns and chatbots.

The study finds that students used a range of prompt types and often revised prompts by small word changes, repeated prompts across chatbots, or layered natural-language instruction with exemplars/questions. No student used all prompt types, and the pathways suggest exploratory trial-and-error rather than sophisticated, systematic prompting. The authors conclude that EFL classroom students would likely benefit from explicit prompt-engineering education so they can better exploit chatbot capabilities for writing support. The paper does not measure writing quality or learning gains; its contribution is descriptive and conceptual, focused on student prompting behavior in a secondary EFL writing context.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies secondary students’ prompting behavior during a writing task, not the quality of the writing product or changes in literacy outcomes. It reports that four EFL students completed a blog-entry task using ChatGPT/SOTA chatbots, but provides no pre/post or comparative literacy outcome data, so no effect on writing performance can be inferred.
finding.measure: prompt types and prompt pathways during a blog-writing task; writing product was collected but not analyzed for outcome effects

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret students’ prompt revisions as evidence of emerging prompt-engineering skill, including trial-and-error exploration, refinement of instructions, and strategic reuse of prompt structures. However, this is a qualitative interpretation of four cases (n=4), not a causal test, so the finding is best understood as descriptive evidence that students engaged in metacognitive prompting behaviors while completing the task.
finding.measure: prompt engineering pathways; prompt sophistication/sequence across turns

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing AI in Secondary Education to Enhance Writing Competence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT may affect writing instruction in secondary education, with a focus on writing competence and the cultivation of a personal writing voice. The authors frame AI as both a potential support for brainstorming, drafting, feedback, and revision, and a potential threat if it encourages shortcutting, plagiarism, or overreliance that weakens student authorship.

The article is primarily a conceptual and practice-oriented discussion rather than an empirical evaluation of a single intervention. It synthesizes prior studies and examples to argue that AI can be useful when integrated into a staged writing process, especially for pre-writing idea generation and revision feedback, but that teacher mediation, process-based assessment, and tightly designed prompts are necessary to preserve learning. It also highlights concerns about cheating detection, the limits of AI-generated feedback compared with human feedback, and the need for tasks that promote authentic expression.

The paper is centered on secondary schooling and repeatedly uses upper-secondary/high-school examples, including argumentative and subject-oriented writing tasks. It references a small number of empirical studies on student use of ChatGPT, teachers’ perceptions, and AI feedback quality, but it does not report original data collection of its own. Its main conclusion is that AI should be treated as a supplementary tool within teacher-led writing instruction rather than a replacement for writing practice or feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI may support some aspects of secondary students’ writing development, especially brainstorming, structuring, revision, and grammar/usage support, but it may also weaken writing competence and authentic voice if students overuse it or copy output uncritically. The article does not present original effect estimates; its claims are based on cited studies and pedagogical reasoning, including an example of a 10th-grade text and a comparison study (Steiss et al., 2024) suggesting human feedback is stronger than ChatGPT feedback.
finding.measure: writing competence, writing voice, feedback quality, structure, grammar, argumentative writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes critical thinking, reasoning, and self-reflection as central writing-related durable skills, arguing that AI can either support or undermine them depending on how it is used. Examples include using AI to generate counterarguments or to compare outputs during revision, but the authors caution that overly open-ended prompting can reduce ownership and depth of thought.
finding.measure: critical thinking, reasoning, self-reflection, use of counterarguments, planning/revision processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly states that AI can reduce teacher workload by providing instant feedback, acting as a teaching assistant, and helping with formative evaluation of student writing. This is presented as a practical advantage for secondary classrooms, particularly when teachers have many students and limited time for individualized feedback.
finding.measure: teacher workload, feedback efficiency, time savings in formative assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests AI may increase student engagement or reduce frustration by helping stuck writers, but it may also create dependency, overwhelm less proficient writers with long responses, or encourage cheating-related attitudes. These claims are conceptual and illustrative rather than based on a new measured sample.
finding.measure: engagement, motivation, frustration, dependency concerns

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that schools need process-based assessment, tighter exam conditions, and clearer rules for AI use because generative AI complicates grading and plagiarism control. It also notes that current detection tools are unreliable and that institutional responses should emphasize teacher judgment and assignment design rather than automated policing alone.
finding.measure: assessment policy, plagiarism control, exam design, institutional handling of AI use

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE), a high-stakes secondary-school leaving exam. The authors use a VNHSGE evaluation dataset containing multiple-choice questions from several subjects and 30 literature essays, and they prompt ChatGPT in zero-shot mode to answer the questions in a structured format. They then compare ChatGPT’s answers against human-derived ground truth and, for several subjects, against Vietnamese student score distributions from prior exam years.

The study is not an intervention study with students; instead, it is a model-performance evaluation of ChatGPT on high-school exam content. The results show that ChatGPT achieved overall passing-level combined scores in both natural-science and social-science groupings across 2019-2023, with combined scores ranging from 6.30 to 6.94. Subject performance varied substantially: English and literature were generally strongest, while chemistry was weakest, and geography/civic education showed more variability and some limitations, especially where image/chart interpretation would be required.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT has clear potential as a support tool for students preparing for high-stakes high-school examinations, but its performance is uneven across subjects and task types. They emphasize that further work is needed to assess more complex questions and to improve capability in areas requiring deeper reasoning or visual information processing. Because the paper evaluates the model on exam items rather than learner outcomes, it primarily provides indirect evidence about AI-supported learning at the secondary level.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT performed strongly on the literature/writing component of the VNHSGE, with scores ranging from 5.63 to 7.50 across 2019-2022 and an average of 6.68. The authors report that ChatGPT’s literature scores were generally higher than the majority of Vietnamese students, except in 2022 where the result was slightly lower.
finding.measure: VNHSGE literature exam score (essay/literature component)

finding.finding_summary: On the English subject, ChatGPT scored between 7.6 and 8.6 across the study years, with an average of 7.92. The paper reports that ChatGPT outperformed the majority of Vietnamese students in English language proficiency, indicating strong performance on this exam-based language task.
finding.measure: VNHSGE English exam score

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s mathematics scores ranged from 5.2 to 6.6 across 2019-2023, with an average of 5.88. The authors state that these scores were lower than the majority of Vietnamese students, suggesting weaker relative performance in mathematics than in language-heavy subjects.
finding.measure: VNHSGE mathematics exam score

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s performance in science-related subjects was uneven. It performed relatively well in biology (scores 5.25-6.0; average 5.8) and physics (5.75-6.5; average 6.1), but less well in chemistry (4.0-6.25; average 4.8), which the authors identify as its weakest subject. Compared with Vietnamese students, the paper describes biology as often better than most students, physics as mostly lower, and chemistry as consistently lower than most students.
finding.measure: VNHSGE physics, chemistry, and biology exam scores

finding.finding_summary: For history, geography, and civic education, ChatGPT showed variable performance. History scores ranged from 4.25 to 7.75 and were usually above the majority of Vietnamese students; geography ranged from 5.0 to 7.5 with one year above most students but generally lower overall; and civic education ranged from 6.0 to 8.25 but remained below most students, especially on problem-solving items requiring higher-order thinking. The paper also notes that geography questions requiring visual/chart interpretation were a limitation for GPT-3.5.
finding.measure: VNHSGE history, geography, and civic education exam scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly attributes weaker performance in some subjects to the need for critical thinking, analytical reasoning, and problem-solving, especially in mathematics and civic education. However, these skills were not measured directly in students; instead, they were inferred from ChatGPT’s exam-item performance, so the evidence is indirect and task-specific rather than a direct student-skill outcome.
finding.measure: Reasoning demands inferred from performance on exam questions requiring analytical/problem-solving skills

paper_profiles.title: Embracing AI in Education: Understanding the Surge in Large Language Model Use by Secondary Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how widely secondary students are using large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama, and Bing Copilot, and what they use them for. The authors are motivated by rapid growth in generative AI use among students, school restrictions on LLMs, and concerns about both cheating and hallucinated or inaccurate outputs. They ask how common LLM use is, which school subjects students use them for, how students perceive their usefulness, and whether usage differs by demographic or school-context factors.

The study uses a survey of 306 U.S. middle and high school students in grades 6-12, collected via a survey platform, local tutoring programs, and social media. It is not an intervention study and includes no comparison group beyond descriptive subgroup comparisons (e.g., by grade band, state technology index, and school type). The results show that 71% of respondents had used an LLM at least once and 9% used one daily; usage was consistent across grades 7-12. Students reported using LLMs for multiple subjects including writing/language arts, history, foreign languages, and math, with 57% of users finding them useful for writing text and 43% for math/STEM questions.

The paper’s conclusions are primarily descriptive and forward-looking: secondary students are already using LLMs widely despite restrictive school policies, and access is unequal across more and less technologically advanced states and between paid and free model users. Students report both benefits and limitations, especially concerns about inaccurate answers and hallucinations in factual or historical contexts. The authors argue for student-adapted models, personalized AI tutoring, and AI classrooms, but they do not test these proposals empirically.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs for writing text/language arts tasks, and 57% of LLM users said the tools were useful for writing text. However, the paper is descriptive and also notes concerns about inaccuracy and hallucinations, so the writing-related experience is not uniformly positive. No direct writing performance outcome, comparator, or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported usefulness for writing text and subject-level usage of LLMs for language arts assignments

finding.finding_summary: Beyond writing, students reported using LLMs for history, foreign languages, and other school subjects. The paper highlights mixed perceptions: students described LLMs as helpful for simplifying complex topics, but also noted incorrect answers and hallucinations, especially in historical contexts. This is a descriptive survey finding with no experimental comparator or effect size.
finding.measure: Self-reported subject areas of LLM use and perceived helpfulness across school subjects

finding.finding_summary: Students’ attitudes toward LLMs were mixed, with an average ethical concern rating of 2.83/5 and school-policy severity rating of 3.48/5. Despite these concerns, usage remained widespread, suggesting that perceived utility outweighed apprehension for many students. No intervention or causal effect on motivation or engagement was tested.
finding.measure: Self-reported ethical concern and perceived school policy severity regarding LLM use

finding.finding_summary: The survey found that LLM use was common despite restrictive school policies, with an average policy severity rating of 3.48/5 and widespread reported use across grades 7-12. The study also identified access gaps by state technology index, school type, and paid-versus-free model access, suggesting institutional and socioeconomic inequality in AI use. These are descriptive comparisons, not causal policy effects.
finding.measure: Self-reported school policy severity, usage prevalence, and subgroup differences by state technology index, school type, and paid access

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs to help with schoolwork efficiently, and many said the tools were useful for answering questions and simplifying complex topics. The paper does not measure time saved or productivity directly, but the descriptive responses imply an operational benefit for completing assignments. No comparator or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported usefulness for schoolwork assistance and answering questions

paper_profiles.title: Product versus Process: Exploring EFL Students’ Editing of AI-generated Text for Expository Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how Hong Kong secondary school students use generative AI chatbots to support expository writing, with a specific focus on the relationship between editing behaviors and final composition quality. The authors ask what kinds of edits students make to AI-generated text during the writing process and whether those process/product editing patterns predict human-rated scores for content, language, organization, and overall quality.

The intervention/approach was a workshop in which students learned prompt engineering and then wrote an expository article using AI chatbots accessed through the POE app. Students could blend AI-generated text with their own words, and the researchers collected both screen recordings of the drafting/revision process and final Google Docs compositions. The study analyzed 39 secondary students overall, with process data available for 25 screen recordings; it used qualitative coding, descriptive statistics, temporal sequence analysis, and multiple linear regression.

The main findings were that students made many edits, but most were short/localized rather than large unit-level revisions. Two editing patterns emerged: one more introduction-oriented and one more body-oriented. In the regression analyses, AI-word count positively predicted all four score dimensions in the final compositions, while most other editing variables had limited predictive power. Process evidence showed that heading edits were positively associated with language and total scores, whereas concluding-paragraph edits were negatively associated with language and total scores. Overall, the study concludes that students’ substantial editing effort does not necessarily translate into better writing quality, suggesting AI supports but does not replace writing skill.

finding.finding_summary: This paper directly studies expository writing quality in secondary EFL students using AI-generated text. In the product-based regression analyses (n=39), the number of AI words positively predicted content, language, organization, and total scores (model p-values .003 to .018; R-squared=.463-.538), while most other edit variables had little unique effect. In the process-based analyses (n=25), heading edits positively predicted language and total scores, but concluding-paragraph edits negatively predicted those same outcomes; the authors conclude that editing effort was substantial but did not consistently translate into better composition quality.
finding.measure: Human-rated expository writing scores for content, language, organization, and total quality; counts of AI words, human words, and edit types/units

finding.finding_summary: The study also substantively examines students’ editing strategies, sequencing, and revision behavior while using AI, which overlaps with metacognitive and self-regulatory writing processes. Temporal sequence analysis identified two distinct patterns: an introduction-oriented pattern and a body-oriented pattern, showing that students differed in how they planned, monitored, and revised their texts over time. However, the paper does not directly measure durable skills with a dedicated scale; it infers them from observable editing behavior and its limited association with outcomes.
finding.measure: Temporal sequence of edits; coding of editing patterns and edit scope

finding.finding_summary: The paper records writing process duration and editing volume but does not evaluate efficiency as a primary outcome in terms of productivity gains or time savings. Total runtime was entered as a predictor in regression models, yet it did not significantly predict any score outcome, and the authors report that most editing variables had minimal explanatory power. This suggests no clear evidence that the AI-supported workflow improved efficiency in a measurable way.
finding.measure: Total runtime of screen-recorded writing sessions; number of edits

paper_profiles.title: Approaching the Limits to EFL Writing Enhancement with AI-generated Text and Diverse Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how Hong Kong secondary school students composed an English feature article using generative AI chatbots alongside their own writing. The central question is not whether ChatGPT improves writing in a controlled experiment, but how students with different academic achievement levels integrate AI-generated text into compositions and whether those interaction patterns are associated with writing quality.

The sample included 59 students from seven Hong Kong secondary schools representing high- and low-achievement bands. Students completed a 500-word feature article writing task after a workshop on writing with ChatGPT support and prompt engineering, and their compositions were analyzed through content analysis, multiple linear regression, and cluster analysis. The paper focused on the quantity and distribution of AI-generated versus human-written words/chunks and their relation to human-rated scores for content, language, organization, and total quality.

Results showed that overall writing scores were mainly associated with the total number of words in a composition, rather than the specific way AI text was chunked or integrated. However, effects differed by school banding: higher-achieving students appeared better able to use AI flexibly, while lower-achieving students were more reliant on AI text and did not benefit as much from AI words, with human revision sometimes associated with lower scores.
