Cluster analyses also suggested that the same AI-writing pattern could help some students but not others. The authors conclude that generative AI can support secondary EFL writing, but its benefits are uneven and depend on students’ existing writing competence and AI literacy.

finding.finding_summary: In 59 Hong Kong secondary school EFL compositions, overall writing quality was associated mainly with total word count rather than the specific way AI-generated text was chunked or integrated. Across all submissions, the partial correlations between total score and AI words (0.417) and human words (0.424) were positive and statistically significant, but AI/human chunk variables were not. By school banding, high-achieving students showed stronger positive associations between score and word counts (e.g., total score with AI words r=0.578 and human words r=0.544), whereas low-achieving students showed weak or non-significant links between AI words and score and some negative associations between human chunks and content/organization.
finding.measure: Human-rated writing quality on HKDSE feature article rubric: content (C), language (L), organization (O), and total score
finding.std_deviation: C SD=1.27; L SD=1.02; O SD=1.10; total SD=3.28

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study asks whether ChatGPT-supported instruction improves EFL students’ academic writing and writing motivation compared with traditional teacher-led instruction. The authors frame ChatGPT as an AI-assisted writing support tool that can provide real-time feedback on grammar, vocabulary, organization, coherence, and sentence structure, potentially functioning like a responsive virtual peer or tutor.

The study involved 50 Chinese undergraduate EFL students at a national university in China, randomly assigned to an experimental group using ChatGPT and a control group receiving traditional instruction. Over 12 weeks, both groups completed similar academic writing activities, but the experimental group could use ChatGPT at home and in class for feedback and revision support, while the control group received teacher feedback only. Pre/post IELTS academic writing tasks and a writing motivation scale were used quantitatively, and interviews with nine experimental participants provided qualitative insight.

Results showed statistically significant advantages for the ChatGPT group on overall writing performance and on writing organization and language use, with a medium-to-large effect on overall writing (d=0.76) and large effects for organization (d=0.84) and language use (d=0.88). Writing content was reported as improved in descriptive comparisons, but the article’s narrative is internally inconsistent about statistical significance for that subscore, so it should be treated cautiously from the excerpt. Writing motivation also improved significantly (d=0.52). Interview data generally reinforced positive perceptions of ChatGPT for immediacy, personalization, and engagement, while also noting concerns about over-reliance and contextual accuracy.

finding.finding_summary: Compared with traditional teacher-led instruction, the ChatGPT group showed significantly higher post-test academic writing performance after 12 weeks. On overall IELTS writing, the experimental group outperformed the control group (M=59.12 vs 45.18), t(48)=3.79, p<0.001, with a large effect size (d=0.76); ANCOVA also found a significant group effect, F(1,47)=19.01, partial eta squared=0.27. Subskills improved significantly for organization (d=0.84) and language use (d=0.88).
finding.measure: IELTS academic writing tasks 1 and 2; overall writing, content, organization, and language use scores
finding.effect_size: d=0.76 overall; d=0.65 content; d=0.84 organization; d=0.88 language use; partial eta squared=0.27 overall
finding.std_deviation: overall writing pre/post SDs: experimental 12.03/14.23, control 17.26/15.62

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-supported instruction significantly increased writing motivation relative to traditional instruction. Post-test motivation scores were higher in the experimental group (M=20.06, SD=3.33) than in the control group (M=18.21, SD=3.58), with t(48)=3.34, p=0.001 and ANCOVA F(1,47)=29.62, partial eta squared=0.38. Interview data also indicated greater enjoyment, confidence, and willingness to engage in writing.
finding.measure: Writing Motivation Scale (adapted from Waller and Papi, 2017); interview themes on motivation/engagement
finding.std_deviation: experimental pre/post SDs: 3.12/3.33; control pre/post SDs: 3.09/3.58

paper_profiles.title: The two faces of Janus? Anxiety and enjoyment in the foreign language classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching
paper_profiles.population: Secondary through Adult (mixed ages; includes teens and adults)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether positive emotion in foreign language learning—foreign language enjoyment (FLE)—is distinct from the well-studied negative emotion of foreign language classroom anxiety (FLCA), and how both relate to learner characteristics. The authors argue that SLA research has focused too heavily on anxiety and propose enjoyment as a complementary construct grounded in positive psychology and flow theory.

Using an internet-based questionnaire, the study collected data from 1,746 multilingual foreign language learners worldwide. Participants completed a newly developed 21-item FLE scale, an 8-item FLCA measure adapted from the FLCAS, and an open-ended prompt about enjoyable classroom episodes. Analyses compared average FLE and FLCA, examined correlations between the two, and tested demographic/experience variables such as number of languages known, number of foreign languages studied, proficiency, relative standing, education level, age, sex, and global-regional background.

Results showed that enjoyment was significantly higher than anxiety and that the two were only modestly negatively related (r = -.36), supporting the claim that they are related but distinct emotions. Higher multilingual experience, greater proficiency, better relative standing, and higher education were associated with more enjoyment and less anxiety; age showed a pattern of increasing enjoyment and declining anxiety in older groups. The qualitative responses suggested that enjoyment was often tied to classroom activities, peer/teacher recognition, progress, teacher skill, and authentic language use. The paper is descriptive and cross-sectional, so it does not test an intervention, but it offers a detailed empirical picture of emotional experience in foreign language classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that foreign language enjoyment (FLE) was significantly higher than foreign language classroom anxiety (FLCA) across 1,746 learners, and that the two were negatively correlated but only modestly so (r = -.36, p < .0001). Multiple learner characteristics were associated with higher enjoyment and lower anxiety, including greater multilingualism, higher proficiency, higher relative standing, older age, and higher education.
finding.measure: Foreign Language Enjoyment scale (21 items); Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale short form (8 items); demographic correlates of affect

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative analysis indicates that enjoyment was frequently linked to classroom interaction, peer collaboration, teacher support, and active participation, all of which are relevant to collaboration and engagement-related durable skills. The most common episode type was specific classroom activities (441/1076, 41.0%), especially role-plays and debates, suggesting that interactive tasks were a major source of positive experience.
finding.measure: Open-ended responses on enjoyable episodes in the foreign language class

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Summarization: Designing AI Support for Real-World Expository Writing Tasks
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual position paper; no study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper argues that expository writing is an important but underexplored target for AI-assisted writing systems, especially in the era of large language models. The authors define expository writing as evidence-driven and knowledge-generating writing that requires authors to read source documents, synthesize evidence, and produce new insights rather than merely summarize existing text.

Rather than reporting an empirical study, the paper sketches a design agenda for AI support across three stages of expository writing: reading and collecting evidence, synthesizing information, and composing text. The authors emphasize that AI should augment, not replace, human judgment, because hallucination, weak reasoning, and overreliance on model output can distort evidence selection and synthesis. They propose modular support that helps writers discover relevant sources, organize and reconcile evidence, and generate short, evidence-aware text in iterative turns.

The paper’s context is broad and domain-spanning, including scientific writing, legal writing, and clinical documentation, but it does not study K-12 classrooms or any learner subgroup. Its main contribution is conceptual: it frames expository writing as a sensemaking process and outlines research and design challenges for future AI writing tools.

paper_profiles.title: Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students’ essays.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether ChatGPT-3 improves student essay writing when used as a writing-assistance tool. The authors compare essay quality, writing time, text authenticity, and text similarity between a small control group writing traditionally and an experimental group using ChatGPT-3.

The sample consisted of 18 second-year master’s students at the University of Split (n=9 control, n=9 ChatGPT), writing an 800–1000 word essay in Croatian on a forensic-science topic. Essays were scored using a rubric covering mechanics, style, content, and format; the study also tracked writing duration, plagiarism/unauthenticity, pairwise similarity, and AI-classifier judgments.

Results showed no significant advantage for ChatGPT on the primary writing outcome. Average scores were slightly higher in the control group (2.39 ± 0.71) than in the ChatGPT group (2.00 ± 0.73), and none of the predictors significantly affected essay scores (group p=0.184, duration p=0.669, module p=0.388, GPA p=0.532). Writing time was similar across groups, and although the ChatGPT group showed somewhat higher text unauthenticity, overall essay similarity was low. The authors conclude that ChatGPT did not improve essay quality in this setting and may have distracted inexperienced users rather than helping them write better.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluated essay-writing quality using rubric-based scores for mechanics, style, content, and format in 18 students (n=9 control, n=9 ChatGPT). Mean essay scores were slightly higher in the control group (2.39 ± 0.71) than in the ChatGPT group (2.00 ± 0.73), and the group effect was not significant (p=0.184).
finding.measure: Rubric-scored essay quality / overall essay score (A-D converted to 1-4)

finding.finding_summary: The paper tested whether ChatGPT reduced the time needed to complete the writing task. Writing duration was similar for the ChatGPT group (172.22 ± 31.59 minutes) and the control group (179.11 ± 31.93 minutes), and duration did not significantly predict essay score (p=0.669).
finding.measure: Writing time to complete the essay

finding.finding_summary: The study included an analysis of whether ChatGPT use related to text authenticity and similarity, which are indirectly tied to drafting practices and self-regulation in writing. The experimental group had slightly higher unauthenticity (11.87% ± 13.45 vs 9.96% ± 9.81), but overall similarity across essays was low (median Jaccard similarity 0.002, range 0–0.054), and the group difference did not translate into significantly better or worse essay scores.
finding.measure: Text authenticity / similarity and AI-classifier judgments

finding.finding_summary: Although not measured with a dedicated motivation or engagement instrument, the paper discusses whether ChatGPT helped students work faster or better and suggests first-time users may have been distracted or over-reliant on the tool. No direct quantitative evidence of engagement or motivation was reported, so any inference here is weak.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing AI in Secondary Education to Enhance Writing Competence
paper_profiles.population: Secondary education (with examples and discussion centered on upper secondary / high school)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI, especially ChatGPT-like chatbots, may influence writing competence and writing voice in secondary education. The authors frame the issue as a tension between using AI as a supportive tool for brainstorming, drafting, feedback, and revision versus the risks of dependency, plagiarism, shallow engagement, and weakened authorial voice.

Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the paper synthesizes prior research and professional examples to argue for a balanced, teacher-guided approach. It discusses where AI may help most in the writing process—especially pre-writing and revision/feedback—and where its use may be problematic, particularly during the actual composing phase and in summative assessment. The paper also highlights classroom implications such as process-based assessment, authentic and personalized assignments, and controlled exam conditions to reduce misuse.

The discussion is explicitly aimed at secondary education and repeatedly references upper secondary / study-preparatory contexts, including a 10th-grade example. It also notes that students who are less creative or less proficient may benefit more from AI-supported idea generation or feedback, while teachers need to maintain oversight to preserve learning goals and writing development. Overall, the article concludes that AI can supplement writing instruction, but the evidence base is still thin and the conclusions are largely interpretive rather than based on direct experimental effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI may support writing competence in secondary education when used for brainstorming, feedback, and revision, but it may also weaken writing development if students rely on it to generate text or bypass composing. No new effect size is reported; the paper is a conceptual review that cites prior studies and one illustrative 10th-grade example rather than presenting an original literacy outcome analysis.
finding.measure: Writing competence, writing voice, writing quality, grammar/structure feedback, and argumentative text development

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes critical thinking, reflection, and authorial ownership as central goals of AI-supported writing, but warns that AI can reduce cognitive effort and depth if it substitutes for student thinking. The evidence discussed is interpretive rather than quantitative, with no study-level effect size reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reflection, problem-solving, and ability to develop a personal voice

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can reduce teacher workload by providing instant feedback, handling standard questions, and supporting formative assessment. This is presented as a plausible operational benefit rather than a directly measured outcome, and no empirical effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, speed of feedback, and efficiency of formative support

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses how schools may need to redesign assessment policies, exam conditions, and assignment design to manage AI use, plagiarism risk, and authenticity in student writing. These are institutional implications drawn from commentary and cited examples, not from a direct policy evaluation, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Assessment design, exam integrity, and school policy responses to generative AI

paper_profiles.title: Approaching the Limits to EFL Writing Enhancement with AI-generated Text and Diverse Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This study examines how Hong Kong secondary school students compose a feature article using generative AI chatbots together with their own words. The authors focus on the structure of human-AI co-authored writing, the interaction patterns students use when integrating AI-generated text, and how those patterns relate to human-rated writing quality.

finding.finding_summary: Across 59 secondary-school compositions, writing quality was positively associated with total word count, regardless of whether words were human- or AI-generated. In the full sample, partial correlations between total score and AI words (r~=0.417) and human words (r~=0.424) were significant, while chunk-level patterns were largely not significant; however, subgroup analyses showed different effects by academic band and AI integration pattern.
finding.measure: HKDSE feature article scores for Content, Language, Organization, and Total writing score; content analysis of AI vs. human words/chunks
finding.std_deviation: Content SD=1.27; Language SD=1.02; Organization SD=1.1; Total SD=3.28

finding.finding_summary: The paper interprets different AI-use patterns as reflecting students' drafting, revising, and independent writing competence. High-banding students showed evidence of more strategic use of AI and some ability to write independently, whereas low-banding students appeared less proficient at integrating AI-generated text and may have been disadvantaged by human revision of AI text.
finding.measure: Cluster analysis and partial correlations linking AI-use patterns to academic band and score profiles

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative case study examines how four secondary-school EFL students in Hong Kong used ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots while completing a familiar timed blog-writing task. The paper focuses on the students’ prompt engineering behavior: what kinds of prompts they wrote, how often they changed prompt types, how they sequenced prompts, and how they used different chatbots during the task.

The intervention/approach was not a classroom AI curriculum or a controlled comparison, but an observation of students’ first-time use of generative chatbots for writing. Students completed a blog entry in a classroom after-school session, using an iPad and the POE app (with ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly). Screen recordings were analyzed to code prompt content (e.g., autocomplete, natural language instruction, questions, search-engine style prompts, and chatbot-generated follow-up prompts) and to map each student’s pathway across turns.

The main conclusion is that the students relied on trial-and-error prompting and used different prompt pathways to complete the same writing task. No student used all prompt types, and the pathways differed in sophistication; some students gradually combined input exemplars with instructions and questions, while others stayed with simpler autocomplete or search-style prompts. The authors conclude that EFL students would likely benefit from explicit prompt engineering education so they can more effectively collaborate with generative chatbots in writing classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: This study did not test whether ChatGPT or other chatbots improved writing quality; instead, it documented how four high-school EFL students engineered prompts to complete a blog-writing task. The paper reports descriptive patterns in writing-task support (n=4 cases; 36 coded turns after excluding 2 accidental prompts), but it provides no comparative effect on writing performance, genre quality, or linguistic accuracy.
finding.measure: Prompt content/types and prompt engineering pathways during a blog-writing task; completed blog entries were collected for triangulation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that students were learning prompt engineering through trial-and-error, showing increasing sophistication in how they combined input exemplars, instructions, and questions while completing the writing task. This is an observational/qualitative finding from 4 cases, not a measured treatment effect; no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Observed prompt engineering behaviors, sequencing of prompt types, and evidence of trial-and-error learning

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that prompt engineering affected how efficiently students progressed through the writing task, but it does not quantify time savings or productivity gains. Students completed the task within 45 minutes, with pathways ranging from 5 to 12 turns; however, the paper only infers efficiency differences qualitatively and does not compare completion speed across conditions.
finding.measure: Number of chatbot turns used to complete the writing task; completion within a 45-minute class session

paper_profiles.title: Exploring AI-Generated Text in Student Writing: How Does AI Help?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Hong Kong secondary school students used AI-generated text while composing English short stories. The authors were interested in whether and how AI-generated text was integrated into student writing, how those patterns varied across students, and whether different patterns were associated with higher human-rated writing quality.

The study involved 23 EFL secondary students from two Hong Kong schools who wrote stories using self-built AI natural language generation tools based on open-source language models. Students received workshops on coding the tools, prompting them, and editing AI output into their compositions. The resulting stories were scored by expert raters on content, language, organization, and an added AI-words criterion; the authors also counted AI chunks and AI words and used multiple linear regression and cluster analysis to examine associations between AI use and writing outcomes.

The main finding was that both human-written words and AI-generated words were positively associated with higher content, language, organization, and total scores, with stronger associations for human words than AI words. Cluster analyses suggested distinct learner profiles: more proficient writers tended to use less AI text but edit it more strategically, while less proficient writers often used more AI text without achieving high scores. The paper concludes that AI-generated text can support some secondary EFL writers, but it does not automatically improve writing quality and appears to work best when students already have sufficient writing competence and editing skill.

finding.finding_summary: In this observational study of 23 Hong Kong secondary EFL students writing short stories with AI-generated text, both human words and AI-generated words were positively associated with higher human-rated writing scores. Multiple linear regression showed significant positive partial correlations between AI words and content/language/organization/CLO scores (about 0.49-0.59) and stronger positive correlations for human words (about 0.91-0.95); however, cluster analysis also showed that high AI use did not guarantee high writing quality, and some high-AI clusters performed poorly.
finding.measure: Human-rated story quality scores for content, language, organization, CLO total, and AI-words criterion; counts of AI words and human words in stories
finding.std_deviation: C: 1.8; L: 1.42; O: 1.6; CLO: 4.74; AI words score: 1.84; grand total: 5.94

finding.finding_summary: The study also examined strategic editing and learner differences in how students integrated AI-generated text, which the authors interpret as a writing-process and metacognitive skill. More proficient writers tended to use AI text less but edit it more effectively, whereas less competent writers often lacked effective strategies for leveraging AI output.
finding.measure: Cluster profiles based on AI-chunk patterns, AI-word percentage, total words, and writing scores

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models for Automated Grading of Student Writing about Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether GPT-4 can reliably grade short student writing assignments in science courses, compared with human instructor grading and existing peer-grading systems. The central problem is the difficulty of assessing writing at scale in online courses, especially MOOCs, where thousands of responses can make instructor scoring impractical.

The study uses writing samples from three Coursera MOOCs in astronomy, astrobiology, and the history/philosophy of astronomy. The authors compare three GPT-4 prompting conditions: model answer only, model answer plus instructor rubric, and model answer plus an AI-generated rubric. They also compare these results to instructor grades and peer grades, using paired nonparametric tests, bootstrapped question-level comparisons, RMS differences, and ICC.

Overall, GPT-4 matched instructor grades when given both a model answer and a rubric, whether the rubric was human-written or AI-generated, and it was more reliable than peer grading. Performance was better on more content-based, structured science writing tasks than on more open-ended history/philosophy prompts. The study concludes that LLMs may be a scalable alternative for grading short science writing in online learning environments, though the work is limited to adult MOOC learners and does not address K-12 classrooms directly.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 produced grades that were not statistically different from instructor grades when provided with an instructor model answer plus a rubric, including an AI-generated rubric. Across the three MOOCs, the intraclass correlation coefficient for grading agreement was 0.92 (95% CI: 0.89–0.94), indicating excellent reliability in scoring science writing tasks.
finding.measure: Agreement/reliability of grades on short science writing assignments in astronomy, astrobiology, and history/philosophy of astronomy MOOCs

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates automated scoring of student writing and finds GPT-4 can closely match instructor ratings on short written responses when the model is given a rubric and exemplar answer. However, performance varied by genre/context: more open-ended prompts in the history/philosophy course showed weaker agreement than the more content-based astronomy and astrobiology prompts.
finding.measure: Accuracy and reliability of automated grading of student writing responses
finding.effect_size: RMS differences ranged from 0.37 to 0.82 depending on prompt and course

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that LLM grading could reduce the burden of assessing large volumes of student writing in MOOCs, where instructor grading is impractical. GPT-4 matched instructor grades closely when prompted with a rubric and model answer, suggesting a scalable automated-grading workflow that could substitute for or support human grading.
finding.measure: Potential scalability and grading burden reduction for large online courses

paper_profiles.title: TEASPN: Framework and Protocol for Integrated Writing Assistance Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes TEASPN, a protocol and open-source framework intended to make it easier to integrate multiple writing-assistance technologies into everyday writing software. The authors argue that a key barrier preventing advances in NLP-based writing support from reaching end users is the high development cost of connecting research models to editors and word processors.

The framework standardizes client-server communication between writing software and writing-assistance technologies such as grammatical error correction, completion, paraphrasing, jump-to-definition/coreference, hover definitions, and external-resource search. The paper also introduces a TEASPN SDK and a demo implementation that combines several NLP components, including LanguageTool for GED/GEC, a neural language model for completion, a seq2seq paraphrase model, coreference-based jumping, WordNet hover definitions, and Tatoeba/Elasticsearch search.

The empirical portion is a small user study with 12 adult participants (college students or NLP researchers) who wrote short English texts in VS Code under two conditions: an integrated TEASPN environment versus a baseline editor with no in-editor assistance but access to outside tools such as Grammarly and web dictionaries. Participants reported generally better writing experience in the integrated condition, and the texts written with TEASPN had lower GPT-2 perplexity (26.4 vs. 37.8), which the authors interpret as more fluent and/or typical English. This study supports the usability of the framework, but it does not investigate K-12 students, high-school writing, or subgroup effects relevant to grades 9-12.

finding.finding_summary: In a small user study (n=12 adults), participants wrote short English texts in an integrated TEASPN environment or in a baseline editor without in-editor tools. Texts produced in the integrated condition had lower GPT-2 perplexity (26.4 vs. 37.8; mean length 335 ± 91 chars vs. 379 ± 116), which the authors interpret as more fluent and/or typical English writing.
finding.measure: Writing fluency/typicality of produced texts, operationalized with GPT-2 perplexity and text length

finding.finding_summary: Participants subjectively rated the integrated environment favorably: 10 of 12 (83.3%) said it provided a better writing experience, and 40% said they wrote a better text in the integrated condition. These responses suggest improved perceived usability and writing experience rather than a direct learning outcome.
finding.measure: Post-task questionnaire on writing experience and perceived text quality

finding.finding_summary: The integrated condition enabled use of multiple embedded tools, with participants reporting an average of 3.2 WAT features used during the task. The study argues that TEASPN reduces friction by bringing tools into the editor, although the written texts were somewhat shorter in the integrated condition, suggesting time was spent exploring features.
finding.measure: Self-reported feature use and observed text length/time-on-task proxy
finding.std_deviation: 3.2 features used on average; 335 ± 91 chars vs. 379 ± 116 chars

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames the system as supporting higher-level writing processes such as rewriting, searching, and selecting among suggestions, but it does not directly measure durable skills. The strongest evidence here is indirect: participants used multiple assistance features and reported improved writing experience, implying reduced cognitive friction during composing.
finding.measure: Indirect inference from multi-tool writing workflow use

paper_profiles.title: Exploring EFL Secondary Students’ AI-generated Text Editing While Composition Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines how Hong Kong EFL secondary school students edit and revise AI-generated text while completing an expository writing task. The authors ask what kinds of edits students make to AI-produced text and what overall editing patterns emerge during machine-in-the-loop writing with generative AI chatbots and related writing-tool suggestions.

The study took place in seven Hong Kong secondary schools during a two-hour AI-assisted writing workshop. Twenty-nine students across grades 1–5 of secondary school were taught basic prompt engineering and then asked to complete a 500-word expository/article writing task using POE, which aggregates chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, plus Google Docs and iOS writing tools. Students recorded their screens as they wrote; 25 usable recordings were analyzed using content analysis and thematic analysis.

The paper identifies 15 distinct edit types across seven categories, including inserting, deleting, and replacing AI-generated text, as well as unanticipated AI-initiated edits from Apple iOS predictive text and Google Docs spelling/grammar/next-word suggestions. It also finds four editing patterns: planning with top-down drafting and revising, top-down drafting and revising without planning, planning with bottom-up drafting and revising, and bottom-up drafting and revising without planning. The authors conclude that students’ use of generative AI in writing is cognitively complex and active rather than passive, but they emphasize that the study is descriptive and does not measure writing quality gains relative to a control condition.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines secondary students’ writing processes and AI-mediated text editing during an expository/article composition task, but it does not compare pre/post writing quality or test a causal effect on literacy outcomes. In the 25 analyzed screen recordings (n=25 usable recordings from 29 participants), students produced 266 edits, including insertions (n=68), deletions (n=58), and replacements (e.g., Replacement AI:Human n=44), showing active revision of AI-generated text rather than passive copying. The evidence supports descriptive insight into writing behavior, not an effect size for writing achievement.
finding.measure: AI-generated text edit types during expository/article writing; screen-recorded composition process

paper_profiles.title: How University Disability Services Professionals Write Image Descriptions for HCI Figures Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can support Disability Services Office (DSO) professionals in writing alternative text (alt text) for complex HCI figures. The motivating problem is that accessibility professionals often need to describe technical visuals from outside their subject expertise, which can make alt text incomplete, generic, or inaccurate. The authors focus on alt text authoring as a real-world accessibility writing task rather than on standalone model performance.

The study has two phases. In Study 1, 12 DSO professionals at higher education institutions wrote alt text for science/HCI figures both without assistance and with ChatGPT-4o support. The researchers collected think-aloud data, interviews, questionnaires, and chat logs to understand workflow, prompting behavior, confidence, and challenges. In Study 2, 11 HCI experts rated selected alt texts using a rubric that emphasized figure type identification, overview and message, key elements, trends/patterns, clarity, details, and contextual relevance.

Findings indicate that AI assistance improved perceived confidence, reduced time and effort, and produced longer alt text that was rated higher in quality by expert reviewers than human-only text. However, the study also shows important limitations: some participants over-relied on AI, many used shallow prompting strategies, and some accepted outputs without sufficiently checking accuracy. The authors conclude that generative AI can be a useful drafting aid for accessibility professionals, but human review and domain checking remain necessary to avoid misleading descriptions.

finding.finding_summary: AI assistance improved DSO professionals’ alt-text writing efficiency and reduced effort. In Study 1 (n=12), participants completed four figures within about 20 minutes with AI support versus using the full 50 minutes without AI support, and two participants could not finish all descriptions in the no-AI condition. The AI-assisted descriptions were also longer on average (mean 140.70 words, std 79.65) than human-only descriptions (mean 104.16 words, std 66.21; t(36)=-2.09, p=0.044).
finding.measure: Alt-text writing time, task completion, and word count of produced alt text
finding.std_deviation: Human-only mean=104.16, std=66.21; AI-assisted mean=140.70, std=79.65

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies accessibility writing for HCI figure descriptions rather than student learning outcomes. Expert raters judged AI-assisted alt text to be superior in quality to human-only alt text, indicating that generative AI can improve the quality of academic figure descriptions. In the expert-evaluation study (n=11), AI-assisted text was rated as better on completeness, clarity, details, and contextual relevance, though some inaccuracies remained.
finding.measure: Rubric-based alt-text quality ratings by HCI experts

finding.finding_summary: The study reports mixed effects on writers’ self-regulation and prompting/metacognitive behavior. Participants with lower HCI knowledge often over-relied on AI and accepted output without sufficient analysis, while more experienced participants used iterative prompting and follow-up questions more effectively. The paper does not report a standardized measure or effect size for this outcome, but qualitative evidence suggests AI can support drafting while also encouraging shallow reliance if users do not critically evaluate outputs.
finding.measure: Think-aloud, interviews, and chat-history analysis of prompting/revision behavior

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Tools on Student Writing Development: A Case Study From The CGScholar AI Helper Project
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This case study examines whether the CGScholar AI Helper, a generative-AI-supported writing feedback tool integrated into the CGScholar platform, can support writing development for high-school students. The paper is situated in broader debates about responsible use of generative AI in education and argues that AI should be mediated through teacher-selected texts, prompts, and rubrics rather than used in an unstructured way.

The study was conducted in a Midwestern U.S. public high school with one ELA teacher and six volunteer 11th-grade students from a socioeconomically underserved school. Students completed a 200-word comparative writing task based on two teacher-selected texts about Indigenous values and agriculture. They received AI-generated feedback aligned to the teacher’s rubric, revised their drafts, received a second round of AI feedback, and then submitted work for teacher review. Data came from draft-to-revision comparisons, student focus group comments, teacher post-survey responses, and researcher observations.

Findings were positive overall but qualitative and small-scale. Five of six students improved on at least one rubric criterion, and one student improved on three criteria. Improvements were most evident in compare/contrast, composing defensible claims, analysis, and introducing/connecting evidence; there were no improvements on the “Identify” and “Support evidence” criteria. Students and the teacher described the feedback as direct, actionable, and useful for revision, though the feedback was also criticized as too long and too linguistically complex. The authors conclude that this mediated generative-AI approach shows promise for high-school ELA writing support, while noting the need for further refinement.

finding.finding_summary: In this 11th-grade ELA case study (n=6), CGScholar AI Helper was associated with improved writing performance on multiple rubric criteria after students revised drafts using AI feedback and resubmitted work. Five students improved in at least one criterion and one student improved in three; gains were reported in compare/contrast, composing defensible claims, introducing/connecting evidence, and analysis, while two criteria showed no improvement. The evidence is qualitative and pre/post within-subject rather than experimental, so no causal effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher rubric ratings of student writing revisions across six criteria (compare/contrast, identify, compose, introduce and connect, support evidence, analyze)

finding.finding_summary: Students and the teacher reported that the AI feedback was helpful, direct, specific, actionable, and encouraging, and that it motivated revision. Focus group comments indicated that the tool gave students something concrete to “go off of” when fixing their writing, suggesting improved willingness to revise and persist through the task. Because this is qualitative self-report evidence from a single small case study, no effect size is available.
finding.measure: Student focus group feedback and teacher post-survey perceptions of motivation to revise and usefulness of feedback

finding.finding_summary: The intervention appears to support higher-order writing processes, especially analysis, comparison/contrast, and claim development. Students revised drafts to include more context, stronger claims, and clearer connections between evidence and argument, indicating gains in analytical reasoning and metacognitive revision behaviors. The study does not report standardized measures or causal estimates, so the finding is based on qualitative rubric-based comparison of drafts.
finding.measure: Rubric-based evidence of analytical writing revision, claim construction, and evidence integration

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI Helper reduced the burden of identifying what to revise by delivering immediate, rubric-aligned feedback during drafting, which may make revision more efficient for students and more workable for teachers. The teacher reported that the tool encouraged revision, but also noted a drawback: the feedback was too long and overly elaborate, prompting later design changes such as chat boxes for summarization and clarification. No quantitative productivity or workload measures were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher and student perceptions of feedback usefulness, clarity, and revision support

finding.finding_summary: Because the writing task centered on comparing two Indigenous-themed texts within ELA content, the study also substantively engages secondary content-area writing. Students improved their ability to connect evidence from the assigned readings to claims about Indigenous culture, traditions, and representations in society. The evidence is based on rubric-scored qualitative revisions rather than standardized content outcomes.
finding.measure: Content-area writing task using two teacher-selected readings about Indigenous culture and agriculture

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Writing Style Development in High School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how writing style develops over time among Danish high school students. The authors ask whether students’ writing becomes more different from their early essays as they progress through high school, whether these changes correlate with simple text-quality indicators, and whether some students show stronger or weaker development trajectories.

To study this, the authors analyze a proprietary corpus of about 131,095 Danish essays written by 10,095 students from Danish high schools. They train a Siamese neural network to estimate pairwise writing-style similarity between texts, then construct a per-student writing-style development profile from each student’s early essays and later submissions. These profiles are clustered into five groups, and the clusters are examined alongside quality indicators such as SMOG grade, noun phrases per sentence, verb phrases per sentence, and text length.

The study finds that writing style generally changes over time during high school, with similarity to early writing typically declining as students submit more essays and write longer texts. Two clusters show the strongest improvement in the quality indicators and are interpreted as more favorable development trajectories, while two other clusters show weaker improvement or even a temporary setback around the first summer vacation. A further analysis of random student pairs suggests that writing styles become more diverse over the course of high school, with first-year and third-year students sometimes remaining as similar as, or more similar than, two third-year students. The paper is an observational analysis rather than an intervention study, so it does not test educational tools or compare instructional conditions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies writing development in Danish high school essays and finds that writing style generally changes over time, with similarity to students’ initial essays declining across high school. Across the five clusters, the authors report both favorable trajectories (C1, C2) with larger gains in quality indicators and weaker trajectories (C3, C4) with smaller gains or a temporary setback after the first summer vacation; sample size was n=3,688 analyzed students, with 131,095 essays in the full corpus.
finding.measure: Writing-style similarity between essays; SMOG grade; noun phrases per sentence; verb phrases per sentence; average words written
finding.study_size: n=3688 analyzed students (131,095 essays total; analysis subset Tanalyze n=3688)

paper_profiles.title: Writing Into Water
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is not an education study. It investigates a physical method for writing lines, letters, and patterns in water by using a movable ion-exchange resin bead to assemble colloidal particles into visible traces.

The authors combine experiments, video tracking, pH microphotometry, and particle-based/continuum modeling to explain how a moving bead generates a diffusio-osmotic flow that attracts tracer particles and leaves behind durable, free-floating lines. They vary bead speed, tracer concentration, particle size, and pen type to map when single lines, split lines, or inverted (negative-contrast) lines appear. The work concludes that hydrodynamic writing in water is possible as a generic physical process, but it has no study of students, classrooms, writing instruction, or AI-supported writing.

Because the paper is entirely about colloidal writing in fluids rather than educational writing tools, there are no relevant K-12 learner subgroups, comparators, or instructional outcomes to extract for the requested high-school AI-writing matrix.

paper_profiles.title: Modifying AI, Enhancing Essays: How Active Engagement with Generative AI Boosts Writing Quality
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how different forms of generative AI (GAI) use during writing relate to the quality of the resulting essays. The authors ask whether students who merely seek AI suggestions, accept them unchanged, or accept and then revise them produce different writing outcomes, and whether those outcomes vary by writing genre and language background.

The study analyzes the CoAuthor dataset, consisting of 1,445 GAI-assisted writing sessions from 63 crowd-sourced writers writing across 20 topics, using GPT-3 suggestions. The authors model three behavioral patterns as treatments: seeking suggestions without accepting them, seeking and accepting suggestions without revision, and seeking and accepting suggestions with modification. They estimate causal effects with X-learner methods, controlling for genre, topic, first-language background, GPT temperature, and frequency penalty.

Across the full sample, accepting AI text without revision is associated with lower lexical sophistication, syntactic complexity, and cohesion, while accepting and revising AI text is associated with improvements on all three measures. All three behaviors reduce gender bias somewhat, with the largest reduction when suggestions are sought but not accepted. Subgroup analyses show that non-native English writers often benefit from AI for lexical sophistication and syntactic complexity, but may show more bias; argumentative writing and some GPT settings also change whether AI use helps or hurts cohesion and complexity. The paper concludes that process matters: active revision of AI output is more beneficial than passive acceptance, and educators should assess how students engage with AI, not only the final written product.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies writing quality in GAI-assisted essay writing using 1,445 sessions from 63 writers. At the average treatment level, seeking suggestions and accepting them without revision reduced lexical sophistication (ATE = -0.086), syntactic complexity (ATE = -0.869), and text cohesion (ATE = -0.007), while seeking suggestions and then revising them improved all three outcomes (lexical sophistication ATE = 0.102, syntactic complexity ATE = 0.963, cohesion ATE = 0.008).
finding.measure: Lexical sophistication (Advanced Guiraud), syntactic complexity (Mean Length of T-Unit), text cohesion (Semantic Overlap)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; discusses primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning contexts rather than studying a specific sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper that examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT and related systems, for education. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors synthesize early use cases and existing literature to discuss how LLMs may support learning, teaching, assessment, feedback, and educational content generation across multiple educational levels.

The paper argues that LLMs could aid students with writing, language learning, problem solving, and personalized support, and could help teachers with lesson planning, feedback, assessment, and content creation. It also highlights major risks, including bias, plagiarism, overreliance, privacy, security, fairness, environmental cost, and difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated text. The conclusion is that LLMs are promising but require careful governance, human oversight, critical-thinking-oriented pedagogy, and further empirical research before responsible large-scale adoption.

Because this is a conceptual/position article, it does not report an original intervention study, sample characteristics, comparator, duration, or quantitative outcomes. It is therefore not a high school empirical intervention paper and should be treated as background/theoretical guidance rather than efficacy evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs may improve institutional practices such as lesson planning, assessment, feedback, and personalized instruction, but also pose substantial governance challenges around privacy, bias, copyright, integrity, and sustainability. No original empirical effect estimate is reported; the claims are conceptual and based on cited prior work rather than a primary intervention study.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of institutional uses and risks of LLMs in education

finding.finding_summary: The authors claim that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by supporting automated feedback, semi-automated grading, quiz generation, and content creation. These are framed as anticipated efficiency gains rather than results from a controlled study, and no quantitative workload reduction estimate is newly produced in this paper.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / grading effort / feedback generation efficiency (conceptual and cited examples)

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence applications in higher education published between 2007 and 2018. The review asks how AI research in higher education has developed, how AI is conceptualized, what ethical issues are discussed, and what kinds of AI applications are being studied. The authors screened 2,656 records, retained 146 journal articles, and coded them for publication patterns, definitions of AI, ethical reflection, and application type.

The review finds that most studies come from computer science and STEM fields, and that quantitative methods dominate the literature. The main AI application areas are profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. The review also notes that only a tiny minority of papers explicitly define AI or critically reflect on ethical issues such as privacy and cost, suggesting that the field is technically rich but educationally and ethically underdeveloped.

Most of the included studies are descriptive, correlational, or short-term implementation studies rather than rigorous intervention trials. The paper concludes that AI in higher education is usually framed as a tool for academic support and institutional efficiency, but that stronger pedagogical grounding, more attention to risks, and more educator-focused research are needed.

finding.finding_summary: The review shows that AI tools in higher education are frequently used to automate or streamline tasks such as assessment, feedback, admission prediction, course scheduling, and other administrative functions. Across the included literature, these applications are presented as improving speed, accuracy, and workload reduction, though the paper does not aggregate a single effect size.
finding.measure: Frequency and functional role of AI applications for assessment, grading, prediction, feedback, and administrative support across included studies

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the reviewed literature focuses on institutional and administrative uses of AI, including admissions, retention, student profiling, and aligning students with programs or labor-market needs. The review characterizes these uses as supporting institutional decision-making and policy-relevant functions, but again does not report pooled effects.
finding.measure: Institutional and administrative applications of AI across included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies multiple writing-related AI applications, especially automated essay scoring and automated feedback for student writing. Individual studies were generally reported as improving efficiency and sometimes encouraging revisions, but the review also notes persistent concerns about feedback quality and usefulness, especially for some learner groups.
finding.measure: Writing assessment, automated essay scoring, and AI-generated feedback for student writing

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies use AI to predict or monitor engagement, motivation, and related learner states, and the review describes these systems as enabling early intervention for at-risk students. The paper does not synthesize causal impacts on motivation or engagement, but it does report that these constructs are common targets of AI-supported monitoring.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, and related learner-behavior indicators

finding.finding_summary: The review includes AI applications for collaboration, self-regulation, and feedback-mediated learning processes, including systems designed to support collaborative writing, peer dialogue, and metacognitive regulation. The narrative synthesis suggests potential benefits, but also emphasizes that the evidence base is short-term and often preliminary.
finding.measure: Collaboration, self-regulation, and related process skills in AI-supported learning environments

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a structured ChatGPT prompt framework can improve second-language learners’ critical thinking and argumentative writing. The authors developed the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW), combining the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model and Tan’s framework for argumentative essays with Hattie & Timperley’s feedback model.

The study used a small quantitative experiment with 10 university students from a state university, randomly assigned to an experimental group using CGCAW-guided ChatGPT prompts and a control group using ChatGPT without guidelines. Participants wrote a short 150–300 word argumentative essay in 40 minutes on social media’s effects on society. Essays were evaluated by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor on different criteria, including clarity, coherence, evidence use, persuasiveness, and thesis/reasoning quality.

Results were mixed across raters. Grammarly slightly favored the control group (mean 92.2 vs. 90.6), ChatGPT favored the experimental group on clarity, coherence, and evidence (mean 74.0 vs. 72.2), and the instructor strongly favored the control group (mean 56 vs. 35). The authors conclude that the CGCAW framework may help some aspects of argumentative writing and critical thinking, but it needs refinement and the evidence is limited by the very small sample, brief task duration, and inconsistent scoring across evaluators.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention produced mixed effects on argumentative writing quality. ChatGPT ratings favored the experimental group on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence (mean total 74.0 vs. 72.2; SD 7.6 vs. 5.5), but Grammarly slightly favored the control group (mean 92.2 vs. 90.6), and the course instructor favored the control group substantially (mean 56 vs. 35).
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality ratings (clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness; plus Grammarly and instructor writing criteria)
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT total SD=7.6 experimental, 5.5 control; subscale SDs reported for clarity/evidence/coherence

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily targets critical thinking in relation to writing, not general literacy alone. The experimental group was reported to improve in clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, which the authors interpret as signs of stronger critical thinking, but other evaluators showed weaker or negative results for the guided framework.
finding.measure: Critical thinking-related dimensions embedded in argumentative writing (clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, thesis development)

paper_profiles.title: eRevise+RF: A Writing Evaluation System for Assessing Student Essay Revisions and Providing Formative Feedback
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th) and Middle School (6-8); not high school
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents eRevise+RF, an automated writing evaluation system designed to assess student argumentative essay revisions and provide formative feedback on both evidence use and revision quality. The main problem addressed is that students often struggle not only to include evidence in response-to-text writing, but also to revise their drafts in ways that meaningfully improve argument quality after receiving feedback.

The system combines evidence-scoring indicators (e.g., number of pieces of evidence and specificity) with revision classifiers to generate feedback across three essay drafts. It was deployed in classrooms with 6 teachers and 406 students in grades 4-8 across three schools in Pennsylvania and Louisiana, writing about two response-to-text prompts (Millennium Villages Project and space exploration) over 3 sessions spanning 3 to 5 days. The evaluation includes NLP component validation and descriptive comparisons of draft quality across sessions; the authors report that essay quality and evidence-use metrics improved across drafts, and that students’ revisions were broadly aligned with the feedback they received. However, the study explicitly lacked a control group, so it is a pilot deployment rather than a causal intervention trial.

finding.finding_summary: In a pilot deployment with 406 students in grades 4-8, essay quality improved across drafts and students’ revisions were responsive to formative feedback. On the MVP essays, average essay word count increased from 293 (draft 1) to 361 (draft 2) to 405 (draft 3), while predicted evidence score (ES) rose from 2.45 to 2.81 to 2.91, NPE from 2.56 to 3.19 to 3.34, and SPC from 8.81 to 12.21 to 13.98. The paper reports similar gains for the SPACE essays (e.g., WC 228→295→338; ES 2.09→2.55→2.85), but provides no inferential test or causal estimate.
finding.measure: Essay quality metrics for response-to-text writing: word count (WC), evidence score (ES), number of pieces of evidence (NPE), and specificity (SPC) across drafts
finding.study_size: n=172 MVP essays used for full three-draft analysis; n=150 SPACE essays used for full three-draft analysis; 406 students deployed overall

paper_profiles.title: Neural Automated Writing Evaluation with Corrective Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a technical system that integrates neural automated writing evaluation (AWE) with grammatical error correction (GEC) to provide instant scoring and corrective feedback for language learners. The main problem addressed is the burden of manual feedback and the separation between scoring and correction in existing tools; the authors argue that combining these functions can support more efficient writing instruction and exam preparation.

The paper describes the architecture of the system and the datasets/models used to build it. For AWE, the authors train and evaluate a RoBERTa-based essay scoring model on ASAP/ASAP++ with denoising, reporting prompt-by-prompt quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) improvements on average from 0.6047 to 0.6143 after cleaning. For GEC, they train seq2seq models with fairseq on BEA 2019 datasets and report a best F0.5 of 65.29 on the BEA 2019 test set.

This is not a true high-school intervention trial: it is primarily a system-description paper with model development, benchmark evaluation, and a planned perception experiment. The paper includes questionnaire items for future learner/instructor perception studies, but it does not report an actual intervention study in grades 9–12 or any student outcome trial. Its conclusions are therefore about feasibility and potential utility of the integrated AWE+GEC system rather than educational efficacy in a school setting.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved automated essay scoring performance after denoising the ASAP dataset. Average prompt-by-prompt QWK increased from 0.6047 on the original text to 0.6143 on the cleaned version (Prompt 1-8 average), with the largest gain on Prompt 1 (0.6187 to 0.7344).
finding.measure: Quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) for automated essay scoring on ASAP prompts
finding.effect_size: 0.6143 QWK average post-cleaning; 0.6047 QWK average original

paper_profiles.title: Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students’ essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether ChatGPT-3 can improve students’ essay writing performance when used as a writing assistant. The authors compare essays written by students using ChatGPT-3 with essays written traditionally, examining overall essay quality, writing time, text authenticity/plagiarism-related indicators, and similarity between essays.

Eighteen second-year master’s students at the University of Split were assigned to two groups of nine each, balanced on module and GPA. The experimental group received ChatGPT assistance (version 2.1.0) while the control group wrote without it; both had four hours to complete an 800–1000 word essay in Croatian on biometric identification in forensic science. Essays were graded by two teachers using a rubric covering mechanics, style, content, and format. The study also measured writing duration, PlagScan-based authenticity, pairwise Jaccard similarity, and AI-classifier judgments.

The main conclusion was that ChatGPT did not improve essay quality or speed. Average essay score was slightly higher in the control group (2.39 ± 0.71) than in the ChatGPT group (2.00 ± 0.73), and the group effect was not significant (P = 0.184). Writing duration was similar across groups, and the experimental group showed slightly more non-authentic text, though similarity across essays remained low overall. The authors conclude that first-time use of ChatGPT in this context did not provide measurable writing benefits and may even be associated with slightly worse performance.

finding.finding_summary: Using ChatGPT-3 as a writing assistant did not improve essay quality. The control group slightly outperformed the experimental group on the overall essay score (2.39 ± 0.71 vs 2.00 ± 0.73), and the group effect was not significant (P = 0.184) in a linear regression model.
finding.measure: Overall essay score based on rubric ratings for mechanics, style, content, and format

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-3 did not reduce the time needed to complete the writing task. Mean writing time was 172.22 ± 31.59 minutes in the GPT-assisted group versus 179.11 ± 31.93 minutes in the control group, and writing duration was not a significant predictor of essay score (P = 0.669).
finding.measure: Essay writing duration

paper_profiles.title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether a brief AI literacy intervention can reduce high school students’ tendency to over-rely on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations. The authors motivate the work by arguing that widespread use of large language models in education may encourage uncritical acceptance of AI output, and that AI literacy might help students evaluate recommendations more critically.

The intervention was a short educational text explaining ChatGPT’s working mechanism, limitations, risks, and how to use it wisely. The control group read a shorter introductory text about ChatGPT’s general usefulness and basic features. Students were 12th-grade Estonian high school seniors (final analytic sample n=36) who were randomly assigned to intervention or control conditions in an online experiment.

After reading the text, students solved eight math logic puzzles with ChatGPT recommendations, four of which were intentionally incorrect. The main outcome was over-reliance on incorrect recommendations, with secondary outcomes including under-reliance on correct recommendations, perceived confidence, and decision time. The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance (48.68% vs 55.88%, d=-0.25) but did significantly increase under-reliance (36.84% vs 19.12%, d=0.78), suggesting the short-form literacy text may have encouraged caution without reducing acceptance of wrong advice. Overall, the paper concludes that brief AI literacy alone is not sufficient to counter over-reliance on ChatGPT in this context.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention did not significantly reduce students’ over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations while solving math puzzles. Over-reliance was 48.68% in the intervention group versus 55.88% in the control group (Welch’s t(28.78) = -0.73, p = .236, d = -0.25), indicating no detectable benefit for accuracy on this numeracy task. However, the intervention significantly increased under-reliance on correct recommendations, suggesting a cautionary shift rather than improved calibrated use of AI.
finding.measure: Acceptance of ChatGPT recommendations on eight math logic puzzles (over-reliance and under-reliance rates)
finding.effect_size: d=-0.25 for over-reliance; d=0.78 for under-reliance
finding.std_deviation: Over-reliance SD intervention=24.26, control=33.69; under-reliance SD intervention=24.11, control=20.78

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined whether a short AI literacy text improved students’ critical evaluation of ChatGPT and altered their reliance behavior. The intervention increased self-reported AI literacy for working mechanism and usage (both p < .05), but did not improve actual calibration of reliance on AI outputs; instead, it increased ignoring of correct recommendations. Correlational analyses also suggested that longer decision times were associated with less over-reliance on incorrect recommendations (rs = -0.41, p = .013).
finding.measure: Self-reported AI literacy, reliance behavior, and initial decision time as an indicator of deliberative thinking
finding.effect_size: d=0.76 (usage), d=0.70 (working mechanism), d=0.19 (limitations), rs=-0.41, rs=0.35
finding.std_deviation: Self-report SDs reported in text; decision time SDs reported as not central

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was designed around ChatGPT understanding and use, and its immediate effectiveness was partly evaluated through self-reported knowledge about how ChatGPT works and how to use it wisely. Students in the intervention group reported higher perceived knowledge of ChatGPT’s working mechanism (M=3.37 vs 2.77, d=0.70) and usage (M=3.42 vs 2.77, d=0.76), but there was no significant improvement in perceived knowledge of limitations and risks (M=2.95 vs 2.77, d=0.19, p = .577).
finding.measure: Self-reported perceived knowledge of ChatGPT working mechanism, usage, and limitations/risks
finding.std_deviation: Working mechanism SDs=0.76/0.90; usage SDs=0.77/0.97; limitations SDs=0.91/1.03

finding.finding_summary: The authors measured initial decision time and total questionnaire time to assess whether the intervention changed how efficiently students interacted with ChatGPT. Mean initial decision time across puzzles was slightly lower in the intervention group (1.56 minutes) than the control group (1.64 minutes), but this difference was not statistically significant (U = 179.5, p = .560).
finding.measure: Initial decision time across all puzzles (dttotal) and total time spent completing the questionnaire
finding.std_deviation: dttotal SD intervention=0.77, control=1.12; total questionnaire time mean=23.6 minutes overall

paper_profiles.title: An Empirical Study to Understand How Students Use ChatGPT for Writing Essays
paper_profiles.venue: ACM conference paper (arXiv preprint; venue not specified in excerpt)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how students actually use ChatGPT while writing essays, with an eye toward the implications for writing instruction and learning. The authors argue that much of the debate about generative AI in education is speculative because researchers and educators have limited visibility into students’ real interactions with tools like ChatGPT during writing tasks.

To study this, the authors built an online writing platform that embedded an in-house ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-turbo) and logged queries, responses, keystrokes, and copy/paste behavior. Seventy-seven U.S. college students recruited from university mailing lists and Prolific wrote an ACT-style argumentative essay for about 30 minutes, while also completing pre- and post-task surveys measuring writing self-efficacy, technology acceptance, perceived ownership, and creativity support. The design was not an intervention trial: all participants used the same tool in the same task, with no randomized comparator condition.

The paper’s main contribution is descriptive and interpretive rather than efficacy-focused. It identifies common usage patterns—planning, translating, reviewing, and “all” or full-essay generation—and shows that a substantial share of participants used ChatGPT to draft large portions or all of their essays. The authors report that higher writing self-efficacy was associated with less ChatGPT use, and that students who used ChatGPT only for ideation or review sometimes reported ownership levels comparable to non-users. Overall, the study raises concerns about dependence, reduced critical engagement, and “vibe writing,” while providing a dataset and framework for future research on regulation and classroom integration.

finding.finding_summary: This study directly examines essay writing behaviors and writing-related perceptions while students used ChatGPT. In a sample of n=77 college students, the authors found that many participants used ChatGPT for planning, translating, reviewing, or generating entire essays, and that some students copied ChatGPT output directly into their essays; however, the study did not test whether writing quality improved or worsened under a comparator condition.
finding.measure: ChatGPT query types, essay composition traces, copy/paste behavior, word counts, perceived ownership, and creativity support during essay writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students’ writing self-efficacy influenced their ChatGPT use: students with higher writing confidence tended to use ChatGPT less. It also measured perceived ownership and creativity support after the essay task, finding that students who used ChatGPT only for ideation or review sometimes reported ownership comparable to non-users, suggesting nuanced effects on students’ feelings about their work and engagement.
finding.measure: Self-Efficacy for Writing (SEWS), perceived ownership questionnaire, Creativity Support Index (CSI)

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that ChatGPT use can displace aspects of critical engagement and independent planning in writing. Across n=77 participants, the authors observed substantial use of ChatGPT for ideation, structuring, and even full-essay generation, which they interpret as potentially reducing opportunities to practice planning, evaluating, and revising writing independently.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of ChatGPT queries (planning, translating, reviewing, all) and analysis of essay-writing traces

paper_profiles.title: ESSAYBENCH: Evaluating Large Language Models in Multi-Genre Chinese Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces ESSAYBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on Chinese essay writing across four genres: argumentative, narrative, descriptive, and expository. The authors argue that existing LLM evaluation methods are too coarse-grained for Chinese essays and do not adequately capture genre-specific rhetorical and structural features.

To address this, they curate 728 real-world essay prompts from chatbot interactions and educational examination materials, then categorize them into open-ended and constrained prompt sets. They design a fine-grained, dependency-aware scoring rubric and validate it through a human agreement study using 14 professional annotators and pairwise comparisons on 5,040 labeled judgments. They also benchmark 15 LLMs on the dataset.

The paper is not an instructional intervention study in schools; it is a benchmark/evaluation paper focused on tool assessment and judge calibration. Its main findings are that the proposed rubric aligns better with human judgments than a coarse baseline, especially for stronger LLM judges, and that the framework distinguishes high-, medium-, and low-quality essays more effectively. In benchmarking, newer proprietary and Chinese models perform best overall, while narrative and descriptive writing remain harder than argumentative and expository writing.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies Chinese essay writing evaluation, which is directly in the literacy domain. In the human agreement study (n=80 prompts sampled for evaluation; 14 annotators; 5,040 pairwise labels), the proposed fine-grained rubric showed stronger alignment with human judgments than the baseline Align-Score, with Spearman ρ improving up to 0.816 and Kendall’s τ up to 0.704 for DeepSeek-R1. The study also found the framework better distinguished high-, medium-, and low-quality essays, indicating improved writing-quality assessment rather than learner writing performance.
finding.measure: Human agreement on essay-quality rankings; sensitivity to high/medium/low essay quality; benchmark scores on Chinese essay writing
finding.study_size: n=80 prompts for agreement study; 14 annotators; 5,040 pairwise annotations

paper_profiles.title: Help Me Write a Story: Evaluating LLMs’ Ability to Generate Writing Feedback
paper_profiles.population: Not a human participant study; English short stories as model inputs with human annotators as evaluators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) can provide useful feedback on creative writing, specifically short stories. It does not study students receiving an intervention; instead, it builds the STORYFEEDBACK benchmark by synthetically corrupting 326 seed stories into four conditions (original, backtranslate, swap, delete), generating feedback from eight LLMs across four prompting setups, and then evaluating that feedback with automatic metrics and human judgments.

The core contribution is an evaluation framework for story-writing feedback, not an instructional intervention trial. The authors analyze whether model feedback is well-formed, specific, correct, able to identify the biggest writing issue, and appropriately positive. Human annotators rated 1,920 feedback samples (3 ratings each), and the study finds that modern LLMs usually produce valid and specific feedback, but they often miss the most salient problem in the story and are not reliable at deciding when positive feedback like “the text is perfect as-is” is warranted.

Because the paper is centered on benchmark construction and model evaluation, it does not report classroom outcomes, student writing gains, or any comparison of student learning against a control group. The evidence is therefore about feedback quality and model behavior in a controlled synthetic setting, rather than efficacy of an AI writing assistant in grades 9–12.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that LLMs can generate usable writing feedback out of the box, which may reduce the effort needed to draft comments for writers. In human evaluation over 1,920 feedback samples, models generally scored high on sanity-check and specificity, with correctness scores around 0.7-0.8 for the strongest models, indicating the outputs were often plausible and actionable.
finding.measure: Human ratings of feedback usefulness/sanity/specificity/correctness on 1,920 model outputs
finding.study_size: n=1,920 feedback samples (3 human annotations each)

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluates LLM-generated feedback on story writing, a literacy task, and finds that the feedback is often specific and reasonably correct but not consistently aligned with the most important writing problems. Human raters gave high specificity scores (up to 0.95 on average for some models) and moderate correctness (roughly 0.73-0.83 for the best models), but lower error-detection and relevance scores, showing mixed quality for writing improvement.
finding.measure: Human ratings of story-writing feedback quality, especially correctness, error-detection, specificity, and relevance
finding.study_size: n=1,920 feedback samples; 326 seed stories expanded to ~1,300 story versions

paper_profiles.title: Work-in-Progress: An empirical study to understand how students use ChatGPT for writing essays and how it affects their ownership
paper_profiles.venue: In2Writing '24 (workshop paper at CHI 2026 listed as forthcoming)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
