This work-in-progress paper proposes a study of how students use ChatGPT while writing essays and how that use relates to students’ perceived ownership of their writing. The paper is framed around two research questions: how students use LLM-powered tools during essay composition, and whether using such tools changes students’ feelings that the essay is their own.

The authors describe a planned user study rather than completed intervention results. Their prototype writing platform embeds a simulated ChatGPT interface alongside a keystroke-level text editor so that the researchers can record queries, responses, edits, timestamps, and patterns of copying/pasting or revision during essay writing. Participants will be students from a university ethics/professionalism course, largely third-year undergraduates, who will write a response to a pre-selected essay prompt using ChatGPT as an optional assistant and then complete an exit survey about ownership and perceptions of ChatGPT.

Because the paper reports only study design and intended analyses, it does not present outcome data or efficacy findings. Its main contribution is methodological: a system for capturing fine-grained writing-process data and a plan to analyze how students integrate LLM assistance into essay drafting, along with perceived ownership. The paper is best understood as a descriptive or observational study proposal rather than a causal intervention trial.

finding.finding_summary: No empirical effect is reported because this is a work-in-progress paper describing a planned study rather than completed results. The paper proposes measuring essay-writing process and perceived ownership during ChatGPT-assisted writing, but no sample data, effect sizes, or outcome results are presented.
finding.measure: Essay writing process; perceived ownership survey; essay drafts and revisions

finding.finding_summary: The paper targets students’ perceived ownership of their writing, which is a self-perception construct closely related to motivation and agency. However, no results are reported, so there is no demonstrated effect of ChatGPT use on ownership in this paper.
finding.measure: Exit survey of perceived ownership of the essay

finding.finding_summary: The study is designed to examine how students integrate ChatGPT into the drafting process, including revision behavior and reliance on AI assistance, which touches on metacognitive and self-regulatory writing behaviors. No empirical findings are reported in this paper.
finding.measure: Keystroke-level writing process logs; query/response logs; revision behavior

paper_profiles.title: Exclusive photoproduction of π0 up to large values of Mandelstam variables s, t and u with CLAS
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a high-statistics measurement of exclusive neutral pion photoproduction on the proton, γp → pπ0, using the CLAS detector at Jefferson Lab. The authors use a tagged photon beam and reconstruct the final state through the π0 Dalitz decay channel π0 → e+e−γ (and related conversion channels), allowing them to extend differential cross-section measurements to large values of Mandelstam variables s, t, and u and across a wide angular range.

The study is not an educational intervention and does not involve students, teachers, schools, or AI tools. Rather, it is a hadronic physics experiment comparing measured cross sections to Regge, handbag/GPD-based, and constituent counting rule models. The main conclusion is that the new data are consistent with s−6.89±0.26 scaling at large angles, broadly support Regge phenomenology, and strongly disagree with the handbag model at the highest available energies.

Because the paper is outside education research, no K-12 outcomes, intervention effects, or AI-related educational impacts are present. It is included here only as a retrieval artifact; there is no relevant empirical evidence for the requested high school AI writing-assistant sub-question.

paper_profiles.title: The Agency Gap: How Generative AI Literacy Shapes Independent Writing after AI Support
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether students’ generative AI (GenAI) literacy helps them write independently after AI support is withdrawn, and whether the type of chatbot support changes that relationship. The authors frame this as an “agency gap”: the extent to which GenAI literacy predicts performance when learners must self-initiate and regulate their writing without immediate AI help.

The study used a two-phase experimental design with 79 higher-education medical and nursing students recruited online. Participants completed multimodal academic writing tasks based on visual data, first with either a reactive chatbot (responds only to user queries) or a proactive chatbot (actively scaffolds through structured questioning and feedback), and then completed a parallel writing task without AI support. Writing was scored on insightfulness, visual data integration, organization/coherence, linguistic quality, critical thinking, and a composite score; GenAI literacy and visualization literacy were also measured.

Results showed that GenAI literacy was positively associated with independent writing performance after AI removal, especially in the reactive condition. In that condition, higher GenAI literacy predicted better post-support writing on visual data integration, critical thinking, and composite score, even after controlling for visualization literacy. In the proactive condition, however, chatbot scaffolding appeared to equalize performance across GenAI literacy levels, and mediation analyses found no indirect effect through AI-supported performance. The paper concludes that GenAI literacy matters most when learners must rely on their own agency, while proactive scaffolding can reduce inequities in access to effective AI support.

finding.finding_summary: GenAI literacy was positively associated with independent academic writing performance after AI support was removed. In the reactive chatbot condition (n=39), higher GenAI literacy correlated with better scores on insightfulness (rs=.41), visual data integration (rs=.40), organization/coherence (rs=.44), linguistic quality (rs=.32), critical thinking (rs=.37), and the composite score (rs=.44); partial correlations controlling for visualization literacy remained significant. In the proactive condition (n=40), no significant associations were found.
finding.measure: Academic writing rubric scores: insightfulness, visual data integration, organization and coherence, linguistic quality, critical thinking, and composite score
finding.effect_size: rs=.41 to .44 (reactive condition, significant dimensions at AI-removal stage); partial rs=.39 to .45

finding.finding_summary: The study directly assessed critical thinking as a writing outcome and found that GenAI literacy predicted stronger critical thinking in independent writing after AI withdrawal. In the reactive condition, the correlation was rs=.37 and the partial correlation controlling for visualization literacy was rs=.40; ordinal logistic regression also showed a significant positive association (b=0.14, SE=0.07, OR=1.15).
finding.measure: Critical thinking rubric score in academic writing

paper_profiles.title: Guardrails for avoiding harmful medical product recommendations and off-label promotion in generative AI models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the risk that generative AI models may produce medically inappropriate recommendations, specifically off-label promotion of medical products. The author argues that because large multimodal models are trained on broad internet-scale corpora with limited human oversight, they can learn and reproduce unvetted product–indication associations that are not approved by regulators such as the FDA.

The paper proposes a detection pipeline to identify potentially harmful off-label promotion in model outputs. The method standardizes user input, runs named entity recognition to identify drug and disease mentions, matches those entities to FDA labeling information, and flags any non-approved product–indication association as possible off-label promotion. The approach is demonstrated on Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet in a shopping-style question-answering setting, using synthetic red-teaming queries generated from 35 pharmaceuticals and 143 known off-label uses.

The evaluation generated 14,300 synthetic queries and found that 15.4% of model responses contained off-label indications according to the proposed detector. On a human-annotated random sample of 2,000 responses, the detector achieved precision 85.75%, recall 80.47%, and F1 83.02%. The paper concludes that guardrails are needed to prevent such outputs from reaching users, and suggests post-hoc filtering as one practical mitigation strategy. The study is primarily a proof-of-concept safety and monitoring paper rather than an educational intervention study.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed post-hoc detection pipeline identified off-label medical-product recommendations in model responses with precision 85.75%, recall 80.47%, and F1 83.02% on a human-annotated sample of 2,000 responses. The broader automated screening over 14,300 synthetic queries flagged 15.4% of responses as containing off-label indications, suggesting the method could efficiently monitor and filter GenAI outputs before user exposure.
finding.measure: Detection performance on human-annotated responses; proportion of responses flagged as off-label
finding.study_size: n=2000 annotated evaluation sample; n=14300 synthetic queries

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI systems should comply with FDA labeling and proposes guardrails to reduce regulatory and public-health risk from off-label promotion. It demonstrates that a general-purpose multimodal model can generate potentially noncompliant recommendations across 35 pharmaceuticals, supporting the need for institutional governance and post-hoc filtering mechanisms.
finding.measure: Frequency of off-label recommendations; compliance-oriented error detection

paper_profiles.title: One Small Step for Generative AI, One Giant Leap for AGI: A Complete Survey on ChatGPT in AIGC Era
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (survey paper; no primary study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of ChatGPT and related generative AI systems, written shortly after ChatGPT’s release. It reviews the underlying technology behind ChatGPT (including Transformer architecture, autoregressive modeling, and the GPT model family), then surveys its applications across scientific writing, education, medical decision support, software development, management, and other domains.

In the education section, the paper discusses how ChatGPT may affect teaching and learning, course material creation, assessment, language learning, and student support, and it cites example works on essay generation, economics and law exams, and other educational uses. However, the article itself does not report a primary empirical intervention, randomized study, or quasi-experimental evaluation in high school settings. It is a descriptive review that synthesizes early claims, demonstrations, and emerging concerns such as hallucination, plagiarism, overreliance, and misuse.

Because the paper is a survey rather than an intervention study, it does not provide original sample characteristics, comparator groups, duration, or effect estimates for educational outcomes. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT represents a major step forward in generative AI, but its educational promise is still preliminary and accompanied by substantial limitations, reliability issues, and ethical risks.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Literacy: A Comprehensive Framework for Literacy and Responsible Use
paper_profiles.venue: ACM (conference paper / manuscript submitted to ACM)
paper_profiles.population: Not a human participant study; framework paper with no direct study population
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging need for a generative AI literacy framework in response to the rapid adoption of ChatGPT-like systems and other large language models. The authors argue that pre-2023 AI literacy guidelines do not sufficiently cover distinctive properties of generative AI, such as hallucinations, context-window limitations, bias, explainability gaps, and broader social impacts.

To develop the framework, the authors conducted a scoping review of 100 pieces of literature and grey literature, then synthesized them into 12 guidelines organized into four areas: tool selection and prompting; understanding interaction with generative AI; understanding outputs; and high-level understanding of generative AI. The paper is a conceptual/guideline synthesis rather than an empirical intervention study, and it does not test an instructional program, compare outcomes across groups, or report participant-level effects. Its main conclusion is that educators, schools, companies, and organizations need updated literacy guidance to support effective, ethical, and informed generative AI use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides a synthesized generative AI literacy framework intended for schools, companies, and organizations, but it does not evaluate implementation outcomes. Its contribution is conceptual and policy-oriented: 12 guideline items meant to inform institutional learning interventions, policies, and responsible-use frameworks.
finding.measure: scoping review / literature synthesis; guideline framework development

paper_profiles.title: Pedagogy-driven Evaluation of Generative AI-powered Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.population: Not reported (review/proposal paper; no primary study participants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews evaluation practices for intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) in the era of generative AI and argues that current benchmarks and metrics are fragmented, subjective, and often poorly aligned with pedagogy. The authors organize the literature into traditional, NLG-based, and pedagogy-oriented evaluation approaches, and they identify major limitations in how response quality, pedagogical value, and learning impact are currently assessed.

Rather than testing a new educational intervention, the paper proposes three research directions: evaluation unification, measuring pedagogical guidance, and measuring active learning. The discussion draws on examples such as dialogue tutoring datasets, teacher-response benchmarks, and prior ITS work, but it does not report a new experiment with students. The only concrete empirical evidence described is cited from another study (e.g., a Turkish high school math field experiment with GPT-4), which is used illustratively rather than as original data.

Overall, the paper concludes that robust, scalable evaluation frameworks for GenAI-powered ITSs are still lacking and that future work should combine learning-science principles with standardized benchmarks and automated metrics. It is best characterized as a conceptual review and position paper about evaluation methodology, not as a direct efficacy study of an AI writing assistant or other classroom intervention.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is primarily about how to evaluate ITSs, not about intervention efficacy. It does not present a primary study measuring productivity or workload outcomes; operational efficiency is only discussed indirectly in relation to the need for scalable and reliable evaluation methods, with no original effect estimate reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that fragmented evaluation practices limit the development, comparability, and scalability of GenAI-powered ITSs, and it proposes unified evaluation frameworks as a path forward. This is a conceptual institutional argument rather than an empirical test, so no study size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: AI vs. Human - Differentiation Analysis of Scientific Content Generation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-generated scientific text can be distinguished from human-written scientific text, and what textual features best separate the two. The authors focus on scientific abstracts and related scientific text, using GPT-3/Text-Davinci-003 and small-scale ChatGPT outputs to generate AI text from paper titles and structured prompts, then comparing these outputs against human-written abstracts and manually assembled examples.

The study is not an educational intervention; it is a text-generation and detection analysis. The authors create a feature framework spanning syntax, semantics, and pragmatics, and they evaluate both human judges and machine detectors on their ability to identify AI-generated text. Human raters achieved 66.1% F1 on 40 mixed scientific/wiki texts, while a perplexity-based approach reached 94.0% F1 on scientific abstracts and a fine-tuned RoBERTa/OpenAI detector reached 94.6% F1 on the abstract dataset. The paper concludes that AI-generated scientific abstracts tend to have a detectable writing-style gap, lower perplexity, and problems with factual accuracy, coherence, and external consistency, while detectors outperform human evaluators.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies AI-generated scientific abstract quality and detectability, not student learning. It finds that AI-generated scientific text can be fluent and sometimes accurate, but it has weaker depth, factual consistency, and argumentative quality than human-written text; human evaluators reached 66.1% F1 on 40 texts, while a perplexity-based detector reached 94.0% F1 on 4,998 scientific abstracts and a fine-tuned RoBERTa detector reached 94.6% F1 on the abstract test set (n=1,994).
finding.measure: Human and model ability to distinguish AI-generated from human-written scientific abstracts; perplexity; detector F1; qualitative assessment of coherence, consistency, and argument logistics
finding.study_size: n=40 human-evaluation texts; n=4,998 abstracts for perplexity analysis; n=3,005 train / n=1,994 test for detector fine-tuning

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that AI writing assistants and automatic detection tools could improve efficiency in scientific writing and review by helping identify machine-generated content and save reviewer time. However, the paper does not test a classroom or workplace productivity intervention; the evidence is indirect and based on detector performance rather than measured workflow outcomes.
finding.measure: Detector performance and qualitative claims about reviewer time and text-generation efficiency

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; no human participants studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper that surveys opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing an intervention, it synthesizes potential educational uses such as content generation, personalized feedback, assessment support, tutoring, and student practice across elementary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning contexts.

The paper focuses on how large language models could support both learners and teachers, including writing assistance, question generation, feedback, lesson planning, and automated assessment. It also discusses risks and constraints such as bias, privacy, cost, sustainability, overreliance, plagiarism, and the difficulty of distinguishing human- from model-generated text.

The article concludes that LLMs have promising educational potential but require careful, ethical, and pedagogically grounded implementation with ongoing human oversight. It is a conceptual and review-style contribution, not an empirical intervention study, so it does not provide causal evidence about student outcomes or high school efficacy.

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a structured ChatGPT-based guideline, the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW), can improve second-language learners’ argumentative essay writing and critical thinking. The authors combine the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model and Tan’s framework for argumentative writing to create prompts intended to help students plan positions, explanations, evidence, and conclusions more deliberately while using ChatGPT.

The study reports a small experiment with 10 university students from a state university, randomly assigned to experimental and control groups of five. Both groups wrote a 40-minute argumentative essay on social media; the experimental group used CGCAW prompts with ChatGPT, while the control group used ChatGPT without structured guidance. Essays were scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor. Results were mixed: Grammarly slightly favored the control group, ChatGPT slightly favored the experimental group on clarity, logical coherence, and evidence, and the instructor strongly favored the control group. The authors conclude that the framework may support some aspects of argumentative writing and critical thinking, but it needs substantial refinement and the study is too small and inconsistent to support strong efficacy claims.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention produced mixed writing outcomes on argumentative essay quality. Grammarly rated the control group slightly higher overall (M=92.2 vs 90.6), while ChatGPT rated the experimental group slightly higher on its own rubric (mean total 74% vs 72.2%), and the course instructor rated the control group much higher (M=56 vs 35).
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and course instructor; subscales included clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness, clear thesis, evidence/reasoning, counterarguments, and summary
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT totals: SD=7.6 (experimental) and SD=5.5 (control); ChatGPT subscales included SDs 1.2-2.4; instructor and Grammarly SDs not fully reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central non-writing outcome is critical thinking in argumentative writing, operationalized through clarity, logical coherence, evidence use, and structured reasoning. The experimental group was described as improving in clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, but the control group performed better on language mechanics and some instructor-rated writing criteria, so the evidence is not uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Critical thinking-related aspects of argumentative writing (clarity, logical coherence, evidence use, position/claim development, reasoning)
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT-rated totals SD=7.6 (experimental) and 5.5 (control); subscale SDs reported for ChatGPT but not for critical thinking as a separate construct

paper_profiles.title: Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students’ essays.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether ChatGPT-3 can improve students’ essay-writing performance when used as a writing assistant. The authors compare essays written traditionally versus essays written with ChatGPT-3 assistance, focusing on overall essay quality, writing time, text authenticity, and similarity among essays.

Eighteen second-year master's students in forensic sciences at the University of Split were assigned to a control group (n=9) or an experimental group (n=9). Both groups wrote an 800–1000 word essay in Croatian within four hours on the same prompt; the experimental group received ChatGPT assistance, while the control group wrote traditionally and was additionally supervised to prevent ChatGPT use. Essays were graded by two teachers using a rubric covering mechanics, style, content, and format, and the study also examined writing duration, plagiarism/authenticity via PlagScan, pairwise similarity via Jaccard index, and AI-classifier outputs.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT did not improve writing performance in this small sample. Essay scores were slightly higher in the control group (2.39 ± 0.71) than in the ChatGPT group (2.00 ± 0.73), and regression results showed no significant effect of group on essay score (P=0.184). Writing time was also similar across groups (172.22 ± 31.59 vs 179.11 ± 31.93 minutes), and the authors report only a slight increase in text unauthenticity in the ChatGPT group, with low overall essay similarity. Overall, the paper is best interpreted as a small pilot RCT showing no detectable benefit of ChatGPT-3 as an essay-writing aid in this context.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-3 assistance did not improve essay quality. The experimental group scored slightly lower than control on the overall essay grade (2.00 ± 0.73 vs 2.39 ± 0.71), and group assignment was not a significant predictor of score in linear regression (P=0.184).
finding.measure: Essay quality/overall essay score based on rubric grades (A-D converted to 4-1) across mechanics, style, content, and format

finding.finding_summary: Using ChatGPT-3 did not reduce writing time. The experimental group took 172.22 ± 31.59 minutes and the control group 179.11 ± 31.93 minutes, and writing duration was not a significant predictor of essay score (P=0.669).
finding.measure: Essay writing duration (minutes)

paper_profiles.title: Machine-Assisted Grading of Nationwide School-Leaving Essay Exams with LLMs and Statistical NLP
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) and statistical NLP tools can be used to machine-assist grading of high-stakes national essay exams in Estonia. The central question is whether automated scoring can approximate human panel scores on curriculum-based rubrics for school-leaving essays, while also providing useful fine-grained feedback and reducing grading burden.

The study uses two full national trial-exam cohorts from Estonia: 781 grade 9 essays and 764 grade 12 essays (1,559 total) from spring 2024. The authors compare several proprietary LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, o4-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro) against human scores using zero-shot rubric-based prompting, and also build supervised statistical NLP regression models for several rubric categories using 10-fold cross-validation. No instructional intervention was delivered to students; the paper is an evaluation of automated scoring methods and a prompt-injection robustness probe, not an educational efficacy trial.

Results suggest that LLMs can achieve near-human grading performance on many rubric categories, with total-score mean absolute errors generally in the 2.66–4.97 range on the 0–27 scale and many predictions falling within the human scoring range more often than not. The statistical NLP models performed slightly better on discrete language-error categories such as punctuation and orthography. The paper concludes that human-in-the-loop machine-assisted grading is technically feasible for national exams, but that rubric clarity, robustness to prompt injection, and governance safeguards are essential for high-stakes deployment.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that LLM-assisted and statistical NLP-assisted grading can approximate human scoring at scale, supporting faster and more consistent evaluation of essay exams. For total essay scores, LLM MAE ranged from 2.66 to 4.97 on the 0–27 scale across models and grades, and predictions often fell within the human score range (e.g., 67% for GPT-4o on grade 9; 55% for Gemini 2 Flash on grade 12), indicating potential to reduce assessor workload in national exam grading.
finding.measure: Mean absolute error on total essay scores; proportion of predictions within the human minimum–maximum range; grading consistency/workflow feasibility
finding.study_size: n=1559 total essays (n=781 grade 9; n=764 grade 12; one grade-9 essay excluded from some analyses due to single rater)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that human-in-the-loop LLM scoring is viable for high-stakes, nationwide exam systems and could support a transition to digital assessment infrastructure. It provides evidence that automated scoring can be integrated into a regulated national examination workflow while maintaining human oversight, and it highlights institutional concerns such as bias, transparency, and prompt-injection risk that must be addressed for adoption.
finding.measure: Comparison of automated scores with official human panel scores; prompt-injection robustness experiment; discussion of deployment feasibility for national exam systems
finding.study_size: n=1559 total essays, plus prompt-injection probe on n=100 grade-9 essays and n=20 generated essays in a separate demonstration

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies writing assessment for academic literacy, showing that both LLMs and statistical NLP can score essay quality in ways that largely track human raters. On the 0–3 rubric scale, model errors were often near human variance, and the system was especially capable on vocabulary, syntax, punctuation, and orthography-related subscores, though performance varied by category and grade level.
finding.measure: Rubric-based essay scores across content, vocabulary/syntax, punctuation, orthography/morphology, and structuring/formatting categories
finding.study_size: n=781 grade 9 essays; n=764 grade 12 essays
finding.std_deviation: 0.03-0.06 range for some cross-validated regression pipelines; human/model score differences reported as MAE rather than SD

finding.finding_summary: The study touches durable-skill-related writing constructs such as argumentation, reasoning, and textual organization, but as a scoring-validation paper these are secondary to literacy assessment. The authors report that models can evaluate rubric dimensions tied to content and argumentation, suggesting automated support for assessing higher-order writing skills, though the paper does not estimate instructional gains in these skills.
finding.measure: Rubric sub-scores for content/argumentation, structure, and related writing dimensions

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can solve the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE), a high-stakes exam used for graduation and university admission. Rather than testing an educational intervention with students, the authors evaluate ChatGPT’s zero-shot performance on a benchmark dataset derived from VNHSGE exam items across multiple subjects and years.

The approach is a model evaluation study using 30 essay items in literature and 1,700 multiple-choice questions across mathematics, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education. The paper reports subject-level scores for ChatGPT from 2019 to 2023 and compares them descriptively with Vietnamese student score distributions from 2019 to 2022. No students were assigned to conditions, and there was no randomized or quasi-experimental intervention.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT would pass the exam overall, with combined scores ranging from 6.35 to 6.94 depending on year and subject combination. Performance was strongest in English and generally weaker in chemistry, with mixed relative performance across subjects when compared to Vietnamese students. The paper argues that ChatGPT shows promise as a support tool for learners, but it is primarily a benchmark/performance analysis rather than an efficacy study of an AI writing assistant or classroom intervention.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was evaluated on high-school exam questions across multiple subjects and was able to pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination. Across 2019-2023, its combined graduation scores ranged from 6.35 to 6.94, exceeding the passing threshold, with subject scores varying by year and discipline.
finding.measure: VNHSGE subject scores and combined graduation scores (GASN/GASS)

finding.finding_summary: On the literature component, ChatGPT scored between 5.63 and 7.5 from 2019 to 2023, with an average of 6.8. The authors report that ChatGPT generally outperformed the majority of Vietnamese students in literature, except in 2022 when its score was slightly lower than student performance benchmarks.
finding.measure: VNHSGE literature exam score

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT achieved its highest performance in English, with scores ranging from 7.6 to 8.6 across 2019-2023 and an average of 7.92. The paper states that it performed better than the majority of Vietnamese students on the English test, indicating strong performance on language proficiency tasks.
finding.measure: VNHSGE English exam score

finding.finding_summary: In mathematics, ChatGPT scored between 5.2 and 6.6 from 2019 to 2023, with an average of 5.88. The authors conclude that these scores were lower than the majority of Vietnamese students, indicating weaker performance relative to human test-takers on mathematics questions.
finding.measure: VNHSGE mathematics exam score

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how four secondary-school EFL students used ChatGPT and other POE-hosted chatbots to complete a familiar blog-writing task for the first time. Rather than testing whether AI writing assistance improves writing outcomes, the authors analyze students’ prompts, prompt sequences, and chatbot switching patterns to characterize “prompt engineering pathways” and the trial-and-error behaviors that emerged during the task.

The study was conducted in a Hong Kong secondary school form-one class with four purposively selected high-achieving students. Students completed a timed in-class writing task (up to 45 minutes) on iPads using Google Docs and the POE app, which included ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly. The main data source was screen recordings of the students’ devices, supplemented by the final written products; the analysis was qualitative content analysis and case-study pattern matching.

The paper identifies nine prompt types, including auto-complete, search-engine style factual queries, greetings, natural-language instructions, and combinations of exemplars, instructions, and questions. Across the four cases, students used different and often trial-and-error pathways, sometimes reusing or modifying earlier prompts and sometimes switching chatbots. The authors conclude that the students were unsophisticated prompt engineers and recommend explicit prompt-engineering instruction in EFL writing classrooms. The study does not evaluate writing achievement effects of the AI tool, so it is not an efficacy trial of AI writing support.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is not an intervention efficacy study of writing quality or achievement; it is a qualitative case study of how four secondary EFL students prompted chatbots while composing a blog entry. The relevant evidence is descriptive only: the authors report 36 coded prompt turns across four cases and discuss how prompt types and pathways varied, but they do not report pre/post writing scores, comparison-group outcomes, or effect sizes for writing performance.
finding.measure: Prompt types, prompt sequences, and completed blog writing task products

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies prompt engineering as a metacognitive/durable skill, focusing on how students trialed different prompt types, refined wording, and used chatbot memory across a writing task. The authors infer that students were learning to craft more sophisticated prompts through exploration, but they provide no quantitative outcome measure or effect size.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of prompt engineering pathways, including prompt content, sequencing, and chatbot switching

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Effects of Generative AI Assistance on Writing Self-efficacy
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines whether different configurations of generative AI assistance affect students’ writing self-efficacy during argumentative writing. The authors focus on a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment manipulating whether AI support is available for idea generation and/or sentence construction, compared with a no-AI condition.

The study recruited 21 Korean undergraduates, of whom 13 were analyzed after exclusions. Participants completed two 30-minute argumentative writing tasks in a 100-minute online session using ChatGPT, with post-task self-efficacy ratings on a 0–100 scale. The intervention was intentionally constrained so that the AI provided only task-focused, neutral assistance and no motivational or evaluative feedback.

Results were exploratory because of the very small sample, but the pattern suggested that AI assistance did not uniformly improve self-efficacy. Ideation-only AI showed the most promising pattern, with higher and increasing self-efficacy over time, while sentence-level AI was associated with declines in self-efficacy. Full-process AI produced the highest average self-efficacy but also signs of reduced ownership, and the no-AI condition showed the lowest mean scores. The paper concludes that where AI intervenes in the writing process matters more than simply whether AI is used.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measured writing self-efficacy during argumentative writing, not writing quality or achievement. Across 13 analyzed undergraduates, full AI had the highest mean self-efficacy (M=82.2, SD=6.4), ideation AI was also high (M=80.1, SD=16.1), sentence AI was lower (M=76.6, SD=7.2), and no AI was lowest (M=61.8, SD=24.0). Change over time was mixed: ideation AI increased (ΔM=+11.1), no AI slightly increased (ΔM=+1.3), full AI was nearly stable (ΔM=+0.5), and sentence AI declined (ΔM=-5.7; all 5 participants declined).
finding.measure: Writing self-efficacy during argumentative writing tasks (0–100 rating scale)
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI [-0.60, 3.07] for Full AI vs No AI

paper_profiles.title: AI-Mediated Feedback Improves Student Revisions: A Randomized Trial with FeedbackWriter in a Large Undergraduate Course
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-mediated feedback can improve the quality of instructor feedback on student writing, compared with traditional human-only feedback. The authors address a practical question in educational AI: instead of generating feedback directly for students, can an LLM assist teaching assistants by suggesting rubric-aligned comments while leaving humans in control of adoption, editing, or dismissal?

To study this, they built FeedbackWriter, a system that surfaces GPT-4o-generated suggestions to TAs as they review knowledge-intensive economics essays. The intervention was deployed in a large introductory economics course at a public R1 university in the United States with 354 undergraduate students and 11 TAs. Students were randomized by section/assignment condition across two essay assignments in a counterbalanced design: one condition used FeedbackWriter (AI-mediated feedback), and the other used a visually matched baseline with the same rubrics and historical feedback but no AI suggestions.

The main outcome was revised draft quality, scored with an LLM-based rubric scorer and checked against human expert ratings on a sample. Students receiving AI-mediated feedback produced significantly higher-quality revisions than students receiving human-only feedback, with Cohen’s d = 0.50. The paper also found that AI-mediated feedback was more actionable and more supportive of independent learning, though it did not produce a statistically significant difference on a post-test measuring learning from the revision process. The study concludes that human-AI collaborative feedback can improve revision quality in a real course setting, but it did not reduce TA grading time and still requires careful rubric design and human oversight.

finding.finding_summary: Students who received AI-mediated feedback via FeedbackWriter produced significantly higher-quality revised drafts than students who received human-only feedback. In the mixed-effects model, condition was associated with a 5% higher final-revision quality and the paper reports Cohen’s d = 0.50, roughly moving a student from the 50th to the 70th percentile.
finding.measure: Final draft quality / revision quality on rubric-based essay scores
finding.std_deviation: First draft quality SD=0.13; final draft quality SD=0.17; improvement SD=0.16

paper_profiles.title: Can Good Writing Be Generative? Expert-Level AI Writing Emerges through Fine-Tuning on High-Quality Books
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can generate creative writing that is preferred over expert human writing, and what happens when expert writers discover that text they judged as better was actually AI-generated. The study is motivated by concerns about whether AI can imitate literary style and voice at a level that is indistinguishable from or superior to human authors.

The authors conducted a three-phase mixed-methods study with 28 expert writers (mostly MFA candidates and one PhD in English) and 131 lay judges. In Phase 1, the experts and three LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro) each wrote 200-450 word excerpts emulating 50 acclaimed authors under two conditions: in-context prompting and fine-tuning (GPT-4o fine-tuned on 30 authors’ books). In Phase 2, blind evaluators compared human-written and AI-generated excerpts for writing quality and stylistic fidelity. In Phase 3, 21 writers participated in retrospective interviews about their reactions after learning that some preferred excerpts were AI-generated.

The study found that in the in-context condition experts preferred human writing, but fine-tuning reversed this pattern: both experts and lay judges preferred AI-generated excerpts, with expert preference shifting strongly toward AI. Qualitative analysis showed that writers often reconsidered their criteria for good writing, attributed AI success to its polished output and different production process, and reported reduced confidence in their ability to distinguish human from AI writing. The paper concludes that author-specific fine-tuning can produce writing that expert readers judge as highly compelling, raising important concerns about creative labor, authenticity, and future writing instruction and publishing practices.

finding.finding_summary: In the blind evaluation task, expert judges preferred human writing over in-context AI output for writing quality (82.7%) but preferred AI-generated writing after fine-tuning (62.2%). For stylistic fidelity, experts also shifted from preferring human writing in the in-context condition (72.0%) to preferring AI in the fine-tuned condition (81.1%), indicating that fine-tuning substantially improved perceived writing quality and style imitation.
finding.measure: Blind pairwise preference judgments of writing quality and stylistic fidelity for literary excerpts
finding.study_size: n=28 expert writers as judges; n=131 lay judges; 150 in-context human-vs-AI evaluations per group; 90 fine-tuned human-vs-AI evaluations per group

finding.finding_summary: The debrief interviews suggest AI-generated text challenged writers’ evaluative confidence and prompted reconsideration of criteria for assessing good writing. Writers reported criteria reframing, expectation violation, and an identity crisis around expertise, which reflects changes in metacognitive judgment rather than direct skill gains.
finding.measure: Retrospective semi-structured interview themes about sensemaking, confidence, and identity

finding.finding_summary: After learning a preferred excerpt was AI-generated, writers reported disappointment, shock, and erosion of aesthetic confidence. The paper characterizes these reactions as expectation violation and identity threat, suggesting a negative emotional impact on participants’ confidence and sense of professional self.
finding.measure: Retrospective interview responses on emotions, confidence, and reactions to AI preference revelations

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that fine-tuned AI can be preferred even by expert writers, implying meaningful consequences for creative labor, publishing, copyright, and educational institutions. Participants recommended disclosure requirements, stronger copyright protections, and changes to creative writing programs, indicating perceived institutional implications rather than a measured policy effect.
finding.measure: Interview themes about future of writing, publishing, copyright, and creative writing education

paper_profiles.title: Fooling LLM graders into giving better grades through neural activity guided adversarial prompting
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates vulnerabilities in large language model (LLM) essay graders and asks whether hidden internal representations can be used to systematically manipulate automated grading outcomes. Rather than studying student learning or instructional effectiveness, the paper develops an attack method that identifies neural activation patterns associated with high essay scores and then optimizes adversarial suffixes to push the model toward those patterns.

The empirical setting uses the Hewlett Foundation Automated Essay Scoring dataset, which contains approximately 2,000 high-school essays per problem set and human expert scores. The authors first train linear readouts on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct hidden states to predict grading outcomes, reporting strong correlations (r = 0.8–0.9) between internal score readouts and final outputs. They then use gradient-based adversarial suffix optimization (GCG) to inflate scores on held-out essays and show transfer to other open- and closed-source models, including Gemini.

The main conclusion is that current LLM-based essay graders are vulnerable to prompt-injection-style attacks and that a seemingly irrelevant token, "user," is a key driver of the attack via chat-template bias. A small modification to the supervised fine-tuning chat template substantially reduces the vulnerability. This is a model robustness and security paper, not an educational intervention study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies automated essay scoring on high-school writing samples and shows that adversarial suffixes can substantially increase LLM-assigned essay grades. Using approximately 1,500 essays for optimization and held-out essays for evaluation, the authors report that the optimized suffixes consistently raise scores on the scoring task, and the attack transfers to other models including Gemini.
finding.measure: LLM-assigned essay scores on automated essay scoring tasks

paper_profiles.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Persian: A Preliminary Study Focusing on ChatGPT
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (Persian NLP benchmark; no K-12 intervention population studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the performance of large language models, especially GPT-3.5-turbo (ChatGPT), GPT-4, and OpenChat-3.5, on a set of Persian NLP benchmarks. The authors study classic tasks (sentiment analysis, emotion recognition, named entity recognition, translation, and reading comprehension), reasoning tasks (textual entailment and multiple-choice math/logic questions), and knowledge tasks (literature and common-knowledge multiple-choice QA). The central question is how well multilingual LLMs work in Persian, and whether prompt language and few-shot demonstrations affect performance.

The study does not test an educational intervention in schools; it is a benchmark/evaluation paper. The authors compare LLMs against task-specific supervised baselines and run zero-shot, one-shot, and three-shot prompting experiments using Persian and English prompts. They also examine whether translating prompts/examples into English improves GPT-3.5 results. GPT-4 is generally strongest, especially on reasoning and math/logic tasks, while task-specific supervised models remain better on several classic language tasks.

The paper includes two new benchmark sets created by the authors: elementary school math questions and a set of mathematical problems drawn from Iranian 7th- and 10th-grade entrance exams plus translated MATH items. However, these are used only as benchmark evaluation sets for models, not as student interventions. Overall, the paper concludes that prompt language matters, GPT-4 benefits more from additional shots than GPT-3.5, and automatic translation to English often improves GPT-3.5 performance. It is primarily a tool/benchmarking study rather than evidence of AI writing-assistant efficacy in high school classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates model performance on math/logic and mathematical problem-solving benchmarks, not student learning. GPT-4 achieved the best reported performance on the math & logic multiple-choice QA task (accuracy=0.725, three-shot, English prompt) and on the math problems dataset (Math metric=0.564, three-shot, English prompt), while GPT-3.5 lagged behind on the latter (best Math metric=0.503). These results indicate stronger model capability for mathematical reasoning under prompting, but they do not constitute an educational intervention effect.
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice math & logic QA; Math metric on mathematical problems; accuracy on elementary school questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper benchmarks reading comprehension, translation, NER, sentiment analysis, and textual entailment, which are literacy-related NLP tasks. On reading comprehension, GPT-4 reached F1=0.687 and GPT-3.5 reached F1=0.644, both below the reported SOTA baseline of 0.691; on sentiment analysis GPT-4 reached macro F1=0.906, exceeding the SOTA baseline of 0.891. These are model-evaluation findings on language tasks rather than learner outcomes.
finding.measure: Macro F1 / F1 / BLEU on sentiment analysis, reading comprehension, named entity recognition, translation, and textual entailment

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s textual entailment and math/logic benchmarks indirectly assess reasoning-oriented capabilities that overlap with durable skills such as inference and problem solving. GPT-4 generally outperformed GPT-3.5, e.g., textual entailment (ParsiNLU) F1=0.636 versus 0.320 for GPT-3.5 in the three-shot English prompt condition, and math/logic accuracy=0.725. However, these are direct model capability tests, not measures of human critical thinking or metacognition.
finding.measure: Macro F1 on textual entailment; accuracy on math/logic QA

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Writing Research Papers: A New Type of Algorithmic Bias and Uncertainty in Scholarly Work
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that generative AI tools used for scholarly writing introduce a new form of context-induced algorithmic bias and uncertainty. The authors discuss how large language models such as ChatGPT and text-davinci-003 can produce biased, hallucinated, or misleading text when prompts include personal, demographic, or institutional context, and how inadvertent red-teaming or limited context can worsen these problems.

The paper is not an intervention study in education and does not test AI writing assistance with students, teachers, or schools. Instead, it is a conceptual paper supported by a small systematic review of scholarly works using ChatGPT or related tools as authorship/writing aids, along with illustrative prompt-based examples of biased or hallucinated outputs. The main conclusion is that generative AI in academic writing may reinforce existing societal biases, create new context-dependent biases, and increase irreproducibility and misinformation in scholarly work.

Because the paper is a commentary/conceptual analysis rather than an empirical trial, it does not provide causal evidence on educational outcomes, student performance, or instructional effectiveness. Its evidence base is centered on examples and literature synthesis about AI-authored research writing, not K-12 learning or high school writing intervention efficacy.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI use in scholarly writing can undermine academic integrity, originality, and reproducibility, and may reinforce bias through a positive feedback loop if AI-generated text re-enters training data. This is presented as a conceptual conclusion rather than a measured effect, with no experimental sample or effect size reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual synthesis of scholarly writing practices and examples of AI-generated text; systematic review count of AI-authored/co-authored works
finding.study_size: n=104 works identified in the authors' systematic review; additional illustrative prompt examples not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on writing quality and scholarly text generation, arguing that AI-assisted writing can introduce hallucinations, biased phrasing, and non-original prose that degrade the quality of written academic output. No direct student writing intervention was tested, so the finding is interpretive rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Scholarly writing output quality, originality, and hallucination/bias in generated text

paper_profiles.title: LCES: Zero-shot Automated Essay Scoring via Pairwise Comparisons Using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes LCES, a zero-shot automated essay scoring framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to compare two essays at a time and then converts those pairwise preferences into continuous scores using RankNet. The core motivation is to reduce reliance on direct score generation, which can be sensitive to prompt wording and model bias, and to improve alignment with human judgments in automated essay scoring (AES).

The empirical evaluation is conducted on two benchmark AES datasets: ASAP, which the authors describe as middle school essays, and TOEFL11, which contains essays written by non-native English speakers. The study is not an instructional intervention or school-based trial; it is a model-development and benchmarking paper using existing essay corpora. The authors compare LCES against zero-shot baselines (Vanilla direct scoring and MTS), several supervised AES models, and alternative latent-score conversion methods (Bradley–Terry and Elo).

Results show that LCES generally outperforms the zero-shot baselines in quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) and Spearman correlation across most prompts and LLM backbones. Performance is especially strong with Llama-3.1-8B and GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini, and the method is reported to be robust to embedding choice and relatively stable across models. The paper also analyzes position bias, agreement with human judgments, and inductive vs. transductive scoring, concluding that LCES can be an effective zero-shot AES approach, though it remains dependent on noisy LLM-generated comparison labels.

finding.finding_summary: LCES improved automated essay scoring accuracy on writing tasks compared with zero-shot baselines. Across ASAP and TOEFL11, it achieved higher average QWK than Vanilla and MTS for most LLM backbones; for example, on ASAP with Llama-3.1-8B, LCES reached avg. QWK = 0.670 versus 0.391 for MTS and 0.194 for Vanilla, and on TOEFL11 with GPT-4o-mini it reached 0.658 versus 0.533 (MTS) and 0.122 (Vanilla).
finding.measure: Quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) and Spearman rank correlation on essay scoring benchmarks
finding.study_size: ASAP n=12,978 essays; TOEFL11 n=12,100 essays (with evaluation subsets/splits as described)
finding.std_deviation: 0.021 (ASAP avg. QWK SD across backbones for LCES); 0.048 (TOEFL11 avg. QWK SD across backbones for LCES)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LCES reduces the need for directly scored essays by using zero-shot pairwise comparisons and a small sampled comparison set (M=5,000) instead of exhaustive scoring. The authors report that performance remains strong even with relatively few comparisons (e.g., M=50 or 100 in sensitivity analysis), suggesting a more computationally efficient and potentially lower-cost scoring pipeline than methods requiring prompt-specific labeled training data.
finding.measure: Computational efficiency, number of pairwise comparisons required, and qualitative comparison of labeling/scoring workflow

finding.finding_summary: Although not the central target, the evaluation rubric used for essay scoring includes dimensions tied to broader writing-quality judgment and relative essay quality. The method improved rank-order consistency with human scoring, with Spearman averages as high as 0.728 on ASAP and 0.730 on TOEFL11 for GPT-4o-based LCES, indicating better preservation of ordinal quality judgments rather than only exact-score matching.
finding.measure: Spearman rank correlation between predicted and gold-standard essay scores
finding.study_size: ASAP n=12,978 essays; TOEFL11 n=12,100 essays

paper_profiles.title: The Psychosocial Impacts of Generative AI Harms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines psychosocial harms associated with generative language models when they are prompted to write short classroom-related stories. Rather than testing an educational intervention, the authors analyze 150,000 generated stories from five LMs (ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Claude 2.0, Llama 2, and PaLM 2) and use a critical qualitative lens to identify representational harms such as erasure, subordination, and stereotyping.

The analysis is grounded in a dataset of 30 classroom prompts spanning 15 academic subjects, with power-neutral and power-laden variants, each sampled 1,000 times per model. The paper focuses on how identity terms and student names are represented in the outputs, highlighting patterns for Indigenous/Native American, Latine, White feminized, and Asian feminized identities. The authors argue that these outputs may contribute to psychosocial harm in educational contexts by reinforcing biased narratives about who belongs, who excels, and who needs help.

The paper does not evaluate student learning outcomes, classroom implementation, or causal effects of AI tools on high school populations. Instead, it is a descriptive/interpretive analysis of model outputs that raises concerns about the educational use of generative AI and calls for future empirical research on user impacts, especially for marginalized students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that biased LM-generated classroom narratives may harm psychosocial well-being by fostering erasure, subordination, and stereotype threat among marginalized students. It does not experimentally measure student outcomes; rather, it infers psychosocial risk from qualitative patterns in 150,000 generated stories across five models.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of representational harms in LM-generated classroom stories

paper_profiles.title: Can Large Language Models Differentiate Harmful from Argumentative Essays? Steps Toward Ethical Essay Scoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) and existing automated essay scoring (AES) systems can distinguish between argumentative essays and harmful essays, and whether they can appropriately score harmful essays. The authors argue that standard AES approaches may reward well-structured but ethically problematic writing because they do not explicitly account for discriminatory content, hate speech, or morally objectionable claims.

To study this, the authors build a new Harmful Essay Detection (HED) benchmark from IELTS-style prompts, generating essays with LLMs using pretending instructions designed to elicit harmful content and then annotating essays as argumentative or harmful. They evaluate several LLMs (GPT-4-turbo, Llama3.1-8B, Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Qwen2-7B) on binary classification and holistic scoring tasks, and compare them with four existing AES models (Hi-att, PAES, NPCR, PMAES). The work is not an intervention trial with students; it is a model evaluation study on essay data, using prompts drawn from IELTS high-school/secondary-level writing contexts.

Main findings are that LLMs still struggle to reliably classify harmful versus argumentative essays, especially when harmful claims are supported with plausible evidence. Persona-related wording can substantially change classification behavior, and some models’ willingness to refuse harmful-generation prompts correlates with better harmful-essay detection. For scoring, existing AES models often assign equal or higher scores to harmful essays than argumentative ones, while LLMs are somewhat more robust but still improve their scores on harmful essays when rubric guidelines are added unless the instructions explicitly incorporate harmful-content criteria.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies essay classification and holistic scoring on writing samples, making literacy the central outcome. In classification, Llama3.1-8B and Llama3-8B achieved better harmful-vs-argumentative detection than other LLMs (macro F1 = 79.01 and 78.62, respectively), while GPT-4-turbo, Qwen2-7B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3 performed worse. In scoring, existing AES models often gave harmful essays similar or higher scores than argumentative essays (e.g., Hi-att 4.32 vs 4.65; PAES 4.74 vs 4.78), whereas LLMs were somewhat more sensitive to harmful content (e.g., Llama3.1-8B 4.83 vs 2.99).
finding.measure: Essay classification F1 / macro F1; holistic essay scores (1-6 scale); QWK on IELTS essays
finding.study_size: HED benchmark: n=290 essays (100 argumentative, 190 harmful); IELTS scoring evaluation across 50 prompts

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence (AI) research in higher education from 2016 through 2022. The authors asked where the studies were conducted, what academic levels and subject domains were represented, who the intended users of AI were, and how AI was being used across the literature. Using PRISMA methods, they screened 371 records and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles for coding and synthesis.

The review found that AI research in higher education grew sharply in 2021–2022, was concentrated in high-income countries, and was most often published by authors from colleges of education and computer science. Undergraduate students were the most common population studied, and language learning was the most common domain. Grounded coding identified five major uses of AI: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The paper is descriptive rather than an intervention study; it does not test causal effects of AI tools on outcomes, and it does not report subgroup findings for multilingual learners or students with disabilities as a focused analytic result.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed higher-education literature, AI was frequently used for writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition, especially in language-learning contexts. Because this is a systematic review, the paper does not estimate a single pooled effect; instead, it reports that language learning was the most common subject domain (17% of studies) and that AI supports included automated feedback and assessment for writing and related literacy tasks.
finding.measure: Frequency and thematic coding of AI uses in language-learning/writing/reading studies

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies studies where AI was used to support persistence, self-regulated learning, and student emotions. For example, the authors note work on emotion control, engagement, and affective responses in AI-assisted learning, but they do not synthesize numeric effects across studies.
finding.measure: Thematic coding of persistence, self-regulation, engagement, and emotion-related uses/outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review includes studies addressing higher-order thinking, reflection, and adaptive support for learning processes, indicating that AI was sometimes used to foster durable skills such as metacognition and problem-solving. However, these are described qualitatively within the review, without pooled estimates or direct experimental comparison.
finding.measure: Thematic coding of reflection, higher-order thinking, and adaptive learning supports

finding.finding_summary: A major finding of the review is that AI was widely used to improve operational efficiency, especially through automatic assessment, feedback generation, question generation, learning analytics, and student-data management. The review reports 26 studies on automatic assessment, 21 on predicting, 18 on intelligent tutoring systems, and 19 on managing student learning, but does not provide pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: Thematic coding of AI applications related to grading, feedback, prediction, learning analytics, and student-data management

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests institutional-level uses of AI in higher education, including admissions prediction, curriculum sequencing, instructional design, and quality assurance/management functions. These findings are descriptive and indicate potential institutional benefits, but the paper does not report causal evidence or quantified institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Thematic coding of managerial and institutional uses of AI

paper_profiles.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces LLaMA, a family of open foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters. The central question is whether strong language model performance can be achieved using only publicly available data and efficient training methods, without proprietary corpora.

The paper describes the model architecture, data mixture, tokenization, optimizer, and several efficiency improvements, then evaluates the pretrained models on a broad set of standard NLP benchmarks. These include commonsense reasoning, closed-book question answering, reading comprehension, math word problems, code generation, and MMLU, along with bias, toxicity, and truthfulness evaluations. The work is about general-purpose model pretraining and benchmarking rather than an educational intervention.

No intervention study in K-12 classrooms is reported, and no grades 9–12 subgroup evidence for multilingual learners or students with disabilities is provided. The paper does include some educationally relevant benchmark results such as RACE high-school reading comprehension and MATH, but these are model-evaluation tasks rather than evidence of AI writing assistant use in instruction. Overall, the paper concludes that larger LLaMA models perform competitively with other frontier models on many benchmarks, while instruction fine-tuning further improves MMLU; it also notes biases and toxicity concerns in the pretrained models.

finding.finding_summary: The models were evaluated on reading comprehension and related language tasks, not classroom writing intervention. On the RACE benchmark, which includes a high-school subset, LLaMA-65B reached 51.6% zero-shot accuracy on RACE-high (and 67.9% on RACE-middle), outperforming GPT-3 175B at 45.5% on RACE-high and approaching PaLM-540B at 49.1%. This is benchmark evidence about reading comprehension ability, not evidence of instructional impact for students.
finding.measure: RACE reading comprehension accuracy (RACE-high / RACE-middle)

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the concerns associated with using ChatGPT in education, treating ChatGPT as an early example of an AI-powered chatbot. The authors ask what risks and limitations arise when chatbots are used for educational purposes, especially in relation to cheating, accuracy, fairness, privacy, and human–machine interaction.

The study uses a three-stage qualitative instrumental case study design. First, it analyzes 2,330 tweets about ChatGPT and education from December 23, 2022 to January 6, 2023 using social network analysis, sentiment analysis, and t-SNE visualization. Second, it conducts content analysis of 19 publicly recruited interviewees who had experience using ChatGPT in education. Third, three experienced educators used ChatGPT for one week in a hands-on user experience investigation across 10 educational scenarios.

The paper does not test a classroom intervention or learning program, and it does not focus on K-12 students, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities as a direct study population. Instead, it identifies perceived benefits and concerns among early adopters, finding that ChatGPT is viewed as potentially useful for instruction, assessment creation, and learning support, but also as prone to inaccurate responses, cheating, manipulation, privacy risks, and inconsistent outputs. The authors conclude that chatbots may have educational value but require careful use, stronger guidance, and more responsible design before broad adoption.

finding.finding_summary: Participants and the user-experience scenarios suggested that ChatGPT can increase efficiency by helping teachers draft materials, create quizzes, provide outlines, and support rapid feedback. However, the same study also showed that outputs can be inconsistent, generic, or inaccurate, which can increase teachers’ burden because results need checking and revision.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview themes and educator user-experience scenarios about instructional preparation, quiz creation, and feedback generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly discusses ChatGPT’s use for writing essays, generating text, and supporting academic writing, but it does not report a controlled literacy outcome measure. In the scenarios, ChatGPT could help produce essays and citations, yet it also generated inaccurate or manipulated text, raising concerns about writing quality and cheating rather than demonstrating improved literacy performance.
finding.measure: Essay/text generation, short-answer response generation, APA citation assistance, and qualitative judgments of writing support
finding.study_size: n=3 educators in user experience; qualitative examples from tweets/interviews

finding.finding_summary: The study emphasizes critical thinking, prompt skill development, and the risk that ChatGPT may reduce students’ reasoning if they rely on it too heavily. Interviewees and the authors argue that users need stronger questioning, evaluation, and critical judgment skills to get useful outputs and avoid overtrusting incorrect answers.
finding.measure: Qualitative themes on critical thinking, prompt skill development, and perceived effects on students’ reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that many participants found interacting with ChatGPT exciting, fun, and emotionally engaging, but also noted disappointment, discomfort, or loss of trust when the system provided wrong or unemotional responses. These are perceived affective responses rather than measured engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Interview themes on personality, emotion, enjoyment, trust, and perceived human-likeness

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on broader institutional concerns including cheating policies, privacy and data governance, fairness/equity, and the need for new teaching philosophies and guidelines for responsible adoption. It argues that schools and universities should adapt assessment practices and governance structures rather than simply banning ChatGPT, but it does not evaluate an institutional policy intervention empirically.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of public discourse, interview themes, and educator scenario analysis about cheating, privacy, fairness, and adoption policy

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty‑first century skills in the post‑pandemic world
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual/review-style paper examining how the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the use of AI-driven educational technologies and why teachers need stronger AI digital competencies to teach effectively in online and blended environments. It argues that AI can support teaching, assessment, feedback, personalization, collaboration, and administrative efficiency, but that these benefits depend on teachers’ ability to select, adapt, and ethically use AI tools.

Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper synthesizes examples from prior research and aligns them with existing competency frameworks, especially DigCompEdu, TPACK, and P21’s twenty-first century skills framework. It proposes that teachers’ AI competence should include not only technical know-how, but also pedagogical design, assessment literacy, ethical judgment, professional engagement, and support for learners’ broader skills such as communication, creativity, collaboration, and self-regulation.

The paper discusses how AI may help learners with diverse needs, including examples of accessibility supports for students with disabilities, but these are cited as illustrative prior examples rather than being directly studied in this paper. Its main conclusion is that educators need broader AI digital competencies and professional development to use AI safely, effectively, and inclusively in the post-pandemic era.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-driven educational tools can reduce teacher workload and improve efficiency by automating grading, generating feedback, supporting assessment, and handling repetitive administrative tasks. These claims are based on cited examples rather than a new empirical test in this paper, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading/feedback automation, administrative efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes prior work suggesting AI can support students’ motivation, self-efficacy, self-regulation, and engagement in online learning environments. It does not present original intervention data; instead, it cites examples of AI systems that provide personalized support and feedback intended to improve these learner dispositions.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-efficacy, self-regulation, engagement

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that AI can foster durable skills such as communication, collaboration, creativity, critical thinking, and problem solving, especially in AI-supported online and blended learning. The paper discusses these as framework-based competencies and supported outcomes from cited studies, but it does not report original effect estimates or sample sizes.
finding.measure: Collaboration, communication, creativity, critical thinking, problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main contribution is conceptual and institutional: it proposes revisions to educator competency frameworks (DigCompEdu and P21) to better incorporate AI. It argues that schools, universities, and policymakers should use these frameworks to guide professional development, curriculum design, standards, and digital transformation, but it does not evaluate institutional outcomes empirically.
finding.measure: Framework development, professional development, policy and curriculum guidance

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review of AI in higher education: it synthesizes 66 evidence syntheses (systematic reviews, scoping reviews, meta-analyses, mapping reviews, and related review types) published in English from January 2018 to July 2023. The authors ask what kinds of AI-in-education evidence syntheses exist in higher education, where they are published, who is producing them, how they are being conducted, and what they conclude about AI applications and research gaps.

The review does not test a single AI intervention directly. Instead, it maps the review literature across major AI application areas in higher education, including profiling and prediction, adaptive systems and personalization, assessment and evaluation, and intelligent tutoring systems. It also evaluates methodological quality using a DARE/AMSTAR-2-informed rubric, finding an average quality score of 6.57/10 and frequent shortcomings in search transparency, inter-rater reliability reporting, quality appraisal, and reflection on limitations.

Across the corpus, the most common focus was general AI in higher education, followed by profiling/prediction and adaptive systems/personalization. The review concludes that the field is growing but uneven, with a strong dominance of systematic reviews and a need for stronger methodological rigor, ethical attention, and more interdisciplinary collaboration. It notes that some reviews addressed accessibility for students with disabilities, but the corpus is not a direct intervention study and does not provide high-school subgroup evidence for multilingual learners or students with disabilities using AI writing assistants.

finding.finding_summary: Across 66 higher-education AI evidence syntheses, the review found that AI is frequently used for institutional efficiency and support functions such as admissions, course scheduling, retention, quality assurance, and automated feedback. However, these are review-level thematic findings rather than a single intervention effect estimate; no pooled effect size for operational outcomes was reported.
finding.measure: Mapped review findings on institutional/administrative AI applications (e.g., admissions, scheduling, retention, quality assurance, automated assessment/feedback)

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that many AI applications in higher education targeted learning support in specific domains such as language learning, nursing, and personalized content delivery, with chatbots and adaptive systems commonly discussed. These are synthesized thematic findings from the included reviews, not direct primary-study effects; no pooled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Mapped review findings on AI applications supporting learning content, personalized instruction, and subject-specific learning tasks
