finding.finding_summary: Several included reviews reported benefits for learner engagement, reduced anxiety, satisfaction, motivation, and related affective outcomes, especially for chatbots/virtual assistants and personalized learning. The paper itself does not pool these results or report a single effect size; it summarizes prior reviews that described positive affective and engagement-related patterns.
finding.measure: Mapped review findings on engagement, satisfaction, anxiety, motivation, and affective responses to AI-supported learning

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that included evidence syntheses reported AI effects on critical thinking, communication skills, and other higher-order learning outcomes, particularly in studies of chatbots and virtual assistants. These are descriptive findings across reviews rather than a pooled intervention estimate, and no effect size is reported in this tertiary review.
finding.measure: Mapped review findings on critical thinking, communication skills, and related higher-order outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students’ essays.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether using ChatGPT-3 as a writing assistant improves students’ essay writing performance, originality, and writing efficiency. The authors compare essays written by students who had access to ChatGPT-3 with essays written traditionally, scoring the essays with a rubric and examining writing time, text authenticity, similarity across essays, and AI-detection outputs.

The sample was 18 second-year master’s students in forensic sciences at the University of Split, Croatia (n=9 control, n=9 experimental). Students wrote an 800–1000 word essay in Croatian within four hours; the experimental group used ChatGPT-3 (version 2.1.0) while the control group did not. Two instructors graded the essays, and the study also analyzed plagiarism/authenticity and pairwise similarity using PlagScan and Jaccard similarity.

Results showed no statistically significant advantage for the ChatGPT group on overall essay score or writing duration. The control group had a slightly higher mean essay score (2.39 ± 0.71 vs 2.00 ± 0.73), and none of the predictors in the regression model were significant. The authors conclude that ChatGPT did not improve essay quality in this setting and may have introduced some authenticity concerns, though essay similarity was generally low. This is a small, single-site intervention with no evidence about multilingual learners or students with disabilities specifically.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluated essay writing performance with and without ChatGPT-3 in a small intervention sample (n=18; 9 control, 9 experimental). Overall essay quality was not improved by the AI assistant: the control group slightly outperformed the ChatGPT group (mean score 2.39 ± 0.71 vs 2.00 ± 0.73), and group assignment was not a significant predictor of score (P=0.184).
finding.measure: Essay rubric score (A-D converted to 4-1; average of mechanics, style, content, format)

finding.finding_summary: The paper assessed whether ChatGPT-3 reduced the time needed to complete the writing task. Writing duration was very similar across groups (172.22 ± 31.59 minutes with ChatGPT vs 179.11 ± 31.93 minutes in control), and writing duration did not significantly predict essay score (P=0.669).
finding.measure: Writing time to complete the essay

finding.finding_summary: The study indirectly examined whether AI use changed higher-order writing-related performance by testing whether duration, GPA, module, and group predicted essay score. None of these predictors were significant in the linear regression model, suggesting no detectable effect of ChatGPT-3 on the broader writing process variables captured here.
finding.measure: Linear regression predictors of overall essay score (group, writing duration, module, GPA)

paper_profiles.title: Towards Explainable AI Writing Assistants for Non-native English Speakers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the challenges non-native English speakers face when using AI writing assistants for paraphrasing, with a focus on why users struggle to evaluate and accept machine-generated suggestions. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors conducted a semi-structured interview study with 15 non-native English speakers who regularly write in English and use tools such as Grammarly, Wordtune, Quillbot, Writefull, Google Translate, and similar systems.

Participants completed think-aloud writing tasks based on email scenarios and then discussed their experiences, challenges, and strategies. The study found that users often doubted whether paraphrased suggestions preserved meaning, tone, and pragmatics, especially when tools provided multiple options without explanations. Lower-proficiency speakers reported more difficulty selecting suggestions, while higher-proficiency speakers experienced less overhead. Users frequently sought external evidence such as dictionary examples, search results, corpora, or human feedback, and many wanted clearer explanations, examples, confidence indicators, or ranking information from the AI tools.

The paper’s main contribution is design guidance for explainable AI writing assistants rather than an evaluated classroom intervention. It proposes explanation features such as confidence scores, example sentences from credible sources, usage-trend visualizations, and textual explanations to support decision-making and learning for non-native writers.

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on writing support for non-native English speakers using AI paraphrasing tools. Participants reported that the tools helped them produce more polished English, but they also struggled to judge whether paraphrases preserved meaning, tone, and contextual appropriateness, especially when multiple suggestions were presented without explanations. No experimental effect on writing quality was measured; the evidence is qualitative and based on interviews with n=15 participants.
finding.measure: Interview-reported writing experiences, perceived paraphrase quality, appropriateness, and challenges in English email writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that participants used metacognitive strategies to evaluate paraphrases, including consulting dictionaries, corpora, search results, and human feedback to decide which suggestion to trust. These strategies suggest active comparison, judgment, and self-monitoring during writing, but the study does not quantify gains in critical thinking or metacognition. Evidence comes from interview data with n=15 non-native English speakers.
finding.measure: Self-reported strategies for evaluating AI suggestions and decision-making during writing

finding.finding_summary: Participants described overhead and friction when selecting among multiple AI-generated paraphrases, particularly when tools lacked explanations or a clear ranking of options. Lower-proficiency users reported greater difficulty and more time/effort in deciding which suggestion to accept, while higher-proficiency users reported less overhead. The study is qualitative and does not report timed efficiency measures or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Perceived overhead and ease/difficulty of selecting among paraphrased suggestions

paper_profiles.title: Stakeholder Perspectives on Whether and How Social Robots Can Support Mediation and Advocacy for Higher Education Students with Disabilities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether and how social robots and related AI tools, including large language models, could support mediation, advocacy, and self-advocacy for disabled students in higher education. The authors frame the work within disability justice and the social model of disability, emphasizing that the goal is not to 'fix' disabled students but to explore how technology might help them navigate institutional barriers, communicate needs, and access accommodations.

The study is an iterative participatory qualitative design conducted at the University of Cambridge. Phase 1 included interviews with four stakeholders: two disability practitioners and two disabled undergraduate students. The interview topics covered advocacy and communication needs, current use of AI tools, potential uses of social robots, robots in student support, and ethical/practical concerns. Thematic analysis produced five themes: empathic understanding, regulatory clarity and transparency, workload/capacity, power dynamics in higher education, and authenticity of AI-supported communication.

The paper finds that participants saw some potential benefits for AI and social robots, especially for repetitive administrative tasks, triaging basic questions, drafting clearer emails, and providing non-judgmental, predictable support. However, they also raised substantial concerns about empathy, privacy, bias, authenticity, and the risk that AI systems trained on existing norms could reproduce ableism and other inequities. The paper does not test an intervention or measure outcomes experimentally; instead, it provides stakeholder perspectives and design implications for future development of AI-supported advocacy tools in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed AI tools and social robots could reduce repetitive advocacy workload by helping draft or send emails, triage basic requests, and answer routine questions. The paper is qualitative and does not report a quantitative effect size; benefits were described as potential improvements in time savings and reduced administrative burden for disabled students and support staff (n=4 interview participants in Phase 1).
finding.measure: Perceived workload, administrative burden, and efficiency in advocacy/support tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-supported advocacy could help students navigate institutional structures more efficiently and potentially improve responsiveness, but participants were also concerned that AI might reproduce existing institutional power imbalances, bias, and inaccessible practices. No quantitative institutional outcome was measured; findings come from thematic analysis of stakeholder interviews (n=4) about higher education disability support systems.
finding.measure: Perceptions of institutional power dynamics, accessibility, and advocacy processes

finding.finding_summary: Participants thought robots might provide a non-judgmental, predictable interaction that could make disclosure and help-seeking easier, but they also worried about reduced empathy, distress, and discomfort. The paper reports no quantitative effect size; these are qualitative themes from interviews with disabled students and practitioners (n=4).
finding.measure: Perceived comfort with disclosure, trust, anxiety, and emotional safety in support interactions

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests AI may support communication clarity and self-advocacy, such as helping students phrase emails or structure requests, but participants worried that automated support could undermine authenticity and agency. No quantitative effect size was reported; findings are based on qualitative interview data (n=4).
finding.measure: Perceived self-advocacy, communication clarity, authenticity, and agency

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Three Pivotal Concepts in K-12 Science State Standards and Maps of Conceptual Growth to Research in Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual and standards-based analysis of K-12 physics learning, focusing on three foundational topics: Newton’s laws (force and motion), conservation of energy, and geometrical optics. The authors compare concept maps from Project 2061 with science standards from four U.S. states (California, Colorado, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin) to identify concepts that are both central to later science learning and commonly included in standards.

The paper does not evaluate an AI intervention or any writing assistant. Instead, it synthesizes prior physics education research on common misconceptions and instructional approaches that have shown some success. For Newton’s laws and conservation of energy, the paper reviews evidence that many students—even in high school and introductory college settings—hold robust misconceptions, such as confusing velocity with force or failing to recognize conservation of mechanical energy in novel contexts.

The context is K-12 science education, with some emphasis on high school physics, but the evidence is drawn from a range of earlier studies and assessments rather than a single intervention study in grades 9-12. The main conclusion is that these foundational physics ideas are prominent in standards, difficult to learn, and best taught through approaches that confront misconceptions directly, such as prediction-based demonstrations and inquiry activities. No evidence is provided about multilingual learners or students with disabilities, and there is no AI-related instructional component.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Newton’s laws and conservation of energy are foundational scientific ideas but are difficult for students to learn because of persistent misconceptions and context-dependent reasoning errors. It summarizes many prior studies (e.g., FCI-based research, conceptual interviews, and classroom explorations) showing that students often fail to apply scientific principles correctly even after instruction, but some prediction-based and exploration-based activities can improve understanding.
finding.measure: Conceptual physics understanding; Force Concept Inventory (FCI); conceptual multiple-choice tests; interviews; classroom explorations

paper_profiles.title: Creating Experience Value to Build Student Satisfaction in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how higher education institutions can create experiential value that leads to greater student satisfaction. The authors frame students as consumers of higher education services and argue that co-creation—students’ active participation in campus activities and interactions with lecturers and staff—should increase the value of their educational experience.

The study uses a survey of 357 students from 32 private universities in South Sumatra, Indonesia. Data were collected with a Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM). The authors test a model in which co-creation predicts experience value, and experience value in turn predicts student satisfaction.

Results show that co-creation has a strong positive association with experience value (estimate = 0.90, t = 11.43, R² = 0.82), and experience value has a strong positive association with student satisfaction (estimate = 0.85, t = 8.29, R² = 0.80). Co-creation does not directly predict student satisfaction in the final model (estimate = 0.05, t = 0.58, not significant), suggesting an indirect pathway through experience value. The paper concludes that universities should emphasize student participation and co-creation to improve the experience students receive and, ultimately, their satisfaction.

finding.finding_summary: Co-creation was positively associated with students’ experience value, which the authors treat as a precursor to satisfaction. In the SEM model, co-creation predicted experience value strongly and significantly (estimate = 0.90, t = 11.43, R² = 0.82) in a sample of n=357 students from 32 universities.
finding.measure: Experience value questionnaire / co-creation survey constructs

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that higher education institutions can improve student satisfaction by designing more co-created campus experiences and involving students in institutional activities. Although the evidence is correlational, the institutional implication is that co-creation and experience design are leverage points for university practice (estimate = 0.85 from experience value to satisfaction; R² = 0.80).
finding.measure: Student satisfaction and institutional co-creation model

paper_profiles.title: The future of generative AI chatbots in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper asks what the future implications of generative AI chatbots, especially ChatGPT-like systems, are for higher education institutions. It is not an intervention study; instead, it uses a narrative literature review to synthesize recent literature on opportunities, risks, and recommended responses for higher education.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that generative AI chatbots can streamline administrative tasks and reduce routine workload in higher education by handling inquiries, course registration support, fee-payment guidance, and appointment scheduling. No original intervention data, sample size, or effect size are reported because this is a narrative review.
finding.measure: Administrative task streamlining and workflow efficiency in higher education

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests generative AI chatbots may support writing and research writing by providing idea generation, drafting assistance, feedback, and improved productivity, but it also emphasizes academic integrity risks and uncertainty about acceptable use. No original study data are reported.
finding.measure: Writing support / research writing assistance in higher education

finding.finding_summary: The review states that chatbots may enhance student learning experiences through personalized, always-available support and instant responses, which could improve engagement and access to help. However, these claims are synthesized from prior literature rather than tested in this paper, so no sample size or effect size is available.
finding.measure: Student learning experience, support access, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The article notes that AI chatbots can prompt critical thinking through interactive conversations that encourage analysis of information and consideration of diverse viewpoints. This is presented as a literature-based claim, not as an empirical intervention result.
finding.measure: Critical thinking / higher-order thinking support

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes institutional opportunities and challenges, including policy, ethics, privacy, academic integrity, resource allocation, training, and governance around AI chatbot adoption in higher education. It concludes that institutions need clear guidelines, stakeholder training, and monitoring to integrate AI responsibly; no original quantitative institutional outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Institutional policy, governance, ethical implementation, and adoption considerations

paper_profiles.title: Specializing Multilingual Language Models: An Empirical Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how to improve pretrained multilingual language models for low-resource languages, especially when the target language is poorly represented in the model’s original vocabulary or uses a non-Latin script. The authors compare two specialization strategies: vocabulary augmentation, where new wordpieces from target-language text are added to multilingual BERT’s vocabulary and the model is further pretrained, and script transliteration, where target-language text is converted to Latin script before further pretraining.

The empirical study evaluates these methods on nine low-resource languages across three scripts, using three NLP tasks: part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, and named entity recognition. The core experimental setup compares unadapted MBERT, language-adaptive pretraining (LAPT), vocabulary augmentation (VA/TVA), fastText, and a scratch-trained RoBERTa-style baseline. Results show that vocabulary augmentation generally improves performance over LAPT and MBERT, with the biggest gains for unseen languages and non-Latin scripts; the gains are associated with better tokenizer coverage. Transliteration also helps for some unseen non-Latin languages, but combining transliteration with vocabulary augmentation often produces negative interaction, so the two methods are not consistently complementary.

finding.finding_summary: Vocabulary augmentation generally improved model performance on the three NLP tasks studied, compared with unadapted MBERT and language-adaptive pretraining (LAPT). Across nine low-resource languages, VA was the top performer in most language-task settings, with especially large gains for unseen/non-Latin languages such as Uyghur, where VA achieved up to a 57% relative error reduction over LAPT on the reported tasks.
finding.measure: Part-of-speech tagging accuracy, dependency parsing LAS, and named entity recognition macro F1
finding.study_size: n=9 languages; 5 random seeds per model
finding.confidence_interval: standard errors reported; exact 95% CI not_reported
finding.std_deviation: standard deviations reported across 5 random seeds

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that vocabulary augmentation offers an appealing balance of performance and cost, and that it is less time- and domain-intensive than linguistically informed transliteration schemes. This is a comparative efficiency claim rather than a direct productivity study, but it is supported by the authors’ interpretation of the intervention costs and relative performance.
finding.measure: Comparative implementation/training cost discussion (no direct workload metric reported)

paper_profiles.title: Exclusive photoproduction of π0 up to large values of Mandelstam variables s, t and u with CLAS
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a high-statistics nuclear/particle physics measurement of exclusive neutral pion photoproduction on the proton, gamma p  ppi0, using the CLAS detector at Jefferson Lab. The goal is to map the differential cross section over a wide range of photon energies and scattering angles, extending previous measurements into kinematic regions where resonance, Regge, and hard-scattering QCD descriptions can be compared.

The approach is an experimental cross-section study, not an educational intervention. The data were collected with a tagged photon beam on a liquid hydrogen target and the neutral pion was reconstructed through its Dalitz decay or external conversion to e+e−gamma. The paper compares the measured cross sections with Regge pole/cut models, a handbag/GPD-based model, and constituent counting rules.

The main conclusions are that the new CLAS data largely agree with Regge-based descriptions in much of the measured range and are broadly consistent with s−7 scaling expected from constituent counting rules at large angles and higher energies. However, the measured wide-angle cross sections are orders of magnitude larger than predicted by the handbag model at the highest energies considered, indicating that the GPD-based description is inadequate in this regime. The paper is purely about hadronic reaction dynamics and contains no educational population, AI system, or K-12 subgroup evidence.

paper_profiles.title: Computers in Secondary Schools: Educational Games
paper_profiles.venue: Encyclopedia of Education and Information Technologies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This encyclopedia chapter provides an overview of educational games in secondary schools, focusing on how digital play is used to support learning. It distinguishes among educational serious games, gamification, game repurposing, and game design/creation, and situates each within secondary education practice.

The chapter is descriptive rather than an empirical intervention study. It summarizes prior literature on digital game-based learning in secondary settings, including examples from mathematics, science, history, and language learning, and notes that gamification research has produced mixed results. The author concludes that secondary education has increasingly integrated game-based approaches and that future work should use stronger empirical methods and learning analytics to better understand their effects.

No AI writing assistant intervention is studied, and the chapter does not report grade 9–12 subgroup findings for multilingual learners or students with disabilities. It is a conceptual review/overview with cited examples of prior game-based learning research, not a direct experimental or correlational study of student outcomes in high school.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter states that game-based learning in secondary education is often associated with learner engagement and motivation, but also notes that gamification studies have shown mixed results. No new empirical data are reported in this chapter; it synthesizes prior literature only.
finding.measure: engagement and motivation (literature synthesis)

finding.finding_summary: The chapter asserts that educational serious games and related approaches can support performance in certain tasks across subjects such as history, science, mathematics, and language learning, but it does not present original outcome data. The discussion is based on examples from prior studies rather than a direct evaluation.
finding.measure: task performance / learning outcomes across subject areas (literature synthesis)

paper_profiles.title: LOLA – An Open-Source Massively Multilingual Large Language Model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces LOLA, an open-source massively multilingual large language model trained on raw text from 167 languages using a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformer architecture. The paper’s core question is whether MoE scaling can improve multilingual generalization while remaining compute-efficient, and whether the model’s expert-routing behavior aligns with language-family structure.

The study does not evaluate an educational intervention or any student-facing AI writing assistant. Instead, it reports model pretraining details, then benchmarks LOLA on 13 multilingual NLP tasks including question answering, reasoning, natural language inference, and reading comprehension. The authors compare LOLA against 17 multilingual models using zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting, and analyze MoE expert activations across languages.

Findings suggest LOLA performs strongly relative to smaller multilingual models and is especially competitive on NLI, reasoning, and reading comprehension tasks, while doing less well on factual Q&A and arithmetic tasks. The expert-routing analysis shows a weak-to-moderate correlation with language-family structure, suggesting the MoE layers capture some implicit linguistic grouping. No subgroup analyses for multilingual learners, students with disabilities, grades 9–12, or classroom implementation are reported.

finding.finding_summary: LOLA was evaluated on multilingual benchmark tasks spanning question answering, reasoning, NLI, and reading comprehension, and the authors report strong overall performance relative to smaller multilingual models. Across 14,000+ evaluation configurations, it especially outperformed Category-1 and Category-2 models, but underperformed larger Category-3 models that had at least five times more active parameters.
finding.measure: Benchmark accuracy / exact match across 13 multilingual NLP tasks

finding.finding_summary: The model showed strong results on reasoning-oriented benchmarks, including commonsense reasoning and cross-lingual inference tasks, indicating improved performance on language-based reasoning rather than classroom skill acquisition. The paper’s own summary states that LOLA is strong in reasoning tasks and competitive with larger models in NLI.
finding.measure: Accuracy on reasoning and NLI benchmarks (e.g., HellaSwag, XCOPA, XStoryCloze, XWinograd, XNLI, PAWS-X)

finding.finding_summary: LOLA was evaluated on reading comprehension and next-word prediction benchmarks, including LAMBADA and Belebele, and the authors report strong performance in reading comprehension. However, the paper does not report a classroom writing or literacy intervention, only benchmark performance on language-model tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy on LAMBADA and Belebele

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a systematic review of research on artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education (HE) published from 2016 through 2022. The authors ask where AI-in-education research in HE has been conducted, who the research focuses on, and how AI is being used across higher education settings. Using PRISMA methods, they screened 371 records and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles for full coding and analysis.

The review is not an intervention study of a single AI tool; instead, it synthesizes the field into broad usage categories such as assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. Most studies were conducted in Asia and North America, most often involved undergraduate students, and most frequently addressed language learning, computer science, and engineering. The review concludes that AI in HE is expanding rapidly, that research leadership has shifted toward China, and that education faculty are now more prominent in the author pool. It also highlights that AI is being used primarily to support students, with fewer studies focused on instructors or managers.

For the specific sub-question about grades 9–12 multilingual learners and students with disabilities, this paper does not provide direct high school evidence or subgroup analyses. Its included studies are in higher education, and the paper reports occasional examples involving diverse or minority learners in HE, but no K-12 intervention findings for multilingual learners or students with disabilities. As a field review, it is useful mainly as background evidence indicating that direct high school AI-writing-assistant evidence is absent in the reviewed literature.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed higher-education literature, AI was frequently used for writing-related tasks such as automated feedback, automatic assessment, translation support, and text generation. The review reports that these applications were often described as helping students improve academic writing, but it does not synthesize a single pooled effect or report a common effect size across the 138 studies.
finding.measure: Writing quality, automated feedback, grading, and language-learning tasks including writing/reading/vocabulary
finding.study_size: n=138 studies reviewed; writing-focused subset not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies used AI to support engagement, persistence, self-regulation, and affect-related outcomes. The review notes examples such as systems that gave personalized feedback, supported self-testing, and helped students regulate effort and emotion, but it does not provide pooled estimates or consistent effect sizes.
finding.measure: Engagement, persistence, self-regulated learning, emotion-related outcomes

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the review is that AI improved efficiency for instructors and administrators, especially through automatic assessment, feedback generation, question generation, learning analytics, and student-data management. The paper emphasizes that these tools can reduce grading and data-analysis burden, but it does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Instructor grading time, feedback generation, question creation, learning analytics, student-data management
finding.study_size: n=138 studies reviewed; operational subset not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies AI uses that touch durable skills such as metacognition, self-regulated learning, and problem solving, especially in intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive feedback systems. However, these findings are descriptive across studies rather than a single evaluated intervention effect, so no pooled effect size is available.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning, metacognitive support, adaptive problem solving

paper_profiles.title: Whatever next? Predictive brains, situated agents, and the future of cognitive science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This is a theoretical target article arguing that brains function as prediction machines, using hierarchical generative models to minimize prediction error. The paper synthesizes work on predictive coding, Bayesian inference, attention, perception, action, and the free-energy principle, and it critiques and extends these frameworks as a unified account of cognition and behavior.

The article does not study an educational intervention, AI writing assistant, or any school-based population. It is a conceptual neuroscience/philosophy paper rather than an empirical study, and the discussion centers on low-level perception, action, and brain computation in general. As such, it provides no direct evidence about high school learners, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities.

Because the paper is not an intervention study and contains no education-specific empirical outcomes, there are no extractable K-12 outcome findings. Any references to machine learning or predictive models are purely analogical and not evidence of AI use in education.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: five priorities for research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a Nature Comment that argues for a research and policy response to ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs). It does not test an educational intervention or report a student outcome study; instead, it synthesizes concerns and opportunities around conversational AI in scientific work, including accuracy, bias, transparency, accountability, open science, and equity.

The authors describe several informal demonstrations in which they prompted ChatGPT to answer research questions or summarize a systematic review, and they observed fabricated, misleading, or incomplete outputs. They use these examples to motivate five priorities: human verification, rules for accountability, investment in open LLMs, embracing benefits of AI, and widening the debate.

The only education-relevant discussion is speculative and policy-oriented: the article suggests AI could support student writing and reasoning, but could also widen inequities if access and capability are uneven. There is no empirical study, no grades 9–12 sample, and no evidence on multilingual learners or students with disabilities in an instructional setting.

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that ChatGPT and similar LLMs could increase productivity by speeding up literature reviews, drafting, code writing, and manuscript preparation, but also warns that outputs are often inaccurate, misleading, or biased. The paper reports informal prompts rather than a controlled study; no sample size, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Illustrative prompt responses to ChatGPT and qualitative assessment of output usefulness/accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes governance, transparency, accountability, and policy changes for research institutions, publishers, and funders in response to LLM use. It provides no empirical evaluation, but makes a strong normative case that institutions should require disclosure, human verification, and open-source development to manage risks and preserve integrity.
finding.measure: Policy and governance recommendations based on qualitative analysis

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests LLMs may support academic skills such as writing, reasoning, and prompt engineering, while potentially reducing the need for skills like literature searching and independent judgment. This is a conceptual claim rather than a measured effect, so no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of writing, reasoning, and prompt-engineering skills

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review article that surveys the educational uses, benefits, and risks of artificial intelligence, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize existing literature on AI technologies in education, including intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading, chatbots, and adaptive learning platforms.

The paper argues that AI has potential to improve learning through personalization, feedback, engagement, and productivity, while also raising important ethical issues such as bias, privacy, transparency, academic integrity, and unequal access. It discusses applications for students, teachers, and administrators, and notes that AI may be especially useful for language learning, feedback, and supporting vulnerable learners, but it does not present original empirical data or a high school intervention study.

For the sub-question on direct high school evidence for multilingual learners and students with disabilities, this paper does not provide an intervention study in grades 9 to 12. It cites prior studies and reviews in general terms, including references to students with dyslexia, autism spectrum disorder, and language-learning applications, but these are not analyzed as subgroup findings from a high school AI writing-assistant intervention. The paper is therefore best characterized as background/review evidence only.

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI tools such as chatbots and writing assistants can support writing and language tasks, including tailored feedback on written assignments, but it does not report original literacy outcomes from a new intervention study. It cites prior work suggesting potential benefits for reading comprehension and writing support, but no effect sizes, sample sizes, or direct high school subgroup results are reported in this paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Lexicon-Based Methods for Sentiment Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents SO-CAL (Semantic Orientation CALculator), a lexicon-based sentiment analysis system for automatically classifying text as positive or negative. The authors’ core question is whether hand-ranked dictionaries of sentiment-bearing words, combined with linguistic rules for negation, intensification, irrealis, repetition, and text-level weighting, can produce robust sentiment classification across domains.

The system is evaluated on several adult consumer-review and opinion-text corpora, including Epinions reviews, movie reviews, camera/printer/stroller reviews, MPQA, MySpace comments, news/blog posts, and headlines. The paper compares alternative dictionary designs and feature settings, showing that the full lexicon-based system generally outperforms simplified versions and is more robust across unseen domains than many domain-specific statistical classifiers, though absolute accuracy varies by corpus.

This is not an educational intervention study and does not involve grades 9–12, students with disabilities, multilingual learners, or AI writing assistance. The evidence is about general sentiment analysis performance in computational linguistics, not K-12 educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: SO-CAL improved automated sentiment classification efficiency and accuracy relative to simpler dictionary variants. On review corpora, the full system reached 78.74% overall accuracy, compared with 75.11% for the Simple dictionary and 73.93% for Only-Adj; on unseen corpora it remained strong at 80.00% on Epinions 2 and 76.37% on the Movie corpus.
finding.measure: Sentiment classification accuracy on review and opinion-text corpora

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Tools on Student Writing Development: A Case Study From The CGScholar AI Helper Project
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This case study examines whether a customized AI writing-feedback tool, CGScholar AI Helper, can support high school students’ writing development in English Language Arts. The paper is situated in a broader software-development project to build a teacher-mediated generative AI system that uses teacher-selected texts, prompts, and a rubric to provide iterative feedback on student writing.

The intervention was piloted with one 11th-grade ELA teacher and six students in a public Midwestern U.S. high school located in a socioeconomically underserved area. Students wrote a 200-word response comparing two assigned texts, received AI feedback through the CGScholar platform, revised, received a second round of AI feedback, and then submitted final work to the teacher. Data came from students’ drafts, researcher observations, a student focus group, and a teacher post-survey.

The study reports that five of six students improved on at least one rubric criterion and one student improved on three criteria. Improvements were most evident in compare/contrast, composing defensible claims, analyzing Indigenous culture, and introducing/connecting evidence. Participants described the AI feedback as direct, specific, actionable, and encouraging, while also noting that it was sometimes too long and linguistically complex. The authors conclude that a mediated, rubric-aligned generative AI writing assistant has promise for supporting K-12 writing, but the evidence is preliminary and based on a small qualitative pilot.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative pilot with 6 11th-grade students, CGScholar AI Helper was associated with improved writing performance on rubric-based criteria after students revised drafts using AI feedback. Five students improved in at least one criterion and one student improved in three criteria, with gains especially in compare/contrast, composing defensible claims, analyzing, and introducing/connecting evidence.
finding.measure: Teacher-rubric scored writing revision on six criteria (compare and contrast, identify, compose, introduce and connect, support evidence, analyze) using a 0-4 star scale

finding.finding_summary: Students and the teacher reported that the AI feedback was helpful, direct, actionable, and encouraging, and that it motivated students to revise their writing. The paper frames revision motivation and willingness to rework drafts as an important benefit of the tool.
finding.measure: Student focus group feedback and teacher post-survey perceptions of revision motivation and usefulness of feedback

finding.finding_summary: The AI feedback supported higher-order writing processes such as comparison, claim composition, analysis, and connecting evidence to claims. These improvements suggest gains in analytical reasoning and metacognitive revision rather than only surface-level editing.
finding.measure: Changes in rubric criteria related to analysis, compare/contrast, composing claims, and connecting evidence

paper_profiles.title: Shaping Human-AI Collaboration: Varied Scaffolding Levels in Co-writing with Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how different granularity levels of AI scaffolding affect human co-writing, focusing on whether large language model (LLM) assistance should be provided at the sentence level or paragraph level. The authors frame the problem as a question of balancing productivity and quality against human agency, satisfaction, and text ownership in AI-assisted writing.

To study this, the authors ran a within-subjects field experiment with 131 adult participants recruited from a large U.S. university health-system community. Each participant completed argumentative writing tasks in three randomly sequenced conditions: no AI assistance, next-sentence suggestions, and next-paragraph suggestions. The custom tool used GPT-3 (Davinci) to generate suggestions on demand. Outcomes included human-rated text quality, edit counts, spelling errors, productivity (words per unit time), satisfaction, ownership, perceived AI influence, and NASA-TLX workload.

The main findings show a U-shaped pattern: sentence-level suggestions did not improve quality or productivity and in some cases worsened text quality, while paragraph-level suggestions improved writing quality and productivity but reduced satisfaction and ownership. The benefits of paragraph-level scaffolding were stronger for non-regular writers and for users with less technology experience. Overall, the paper concludes that more substantial AI scaffolding can improve writing performance, but at the cost of weaker perceived authorship, suggesting that writing assistants should be designed with adaptive, personalized support rather than a one-size-fits-all level of help.

finding.finding_summary: This within-subjects experiment found a U-shaped relationship between AI scaffolding and writing quality. Relative to no AI assistance, sentence-level suggestions reduced human-rated text quality by 0.29 points (p=0.02), while paragraph-level suggestions increased quality by 0.18 points (p=0.02); the analysis used N=393 condition-level observations from 131 participants.
finding.measure: Human-rated text quality of argumentative writing; supporting automated cohesion/lexical sophistication metrics (TAACO, TAALES)
finding.effect_size: sentence: -0.29 quality points; paragraph: +0.18 quality points

finding.finding_summary: AI-assisted writing reduced user satisfaction and perceived text ownership compared with no AI assistance. Satisfaction declined by -2.14 in the sentence condition and -1.89 in the paragraph condition, and ownership declined by -3.66 and -5.65 respectively (all relative to control), indicating a consistent negative effect on user experience despite improved quality in the paragraph condition.
finding.measure: Post-task satisfaction and perceived ownership ratings

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests AI scaffolding changed how participants managed the writing task, but not uniformly in a positive way. Text quality improved with paragraph-level support and worsened with sentence-level support, and the authors interpret these effects as reflecting differences in how AI support shaped planning and sustained engagement with the argument; however, direct measures of critical thinking or collaboration were not central outcomes.
finding.measure: Argumentative writing quality and sequence-position effects during co-writing
finding.effect_size: paragraph quality: +0.18; sentence quality: -0.29; previous sentence→paragraph transition: +0.52

finding.finding_summary: Paragraph-level scaffolding improved productivity, defined as words per unit time, by 0.07 (p=0.01) relative to the no-AI condition. The sentence-level condition did not significantly improve productivity, and both AI-assisted conditions substantially reduced the number of edits compared with control (-334.14 for sentence and -795.04 for paragraph, both p<0.0001).
finding.measure: Productivity (words/time) and number of edits

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how four secondary school English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students in Hong Kong used ChatGPT and other proprietary chatbots to complete a timed blog-writing task for the first time. The authors are interested in the prompt content students chose, the sequence of prompts they used, and how their prompt engineering pathways differed as students iteratively refined their requests through trial and error.

The study is a qualitative case study based on iPad screen recordings and students’ completed writing tasks. Students were given a blog-entry prompt and could use the POE app (which included ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly) during an after-school lesson. The analysis coded 36 valid prompt turns into types such as auto-complete, natural language instruction, questions, greetings, search-engine style prompts, and chatbot-suggested follow-ups.

The main finding is that students used a small set of prompt types, often by experimenting across turns and across chatbots, rather than by applying systematic prompt-engineering strategies. The authors argue that the pathways ranged from less to more sophisticated, with many prompts relying on simple auto-complete or basic natural-language instructions. They conclude that students need explicit prompt-engineering instruction to make better use of generative AI for writing in EFL classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies students’ use of AI chatbots to support a writing task, focusing on how they generated blog text through prompting rather than on writing quality outcomes. Across four students, 36 valid prompt turns were coded, and the authors describe pathways that ranged from simple auto-complete to more sophisticated combinations such as AC + NLI + Q. The study provides process evidence that ChatGPT and other chatbots were used as writing support, but it does not report direct pre/post measures of writing performance, so the academic-literacy effect on writing achievement is not quantified.
finding.measure: Prompt content and sequencing during a blog-writing task; completed writing task qualitatively reviewed

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Legal Writing Evaluation of LLMs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies whether large language models can be used as automated judges for legal writing in the Brazilian Bar Examination. The authors introduce oab-bench, a benchmark built from 105 open-ended questions across seven law areas from the 39th, 40th, and 41st editions of the exam, together with official commented answers and score-distribution tables used for grading.

The main intervention is not an educational treatment for learners, but an evaluation pipeline in which LLMs first generate answers as examinees and then a strong LLM judge (o1) scores those answers using the official grading rubric. The paper compares multiple candidate models on the benchmark and also compares LLM-judged scores against human scores on a small set of handwritten, manually transcribed, previously graded student responses from older exam editions.

The paper finds that Claude-3.5 Sonnet performed best as a candidate answer generator, while o1 aligned reasonably well with human grading on approved human responses, though it sometimes over- or under-scored compared with human examiners. The study concludes that frontier LLMs can approximate human scoring on this specialized legal writing task, but the work is primarily a benchmark/evaluation study rather than an intervention study in K-12 education. It does not study multilingual learners or students with disabilities, and it reports no subgroup analyses for those populations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLMs on a legal writing exam benchmark (oab-bench) and reports that Claude-3.5 Sonnet achieved the highest average score, 7.93/10, passing all 21 exams. This reflects performance on specialized open-ended writing tasks rather than an instructional effect.
finding.measure: OAB legal writing exam scores on open-ended legal essay and discursive questions
finding.study_size: n=21 exams (105 questions across 3 exam editions)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM judges can automate scoring of legal writing, reducing reliance on human examiners. In the human-vs-LLM comparison, o1 showed reasonable alignment with human scores on three real exam responses, with MAE ranging from 0.04 to 0.28 across the three examined exams, suggesting potential efficiency gains in grading workflows.
finding.measure: Agreement between human and LLM judge scores; mean absolute error (MAE) in scoring
finding.study_size: n=3 human-written exams for judge comparison

paper_profiles.title: Is Your Writing Being Mimicked by AI? Unveiling Imitation with Invisible Watermarks in Creative Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of protecting creative writing from unauthorized AI imitation. The authors argue that existing watermarking and membership-inference methods are designed mainly for visual or multimodal data, or for detecting whether text is AI-generated, and do not adequately verify ownership of stylistic essence in creative writing.

To solve this, the paper proposes WIND (Watermarking via Implicit and Non-disruptive Disentanglement), a watermarking framework that uses an encoder plus a frozen LLM to extract five style elements from texts: vocabulary/word choice, syntactic features, rhetorical/stylistic choices, tone/sentiment, and rhythm/flow. These condensed style descriptions are mapped into a disentangled watermark space and compared against suspicious texts using Hamming distance. The method is evaluated on human-written creative writing datasets (Shakespeare and ROCStories) with AI-rewritten imitation texts generated by GPT-3.5, Grok, and OPT, showing high watermark verification performance and strong robustness to several perturbation attacks.

The study is not an education intervention and does not involve students, classrooms, or instructional use of AI writing assistants. There are no direct data on high school learners, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities. The empirical results are about copyright verification for creative writing datasets, not educational outcomes, though the paper includes comparisons against baseline detectors and watermarking methods that show WIND performs substantially better in identifying imitation texts.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed WIND framework substantially improves verification efficiency and reliability for detecting AI imitation of creative writing compared with baseline classifiers and watermarking methods. In the main experiments, WIND reached very high F1 scores with low false-positive rates, for example F1=94.72 with FPR=2.99 at num=6 on SP when GPT-3.5 generated the imitation texts, while baseline BERT and T5 were much weaker; the paper also reports about 23 minutes training time for a representative SP run with 10 samples.
finding.measure: F1, true positive rate (TPR), false positive rate (FPR), and wall-clock training time for copyright verification
finding.std_deviation: reported in tables as standard deviations for F1/TPR/FPR, but not aggregated into a single value

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that WIND provides a practical copyright-protection mechanism for creative writing datasets and could help institutions or content owners verify ownership against AI imitation. Empirically, it outperformed existing watermarking baselines such as KGW, Unigram, EWD, SynthID, and Unbiased at both FPR@10% and FPR@1% operating points, supporting its use as a stronger institutional safeguard for textual IP.
finding.measure: Verification performance against watermarking baselines at FPR@10% and FPR@1% operating points
finding.std_deviation: reported in tables as standard deviations for some comparisons, but not summarized

paper_profiles.title: Igniting Creative Writing in Small Language Models: LLM-as-a-Judge versus Multi-Agent Refined Rewards
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how to improve creative writing in a 7B-parameter small language model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) using AI-generated feedback rather than human feedback. The authors compare two reinforcement-learning-from-AI-feedback (RLAIF) strategies for generating Chinese greetings: (1) a reward model trained on preference data curated by a multi-agent evaluation pipeline, and (2) a principle-guided LLM-as-a-Judge that directly provides reward signals after adversarial optimization with reflection.

The study uses large-scale online Chinese greeting data to build a retrieval corpus, preference pairs for reward-model training, and train/test splits for policy optimization. The core experiments evaluate output quality with automatic metrics and human judgments across language quality, creativity, emotional resonance, cultural appropriateness, and content richness. The paper reports that both AI-feedback approaches improve over baseline SFT-only models, and that the LLM-as-a-Judge approach generally performs best, with higher excellence rates and better human-rated scores than the refined reward-model approach.

The context is not classroom-based and does not involve K-12 learners, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities. Instead, it is a generative language-model training paper focused on Chinese greeting generation, efficiency, and alignment between automated and human evaluation. The paper concludes that principle-guided LLM-as-a-Judge reward signals can be a more efficient and effective alternative to conventional reward-model pipelines for creative text generation.

finding.finding_summary: Both AI-feedback methods improved creative writing quality for Chinese greeting generation compared with baselines, and the LLM-as-a-Judge + RL approach performed best. Human experts rated the model highest on language quality, and the paper reports higher excellence rates and average human scores for LLM-as-a-Judge + RL than SFT-only or reward-model-based variants.
finding.measure: Human expert ratings of generated Chinese greetings on language quality and overall excellence rate; five-dimensional rubric including language quality, creativity, emotional resonance, cultural appropriateness, and content richness

paper_profiles.title: Understanding EFL Students’ Idea Generation Strategies for Creative Writing with NLG Tools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study asks how English as a foreign language (EFL) secondary students search for, evaluate, and select ideas when using natural language generation (NLG) tools for creative writing. The paper is framed around a gap in the literature: although AI writing tools may support idea generation, little is known about how novice EFL writers actually interact with them during classroom-style creative writing tasks.

The authors organized seven voluntary workshops in an all-girls secondary school in Hong Kong. Four students in grades secondary 1, 3, 5, and 5 (ages 12–17) wrote short English stories of up to 500 words using their own words plus text generated by four custom NLG tools built on Hugging Face (e.g., next sentence, next word, and next paragraph generators powered by open-source language models such as GPT-J, GPT-Neo, GPT-2 Large, and BERT). Students reflected in writing after workshops, and the researchers conducted thematic analysis of the reflections and workshop recordings.

The study found that students generally approached NLG tools with relatively underdeveloped idea-search strategies focused on language fragments rather than story structure. When evaluating AI output, they tried to fit it into existing story ideas, and some were wary of novel or surprising suggestions. Students preferred tools that produced more ideas, which they could then filter. The paper concludes that EFL students may need explicit instruction on prompting, evaluating, and using NLG tools for creative writing, but it is exploratory and does not test learning gains with a comparator.

finding.finding_summary: The study examined students’ use of NLG tools for English creative writing and identified strategies for idea generation, evaluation, and tool selection, but it did not measure writing quality with pre/post tests or a comparison group. Across four secondary students (n=4), reflections suggested that AI output could help generate usable words, sentences, and paragraphs, yet students also showed aversion to some outputs and relied on existing ideas to judge fit.
finding.measure: Written reflections and workshop discussion about short-story writing with NLG tools

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focused on students’ metacognitive and strategic behaviors while writing with AI, including prompting, evaluating outputs, and selecting among tools. Thematic analysis showed students used existing schemas to judge AI suggestions and varied in openness to novel ideas, but no standardized outcome measure or causal estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of reflection responses on strategy use, evaluation, and tool choice

paper_profiles.title: Writing-RL: Advancing Long-form Writing via Adaptive Curriculum Reinforcement Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes Writing-RL, an adaptive curriculum reinforcement learning framework for improving long-form writing in large language models. The authors argue that supervised fine-tuning for long-form generation is limited by data saturation and teacher-model ceilings, and they introduce three components to address this: margin-aware data selection, pairwise comparison rewards, and dynamic reference scheduling.

The study is conducted on 7B-scale writer models initialized from writing-oriented supervised fine-tuned checkpoints. Training uses two generative writing datasets (LongWriter and WritingBench) and compares RL training with PPO against supervised fine-tuning baselines and alternative curriculum/reward designs. The paper reports that RL-trained models outperform SFT baselines on writing benchmarks and also generalize better to long-context reasoning tasks, but the work is a model-training study rather than an educational intervention study.

The context and evaluation are entirely about AI model capability for writing, using benchmark tasks and LLM-as-a-judge scoring. No school-based population, classroom implementation, or learner subgroup analysis is reported. For the requested sub-question, this paper does not provide direct high school evidence for multilingual learners or students with disabilities; it only offers baseline/non-AI educational evidence? No—the paper contains no educational learner evidence at all, only model-training evidence.

finding.finding_summary: Writing-RL improved long-form writing performance over supervised fine-tuning baselines on benchmark evaluations. For example, Qwen2.5-7B-Writing-RL reached 87.23 on WritingBench, 73.19 on EQ-Bench, and 93.06 on LongBench-Write (average 84.49), compared with its SFT counterpart at 83.71, 70.02, and 92.22 (average 81.98). Llama3.1-8B-Writing-RL similarly improved to 87.40 average versus 84.25 for SFT.
finding.measure: WritingBench score, EQ-Bench creative writing score, LongBench-Write quality score, average benchmark score

finding.finding_summary: The paper also reports improved generalization from long-output writing training to long-input reasoning tasks on LongBench v2. RL-trained models outperformed their SFT-trained counterparts, such as Qwen2.5-7B-Writing-RL scoring 31.8 overall versus 27.6 for SFT, and Llama3.1-8B-Writing-RL scoring 32.8 overall versus 28.4 for SFT. This is presented as a transfer effect across long-context tasks rather than a direct educational outcome.
finding.measure: LongBench v2 reasoning benchmark scores (easy, hard, short, medium, long, overall)

paper_profiles.title: AI-Mediated Feedback Improves Student Revisions: A Randomized Trial with FeedbackWriter in a Large Undergraduate Course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether AI-mediated feedback, delivered through a human-in-the-loop system, improves student writing revisions more than traditional human-only feedback. The core problem is that producing high-quality, rubric-aligned feedback on long, knowledge-intensive essays is time-consuming for instructors and teaching assistants (TAs), and fully automated AI feedback can be inaccurate or misaligned with course goals.

To address this, the authors built FeedbackWriter, a system that generates GPT-4o-based feedback suggestions for TAs while allowing them to adopt, edit, or dismiss the suggestions. The system was deployed in an introductory economics course (ECON101) at a large public U.S. university with 354 undergraduates and 11 TAs. Students completed two writing assignments with a first draft, TA feedback, and a revised final draft; conditions were counterbalanced across assignments so each TA experienced both the AI-mediated and baseline non-AI workflow.

The main outcome was revised draft quality, with a secondary learning outcome measured by a post-test. Students receiving AI-mediated feedback produced higher-quality revisions than those receiving human-only feedback, with a reported effect size of Cohen’s d = 0.50. However, the AI-mediated condition did not produce a statistically significant difference on post-test learning. The study also found that AI-supported feedback was more actionable and more supportive of independent learning, and that TAs found the suggestions useful for spotting missed issues and clarifying rubric expectations.

finding.finding_summary: Students who received AI-mediated feedback through FeedbackWriter produced significantly higher-quality revised drafts than students who received human-only feedback. The main revision-quality outcome improved by about 5 percentage points, with a reported effect size of Cohen’s d = 0.50; the study included 354 undergraduate students and 1,366 essays.
finding.measure: Final draft quality / revised writing quality scored with an LLM-based rubric scorer

finding.finding_summary: Although higher-quality revisions were associated with learning, the post-test administered after revision showed no statistically significant difference between AI-mediated feedback and human-only feedback. Learning was measured with a post-test containing multiple-choice and open-ended questions on course knowledge components, and 262 students completed it for Assignment 1 and 305 for Assignment 2.
finding.measure: Post-test score after revision

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to support TA feedback provision, and qualitative/behavioral analyses indicated that TAs found AI suggestions useful for spotting overlooked issues and clarifying rubrics. However, the paper reports that grading time did not decrease in the experiment, so the operational efficiency effect was not a measured time-saving gain in this study.
finding.measure: TA grading time / system logs of TA interactions

paper_profiles.title: Breaking Barriers: Assistive Technology Tool as Educational Software to Support Writing
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Computer Engineering & Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the development of a Thai word prediction assistive technology tool designed to support writing for students with learning disabilities. The authors frame the work as addressing a lack of affordable, Thai-language writing support tools in Thailand, where most available word prediction products are English-oriented and expensive.

The paper includes usability testing with four information technology students and then a small classroom experiment with five grade 5 students with learning disabilities in Bangkok. In the experiment, students practiced typing essay-style messages on Notepad with and without Thai Word Prediction, and the authors compared keystroke reduction and essay-writing errors across pretest/posttest conditions.

Results are reported descriptively for three focal students. The program reduced keystrokes by 49.31% and 11.83% for Student #1 across two messages, 12.87% and 25.51% for Student #2, and 22.95% and 18.23% for Student #3. Essay-writing errors declined from 6 to 0 for Student #1, 11 to 1 for Student #2, and 4 to 2 for Student #3, which the authors interpret as improved writing accuracy and faster, easier word selection. The study does not report comparison analyses, subgroup contrasts, or any evidence specific to multilingual learners or students with disabilities beyond the inclusion of students with learning disabilities in the intervention group.

finding.finding_summary: In a small pretest/posttest classroom experiment with students with learning disabilities, Thai Word Prediction was associated with fewer essay-writing errors and improved word selection. For three reported students, errors decreased from 6 to 0, 11 to 1, and 4 to 2; the authors also report keystroke reductions of 49.31%/11.83%, 12.87%/25.51%, and 22.95%/18.23% across two typing messages.
finding.measure: Essay-writing errors; typed essay accuracy; keystroke reduction during writing
finding.study_size: n=5 (intervention group); detailed results reported for 3 students

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that the word prediction tool reduced typing effort and sped up written output for students with learning disabilities. Across the three students with reported data, keystroke reductions ranged from 11.83% to 49.31% on one message and from 18.23% to 25.51% on the other message, indicating improved efficiency in composing text.
finding.measure: Keystroke counts / keystroke reduction during typing practice
finding.study_size: n=3 reported in the table; n=5 in the experiment overall

paper_profiles.title: Writers Gonna Wait: The Effectiveness of Notifications to Initiate Aversive Action in Writing Procrastination
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether notifications and related interface supports can reduce procrastination on aversive writing tasks. The authors argue that while notifications are common in behavior-change applications, it is unclear whether they help when users already find the task unpleasant and have little intrinsic motivation to begin. To test this, they built a custom text editor that logged writing behavior and embedded several persuasive supports: standard clickable notifications, actioned notifications that asked for immediate text input, a goal progress bar, distraction-free mode, and an AI-/text-mining-based writing assistance system.

The study used 21 college students in a ubiquitous computing course who completed two graded 3000-word writing assignments over two nine-day periods. The first phase served as a baseline with no notifications; the follow-up phase introduced notifications, with one group receiving standard notifications only and the other receiving both standard and actioned notifications. The editor also generated concept-based writing assistance after enough text had been written. The paper reports that standard notifications were mostly ignored, actioned notifications were only occasionally answered, and neither notification type meaningfully reduced procrastination behavior. In contrast, the writing assistance features and goal progress bar were perceived more positively, with qualitative and survey evidence suggesting reduced aversion, better focus, and some help overcoming writer’s block.

Overall, the main conclusion is that notifications alone are weak tools for starting aversive writing tasks, especially when users are already busy or mentally blocked. The authors suggest that systems should reduce barriers, offer clear goals, and provide nonjudgmental assistance rather than rely on reminders. The study is exploratory and focused on undergraduate writing; it does not include high school students, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies writing performance and writing process during two graded 3000-word assignments. Compared with the baseline/no-notification phase, the follow-up notification intervention produced very little to no change in procrastination-related writing behavior; GRP1 averaged 2.29 writing sessions (sd=1.82, n=7) and GRP2 averaged 2.43 sessions (sd=0.9, n=7), with similar average writing time per participant. The authors conclude that notifications did little to decrease writing procrastination, while the writing-assistance features were perceived as helpful for overcoming writer’s block and structuring writing.
finding.measure: Writing behavior during graded 3000-word assignments (word count, number of sessions, typing time, start time) and self-reported PASS procrastination related to writing
finding.study_size: n=14 analyzed in follow-up; n=21 recruited
finding.std_deviation: GRP1 sessions sd=1.82; GRP2 sessions sd=0.9; SUS mean=60.7, sd=12.30

finding.finding_summary: The intervention had mixed effects on task aversion and satisfaction. Notifications were largely ignored and sometimes increased annoyance or negative feelings, but the writing-assistance system significantly decreased task aversiveness and difficulty in decision making compared with baseline (p<0.05). PASS self-reports suggested procrastination levels changed little overall, while qualitative comments indicated reduced aversion for some users and increased annoyance for others.
finding.measure: PASS procrastination survey, qualitative comments about aversion/annoyance, and user satisfaction (SUS)
finding.study_size: n=14 analyzed in follow-up; baseline n=21
finding.effect_size: p<0.05 for reduced task aversiveness and decision difficulty from writing assistants
finding.std_deviation: PASS high procrastination mean=8.2, sd=0.45; low procrastination mean=6.6, sd=1.52; SUS mean=60.7, sd=12.30

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that several UI supports helped students manage the writing task more effectively, especially the goal progress bar and distraction-free mode. Participants reported that the goal bar helped them evaluate writing time better (80% agreed) and motivated them to reach their goal (73.33% agreed), while distraction-free mode helped them focus (60% agreed) and write faster (40% agreed). The writing-assistance system also helped some participants structure thoughts and overcome writer’s block.
finding.measure: Survey responses about goal progress bar, distraction-free mode, and writing-assistance supports

finding.finding_summary: Operationally, the system captured writing process data and showed that notifications did not meaningfully improve efficiency in getting students started, but some assistive features improved perceived efficiency. Standard clickable notifications were immediately dismissed by all 118 instances, actioned notifications were responded to in 9 of 25 cases, and writing assistance was seen as useful for planning and generating content. The authors therefore conclude that notifications alone are not enough to improve task initiation efficiency, whereas tool supports such as concept mining and goal feedback can reduce effort and burden.
finding.measure: Notification dismissal/response rates, writing sessions, and self-reported usefulness of editor features
finding.study_size: n=14 analyzed in follow-up; 143 notifications delivered

paper_profiles.title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper conducts a systematic review of empirical research on artificial intelligence in STEM education published from 2011 to 2021. The authors use a general systems theory framework to organize AI-STEM studies around five system elements: technology, subject (instructor and learner), information (learning content), medium, and environment. Their goal is to understand not only what AI techniques are being used in STEM education, but also how those techniques interact with instructional contexts and what effects they have on learning and teaching.

Across 63 empirical studies, the review identifies six categories of AI applications: learning prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, student behavior detection, automation, educational robots, and a small set of other applications. The studies span multiple STEM subjects, with most work concentrated in science, technology, and engineering, and most use computer-based or web-based environments. The review also shows that instructors usually support the interventions, lecturing is the most common instructional strategy, and higher education is the most common population studied, though a smaller number of K-12 studies are included.

In terms of effects, the review reports that most empirical studies found positive effects of AI tools on learning performance, affective outcomes such as motivation and interest, and higher-order thinking skills. Some studies also found AI useful for detecting learning behaviors and predicting performance, while technological results generally showed that machine learning methods and automated assessment systems can work effectively in STEM contexts. However, a few studies found no significant learning gains, and the review concludes that evidence is promising but uneven across AI types, contexts, and outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review included some studies that directly involved writing and argument assessment in STEM contexts, but the paper is not a focused writing-intervention review. One empirical study of automatic argument assessment for computer engineering final reports reported that the system helped students improve statement and justification abilities in writing, while the review also notes that some AI-enabled assessment studies produced no significant learning gains overall.
finding.measure: Argument assessment of computer engineering final reports; writing/argumentation abilities

finding.finding_summary: Across 42 studies reporting educational effects, most AI applications were associated with positive affective outcomes such as attitude, interest, motivation, and satisfaction. The review highlights studies in which students expressed positive feedback toward learning analytics, adaptive learning systems, personalized learning environments, and robot tutors, suggesting improved engagement and motivation in STEM learning contexts.
finding.measure: Questionnaires, surveys, interviews, and mixed-method attitude/motivation measures

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI interventions often supported higher-order thinking, including problem-solving, computational thinking, and self-regulated learning. For example, the cited studies found better problem-solving in a flowchart-based ITS, improved computational thinking with deep-learning recommendations in AR, and more self-regulated learning behaviors with adaptive robotic scaffolding.
finding.measure: Problem-solving ability, computational thinking, self-regulated learning behaviors

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed empirical studies focused on mathematics learning and mathematics-related performance, and the overall pattern reported in the review was positive. The review cites adaptive learning and intelligent tutoring applications in math that improved learning gains, though it also notes that not all AI tools produced significant effects.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning gains, course performance, and math problem recommendation outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that many AI-STEM studies in science and engineering reported improved academic performance, including science achievement and reasoning-related outcomes. Examples include a context-aware ubiquitous learning system in geoscience with significantly positive effects on learning achievements and automated assessment work in biology that evaluated scientific explanations; however, some studies showed null effects.
finding.measure: Science achievement, learning performance, and reasoning-related STEM assessment outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review includes some literacy-adjacent evidence in STEM, especially automated assessment of written explanations and reports, but it does not synthesize a dedicated writing or reading-to-write intervention literature.
