The clearest result is that automatic argument assessment improved computer engineering students' writing argumentation ability, while other automated scoring studies showed mixed accuracy and occasional null learning effects.
finding.measure: Writing quality, argumentation in reports, automated scoring of written scientific explanations

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examined whether ChatGPT-supported writing instruction improves academic writing performance and writing motivation for Chinese English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. The authors motivated the study by noting that writing feedback is time-consuming and often difficult to individualize, and argued that AI tools may provide immediate, personalized support for writing development.

Fifty undergraduate EFL students at a Chinese university were randomly assigned to either an AI-assisted condition using ChatGPT or a traditional teacher-led condition. Over 12 weeks, both groups completed similar writing tasks and received feedback, but the experimental group received real-time AI feedback on grammar, vocabulary, coherence, organization, and sentence structure, while the control group received teacher feedback. Quantitative data came from IELTS academic writing pre/post tests and a writing motivation scale; qualitative data came from interviews with nine students in the AI group.

Results showed that the ChatGPT group outperformed the control group on overall writing performance, writing organization, language use, and writing motivation, with a smaller but still significant advantage for writing content. Reported effect sizes ranged from d=0.52 for motivation to d=0.88 for language use. Interview data suggested that students viewed ChatGPT as innovative, helpful, and motivating, while also expressing caution about over-reliance and contextual accuracy. The study concludes that AI-assisted writing feedback can support EFL writing development and motivation, though the authors note the need for careful, ethical use of such tools.

finding.finding_summary: The ChatGPT-assisted group showed significantly higher academic writing performance than the control group after the 12-week intervention. On overall writing, the experimental group scored higher than the control group (M=59.12 vs. 45.18), t(48)=3.79, p<0.001, d=0.76; ANCOVA also found a significant group effect on post-test writing scores, F(1,47)=19.01, partial eta squared=0.27. The writing assessment used IELTS academic writing Tasks 1 and 2, with subscores for content, organization, and language use.
finding.measure: IELTS academic writing Tasks 1 and 2; overall writing score and subdomains (content, organization, language use)

finding.finding_summary: Writing motivation improved significantly more in the ChatGPT group than in the traditional instruction group. The experimental group’s motivation score was higher at post-test (M=20.06 vs. 18.21), t(48)=3.34, p=0.001, d=0.52, and ANCOVA confirmed a significant group effect, F(1,47)=29.62, partial eta squared=0.38. Interview evidence also indicated that students felt more engaged, confident, and motivated when using AI-supported feedback.
finding.measure: Writing Motivation Scale (WMS)

paper_profiles.title: Automated feedback and writing: a multi-level meta-analysis of effects on students’ performance
paper_profiles.population: Primary through post-secondary students; includes secondary (high school) and tertiary samples
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether automated writing evaluation (AWE) systems that provide individualized, timely feedback improve students’ writing performance. The authors note that teachers often lack the time and resources to provide frequent, process-oriented writing feedback, and that AI-based feedback tools may help fill that gap.

The study is a multi-level meta-analysis of 20 experimental or quasi-experimental studies (84 effect sizes; N=2,828) published in scholarly journals. The included interventions used AWE tools that produced automated feedback on student writing, compared against no feedback or alternative feedback conditions, and measured outcomes on revision tasks and transfer tasks, with some studies also including follow-up measures. The meta-analysis found an overall positive effect of AWE feedback on writing performance (g=0.55, 95% CI [0.19, 0.91]), with substantial heterogeneity across studies.

Moderator analyses suggested that AWE tends to work better in longer interventions, in L2 contexts, on transfer tasks, and for analytic as well as holistic writing outcomes, while short interventions and revision/performance outcomes showed weaker effects. The follow-up effect was positive but not statistically significant, indicating limited durability evidence. Overall, the review concludes that AWE is promising for writing instruction, but its effects are variable and depend on context and implementation.

finding.finding_summary: Across 84 effect sizes from 20 studies (N=2,828), automated feedback produced a medium positive effect on writing performance when pre-test values were included (g=0.55, SE=0.17, 95% CI [0.19, 0.91]). Without pre-test values, the pooled effect was larger (g=0.77, SE=0.20, 95% CI [0.35, 1.18]), suggesting that ignoring baseline differences can overestimate impact.
finding.measure: Writing performance on revision and transfer tasks; holistic and analytic writing scores

paper_profiles.title: A systematic mapping review at the intersection of artificial intelligence and self-regulated learning
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic mapping review of research at the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and self-regulated learning (SRL). Rather than estimating an intervention effect, it catalogs 84 empirical studies published from 2018 to 2024 and organizes them using a Who/What/How/Why framework to show which stakeholders were studied, which SRL theories were used, how AI was implemented, and what purposes it served.

The review finds that AI-SRL research is heavily concentrated in higher education, with relatively little work in K-12 and especially little in primary school. Most studies use AI as an intervention, especially adaptive systems/personalization, profiling/prediction, and intelligent tutoring systems; the most common intended effects are supporting cognitive and metacognitive aspects of SRL, and improving outcomes such as academic performance, engagement, motivation, and collaboration.

Because this is a mapping review, it does not synthesize causal effects of a single intervention and does not focus on one domain such as writing. The paper does note that AI-supported SRL has been used to support writing-related learning in some studies, but the review’s own evidence is broad and mostly centered on STEM and higher education rather than high school content-area writing. The authors conclude that the field needs more theory specification, more qualitative and longitudinal work, greater attention to educators and younger students, and stronger ethical/data-transparency practices.

finding.finding_summary: Across the 84 studies in the mapping review, AI-supported SRL was often associated with improved academic performance in domain-specific learning contexts, including some writing-related learning activities. However, the review does not report a pooled effect size for writing or content-area literacy, and it is not a single intervention study of high school writing; instead, it summarizes heterogeneous studies where academic outcomes were frequently positive.
finding.measure: Academic performance / domain-specific learning outcomes
finding.study_size: n=84 studies (review-level); writing-specific sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI-supported SRL was frequently linked to improved motivation, engagement, emotions, and related self-regulatory processes. Specifically, motivation was examined in 20 studies, engagement in 10, and emotional outcomes in 9, and the overall pattern reported by the authors was generally positive rather than negative or null.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, emotions, and SRL-related attitudes/self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: This review centrally addresses SRL, metacognition, collaboration, and related durable skills. The authors report that AI was most often used to support cognitive and metacognitive aspects of SRL, and that some studies also found benefits for collaborative learning and reasoning skills; however, no pooled effect sizes are provided because the paper is a mapping review.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning, metacognition, collaboration, reasoning, and related durable skills

finding.finding_summary: A smaller set of included studies examined dashboards, automated feedback, and other AI tools that can streamline feedback and monitoring, suggesting potential operational benefits such as scalable support and reduced workload. The review explicitly frames AI as enabling timely, scalable feedback and assessment support, but it does not provide a pooled quantitative estimate of workload reduction.
finding.measure: Feedback delivery, dashboard support, assessment/evaluation efficiency, workload-related indicators

paper_profiles.title: A pedagogical design for self-regulated learning in academic writing using text-based generative artificial intelligence tools: 6-P pedagogy of plan, prompt, preview, produce, peer-review, portfolio-tracking
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of how students should use text-based generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, in academic writing without undermining writing quality or academic integrity. The authors argue that because generative AI can produce fluent text with minimal prompting but can also hallucinate, fabricate references, and tempt inappropriate use, students need a structured pedagogy that teaches responsible, critical, and self-regulated use rather than prohibition alone.

The paper proposes a conceptual six-phase framework called the 6-P pedagogy: plan, prompt, preview, produce, peer-review, and portfolio-tracking. The framework is grounded in Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning model and the authoring cycle, and it is intended to help students remain in control of the writing process while using AI as an assisting tool. The phases emphasize planning the thesis and structure, crafting and revising prompts, verifying AI output, synthesizing and producing the final text, receiving peer feedback, and reflecting on the process through portfolios.

The paper is not an empirical intervention study. It does not report a sample, comparison condition, or measured outcomes from classrooms; instead, it advances a pedagogical design and discusses implications for teachers, student development, and future research. The authors note that the framework has not yet been validated in a real-world setting, though they mention that a university in Hong Kong has adopted it for undergraduate general education. Overall, the paper concludes that generative AI literacy, self-regulation, and critical thinking are necessary for effective and ethical academic writing with AI tools, but the claims are theoretical rather than evidence-based.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report an empirical effect on writing quality or other literacy outcomes; it proposes a pedagogical framework for AI-supported academic writing. The authors argue that the 6-P model is intended to support better planning, drafting, revising, and reflection, but they explicitly state that the framework lacks real-world validation and provide no sample, effect size, or outcome data.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally focuses on self-regulated learning as a design principle, especially planning, monitoring, self-reflection, and adaptive reaction. However, it offers no empirical test of changes in motivation, engagement, persistence, or self-regulation, so there is no measured intervention effect to extract.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Critical thinking is a major theoretical focus of the paper, framed as essential for evaluating AI-generated text and avoiding hallucinations or hallucinated references. Yet the article provides no empirical evidence that the 6-P pedagogy improved critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration, or transfer; it only proposes these as intended outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses generative AI as a potential aid to productivity in writing, but it does not measure time savings, efficiency, or workload. The framework is presented as a way to structure AI use, not as an evaluated intervention with operational outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses institutional policy implications, including guidelines for acceptable AI use, academic integrity, and the need for teacher/student development. These are recommendations only; the paper reports no policy intervention, governance outcome, or institutional measurement.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: The Notorious GPT: science communication in the age of artificial intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This essay examines the rise of ChatGPT and generative AI and considers what it means for science communication practice, research, and the broader information ecosystem. The paper asks how these tools may change the production, translation, and public circulation of science-related content, while also highlighting risks such as factual inaccuracies, fabricated references, misinformation, and labor-market disruption for communicators.

Rather than reporting an intervention study, the article is a conceptual and field-scanning essay grounded in recent examples, early studies, and commentary about generative AI. It outlines possible uses of AI for summarizing science, translating technical language, creating multimodal content, and enabling dialogical communication at scale, but argues that science communication research has largely neglected AI so far.

The author concludes that researchers should urgently study four areas: public communication about AI, communication with AI, AI’s impact on science communication practice and ecosystems, and the conceptual/theoretical challenges AI raises for communication scholarship. Overall, the paper is a call for a research agenda, not an empirical evaluation of AI in education or writing instruction.

paper_profiles.title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (the paper is a conceptual review/framework article, not an empirical study of a student population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a broad problem in educational technology research: why digital tools sometimes improve learning and how researchers can explain those effects beyond simple comparisons of tool use versus no tool use. The authors argue that studies often focus on outcomes without specifying the cognitive processes and learning activities that mediate learning, making it difficult to identify the mechanisms by which digitally enriched instruction works.

To address this, the paper proposes the CoDiL framework, which integrates ideas from the knowledge-learning-instruction framework, the selection-organization-integration model, and utilization-of-learning-opportunity perspectives. The framework emphasizes that digital tools should be analyzed in terms of their instructional features, the learning activities they stimulate, and the cognitive processes linking those activities to knowledge acquisition. The article illustrates the framework with examples from math, science, and other domains, and it recommends that researchers specify content knowledge components, define relevant learning activities, design tools to elicit those activities, and collect process data to examine student-tool interaction.

The article is not an intervention study and does not test an AI writing assistant or any educational technology in grades 9-12. Instead, it is a theoretical synthesis and research-guidance paper intended to support future empirical work on digital learning mechanisms. Its main conclusion is that valid explanations of learning with digital tools require content-specific theories, process data, and careful alignment between instructional features and the cognitive activities they are meant to stimulate.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT versus human essayists: an exploration of the impact of artificial intelligence for authorship and academic integrity in the humanities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether GPT-4 can produce humanities essays comparable to those written by undergraduate students, and whether experienced human markers and commercial AI detectors can distinguish between the two. The authors focus on close-reading/commentary essays on passages of Old English poetry, a task central to first-year English literature assessment at the University of Oxford. Student essays submitted before the release of ChatGPT were compared with GPT-4-generated essays written from similar prompts, and all essays were blind-marked by experienced assessors.

The study finds that AI-written essays scored similarly to student essays on the UK grading scale, with no statistically significant difference (AI mean 60.48 vs. human mean 63.57, p = 0.10). However, qualitative analysis suggests that the AI responses were stronger on structure, register, and organization, while student work showed more nuanced cultural contextualization, deeper critical analysis, and more precise attention to poetic style and effect. Human markers identified authorship correctly 79.41% of the time, and the best detector tested (Quillbot) achieved 95.59% accuracy.

The paper concludes that generative AI can already produce convincing humanities commentary at roughly undergraduate quality, but still falls short in close textual analysis and contextual interpretation. The authors argue that assessment design in higher education should shift toward tasks that emphasize higher-order thinking, unseen prompts, and other formats less vulnerable to AI-generated prose, while also acknowledging that current detection tools and human judgment remain imperfect.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4-generated commentary essays on Old English poetry were scored comparably to student essays, with no statistically significant difference in average marks (AI mean 60.48, human mean 63.57; t = -1.67, p = 0.10). Qualitatively, AI essays were stronger in formal structure and academic register but weaker in detailed close reading, nuanced contextualization, and analysis of poetic style and effect.
finding.measure: Essay scores on the UK university grading scale; qualitative assessment of writing quality, organization, and textual analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on critical analysis, interpretation, and argumentation in close-reading essays. AI outputs were judged to have acceptable organization and academic tone, but they lacked the depth, incisiveness, and nuanced reasoning seen in stronger student essays; these cognitive differences were a major basis for distinguishing human from AI work.
finding.measure: Qualitative rubric dimensions including engagement, argument, information, organization, clarity, coherence, depth, accuracy, and incisiveness

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that generative AI poses a significant challenge to assessment integrity in higher education because AI-written essays can achieve marks similar to authentic student work. The authors argue for assessment redesign, including unseen prompts, in-person examination, and greater emphasis on higher-order thinking, to better protect academic integrity.
finding.measure: Comparative essay performance and authorship-detection outcomes informing assessment policy implications
finding.study_size: n=68 essays (40 AI, 28 student) plus 7 human markers

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Large Language Model and Story-Based Gamification in Intelligent Tutoring System to Scaffold Introductory Programming Courses: A Design-Based Research Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This design-based research study examines whether AI-enhanced gamification can scaffold learning in introductory programming (CS1) courses and improve Chinese international students’ sense of belonging. The paper is motivated by challenges these students face in adapting to programming instruction, including limited prior coding knowledge, language barriers, reduced interaction, and low academic confidence.

Across three iterative phases, the study first surveyed 57 Chinese international students and interviewed nine to identify key barriers to success and belonging. It then designed and evaluated a two-week story-based gamification prototype in Blackboard with 34 students, using narrative scenarios, role-play, leaderboards, teamwork, and feedback. Finally, it developed a more advanced intelligent tutoring system using GPT-3, with multiple chatbots and personalized feedback, and evaluated it through computer simulation and a pilot user study with stakeholders.

The main findings were that story-based gamification was perceived positively and appeared to improve engagement, motivation, and sense of belonging in the course. The GPT-3-enhanced intelligent tutoring system also showed promise for providing feedback and holding useful conversations, though performance depended on question quality and the system’s domain knowledge was limited. The paper concludes that AI-enhanced gamification may help support inclusive learning and belonging in introductory programming, but it calls for more real-world studies on long-term learning outcomes, transfer, and durability.

finding.finding_summary: The formative survey and prototype evaluation suggest that the AI-enhanced gamification design improved Chinese international students’ motivation, engagement, and sense of belonging in CS1. In the prototype study (n=32 questionnaire; n=32 focus groups; 34 enrolled), most students reported feeling more motivated, more engaged, more connected to classmates, and having a greater sense of belonging after the story-based activities.
finding.measure: Survey responses, focus groups, and participatory observation on sense of belonging, motivation, engagement, and academic emotions
finding.study_size: n=57 survey; n=9 interviews; n=34 enrolled in prototype study; n=32 questionnaire; n=32 focus groups

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Antitrust and Platform Power in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: 1st Workshop on Generative AI and Law, co-located with ICML
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines market dominance and platform power in the generative AI ecosystem from an antitrust law perspective. The authors argue that a small number of large technology companies control key layers of the generative AI stack, including data, talent, infrastructure, funding, and model development, which may reinforce concentration and make entry difficult for new competitors.

The paper is a policy and legal analysis rather than an empirical study of an educational intervention. It discusses how incumbents such as Google, Microsoft, Apple, and other major firms may leverage existing advantages from adjacent markets to strengthen their position in generative AI. The authors also consider how current antitrust doctrine, vertical integration, and emerging EU AI regulation could shape competition, concluding that more quantitative market analysis is needed and that current regulatory approaches may unintentionally favor already well-resourced firms.

The paper does not study students, educators, schools, or classroom implementation, and it contains no intervention, outcome measures, or empirical evidence about writing instruction or AI writing assistants. Its relevance to education is indirect, through broader governance and market-structure considerations for generative AI tools.

paper_profiles.title: AbuseGPT: Abuse of Generative AI ChatBots to Create Smishing Campaigns
paper_profiles.venue: IEEE 12th International Symposium on Digital Forensics and Security (ISDFS 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether modern generative AI chatbots can be abused to help attackers create SMS phishing (“smishing”) campaigns. The authors focus on prompt-injection and jailbreak strategies intended to bypass chatbot safety guardrails and elicit harmful outputs such as smishing text templates, campaign ideas, attack tool recommendations, fake URL suggestions, and multi-step attack guidance.

The study uses ChatGPT 3.5 as the main case study, with additional exploratory tests on Google Bard. The paper is framed around four research questions: whether chatbots can be jailbroken, whether they can generate smishing messages, whether they can recommend relevant toolkits, and whether they can suggest fake URLs. The authors report that some jailbreak prompts successfully produced unethical outputs in ChatGPT, while Bard often resisted or gave limited responses, though a few prompts yielded partially useful or disguised outputs.

This is not an educational intervention study and does not involve students, schools, or classroom writing outcomes. It is a cybersecurity abuse case study with no human-subject experiment measuring downstream attack success; the authors explicitly note that they did not test the smishing messages on real users. The paper’s main conclusion is that current AI chatbots can be manipulated to support more craftful smishing campaigns, underscoring the need for stronger safeguards and defensive monitoring.

paper_profiles.title: Learning From Failure: Integrating Negative Examples when Fine-tuning Large Language Models as Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can learn from failed trajectories when fine-tuned as agents, rather than discarding those negative examples. The authors argue that prior agent-tuning pipelines waste information by keeping only successful trajectories, and they propose negative-aware training (NAT), which explicitly labels positive versus negative trajectories by adding a prompt suffix indicating whether the model should generate a correct or incorrect solution path.

The method is evaluated on math reasoning, multi-hop question answering, and strategic question answering tasks using LLaMA-2-Chat 7B and 13B models fine-tuned on trajectories generated largely by GPT-3.5. Across these benchmarks, incorporating negative examples usually improves performance over positive-only fine-tuning, and NAT performs better than naively mixing positive and negative examples without labeling. The paper also shows that data quality matters substantially, that the model mainly learns better reasoning/planning rather than action execution, and that finer-grained labeling of negative examples can further improve results.

The study is not an educational intervention study in classrooms; it is an NLP/agent-tuning paper using benchmark tasks. Its conclusions are methodological: failed trajectories can be useful training data if they are differentiated from successful ones, and the benefit depends on both the amount and quality of negative data. The authors also show preliminary transfer to chain-of-thought prompting, suggesting the approach is broadly applicable across agent-style and reasoning-style fine-tuning setups.

finding.finding_summary: Negative-aware training improved math word-problem accuracy over positive-only fine-tuning and naive inclusion of negative examples. For LLaMA-2-7B with 2k positive examples, average accuracy rose from 55.90 (Vanilla) to 64.64 (NAT), with similar gains for 13B models and additional improvement in a CoT setting (52.69 to 59.37 average accuracy).
finding.measure: Math word-problem accuracy on GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, and MultiArith; exact match-style accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved performance on multi-hop and strategic question answering tasks, showing that NAT helps answer complex reasoning questions beyond math. On HotpotQA, NAT/NAT-2 improved EM and F1 relative to positive-only training; on StrategyQA, NAT improved accuracy from 55.40/53.40 (Vanilla) to 65.80/64.60 (7B/13B).
finding.measure: HotpotQA exact match and F1; StrategyQA accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret the gains as improved reasoning and planning rather than better tool execution, which is a form of durable cognitive skill. Table 6 shows that NAT increased accuracy on GSM8K to 46.93 from 35.63 (Vanilla) while reducing action errors relative to NUT (7.90% vs. 10.47%), suggesting better thinking about how to solve problems.
finding.measure: Action error rate, average turns, and solution accuracy on GSM8K trajectories

paper_profiles.title: The future of generative AI chatbots in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the future implications of generative AI chatbots, especially ChatGPT, in higher education institutions. It asks how these tools may affect teaching and learning, student support, research writing, and administrative efficiency, while also identifying risks such as academic integrity concerns, privacy issues, bias, and difficulties interpreting user input.

The paper uses a narrative literature review methodology to synthesize prior publications from academic databases. It is not an intervention study and does not present original empirical data; instead, it organizes the literature into opportunities, challenges, and proposed mitigation strategies, including ethical guidelines, stakeholder training, collaboration across disciplines, human oversight, and continued research.

The population/context is higher education, with discussion focused on students, academics, and institutional leaders rather than K-12 learners. The main conclusion is that generative AI chatbots have promise for personalized support, research assistance, and operational streamlining, but responsible adoption requires policy development, training, monitoring, and further empirical research in real educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that generative AI chatbots may improve operational efficiency in higher education by streamlining administrative tasks, supporting research writing, and reducing routine workload. At the same time, it notes substantial implementation burdens, including resource allocation, training, monitoring, and the need to redesign assessment and support processes.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of reported administrative, support, and research-writing functions

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on institutional-level implications of generative AI chatbot adoption, including academic integrity policy, ethical governance, privacy, staff training, and institutional readiness. It concludes that HEIs must develop clear guidelines and oversight structures to integrate AI responsibly and equitably.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of institutional policy, governance, and implementation issues

paper_profiles.title: Confirmation Bias in Generative AI Chatbots: Mechanisms, Risks, Mitigation Strategies, and Future Research Directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective article examines the phenomenon of confirmation bias in generative AI chatbots. Rather than testing a classroom intervention, it synthesizes prior work from cognitive psychology, human-computer interaction, and NLP to argue that chatbots can reproduce and amplify users' preexisting beliefs because their generative architecture prioritizes contextual consistency, user satisfaction, and conversational coherence.

The paper discusses several hypothetical mechanisms for how confirmation bias may arise, including prompt framing, multi-turn conversational reinforcement, training-data skew, and alignment methods that favor helpful or agreeable responses. It also outlines risks such as misinformation reinforcement, polarization, and reduced user autonomy, especially in high-stakes domains. Mitigation ideas proposed include detecting loaded assumptions, offering counterarguments, presenting multiple perspectives, transparency about sources, and policy or auditing frameworks.

The article is conceptual and forward-looking, not an empirical study of students or teachers, and it does not report original data, experiments, or effects in educational settings. Its main contribution is a research agenda for future empirical work on confirmation bias in generative AI systems.

paper_profiles.title: Contextualizing Problems to Student Interests at Scale in Intelligent Tutoring System Using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of scaling problem contextualization to student interests in intelligent tutoring systems. The authors argue that teachers can improve engagement and learning by tailoring algebra word problems to students’ interests, but that doing this manually is time-consuming and difficult to scale.

To address this, the paper explores using GPT-4, accessed through the OpenAI API, to automatically rewrite algebra problems in CTAT so that the cover stories match different student interests while preserving the original mathematical structure, difficulty, and values. The work focuses on prompt engineering across four problem sets in TutorShop and presents example outputs for interests such as TikTok, NBA, and video games.

The paper is primarily a system/design and proof-of-concept paper rather than a student outcome study. The authors report that GPT-4 can produce meaningful contextualizations and note limitations, especially for geometry and diagram-based problems. They explicitly state that future work should run systematic studies to measure effects on student learning outcomes, engagement, and efficiency, but no empirical intervention results with learners are reported in this paper.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes that GPT-4 can scale contextualization of existing tutor problems, reducing the manual effort needed from teachers or instructional designers. The authors report that their iterative prompt engineering produced meaningful contextualizations across four problem sets while preserving problem intent and difficulty, suggesting potential gains in authoring efficiency, but they do not provide student or workload outcome data.
finding.measure: Ability to generate contextualized versions of existing problems in CTAT/TutorShop; authoring workflow feasibility

paper_profiles.title: Pedagogy-driven Evaluation of Generative AI-powered Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (no learner population studied; conceptual/review paper on ITS evaluation)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core problem in AI in education: how to evaluate generative AI-powered intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) in ways that are pedagogically meaningful, reliable, and scalable. The authors argue that current evaluation practices are fragmented, over-rely on self-report or generic natural-language metrics, and do not adequately capture important educational qualities such as metacognitive support, active learning, factual correctness, or contextual relevance.

Rather than testing a specific tutoring intervention with learners, the paper synthesizes prior AIED and learning-science work and proposes a framework for evaluation. It reviews traditional, NLG-based, and pedagogy-oriented evaluation methods, highlights challenges in benchmark creation and metric unification, and proposes three future research directions: evaluation unification, measuring pedagogical guidance, and measuring active learning. The paper is positioned as a roadmap for future ITS evaluation rather than an empirical study of student outcomes.

The paper includes illustrative examples from prior studies and datasets, including existing tutoring benchmarks and a Turkish high-school GPT-4 math-tutoring field experiment cited as motivation. However, it does not report original experimental results on writing, transfer, or durability, nor does it study high school content-area writing classrooms. Its main contribution is conceptual and methodological: defining how the field should evaluate GenAI tutors going forward.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not empirically measure durable skills in learners; instead, it argues that future ITS evaluation should assess metacognition and active learning as proxies for deeper learning and transfer. The paper is conceptual and provides no learner outcome data, effect sizes, or follow-up measures.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses engagement, sentiment, and supportiveness as features that future evaluation systems should measure, but it does not present empirical evidence about student motivation, engagement, or persistence. No original participant data or outcome estimates are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Impact of ChatGPT on ESL students’ academic writing skills: a mixed methods intervention study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed methods intervention study examines whether ChatGPT can improve undergraduate ESL students’ academic writing when used as a formative feedback tool. The paper addresses a practical problem in large writing classes: providing timely, individualized feedback on content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary. The author frames ChatGPT as a dialogic feedback assistant that may help students self-assess and peer-assess their writing more efficiently than traditional instructor-only feedback.

The intervention was conducted in a first-year science and engineering writing course at a private university in India. An intact class was assigned to an experimental group (n=35 analyzed) and a comparison group (n=37 analyzed). Across six hours of instruction over about a month, students practiced process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraphs, with the experimental group using ChatGPT for self- and peer-assessment after a short training session. Data came from pre-test, post-test, delayed post-test writing measures and three focus group discussions.

Quantitatively, the experimental group improved substantially from pre-test to post-test and delayed post-test, and outperformed the comparison group at both post-test and delayed post-test. The author reports a large within-group effect over time (RM ANOVA η²=0.902) and very large pairwise effects for pre/post and pre/delayed post comparisons. Qualitatively, students described ChatGPT as helpful for generating ideas, staying on topic, organizing paragraphs, improving grammatical accuracy, and explaining language errors. Minor concerns included possible dependence on the tool and reduced creativity. The study concludes that, with training and appropriate use, ChatGPT can support academic writing development and sustained gains in similar higher-education ESL settings.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention produced large gains in academic writing performance. In the experimental group (n=37 with complete quantitative data), mean writing scores increased from 12.581 at pre-test to 19.216 at post-test and 20.419 at delayed post-test. The repeated-measures ANOVA showed a significant effect over time (F(2,72)=330.704, p=5.146e-37, η²=0.902), and post-hoc tests showed significant improvements from pre-test to post-test (d=-3.300) and pre-test to delayed post-test (d=-3.898).
finding.measure: Three writing tests with tasks on process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraphs; scored for content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary
finding.study_size: n=72 quantitative completers for within-group analysis (EG n=37, CG n=35)
finding.std_deviation: Pre-test SD=0.833; post-test SD=2.485; delayed post-test SD=2.575

finding.finding_summary: Students reported overwhelmingly positive perceptions of ChatGPT’s impact on their writing, including increased confidence, autonomy, and faster task completion. They also noted that the tool reduced anxiety about asking for help and supported independent work, although a few concerns about dependence and reduced motivation to think were raised. These perceptions came from three focus group discussions with five participating experimental-group students.
finding.measure: Focus group discussion themes on autonomy, collaboration, motivation, and dependence

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examined skills related to organization, idea generation, peer collaboration, and metalinguistic reflection during writing. Students said ChatGPT helped them generate focused ideas, stay on topic, connect main ideas to supporting details, use signposts appropriately, and discuss writing choices with peers. The only negative notes were that the tool could impose a fixed pattern and potentially hinder creativity.
finding.measure: FGD-coded themes and writing-task feedback related to content organization, collaboration, and self/peer assessment
finding.study_size: n=5 FGD participants; intervention group n=37 quantitative completers

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived ChatGPT as saving time and speeding up brainstorming and paragraph completion. The focus group coding explicitly identified faster writing speed and time-saving in brainstorming as positive effects, suggesting improved task efficiency during writing activities. No direct teacher workload measure was reported, but the tool was presented as reducing the time needed to provide individualized feedback in a large class.
finding.measure: FGD-coded themes on faster writing speed and time-saving in brainstorming

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular focus on chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors synthesize existing literature to describe what AI can do in educational settings, including personalized learning, automated feedback, assessment support, student engagement, and administrative assistance.

The paper discusses AI applications across educational levels and functions, using examples such as intelligent tutoring systems, chatbot-based supports, automated grading, and AI-assisted feedback on writing and language learning. It also emphasizes ethical and practical concerns, including bias, privacy, academic integrity, over-reliance on technology, and the need for teacher preparation.

Because the article is a conceptual review, it does not report a participant population, intervention sample, or original empirical effects. Its main conclusion is that AI and ChatGPT have promise for improving instruction and efficiency, but responsible implementation requires attention to ethics, pedagogical alignment, and teacher support.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools and chatbots can reduce teacher and administrator workload by automating grading, scoring, assignment evaluation, and some student support tasks. These claims are synthesized from prior literature rather than tested in this paper; no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / assignment grading and administrative task efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The article describes AI-based writing support tools such as Grammarly, InstaText, QuillBot, and chatbot-supported writing instruction as promising for improving written assignments and feedback processes. However, the paper does not present original data on writing quality, transfer, or durability; it only cites prior studies and examples.
finding.measure: Writing quality / written assignments

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes literature suggesting AI can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and self-regulation through personalized learning and instant feedback. No original measure is reported in this article, and no effect size or sample size is available.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, confidence, self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: The article states that AI may foster critical thinking, creativity, self-reflection, and self-directed learning, but these are presented as anticipated benefits from the literature rather than findings from an empirical study. The paper does not report outcome measures, effect sizes, or sample sizes.
finding.measure: Critical thinking / creativity / self-reflection

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of how artificial intelligence can be integrated into education, with a particular emphasis on higher education. It addresses the challenges created by tools such as ChatGPT, especially concerns about student overreliance, hallucinations, plagiarism, unclear expectations, and uneven educator preparedness. The paper argues that simply banning or fully allowing AI is inadequate; instead, institutions need a middle-ground policy approach that emphasizes transparency, ethical use, and explicit student guidance.

The article is built around a case study from a Swiss University of Applied Sciences and a narrative literature review. The case study describes how the institution developed internal AI guidelines for student writing, including rules about allowed use, disclosure of tools, documentation of prompts and purposes, and critical evaluation of AI outputs. The author then broadens the discussion to suggest workshops, regular updates, dedicated staffing, and AI literacy initiatives as ways to create a durable institutional culture around responsible AI use.

The paper’s pedagogical core is that students should learn three related skills: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It presents AI literacy as foundational knowledge about how AI works, what it can and cannot do, and its ethical and societal implications; prompt engineering as a way to interact more effectively with AI systems; and critical thinking as the essential safeguard against uncritical acceptance of machine-generated outputs. The article is primarily theoretical and practical rather than empirical, and it does not test an intervention or report outcome data on student learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes an institutional response to generative AI at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences: internally developed AI guidelines that permit AI use but require transparency, documentation, and critical reflection. The discussion suggests this middle-ground governance approach may help regulate use and encourage responsible behavior, but no empirical evaluation of policy effects is reported.
finding.measure: institutional policy / AI guidelines adoption and implementation

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and especially critical thinking are essential student competencies for responsible AI use. However, these claims are conceptual and supported by cited literature and the author’s case-based observations rather than by direct outcome measurement in this paper.
finding.measure: conceptual discussion of critical thinking, AI literacy, and prompt-use practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on AI use in academic writing, especially how students can use AI as a 'sparring partner' while avoiding direct copy-paste and maintaining authorship. It does not measure writing quality empirically, but it does provide detailed guidance intended to improve the process and integrity of written assignments.
finding.measure: academic writing practices and documentation requirements

paper_profiles.title: Shaping integrity: why generative artificial intelligence does not have to undermine education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual/opinion paper; no empirical study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion/conceptual article arguing that generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in education does not have to undermine academic integrity if it is used responsibly. Rather than presenting original empirical evidence, the authors synthesize ethical frameworks and learning theories—including deontological ethics, consequentialism, constructivism, and self-determination theory—to make the case that AI can support learning, digital literacy, and authentic engagement.

The paper discusses classroom examples across history, language arts, science, and business to illustrate how AI tools might be used for interactive timelines, writing feedback, virtual labs, collaborative projects, and personalized learning. It emphasizes that educators should set clear boundaries, teach ethical use, and design assessments that prioritize authentic learning, transparency, and critical thinking.

Because the article is not an intervention study and includes no original sample, measures, or effect estimates, it does not provide empirical evidence on student outcomes such as writing quality, transfer, or durability. Its main contribution is a normative and practical framework for responsible AI integration, along with recommendations for educator professional development, policy, and iterative evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report an empirical intervention or measured effect on writing or reading outcomes. It discusses AI-assisted writing as a conceptual example and cites prior work, but provides no original data on writing quality, organization, argumentation, transfer, or durability.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article argues conceptually that responsible GAI use may foster autonomy, competence, relatedness, and intrinsic motivation, which in turn could support academic integrity. However, these claims are theoretical and illustrated with examples rather than tested in an intervention study.
finding.measure: motivation, autonomy, competence, relatedness (theoretical discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes that GAI can support critical thinking, collaboration, and digital literacy through constructivist and project-based uses, but it does not present empirical evidence. No sample, effect size, or outcome measure is reported for these durable-skill claims.
finding.measure: critical thinking, collaboration, digital literacy (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The authors recommend institutional policies, educator professional development, transparency guidelines, and iterative evaluation for AI integration in schools. These are prescriptive recommendations rather than measured institutional outcomes, so no effect estimates are reported.
finding.measure: policy, governance, professional development (recommendations)

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not specified (broad human learning / K-12 through higher education and beyond)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the opportunities and risks of generative AI for human learning, rather than testing a single intervention. The authors synthesize emerging work on large language models and other generative systems across learning support, learning-resource creation, feedback, and assessment, arguing that GenAI could personalize instruction, diversify materials, speed feedback, and enable more authentic assessment.

The paper’s central question is how GenAI should be integrated into education so that it strengthens, rather than undermines, human cognition, metacognition, creativity, and agency. It highlights concerns about hallucinations, privacy, bias, transparency, overreliance, and disruption of assessment, and calls for AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and methodological rigor in future research.

Because the article is a high-level perspective grounded in prior studies rather than an empirical intervention study, it does not report original sample-based effects for a specific population or classroom context. Its main contribution is framing a future research agenda for human-AI learning across educational levels, including the need for rigorous longitudinal and randomized studies in authentic settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses GenAI for writing and feedback, citing prior studies showing that ChatGPT/LLM feedback can improve secondary students’ text revision and that LLMs can generate fluent, in-depth feedback. However, these are cited examples rather than new findings from this paper, and the article itself does not report original writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Writing feedback, text revision, writing quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can increase learner engagement and satisfaction in some contexts, but also warns that overreliance may reduce learner agency, critical thinking, and creativity. These claims are based on cited prior studies and conceptual synthesis rather than original data in this article.
finding.measure: Engagement, satisfaction, agency

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is the impact of GenAI on durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, problem-solving, and creativity. The paper does not present new effect estimates; instead, it synthesizes evidence and argues that AI assistance may support learning in the short term while potentially weakening these skills through overreliance, with the need for future rigorous studies explicitly emphasized.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, problem-solving, creativity, self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: The article states that GenAI can scale personalized support, create learning resources, and provide timely feedback more efficiently than traditional approaches, potentially reducing educator workload. These are conceptual claims supported by cited examples, not original empirical estimates in this paper.
finding.measure: Feedback efficiency, resource creation efficiency, workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI may disrupt conventional assessment and require institutional changes in evaluation, policy, privacy, and AI literacy. It emphasizes the need for regulations, ethical guidelines, and evidence standards, but does not report original institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Assessment validity, policy/ethics considerations, institutional readiness

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how secondary EFL students prompt ChatGPT and other chatbots while completing a writing task, and what patterns emerge in their prompt-engineering pathways. The authors frame the work as a machine-in-the-loop writing process in which students alternate between prompting a chatbot, evaluating the output, and continuing the draft.

The study uses a qualitative case-study design with four Hong Kong secondary school students completing the same timed blog-entry writing task for the first time with SOTA chatbots. Data came from iPad screen recordings and the completed writing products; the analysis coded 36 prompt turns and traced prompt types, sequencing, and changes over time. Six prompt types were identified (e.g., auto-complete, natural language instruction, question, search-engine style prompts, greetings, and chatbot-suggested prompts), with students showing trial-and-error exploration and increasing sophistication in some pathways.

The main conclusion is not that ChatGPT improved writing quality, but that students used a limited and uneven range of prompting strategies and often learned by experimenting with different prompt forms. The authors argue that students did not appear to know many potentially effective prompting strategies (such as few-shot or chain-of-thought prompting), did not explicitly seek language-support functions like proofreading, and would likely benefit from prompt-engineering instruction in EFL writing classrooms. The paper is primarily descriptive and ends by calling for future research on writing products, output evaluation, and broader prompt-engineering development.

finding.finding_summary: The study did not test whether ChatGPT improved students’ writing quality; instead, it descriptively examined how four secondary EFL students used prompts while composing blog entries. The only literacy-related evidence is that students completed a writing task and produced written blog entries, but no comparison, rubric score, or pre/post change in writing quality was reported.
finding.measure: Writing task completion / written blog entry quality not systematically assessed

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines prompt engineering as a skill involving trial-and-error, sequencing, and refinement of prompts, which the authors interpret as students learning more sophisticated prompting strategies over time. Evidence is qualitative and case-based only: across 36 coded turns from n=4 students, some pathways showed greater sophistication, minor word modifications, and more strategic use of prompt types, while others remained limited or exploratory.
finding.measure: Prompt engineering pathway quality, prompt type variety, sequencing, and refinement

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports how many turns students needed to complete the task and suggests that prompt engineering may help students work more effectively with chatbots, but it does not measure productivity gains, time savings, or workload changes against a baseline. Students completed the writing task in 5 to 12 turns, but no efficiency outcome was compared across conditions or linked to performance.
finding.measure: Number of prompt turns to complete the task

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE), a high-stakes exam spanning multiple subjects and including both multiple-choice and literature essay components. The motivation is to understand the potential of large language models as educational support tools and to benchmark them on an authentic high-school assessment context.

The authors evaluate ChatGPT in a zero-shot setup using the VNHSGE dataset, which includes 30 literature essays and 1,700 multiple-choice questions from subjects such as mathematics, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, civic education, and literature. Responses were graded against human expert ground truth, with subject scores computed on a 10-point scale and combined according to the Vietnamese graduation scoring formula. No instructional intervention was implemented with students; the study is a direct model-performance evaluation.

Results show that ChatGPT generally achieved passing-level performance, with average subject scores ranging from 4.8 to 7.92 and combined graduation scores around 6.3 to 6.9 across years 2019-2023, indicating it could pass the exam under the paper’s assumed scoring conditions. The model performed especially well in English and literature, and less well in chemistry, physics, and some higher-order problem-solving or image/chart-based geography items. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has promise as an educational support tool, but its performance remains uneven and should be tested further on more complex and context-dependent exam questions.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT performed strongly on the literature/writing component of the VNHSGE, with reported scores ranging from 5.63 to 7.5 across 2019-2023 and an average score of 6.8 on the 10-point scale. The paper states that on the literature test case, ChatGPT scored higher than the GRE Writing benchmark and generally higher than the majority of Vietnamese students, suggesting solid performance on text-based composition/comprehension tasks.
finding.measure: Literature exam score / essay performance on VNHSGE literature component

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s mathematics performance was weaker than its language performance, with scores ranging from 5.2 to 6.6 from 2019-2023 and an average score of 5.88 on the 10-point scale. The authors report that these results were lower than the majority of Vietnamese students, indicating that the model was only moderately successful on math content and did not match typical student performance.
finding.measure: Mathematics exam score on VNHSGE

finding.finding_summary: Performance on science subjects varied by domain. ChatGPT scored relatively well in biology (5.25-6.0, average 5.8) and physics (5.75-6.5, average 6.1), but the paper reports lower performance in chemistry (4.0-6.25, average 4.8), with chemistry described as its lowest subject overall. The authors also note that ChatGPT often scored below the majority of Vietnamese students in physics and chemistry, while biology results were comparatively stronger.
finding.measure: Physics, chemistry, and biology VNHSGE scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates non-language, non-STEM school subjects including history, geography, and civic education. ChatGPT’s history scores ranged from 4.25 to 7.75 (average 5.65) and were often above the majority of Vietnamese students, while geography ranged from 5.0 to 7.5 (average 6.15) and civic education from 6.0 to 8.25 (average 7.05), though both geography and civic education were still generally below the majority of students in the authors’ comparisons. Geography performance was constrained by the model’s inability to interpret images/charts in atlas-based items.
finding.measure: History, geography, and civic education exam scores on VNHSGE

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret performance differences as reflecting analytical and higher-order thinking demands, especially in mathematics, physics, civic education, and geography. They specifically attribute weaker performance in some subjects to limitations in critical thinking, problem solving, and visual analysis, but these constructs are inferred from exam performance rather than directly measured with a durable-skills instrument.
finding.measure: Performance on exam items requiring analysis, problem solving, and interpretation

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that ChatGPT could pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination, with combined graduation scores ranging from 6.35 to 6.94 for the natural/social subject combinations across 2019-2023. The authors argue this implies potential educational utility for exam preparation and broader institutional use, though they also caution that further research is needed before practical adoption.
finding.measure: Computed graduation score (GASN/GASS) using VNHSGE scoring formula

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper examines ChatGPT’s outputs in response to a set of science-education prompts and reflects on its potential uses for educators and researchers. The author asks three questions: how ChatGPT answers science education questions, how educators might use ChatGPT to generate teaching resources, and how ChatGPT itself can function as a research tool. The study uses a self-study methodology rather than a student outcome trial, so the unit of analysis is the AI-generated text and the author’s interpretation of it.

The paper shows that ChatGPT often produces responses that align with established science education themes, such as inquiry-based learning, real-world connections, differentiation, collaboration, and formative assessment. It also demonstrates that ChatGPT can rapidly generate a unit plan, rubric, and quiz for a Year 7 renewable/non-renewable energy topic, which the author views as potentially useful starting points for teachers. However, the paper repeatedly stresses that the outputs are generic, may lack evidence or context sensitivity, and should be critically evaluated and revised by educators.

The main conclusions are cautious and practical. ChatGPT may help educators brainstorm lesson ideas, scaffold writing, or streamline editing, but it is not a substitute for teacher expertise, evidence-based pedagogy, or contextual judgment. The author also raises concerns about hallucinated citations, bias, authorship, transparency, and broader ethical issues around generative AI in education and research.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT produced responses that largely aligned with established science education themes, including inquiry-based learning, real-world connections, and assessment for learning. The paper is exploratory and non-experimental, so it does not estimate student achievement effects; instead, it qualitatively judges the AI outputs as useful but often generic and lacking evidence grounding.
finding.measure: Quality and content of ChatGPT-generated science education responses; alignment with science education literature

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT successfully generated a Year 7 science unit on renewable and non-renewable energy sources, a rubric, and a multiple-choice quiz with answer key. The author judged these outputs to be workable starting points for curriculum materials, though they required refinement and contextual adaptation.
finding.measure: Generated instructional materials (unit plan, rubric, quiz) for Year 7 renewable and non-renewable energy

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT may support learner engagement and reduce barriers such as writer’s block by serving as a learning scaffold. These claims are speculative and based on author reflection rather than direct measurement of student engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Author reflection on potential student engagement and support functions of ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support critical thinking when used as a scaffold, but it can also undermine it if students accept AI-generated text uncritically. The author emphasizes the need for educators to model responsible use, encourage critique of AI outputs, and retain human judgment in pedagogical decisions.
finding.measure: Critical evaluation of ChatGPT outputs; reflection on critical thinking and responsible use

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was used as an editing aid and was described as helpful for improving phrasing, flow, and word choice during writing. The paper also suggests it may help teachers quickly generate lesson ideas, rubrics, and quizzes, potentially reducing preparation time, though no workload metric was measured.
finding.measure: Author-reported editing assistance and content-generation utility

paper_profiles.title: Automated feedback and writing: a multi-level meta-analysis of effects on students’ performance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether automated writing evaluation (AWE) feedback improves students’ writing performance and whether effects differ by learner, intervention, and outcome characteristics. The motivation is that writing instruction and individualized feedback are time-intensive for teachers, making AI-supported automated feedback an appealing tool for formative assessment.

The authors conducted a multi-level meta-analysis of 20 experimental or quasi-experimental studies published in scholarly journals, yielding 84 effect sizes from 2,828 learners. Across studies, automated feedback produced a medium positive effect on writing performance overall (g = 0.55 with pre-test adjustment; 95% CI 0.19 to 0.91). A robustness check without pre-test values produced a larger overall effect (g = 0.77), but this did not differ significantly from the main estimate.

Moderator analyses suggested meaningful descriptive differences, though none of the subgroup contrasts were statistically significant. Longer interventions, post-test outcomes, transfer/learning tasks, and language-focused outcomes tended to show stronger effects than short interventions, follow-up outcomes, and revision/performance tasks. The authors conclude that AWE is beneficial on average, but its impact varies and should not be treated as a one-size-fits-all intervention; they recommend more primary studies that report intervention details and compare feedback types.

finding.finding_summary: Across 84 effect sizes from 20 studies (N=2,828), automated feedback improved students’ writing performance with a medium overall effect of g=0.55 (SE=0.17, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.91) in the main analysis that adjusted for pre-test performance. A robustness check using post-test only produced a larger effect (g=0.77, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.18), but this did not significantly differ from the main estimate.
finding.measure: Writing performance (holistic and analytic writing outcomes on revision or transfer tasks)

paper_profiles.title: The relationship between student interaction with generative artificial intelligence and learning achievement: serial mediating roles of self-efficacy and cognitive engagement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether students’ interaction with generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is associated with learning achievement, and whether that relationship operates through self-efficacy and cognitive engagement. The authors motivate the study by arguing that GAI tools such as ChatGPT offer personalization, real-time interactivity, and instant feedback, but note that there has been limited empirical evidence on how these tools relate to academic outcomes.

Using two-wave online survey data from 389 Chinese undergraduates, the study measures student–GAI interaction, self-efficacy, cognitive engagement, and learning achievement (defined as the change in GPA from 2022 to 2023). The analysis uses regression, bootstrap mediation testing, and propensity score matching to address self-selection bias. Results show a positive association between student–GAI interaction and learning achievement, with partial mediation through self-efficacy and cognitive engagement, including a serial mediation path from interaction to self-efficacy to cognitive engagement to achievement.

The paper concludes that greater interaction with GAI is associated with higher achievement, and that cognitive engagement is the stronger mediator relative to self-efficacy. It recommends that educators help students use GAI in structured, goal-oriented, and reflective ways that promote deeper thinking and confidence, rather than simply banning these tools. The study also suggests that instructional design should leverage GAI to support challenging tasks, feedback, and exploration.

finding.finding_summary: Student–GAI interaction was positively associated with learning achievement among 389 undergraduates. In the main regression, the interaction coefficient predicting GPA change was β=0.146 (p<0.01), and the association remained positive though smaller after adding mediators (β=0.073, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Change in academic-year GPA (2023 GPA minus 2022 GPA, z-standardized)

finding.finding_summary: Student–GAI interaction was associated with higher self-efficacy, and self-efficacy in turn predicted higher learning achievement. The indirect effect through self-efficacy was significant (0.0154; 95% bootstrap CI 0.0029 to 0.0312), and the propensity-score-matched treatment effect on self-efficacy was also positive (ATT=0.1703, t=2.03).
finding.measure: Self-efficacy scale (10-item Likert scale); bootstrap indirect effect; PSM ATT

finding.finding_summary: Student–GAI interaction was associated with higher cognitive engagement, and cognitive engagement strongly predicted learning achievement. The indirect effect through cognitive engagement was significant (0.0463; 95% bootstrap CI 0.0237 to 0.0736), and the PSM analysis showed a positive treatment effect on cognitive engagement (ATT=0.2170, t=2.72).
finding.measure: Cognitive engagement scale (Likert scale); bootstrap indirect effect; PSM ATT

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence (AI)-integrated educational applications and college students’ creativity and academic emotions: students and teachers’ perceptions and attitudes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examines how AI-integrated educational applications influence undergraduate students’ creativity and academic emotions, from both student and teacher perspectives. The authors frame the issue as a tension between AI’s potential to support learning through personalization, feedback, and engagement, and its potential to constrain creativity, increase anxiety, and reduce human connection.

In the qualitative phase, the researchers interviewed 15 undergraduate students and 8 teachers at Wenzhou University using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis. In the quantitative phase, they administered a Likert-scale survey to 120 students and 30 teachers to gauge attitudes toward AI applications’ constraints and merits. The AI tools discussed include adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring systems, NLP-based applications, AI-enhanced collaborative platforms, and predictive analytics, but the paper does not isolate effects by tool type or implementation condition in an experimental way.

Across both phases, participants reported a dual-edged impact: AI applications can stimulate creativity, increase engagement, provide personalized feedback, support emotional well-being, facilitate collaboration, and broaden access to learning resources. At the same time, they can impose rigid structures that constrain creative thinking, create emotional disengagement, heighten performance anxiety, cause technical frustration, encourage over-reliance, worsen inequities through the digital divide, and raise ethical concerns. The study concludes that AI can be beneficial in higher education, but implementation should be thoughtful and balanced to avoid undermining creativity and academic emotions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that AI-integrated educational applications can stimulate creativity by introducing new ideas and problem-solving techniques, but can also constrain creativity when they impose rigid frameworks. In the quantitative survey, 40% of teachers and 40% of students agreed that AI stimulates creativity, while 25% of teachers and 20% of students strongly agreed; however, 25% of teachers and 25% of students agreed that AI applications constrain creativity, with an additional 15% strongly agreeing in both groups.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creativity constraints and stimulated creativity from interviews and Likert-scale survey responses
finding.study_size: n=23 qualitative; n=150 quantitative (120 students, 30 teachers)

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses centrally on academic emotions, especially emotional disengagement, anxiety, motivation, enjoyment, and emotional resilience. Participants reported that AI can reduce anxiety through constant availability and gamified elements, but can also increase emotional disengagement, performance anxiety, and frustration when interactions feel repetitive or overly evaluative. Survey responses showed substantial agreement that AI both supports emotions and creates emotional strain, indicating a clearly mixed pattern.
finding.measure: Academic emotions and related attitudes (anxiety, engagement, emotional support, resilience) via interviews and Likert-scale survey items
finding.study_size: n=23 qualitative; n=150 quantitative (120 students, 30 teachers)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly discusses durable skills, especially critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and self-initiative. AI was described as supporting collaborative creativity and innovative problem-solving, but also as encouraging over-reliance that could reduce independent thinking and self-initiative. Survey results reflected this dual pattern: 35% of teachers and 30% of students agreed that over-reliance on AI is a concern, while 35% of teachers and 35% of students agreed that AI facilitates collaborative creativity.
finding.measure: Perceptions of collaboration, critical thinking/self-initiative, and creative problem-solving
finding.study_size: n=23 qualitative; n=150 quantitative (120 students, 30 teachers)

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceived a GenAI-powered creative mathematical writing activity in classroom settings. The central question is not whether the tool improves test scores, but how participants experienced the learning process, what benefits they perceived, and what challenges emerged when using generative AI to support math story writing.

The study implemented a three-step learning design—Ask, Represent, Transform—across six 5th-grade classrooms in two U.S. schools, involving 79 students and 6 teachers. Students used a system built with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to draft, revise, and illustrate culturally relevant math stories, then evaluated the AI-generated outputs with a checklist. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations, analyzed thematically.

Findings indicate that participants perceived several benefits, including enhanced creativity, deeper mathematical understanding, improved AI literacy, and increased interest, curiosity, and ownership in learning. At the same time, they identified challenges such as students’ limited critical evaluation of AI output, difficulty generating coherent stories, AI systems being perceived as "too perfect," insufficient pedagogical feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connection features, and limited communication options. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI can support creative mathematics learning, but only when instructional design and system features deliberately support revision, feedback, autonomy, accessibility, and social interaction.

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing helped students understand mathematical problems, represent mathematical ideas, and uncover misconceptions. The study used qualitative evidence from 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers across six classrooms; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of mathematical understanding, problem representation, and misconception detection during story-based math writing
