finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied creative mathematical writing, a writing-based academic task, and found that students and teachers perceived GenAI as supporting story drafting, originality, and revision in the writing process. Across interviews and observations with 79 students and 6 teachers, participants described the tool as helping students create and improve math stories, though no quantitative outcome data were reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creative mathematical writing quality, drafting, and revision with GenAI

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that the GenAI activity increased interest, curiosity, and ownership in math learning. Participants described the activity as fun and engaging, and teachers noted stronger attention and motivation; the evidence is qualitative from 79 students and 6 teachers.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning

finding.finding_summary: The study found gains in AI literacy and prompting behavior, but also reported weaknesses in students’ critical evaluation and story-generation competence. Students learned to make more specific prompts and recognized AI strengths and weaknesses, yet some struggled to revise imperfect AI outputs or formulate coherent stories; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI-generated content

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how secondary school EFL students prompt ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots while completing a writing task for the first time. The authors ask what kinds of prompt content students use and what patterns emerge across students’ prompt engineering pathways, with a particular interest in the trial-and-error process of learning to collaborate with generative AI in writing.

The study uses a qualitative case-study design with four Hong Kong secondary school students in a form one English class. Students completed a timed blog-writing task in class using iPads and the POE app, which included ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly. The authors analyzed screen recordings and the students’ written products, coding 36 usable prompt turns into categories such as auto-complete, natural language instruction, questions, greetings, search-engine style prompts, and chatbot-suggested follow-up prompts.

The main finding is that students used a limited and uneven range of prompting strategies, typically learning through trial and error rather than through prior instruction. Some pathways appeared more sophisticated than others, especially when students combined input exemplars with natural language instructions and questions, reused successful prompt structures, or carried ideas forward across turns and chatbots. The paper concludes that prompt engineering education would likely help EFL students move beyond ad hoc experimentation and use chatbots more effectively for writing support.

finding.finding_summary: The study does not test writing quality with a pre/post design, but it provides qualitative evidence that students used ChatGPT and other chatbots to support a writing task through trial-and-error prompting. Across 36 coded turns from four students, the authors found six distinct prompt types and noted that more sophisticated pathways combined input exemplars with natural language instruction and questions, suggesting potential support for writing development, but the paper does not report effect sizes on writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Prompt types and sequencing during an EFL blog-writing task; completed blog entries as contextual evidence

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines prompt engineering as a form of strategic, iterative problem solving and metacognitive regulation while completing a writing task. Students explored different prompt types, revised prompts by making minor changes, and sometimes reused or extended prior prompts across chatbots, indicating developing prompt sophistication; however, the study is descriptive and does not quantify gains in critical thinking or metacognition.
finding.measure: Prompt engineering pathways, including prompt variety, sequencing, and revisions across turns/chatbots

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret students’ behavior as trial-and-error learning, with some pathways reflecting exploration, persistence, and adaptation while completing a timed task. The paper suggests that classroom support and prompt-engineering education could help students become more confident and effective users, but it does not directly measure motivation, engagement, or self-efficacy.
finding.measure: Observed trial-and-error prompting behavior and task completion during a timed classroom activity

paper_profiles.title: Exploring EFL Secondary Students’ AI-generated Text Editing While Composition Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how Hong Kong EFL secondary students edit AI-generated text while completing an expository writing task. The authors focus on machine-in-the-loop writing: how students use generative AI chatbots, Google Docs suggestions, and Apple iOS predictive text during drafting and revision, and whether students passively accept AI output or actively manipulate it.

The study used an exploratory mixed-methods design with screen recordings from 29 secondary students across seven Hong Kong schools after an AI-assisted writing workshop. Students received instruction on process-based or genre-based writing, prompt engineering, and then completed a 500-word expository writing task using POE chatbots and Google Docs. The researchers content-analyzed 25 usable recordings (10 hours total) to identify edit types and used thematic analysis plus multiple case studies to classify editing patterns.

The paper identifies 15 edit types across seven categories, including insertions, deletions, replacements, formatting, and AI-initiated suggestions from iOS and Google Docs. The authors conclude that students’ writing with generative AI is more cognitively complex than simple copy-paste and that some students strategically evaluate and revise AI output. Four broad patterns emerged: planning with top-down drafting and revising, top-down drafting and revising without planning, planning with bottom-up drafting and revising, and bottom-up drafting and revising without planning. The study argues for explicit instruction in AI text-editing strategies, prompt engineering, and maintaining authorial voice and agency.

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that 25 of 29 students produced and edited AI-generated text while composing, and the researchers identified 266 edits across 15 edit types. Students did not merely paste complete AI essays: they frequently inserted AI text (n=68), deleted AI text (n=58), and replaced AI text with human text (n=44), indicating active engagement with writing processes rather than passive acceptance.
finding.measure: Screen-recorded composition writing behaviors and qualitative coding of AI-generated text edits

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that students’ interactions with AI-generated text involve complex cognitive processes such as planning, evaluation, revision, and maintaining agency. Four editing patterns were identified based on planning and drafting orientation, suggesting variation in metacognitive writing strategies rather than simplistic use of AI.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of planning/drafting/revision patterns in screen recordings

finding.finding_summary: The discussion concludes that many students maintained agency over the machine-in-the-loop writing process and actively evaluated AI output, rather than passively consuming it. However, the study does not directly measure motivation or self-efficacy, so this is an indirect finding about agency and persistence in writing with AI.
finding.measure: Observed agency and active evaluation during AI-assisted writing

paper_profiles.title: Exploring EFL Students’ Prompt Engineering in Human-AI Story Writing: An Activity Theory Perspective
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study investigates how English as a foreign language (EFL) secondary school students decide when and why to prompt generative AI tools during short story writing. Using Activity Theory, the authors ask what conditions or purposes drive students’ prompt engineering and what shared qualities characterize the activity systems in which those prompting decisions occur.

The study was conducted with 67 Hong Kong secondary school students during the 2022–23 academic year. Students completed two workshops: first, they built their own simple generative-AI story tools using Python and open-source language models on Hugging Face; second, they used those tools to write short stories and then reflected on how they chose what text to prompt into the AI. Data included the students’ tools, stories, and open-ended reflections. The authors used thematic analysis for the prompting purposes and matrix comparisons for activity-system qualities such as school achievement level, tool sophistication, story completeness, number of AI words, and overall writing quality.

The analysis identified three main prompting purposes: unawareness of rules, overcoming writer’s block, and developing/expanding/improving the story. Students prompting to overcome writer’s block or develop their stories tended to use more sophisticated tools and produce higher-quality writing than students who reported no clear prompting rules. The paper concludes that teachers should provide tailored instruction and scaffolded guidance for prompt engineering, especially for students who are unsure when or how to prompt AI, and that NLG tool designers should build in differentiated prompt instructions for users at different stages of story development.

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on EFL story writing with generative AI and reports that students’ prompting purposes related to writing development, idea generation, and elaboration. Among 34 analyzed stories, students who prompted to overcome writer’s block or to develop/improve stories tended to produce higher-quality writing and more complete stories than students who reported unawareness of rules, but the paper does not report inferential statistics or a causal effect size.
finding.measure: Short story quality rubric scores, story completeness, and AI-word usage in student-written stories
finding.study_size: n=67 participants; n=34 stories analyzed for object variables

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant, can support K-12 students’ writing through formative feedback. The core question is not whether the system improves test scores in a controlled experiment, but how students and teachers experience AI feedback when it is aligned with classroom rubrics, teacher materials, and subject-specific writing tasks.

The study piloted CyberScholar in four public schools in the United States: three high schools and one middle school in the Midwest and Northwest. A total of 121 students and 4 teachers participated in implementation, observations, surveys, and interviews, though only 54 students and 3 teachers completed the post-survey and 8 students plus 1 teacher were interviewed. The tool was configured through retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering to incorporate teacher rubrics, instructional materials, and writing prompts so that feedback matched classroom expectations.

Findings from thematic qualitative analysis suggest that students viewed CyberScholar as helpful because it gave detailed and specific feedback, enabled interactive follow-up questions in some settings, supported revision, and made rubric criteria more visible. Students also reported perceived improvements in grammar, transitions, wording, and overall writing quality. At the same time, some students found the star ratings inconsistent across repeated submissions, indicating that the tool’s scoring could be unstable. Overall, the paper concludes that CyberScholar has potential as a complement to teacher feedback, especially when AI feedback is detailed, rubric-aligned, and embedded in iterative revision routines.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students perceived CyberScholar as supportive of writing development through detailed, specific, and rubric-aligned feedback. Across 121 students, 36 said they would like to use the tool again, and several examples suggested improved revision quality, grammar, transitions, and clarity after AI feedback; however, these were qualitative perceptions rather than controlled score gains.
finding.measure: Student surveys, interviews, and observed revisions of writing assignments; rubric-based feedback and repeated draft submissions
finding.study_size: n=121 students, n=4 teachers (post-survey n=54 students, n=3 teachers; interviews n=8 students, n=1 teacher)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that CyberScholar promoted metacognition and self-regulation by helping students reflect on writing quality, revise iteratively, and ask follow-up questions to clarify feedback. Students described using the tool to identify weaknesses, refine drafts, and compare versions, suggesting increased reflective engagement during revision, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Interview and survey comments about revision, clarification-seeking, and perceived writing improvement

finding.finding_summary: Students often described CyberScholar as helpful, motivating, and time-saving, which suggests positive effects on engagement and persistence during writing tasks. The tool’s interactive nature and immediate feedback were perceived as making revision more engaging, though some students were uncertain because of inconsistent ratings on repeated submissions.
finding.measure: Student post-survey responses and interviews on usefulness, motivation, and engagement with writing revisions

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that CyberScholar could improve instructional efficiency by providing quick, detailed formative feedback and reducing some of the burden of first-pass commenting. Students also described the system as faster and easier to work with than peer or self-analysis, and the discussion frames the tool as supporting teachers by shifting them toward managing AI feedback loops rather than providing all feedback themselves.
finding.measure: Teacher and student perceptions of speed, convenience, and workload; classroom observations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that a teacher-aligned GenAI feedback system may help address equity and access issues by providing scalable formative support across diverse school contexts, including underserved and mid-poverty schools. This is presented as a conceptual and implementation-level contribution rather than an evaluated institutional outcome, so no quantitative institutional effect was reported.
finding.measure: Implementation observations and contextual discussion of diverse school settings, equity, and scalability

paper_profiles.title: Approaching the Limits to EFL Writing Enhancement with AI-generated Text and Diverse Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks how secondary school EFL students combine their own writing with AI-generated text when composing a feature article, and whether particular interaction patterns are associated with better writing quality. The authors focus on machine-in-the-loop writing with generative AI chatbots, especially ChatGPT-style tools, and investigate the relationship between the amount/structure of AI-generated text and human-rated writing scores.

The sample included 59 Hong Kong secondary school students from seven schools with differing academic achievement levels. Students attended a workshop on writing with ChatGPT support, learned prompt engineering and an explicit writing approach, then completed a feature-article task using their own words plus at least one AI chatbot. The paper analyzes the compositions with content analysis, multiple linear regression, and cluster analysis, using content, language, organization, and total score as outcomes.

The main finding is that writing quality was driven primarily by overall word volume rather than by how AI text was chunked or integrated. Across all students, both AI words and human words were positively associated with scores, but the chunk-level variables were not significant. When students were separated by school academic banding, high-banding students showed stronger positive associations between word count and scores, while low-banding students did not gain similarly from more AI text and in some cases human revision of AI text was negatively associated with scores. Cluster analysis suggested that the same AI-use pattern could help some students but not others, and that more academically successful students had more flexible ways of leveraging AI, whereas lower-achieving students relied more heavily on AI-generated text and had less effective drafting/revision strategies.

finding.finding_summary: Writing quality depended mainly on total word count rather than on the way AI-generated text was chunked or integrated. Across all 59 compositions, AI words and human words were both positively and significantly associated with content, language, organization, and total scores (partial correlations around 0.39-0.44, p<0.01), but chunk-level variables were generally not significant.
finding.measure: Human-rated feature-article writing scores (Content, Language, Organization, Total) and text features from student compositions

finding.finding_summary: The paper interprets results in terms of students' drafting, revising, and prompt-engineering competence when using AI. High-banding students appeared more capable of independently writing and strategically integrating AI text, while low-banding students appeared less able to revise AI output effectively; these patterns were inferred from regression and cluster analyses rather than directly tested as an instructional intervention.
finding.measure: Interaction patterns with AI-generated text, including chunk length, word counts, and cluster profiles linked to writing performance

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that benefits of AI-assisted writing are unevenly distributed across academic profiles, implying that school-level achievement context and AI literacy shape who benefits from generative AI writing support. Low-banding schools showed weaker model fit and less evidence that more AI text improved scores, suggesting institutional differences in readiness for AI-supported writing pedagogy.
finding.measure: Comparisons across high-banding and low-banding school groups using partial correlations and cluster analysis

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school students (middle and high school)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to teach K-12 students how to use AI chatbots responsibly and effectively for learning, with particular attention to prompting literacy. The authors argue that students need instruction not only on what AI can do, but also on when to use it and how to craft prompts that elicit useful learning support rather than direct answers or low-quality outputs.

To address this, the paper introduces a web-based AI literacy module built around three scenario-based prompt-writing activities. Students interact with a general-purpose LLM chatbot, submit prompts, and receive immediate AI-generated auto-grading plus detailed feedback against scenario-specific rubric dimensions such as relevance, purpose, conciseness, background/context, elaboration, and avoiding explicit direct-answer seeking. The module was deployed in two classroom studies across 11 authentic secondary classrooms in East Asia, with Study 1 (n=111 valid students) evaluating auto-grader accuracy, student prompting performance, confidence changes, and student perceptions, and Study 2 revising the assessment instrument and evaluating item quality.

The main findings were that the AI auto-grader achieved high agreement with human grading on most dimensions, students improved especially in including background/context information in prompts, and self-reported confidence in using AI for learning increased significantly after the activity. However, gains on some prompt dimensions were limited, suggesting dosage and exposure matter, and the authors note the need for more varied and larger-scale studies. Study 2 found that replacing multiple-choice items with true/false and open-ended items improved difficulty and discrimination, although reliability remained only moderate.

finding.finding_summary: The prompting literacy module improved students' ability to construct learning-oriented prompts, especially by embedding background/context information. In Study 1, prompt scores showed a significant gain for the Background dimension from Q1 to Q3 (p = .039), and overall prompt-writing practice plus feedback was associated with higher-quality prompts across repeated attempts.
finding.measure: Prompt-writing rubric scores for scenario-based AI prompts (Relevance, Purpose, Conciseness, Background, Elaboration, No Direct Answer)
finding.study_size: n=111 valid students in Study 1; 483 unique prompts; 98 students for pre/post test

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased confidence in using AI for learning after the module. Self-reported confidence increased by 10.4% on average, with a significant Wilcoxon test result (p < .001), indicating the activity improved students' perceived readiness to use AI appropriately for learning.
finding.measure: 5-point Likert self-report confidence item ('I know how to use AI to help me learn')
finding.study_size: n=111 valid students in Study 1; 98 students completed pre- and post-test comparisons

finding.finding_summary: The intervention supported students' metacognitive and prompting skills, including understanding how to ask better questions and when not to request direct answers. Survey responses indicated students learned prompting strategies such as adding context and avoiding asking AI to solve tasks outright, suggesting gains in strategic thinking about AI use.
finding.measure: Open-ended self-reflection survey responses; prompt rubric performance
finding.study_size: n=131 students provided self-reflection responses; n=111 valid students in main study

finding.finding_summary: The AI-based auto-grader was able to evaluate student prompts with generally high accuracy, suggesting the approach could reduce grading burden and provide immediate feedback at scale. Average auto-grading accuracy across dimensions was 0.92, with several dimensions above 0.90, though Purpose and No Direct Answer were weaker.
finding.measure: AI auto-grader accuracy against human ratings

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the module and assessment pipeline are scalable and useful for classroom implementation, and that iterative classroom data can inform better assessment design. Study 2 improved item quality by replacing MCQs with TF and open-ended items; 60% of OE and 30% of TF items met difficulty/discrimination criteria, compared with none of the MCQs.
finding.measure: Assessment item difficulty, discrimination index, and Cronbach's alpha
finding.study_size: Two classroom studies; Study 1 n=111 valid students; Study 2 similar population

finding.finding_summary: The module improved prompting literacy in the context of AI use for learning across biology, geography, and math scenarios, but the paper's strongest evidence is about learning to use AI as a tool rather than mastery of domain content. Students also showed initial baseline knowledge but varied ability to write effective prompts, and the revised assessment better captured these learning objectives.
finding.measure: Scenario-based prompting literacy assessments and student prompt quality
finding.study_size: n=111 valid students; Study 2 similar classroom sample

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not a human-subject study; discusses K-12, tertiary, and professional education contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT/GPT-3-style systems, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes emerging examples and theoretical considerations to argue that LLMs may support learning, teaching, assessment, and educational content creation while also introducing risks related to bias, privacy, copyright, integrity, overreliance, and unequal access.

The paper discusses potential uses across learner and teacher perspectives, including personalized feedback, tutoring, lesson planning, automated quiz and question generation, writing support, and adaptive assistance in collaborative or remote learning. It also reviews a small set of early research examples on chatbot-like systems, automated feedback, and assessment support, but these are presented as illustrative prior work rather than as a systematic empirical comparison of implementation conditions.

Because the paper is a conceptual/position piece, it does not report original sample-based results or effect sizes. Its main conclusion is that LLMs have promise in education if they are integrated with human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, ethical safeguards, and careful attention to transparency, fairness, sustainability, and access.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by helping with lesson planning, feedback generation, automated grading support, quiz creation, and drafting educational materials. These claims are supported by cited examples rather than original experiments; no study-level effect sizes or samples are reported in the paper itself.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and content-generation efficiency (conceptual/reviewed examples)

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights potential benefits for writing and reading-related learning, including syntactic and grammatical correction, style improvement, summaries, outlines, and reading-comprehension support. These are presented as opportunities and examples from prior work, not as directly tested outcomes in this position paper.
finding.measure: Writing quality, reading comprehension support, summaries, outlines, grammar/style assistance

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact-checking when used as complementary tools, but may weaken these skills if learners rely on them too heavily. No original empirical estimate is reported; the discussion is theoretical and based on cited examples and risk analysis.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, fact-checking, and independent inquiry (conceptual)

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims LLM-based tools may improve student engagement, curiosity, and participation, and reduce language-learning anxiety in some contexts. These effects are described as plausible or supported by cited prior studies, but the position paper does not present new empirical data.
finding.measure: Engagement, curiosity, participation, and language-learning anxiety (conceptual/reviewed examples)

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is institutional implications: governance, privacy, copyright, fairness, sustainability, access, and the need for human oversight and policy. The paper does not provide empirical estimates, but it strongly argues that successful adoption depends on institutional rules, transparent practices, and educator training.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy, fairness, access, and institutional readiness (conceptual)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is an early peer-reviewed discussion of ChatGPT and higher education. It asks what ChatGPT is, how it works, what its strengths and limitations are, and what its emergence may mean for learning, teaching, and assessment. The paper is primarily a desktop analysis and literature review, supplemented by the authors’ informal testing of ChatGPT on a small set of prompts.

The paper situates ChatGPT within the broader history of artificial intelligence in education, especially teacher-facing and student-facing tools such as automated essay scoring, automated written corrective feedback, Grammarly, and Wordtune. It argues that ChatGPT resembles earlier AI writing tools in some respects, but is more capable of generating fluent, human-like text, raising concerns about academic integrity and the viability of conventional essay assessments.

The article’s central conclusion is that ChatGPT is not a reliable source of factual truth or deep reasoning, but it is likely to become an important educational technology. The authors recommend that higher education instructors and institutions adapt assessments, use flipped and in-class tasks, and treat AI as a tool to be managed and integrated rather than simply banned. The paper is conceptual rather than empirical, so it does not provide strong causal evidence about learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can generate fluent prose, conceptual explanations, and short essays quickly, but its writing is often generic, descriptive, shallow, and sometimes inaccurate. In the authors’ informal prompt tests, ChatGPT produced an approximately 500-word essay in under 120 seconds for a 2000-word request, but it lacked depth and reliable citations; in a Chinese writing task, the output was grammatically poor and illogical.
finding.measure: Informal prompt-based writing tasks and qualitative evaluation of generated text quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames ChatGPT as inadequate for higher-order writing demands such as critical and analytical thinking. In the authors’ testing, the model could explain concepts and draft text, but it struggled with tasks requiring argument quality, evidence use, and sophisticated reasoning, which the authors interpret as a limitation for durable-skill development.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of task performance on prompts requiring critical/analytical writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT can improve efficiency by generating explanations, drafting text, answering questions, and reducing some writing and feedback burdens for teachers and students. The authors describe responses appearing within roughly 60-120 seconds and argue that AI writing tools can save time, support drafting, and help automate some assessment-related and feedback-related tasks.
finding.measure: Qualitative observations of response speed and workflow utility

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that ChatGPT is likely to disrupt assessment policies, academic integrity practices, and institutional responses to AI use. It recommends that institutions revise assessment design, consider policies for appropriate use, and prepare for broader adoption rather than relying on plagiarism detection alone, but these are conceptual recommendations rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of assessment and institutional policy implications

paper_profiles.title: Shaping integrity: why generative artificial intelligence does not have to undermine education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper argues that generative artificial intelligence (GAI) does not inherently undermine academic integrity and can instead support learning when used responsibly. The authors frame the issue as an ethical and pedagogical one: rather than treating AI as a shortcut for completing assignments, educators should integrate it in ways that promote authentic learning, digital literacy, and student agency.

The paper does not report a primary empirical study; instead, it synthesizes ethical frameworks (e.g., deontological ethics, consequentialism), learning theories (constructivism, self-determination theory), and prior literature to propose principles for responsible classroom use. Across examples from history, language arts, science, business, and other subjects, the authors argue that AI tools can support personalized feedback, interactive exploration, collaboration, and reflection, which may strengthen motivation, competence, and integrity. They also emphasize policy, transparency, educator professional development, and iterative evaluation as conditions for responsible implementation.

Although the paper is relevant to high school practice, it is not a comparison of implementation moderators and does not provide experimental evidence on teacher mediation, prompt training, feedback specificity, revision stage, dosage, or differences among AI tool types. Its contributions are conceptual and normative rather than empirical.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that responsible use of GAI can foster intrinsic motivation by supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness, which in turn may reduce academic dishonesty. No new empirical estimate is reported; the claims are drawn from prior theory and illustrative examples rather than a primary study.
finding.measure: Intrinsic motivation, autonomy/competence/relatedness, academic integrity attitudes

finding.finding_summary: GAI is presented as supporting constructivist learning, critical thinking, reflection, collaboration, and knowledge construction through interactive and personalized tasks. The paper cites prior work but does not report original outcome data, effect sizes, or sample sizes.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reflection, collaboration, knowledge construction

finding.finding_summary: The paper specifically discusses language arts and creative writing uses of GAI, claiming that AI feedback on grammar, tone, and narrative structure can help students improve writing skills. However, this is presented as a conceptual argument with no original empirical results, sample size, or effect estimate.
finding.measure: Writing quality, grammar, tone, narrative structure

finding.finding_summary: The paper recommends transparency, institutional guidelines, educator professional development, and iterative evaluation to govern AI use in schools. These are policy-oriented recommendations rather than measured outcomes, so no quantitative effect is reported.
finding.measure: AI governance, policy guidance, educator training, implementation practices

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a PRISMA-guided systematic review of artificial intelligence (AI) research in higher education published from 2016 through 2022. The authors asked three main questions: where the studies were conducted, who authored them and what academic levels and subject domains were studied, and how AI was being used in higher education.

The review screened 371 records and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles. The studies were mostly conducted in Asia and North America, with China emerging as the leading country in the final set. Undergraduate students were the most common population studied, and language learning, computer science, and engineering were the most frequent subject domains. The first authors were most often affiliated with colleges of education, followed by computer science.

Using grounded coding, the authors identified five major uses of AI in higher education: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistant, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The review concludes that AI in higher education is still being used primarily to improve or automate existing practices, such as grading, feedback, prediction, and personalized support, while newer possibilities remain underexplored. The paper does not test a single intervention or estimate causal effects; instead, it maps trends and gaps in the field and calls for more work on tools such as ChatGPT, graduate education, and underrepresented regions and disciplines.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI was frequently used for writing, reading, and vocabulary-related tasks in higher education, especially within language learning. The review reports that automatic assessment and AI feedback were used to improve academic writing skills, but it does not synthesize a single pooled effect size across studies.
finding.measure: Writing, reading, and vocabulary outcomes; automated writing assessment/feedback
finding.study_size: 138 studies reviewed; several literacy-focused primary studies cited, exact pooled n not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies studies using AI to support student persistence, emotion control, and engagement, including systems that provided immediate answers, personalized feedback, and support for learners' emotions and self-regulation. One example discussed an AI change agent organized around goal initiation, goal formation, action control, and emotion control, but the review does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Persistence, emotion control, engagement, self-regulated learning
finding.study_size: 138 studies reviewed; exact n for social-emotional studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review describes AI uses that supported higher-order thinking, collaboration, and learning strategies, including online collaborative reflection, goal setting, and adaptive guidance. These findings suggest AI often supported durable skills as part of broader learning environments, though the paper provides no synthesized quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking, collaborative reflection, goal setting, adaptive learning support
finding.study_size: 138 studies reviewed; exact n for durable-skill studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the review was that AI improved operational efficiency by reducing instructor grading time, generating test questions, providing immediate feedback, and helping manage student data. The authors note that assessment/evaluation was the most common use of AI and that AI also supported learning analytics, curriculum sequencing, and instructional design, but the review does not report pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: Instructor workload, grading time, question generation, learning analytics, curriculum sequencing, instructional design
finding.study_size: 138 studies reviewed; 26 studies in automatic assessment and 19 studies in managing student learning

finding.finding_summary: The review found AI was used for institutional purposes such as predicting dropout risk, admissions, and managing large student datasets, with 19 studies focused on managing student learning and 12 studies on prediction-related managerial uses. These uses suggest AI can inform institutional decision-making and student support systems, but the paper does not estimate causal or comparative institutional effects.
finding.measure: Dropout prediction, admissions, student data management, institutional analytics
finding.study_size: 138 studies reviewed; managerial subset includes 19 studies on student learning management and 12 prediction studies on managerial topics

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (literature review; education broadly, including K-12 and higher education examples)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines the emergence of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. The authors synthesize existing literature on AI technologies, outlining how these tools may support teaching, learning, feedback, assessment, personalization, and administrative efficiency, while also highlighting ethical and practical concerns such as bias, privacy, academic integrity, and the need for teacher preparation.

Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper surveys a broad range of AI-in-education applications, including intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading, personalized learning platforms, and conversational agents like ChatGPT. The discussion is largely conceptual and literature-based, drawing on prior studies across educational levels and contexts to argue that AI can improve engagement, feedback, and workload efficiency when used responsibly and in alignment with pedagogical goals.

The paper’s main conclusion is that AI has substantial promise for education, but benefits depend on careful integration, ethical safeguards, and adequate support for educators. It does not present original empirical data on student outcomes or compare implementation conditions; instead, it calls for more research to determine how tools like ChatGPT should be effectively and responsibly used in educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI tools such as chatbots and automated grading systems can reduce teacher workload by evaluating assignments, scoring work, and providing feedback. It cites examples such as Gradescope, Autolab, AutoGradr, and Repl.it as tools that can save teachers substantial time for lesson planning and student support, but it does not report original effect sizes or sample sizes.
finding.measure: teacher workload; grading/scoring efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses chatbots and ChatGPT as tools that can support writing-related learning through feedback, text generation, summarization, and language-related assistance. It cites prior studies and examples such as Grammarly, InstaText, QuillBot, and a study on post-secondary writers, but provides no original quantitative estimate in this article.
finding.measure: writing skills; written assignment feedback; language support

finding.finding_summary: The review states that chatbots can support language learning, including speaking and communication practice, and cites studies where AI chatbots improved learners’ speaking performance and punctuation learning in Spanish. No original data are reported in this article, and no effect sizes are given.
finding.measure: speaking performance; communication skills; punctuation learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI can increase motivation, engagement, self-confidence, and reduce anxiety by creating personalized and interactive learning environments. These effects are described as findings from prior literature, including chatbot and AI tutor studies, but this review itself reports no new sample size or effect size.
finding.measure: motivation; engagement; anxiety; self-confidence

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests AI can foster durable skills such as critical thinking, creativity, self-regulation, self-reflection, and self-directed learning by providing individualized feedback and step-by-step guidance. This is a synthesis claim rather than an original empirical test, and no quantitative estimate is reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking; creativity; self-regulation; self-directed learning

paper_profiles.title: The future landscape of large language models in medicine
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective article examines how large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT and GPT-4, may affect medicine across three domains: patient care, medical research, and medical education. The paper is not an empirical evaluation of an intervention; instead, it synthesizes early evidence, examples, and concerns about LLM capabilities, limitations, risks, and potential use cases.

In the education section, the authors argue that LLMs can support learning by generating explanations, summaries, step-by-step guides, individualized feedback, simulations, and revision aids. They also warn that students may misuse LLMs, which could undermine critical thinking, creativity, and reasoning, especially if LLMs become a crutch for assignments. The paper emphasizes the need for responsible use guidelines, prompt-engineering instruction, transparency, and institutional regulation, but it does not report original data on students, teachers, or classrooms.

Overall, the article concludes that LLMs have promising educational and clinical applications, but their current limitations—especially hallucinations, bias, lack of transparency, and weak factual reliability—make careful governance essential. Because it is a perspective/commentary, it offers no experimental estimates of effect, and its claims about benefits and risks are conceptual rather than empirical.

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that LLMs may support engagement through personalized explanations, interactive simulations, and individualized feedback, but it also warns that overreliance could reduce students' motivation to think independently and weaken creativity. No primary data, sample size, or effect size are reported because this is a perspective piece rather than an empirical study.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on critical thinking and reasoning as key durable skills potentially affected by LLM use in education. It contends that LLMs can assist reasoning through explanations and contextualization, but inappropriate use as a crutch may externalize reasoning and decrease students' critical thinking and creativity; no empirical effect sizes or sample are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how fifth-grade students and their teachers perceived a generative AI-powered tool designed to support creative mathematical writing. The study asks what educational benefits and challenges emerged when students used the system to ask questions about math story problems, represent their thinking with visual tools, and transform their ideas into culturally relevant math stories drafted with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3.

The implementation took place across six elementary classrooms in two U.S. schools with 79 fifth-grade students and six teachers. Students used the system over four class periods in one school and eight sessions in the other, after which a subset of students participated in focus-group interviews and all teachers were individually interviewed; survey responses and classroom observations were used to triangulate the qualitative data.

The study concludes that GenAI-supported mathematical creative writing was perceived to foster creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and positive affective experiences such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. At the same time, participants identified important challenges: students sometimes failed to critically evaluate AI output, struggled to generate coherent stories, and wanted more room for improvement, adaptive feedback, autonomous creation, social interaction, and accessible communication options. The authors argue that educational value depends not just on advanced AI capabilities, but on deliberate instructional and interface design that preserves learning opportunities and human collaboration.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived the GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing activities as strengthening mathematical understanding. The Ask and Represent steps helped students break down problems, visualize quantities and relationships, and surface misconceptions; however, this is based on qualitative perceptions rather than test-based outcomes, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student and teacher interview perceptions of mathematical understanding, problem decomposition, representation, and misconception detection
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=6 teachers (interviews from a subset of 10 students and all 6 teachers)

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on creative mathematical writing and reports that GenAI supported students in drafting, modifying, and improving stories, including adding detail and making narratives more original. Participants described the system as helping them write more fluently and creatively, but the evidence is qualitative and does not include standardized writing measures or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Interview and open-ended survey perceptions of story drafting, revising, originality, and creative writing process

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that working with GenAI made math feel more interesting, enjoyable, and curiosity-provoking, and it increased students’ sense of ownership over their learning. Students said the activity reduced pressure, encouraged experimentation, and made them feel like authors responsible for their own work, but these outcomes were captured through thematic analysis rather than quantitative scales.
finding.measure: Interview and open-ended survey perceptions of interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning

finding.finding_summary: The study found that GenAI-supported writing promoted several durable skills, especially divergent and flexible thinking and prompt engineering. Students learned through trial and error to make prompts more specific and to evaluate strengths and weaknesses of AI output, but the study did not quantify gains with a standardized critical-thinking measure.
finding.measure: Interview and observation themes on prompt engineering, critical evaluation of AI output, divergent/convergent/flexible thinking

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students indicated that the system could speed up initial story generation and provide quick drafts, which reduced the burden of starting from scratch. However, the same paper also notes that the system lacked timely feedback and sometimes required teacher intervention, so the operational benefit is limited and context-dependent rather than clearly demonstrated quantitatively.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of drafting speed, prompt iteration, and need for teacher assistance

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Tools on Student Writing Development: A Case Study From The CGScholar AI Helper Project
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This case study examines whether the CGScholar AI Helper, a web-based AI writing feedback tool, can support 11th-grade students’ writing development in English Language Arts. The study is framed around a broader CGScholar development effort and asks how customized, teacher-mediated generative AI feedback can be calibrated to fit classroom writing instruction rather than functioning as an unmediated chatbot.

The intervention involved one ELA teacher and six 11th-grade students in a socioeconomically underserved public school in the U.S. Midwest. Students completed a 200-word writing task comparing two teacher-selected texts and received two rounds of AI-generated feedback aligned to the teacher’s prompt, rubric, and source materials through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The research team also trained the teacher and students to use the platform and observed the implementation. Data came from students’ original and revised drafts, focus group comments, teacher post-survey feedback, and researcher observations.

Findings indicate that the AI Helper generally supported writing improvement: five of six students improved on at least one rubric criterion, and one student improved on three. Improvements were most evident in compare/contrast, composing defensible claims, analysis, and introducing/connecting evidence. Participants described the feedback as direct, specific, actionable, and encouraging revision. The paper concludes that a mediated, teacher-calibrated form of generative AI has promise for supporting K-12 writing development, while also noting usability concerns such as feedback that was too long and too elaborate.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative case study of six 11th-grade students, the CGScholar AI Helper was associated with improved writing development across several rubric criteria. Five students improved in at least one criterion and one student improved in three; gains were especially visible in compare/contrast, composing defensible claims, analysis, and introducing/connecting evidence after two rounds of AI feedback.
finding.measure: Teacher rubric-scored writing performance on a 0-4 star scale across six criteria; comparison of initial and revised drafts

finding.finding_summary: Students and the teacher reported that the tool encouraged revision and made it easier to identify what needed fixing. Focus group comments described the feedback as helpful, direct, and motivating for revision, suggesting positive effects on writing engagement and persistence during revision.
finding.measure: Focus group feedback, teacher post-survey, and researcher observations of student revision behavior

finding.finding_summary: The AI Helper appeared to support students’ analytical and revision skills by prompting them to compare texts more effectively, formulate more defensible claims, and connect evidence to claims. The authors interpret these changes as evidence that teacher-calibrated AI feedback can strengthen students’ capacity to revise independently and engage in more analytical writing.
finding.measure: Changes in rubric criteria related to compare/contrast, composing claims, analyze, and introduce/connect

paper_profiles.title: Shaping Human-AI Collaboration: Varied Scaffolding Levels in Co-writing with Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how different levels of AI scaffolding affect human writing performance and user experience in a co-writing setting with large language models. The core question is whether sentence-level suggestions or paragraph-level suggestions are more effective than no AI assistance, and whether the effects vary by writer expertise, technology familiarity, and order of exposure. The authors frame the work as a study of human-AI collaboration and scaffolding, with implications for the design of AI writing assistants.

The study used a within-subjects field experiment with 131 adults recruited from a large public university health-system. Participants completed argumentative writing tasks under three randomized conditions: no AI assistance, next-sentence suggestions, and next-paragraph suggestions. The custom tool used GPT-3 (Davinci) to generate suggestions, and the researchers measured text quality, number of edits, spelling errors, satisfaction, ownership, cognitive load, influence of AI suggestions, and productivity (words per time).

Results show a U-shaped pattern: sentence-level scaffolding did not improve writing quality and actually reduced it slightly, while paragraph-level scaffolding significantly improved quality and productivity. Both AI conditions reduced satisfaction and perceived ownership, with stronger ownership loss under paragraph-level support. Effects were stronger for non-regular writers and users with little or no prior technology use, while professional writers saw little quality benefit. The paper concludes that AI writing support should be personalized and that more comprehensive scaffolding may help some users but can also reduce authorship feelings and satisfaction.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluated writing performance across three conditions (no AI, sentence-level suggestions, paragraph-level suggestions) using human-rated text quality plus automated cohesion/lexical sophistication metrics. Sentence-level scaffolding reduced text quality by 0.29 points versus control, while paragraph-level scaffolding increased quality by 0.18 points (N=393 observations from 131 participants), yielding a U-shaped effect on writing quality.
finding.measure: Human-rated argumentative text quality; TAACO cohesion; TAALES lexical sophistication
finding.effect_size: Paragraph: +0.18 quality points; Sentence: -0.29 quality points

finding.finding_summary: Both AI-assisted conditions lowered user satisfaction and perceived ownership relative to no AI assistance. Satisfaction dropped by 2.14 points in the sentence condition and 1.89 points in the paragraph condition; ownership dropped by 3.66 and 5.65 points respectively (N=393), indicating that stronger AI scaffolding improved output but reduced positive user experience and sense of authorship.
finding.measure: Post-task satisfaction and ownership ratings
finding.effect_size: Satisfaction: sentence -2.14, paragraph -1.89; Ownership: sentence -3.66, paragraph -5.65

finding.finding_summary: The paper measures cognitive load and influence/persuasion effects during AI co-writing, which are relevant to self-regulation and authorship control. NASA-TLX cognitive load did not differ significantly across conditions, but AI influence on the final response increased substantially in both AI conditions, especially paragraph mode (5.91 vs 5.07 in sentence mode), suggesting stronger delegation to the AI with higher scaffolding.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX cognitive load; AI influence on final text

finding.finding_summary: AI scaffolding reduced editing burden and improved productivity, especially in paragraph mode. Compared with no AI assistance, sentence-level suggestions reduced edits by 334.14 and paragraph-level suggestions reduced edits by 795.04; paragraph scaffolding also increased productivity by 0.07 words per unit time (sentence mode showed no significant productivity gain).
finding.measure: Number of edits; productivity (words/time)
finding.effect_size: Edits: sentence -334.14, paragraph -795.04; Productivity: paragraph +0.07 words/time

finding.finding_summary: The study includes spelling error counts as a secondary output-quality outcome, but AI scaffolding did not significantly change spelling errors across conditions. This suggests the intervention affected higher-level composition more than low-level correctness, with no detectable benefit or harm on spelling accuracy.
finding.measure: Number of spelling errors

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how four secondary school EFL students in Hong Kong used ChatGPT and other proprietary chatbots to complete a timed blog-writing task for the first time. The authors are interested not in writing quality outcomes per se, but in the kinds of prompts students generated, how those prompts changed over time, and what prompt-engineering pathways emerged as students tried to elicit useful output from the chatbots.

Using iPad screen recordings and the students’ completed writing products, the study conducts a qualitative case analysis of 36 coded prompt turns across four students. The paper identifies six distinct prompt types (e.g., auto-complete, natural language instruction, questions, search-engine-like prompts, greetings, and chatbot-suggested follow-up prompts) and several more complex combinations of these types. It finds that students generally learned through trial-and-error, often beginning with a prompt type and then refining or repeating it, but no student used all prompt types and most did not use more advanced strategies such as few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought, or explicit role prompting.

The main conclusion is that secondary EFL students are unsophisticated prompt engineers when first introduced to ChatGPT-like systems, and that prompt engineering education would likely help students move beyond exploratory trial-and-error. The paper argues that classroom instruction should introduce students to chatbot capabilities, prompt types, and ways to match prompts to writing-task needs, while also noting that future work should examine how students evaluate chatbot outputs and integrate them into writing products.

finding.finding_summary: The study does not test whether ChatGPT improves writing performance; instead, it qualitatively documents how four high-school EFL students used prompt engineering to complete a writing task. The evidence centers on prompt content and sequencing during writing, not on measured gains in writing quality, so no causal literacy effect is reported.
finding.measure: Prompt types and sequences during a blog-writing task; completed writing samples were collected but not analyzed for writing-quality outcomes in the reported findings

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that students engaged in trial-and-error prompt refinement, showing exploratory learning and adaptation as they tried different prompt forms and repeated or modified prompts to elicit better chatbot output. These behaviors are interpreted as developing prompt engineering skill, a durable skill involving strategic problem solving and metacognitive adjustment, but the study does not quantify gains with effect sizes.
finding.measure: Observed prompt engineering pathways, including prompt-type changes, repetition, and refinement across turns

paper_profiles.title: Neural machine translation for automated feedback on children’s early-stage writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to automatically support teachers in giving formative feedback on children’s early-stage writing. The core challenge is that emergent writing often includes phonetic spelling, missing grammar, punctuation, and spacing, making standard linguistic analysis difficult. The authors frame the problem as a sequence-to-sequence translation task: convert student writing into conventional teacher-like writing so that downstream readability and text-quality metrics can be computed more reliably.

The study uses a large dataset of 36,610 student–teacher text pairs collected from a digital learning platform, with about 25% of pairs estimated to be noisy or mismatched. The authors fine-tune a pretrained BART model, compare it with baselines including identity copying, untuned BART, and ChatGPT-generated reconstructions, and evaluate a robust likelihood that explicitly handles noisy pairs. They also test synthetic data augmentation, temperature scaling, and deep ensembles. Results show that fine-tuned BART substantially improves reconstruction accuracy over baselines, synthetic pretraining plus fine-tuning performs best overall, and the translated texts yield much better estimates of readability metrics (Flesch-Kincaid and LIX) than using student text directly. The robust likelihood gives slight additional gains, and average log-likelihood can be used as a reject criterion to avoid poor translations, though calibration improvements do not clearly change that decision behavior.

finding.finding_summary: The model substantially improved reconstruction of children’s early writing and improved downstream readability estimation. On the test set, fine-tuned BART reduced mean normalized edit distance from 0.16 for the identity baseline and untuned BART to 0.09, and synthetic-data fine-tuning further improved it to 0.08; corresponding median NED fell to 0.01. Using reconstructed text also lowered readability-metric error versus using student text directly (e.g., FK MAE 0.58 and LIX MAE 2.88 for BART fine-tuning, compared with 1.36 and 5.66 for the identity baseline).
finding.measure: Normalized edit distance (NED) for text reconstruction; mean absolute error (MAE) for Flesch-Kincaid (FK) and LIX readability metrics
finding.confidence_interval: mean±SE reported: NED 0.09±0.00; FK MAE 0.58±0.03; LIX MAE 2.88±0.14

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s primary educational implication is teacher workload reduction: it proposes automated feedback generation for early writing, and the model can reconstruct conventional text accurately enough to support formative feedback and automated readability assessment. The robust likelihood and log-likelihood-based rejection option aim to reduce the burden of handling noisy or low-quality predictions by filtering poor translations before they are used in feedback workflows.
finding.measure: Model reconstruction performance and rejection-based decision-making for automated feedback workflows
finding.study_size: n=36,610 total pairs; n=2,767 test pairs

paper_profiles.title: Read, Revise, Repeat: A System Demonstration for Human-in-the-loop Iterative Text Revision
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents R3 (Read, Revise, Repeat), a human-in-the-loop system for iterative text revision. The authors argue that prior neural text revision systems are mostly one-shot and do not adequately model the iterative way humans revise text or incorporate feedback at each step. R3 instead generates sentence-level edit suggestions with explicit edit intentions and lets users accept or reject the edits across multiple revision depths.

The system combines edit-intention classification with a PEGASUS-based revision generator, trained on an iterative revision dataset collected from three domains (ArXiv, Wikipedia, and Wikinews). The user study involved three linguistic experts who reviewed model-generated edits and compared them with human-written revision sequences, while a second group of three annotators judged final document quality. The paper reports that R3 performs comparably to human revisions at early depths (1 and 2), but acceptance drops at depth 3. Human feedback improves final revision quality and reduces the number of iterations and edits needed. The study also finds that fluency edits are most readily accepted when human-authored, while system-generated style edits are relatively rare but accepted at a comparatively high rate. Overall, the work is a systems/HCI demonstration showing that lightweight human oversight can improve iterative revision quality, but it also highlights limitations in deeper revision steps and in the model’s handling of fluency edits.

finding.finding_summary: R3 improved writing/revision quality in an iterative text revision task, with human-in-the-loop revisions producing better final documents than system-only revisions. The system was rated comparable to human revisions at early depths (t=1 and t=2), but performance weakened by depth 3, indicating benefits for early-stage writing support but limitations for deeper iterative revision.
finding.measure: Acceptance rate of suggested edits; human judgments of final revised document quality; SARI/BLEU/ROUGE-L for the generation model
finding.study_size: n=3 linguistic expert users; n=10 documents for final-quality comparison; revision corpus: 44,270 training docs, 5,152 validation docs, 6,226 test docs

finding.finding_summary: Human feedback reduced the amount of revision work needed and improved efficiency in the revision process. SYSTEM-HUMAN produced better-quality final documents with fewer iterations and fewer accepted edits than SYSTEM-ONLY (avg. depth 2.5 vs 2.8; 148 vs 175 edits), suggesting that lightweight human review can make iterative revision more efficient.
finding.measure: Average revision depth, number of accepted edits, user-rated convenience/productivity, and final document quality
finding.study_size: n=3 linguistic expert users; n=3 annotators for quality comparison; n=10 documents for final-quality comparison

finding.finding_summary: The system supported controlled reviewing and decision-making during revision, but the paper does not provide strong direct evidence on broader durable skills outcomes. User feedback suggests the interface was convenient and could support productivity for familiar topics, yet users still needed to verify meaning and sometimes experienced friction from edit presentation, indicating mixed support for metacognitive editing practices.
finding.measure: User questionnaire ratings of convenience, satisfaction, productivity, and retention; qualitative comments

paper_profiles.title: Understanding EFL Students’ Idea Generation Strategies for Creative Writing with NLG Tools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines how English as a foreign language (EFL) secondary students use natural language generation (NLG) tools to support idea generation in creative writing. The authors focus on a gap in the literature: while NLG tools can generate text for writers, there is little empirical evidence on how novice EFL writers actually search for, evaluate, and select AI-generated ideas when composing stories.

The study took place in an all-girls secondary school in Hong Kong. Four students participated in seven voluntary, hour-long workshops where they learned about story writing, AI concepts, prompting, and digital writing practices, and then wrote short stories using their own words alongside text generated by four open-source NLG tools with different output lengths and generation styles. Students completed written reflections after workshop sessions, and the authors conducted thematic analysis of these reflections, supplemented by workshop audio/video and screenshots.

The findings suggest that students often approached prompting as a language-level task rather than a story-planning task, using sentence-level or paragraph-level inputs depending on what they wanted from the tool. When evaluating output, students generally tried to fit AI-generated text into their existing story ideas and differed in how open they were to novel or unexpected ideas. Tool selection was shaped mainly by the desire for more output to choose from, and no student preferred the next-word generator. The authors conclude that EFL students may need explicit instruction in prompt crafting, idea evaluation, and openness to AI-generated novelty, and they argue that NLG tools should be treated as scaffolds rather than replacements for planning and peer support.

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that EFL students used NLG tools to support story writing, but their strategies were mainly at the level of language units rather than narrative structure. Across 4 students and 12 reflection instances, students often searched for words, sentences, or paragraphs to complete creative writing tasks, evaluated output by checking whether it fit existing story ideas, and preferred tools that produced more ideas to select from.
finding.measure: Student written reflections, workshop discussions, and screenshots of AI-assisted short-story writing

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing English Writing Proficiency in China’s Polytechnic Students: An In-Depth Literature Review on the Application of the Input Hypothesis
paper_profiles.population: Polytechnic students (higher vocational / technical college students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Krashen’s Input Hypothesis can help improve English writing proficiency among polytechnic students in China. The central question is whether providing comprehensible input that is slightly above learners’ current level can support development in vocabulary, grammar, and idea organization for writing.

The paper is an in-depth literature review rather than a new empirical study. It synthesizes prior work on input-based language learning, writing challenges in vocational higher education, and a small number of related empirical studies in reading, output, and peer feedback. The author argues that polytechnic students face substantial writing difficulties due to limited exposure to English, low motivation, and traditional instruction, and that input-rich, scaffolded writing instruction could address these issues.

The review concludes that the Input Hypothesis is promising for writing instruction but that direct evidence on writing outcomes for polytechnic students is scarce. The paper recommends more controlled and longitudinal studies, especially on adapted materials, scaffolded tasks, and feedback approaches, to determine whether input-based methods reliably improve writing proficiency in this context.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that comprehensible input may support English writing development by improving vocabulary, grammar, and organization, but it also explicitly states that direct empirical evidence on polytechnic students’ writing proficiency is scarce. The paper cites related studies (e.g., reading and peer feedback research) but does not report a direct experiment on writing outcomes in this review itself.
finding.measure: English writing proficiency; vocabulary, grammar, and organization in writing

paper_profiles.title: How to Prompt? Opportunities and Challenges of Zero- and Few-Shot Learning for Human-AI Interaction in Creative Applications of Generative Models
paper_profiles.venue: CHI’22 Workshops (GenAICHI: Generative AI and Computer Human Interaction)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper argues that prompting should be treated as a new human-AI interaction paradigm, especially for creative applications of generative models. The authors focus on zero-shot and few-shot prompting with large language models and other generative systems, and they describe how prompts can support ad hoc tool creation, extend creative expressiveness, and provide inspiration and feedback during creative work.

Rather than reporting an intervention study, the paper synthesizes prior HCI/AI work and the authors’ own brainstorming sessions with five HCI researchers. From this analysis, it proposes four design goals for user interfaces that support prompting: helping users formulate prompts, combine prompts, apply prompts in context, and represent prompts in the interface. The examples are illustrated with creative-writing scenarios, but the paper’s contribution is primarily conceptual and design-oriented, not empirical.

The paper does not study K-12 learners, teachers, or classroom use directly. Its main conclusion is that effective prompting requires better user interfaces and interaction models because current prompting is often trial-and-error, hard to control, and difficult to generalize across models. It highlights opportunities and challenges around prompt composition, prompt representation, asynchronous use, and the cognitive/creative workflow of users interacting with generative models.

finding.finding_summary: This is not an empirical outcomes study; it is a qualitative workshop paper proposing interface design goals for prompt-based human-AI interaction. It discusses creative writing workflows and prompt engineering concepts, but reports no measured effect on critical thinking, collaboration, metacognition, or other durable skills.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper speculates that better prompting interfaces could reduce trial-and-error and support quicker prompt formulation, but it does not test productivity, task efficiency, or workload in an empirical study. No quantitative evidence is reported for changes in efficiency.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: CS4: Measuring the Creativity of Large Language Models Automatically by Controlling the Number of Story-Writing Constraints
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces CS4, a benchmark for evaluating the creativity of large language models (LLMs) in story writing under increasingly specific prompts. The core idea is that adding more constraints to a prompt makes it harder for models to rely on memorized training examples, thereby revealing whether they can produce original, coherent stories rather than simply reproducing high-quality text from training data.

The benchmark includes two constraint-generation strategies: an instruction-based approach and a story-based approach. For each, the authors synthesize 7, 15, 23, 31, and 39 constraints per prompt, producing 500 unique prompts total. They then ask GPT-4 to generate a base story and have six 7B models (LLaMA-2, Gemma, Mistral, and three OLMo variants) revise the story to satisfy the constraints. Stories are evaluated with LLM-as-a-judge methods on constraint satisfaction, coherence, grammar, likability, and diversity.

The main finding is that all models perform worse as prompt specificity increases, but they degrade at different rates. Gemma-7B and Mistral-7B show stronger performance under heavy constraint loads and slower quality decay than LLaMA-2-7B, suggesting greater creativity by the paper’s definition. The paper also finds that learning from human feedback helps more when prompts have fewer constraints, and that this advantage diminishes as prompts become more specific. The study is about LLM story generation, not educational use or high-school classroom interventions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates story-writing quality in large language models, a writing/literacy task. Across 500 prompts (7, 15, 23, 31, 39 constraints) and six 7B models, performance generally drops as constraints increase, but some models (notably Gemma-7B) retain better coherence and constraint satisfaction than others. Example reported results include a ~35% drop in constraint satisfaction for LLaMA-2 7B from 7 to 39 constraints, versus ~20% for Gemma-7B.
finding.measure: Story coherence, constraint satisfaction, grammar, likability, and story-writing diversity

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Taiwanese Hokkien Dual Translation by Exploring and Standardizing of Four Writing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of machine translation for Taiwanese Hokkien, a low-resource language with multiple competing writing systems (Hokkien Han, Tâi-lô, Pĳeh-ōe-jī, and Hàn-lô) and limited standardized corpora. The authors ask whether a large language model adapted from a Mandarin-centric base model can improve dual translation between Taiwanese Hokkien, Mandarin Chinese, and English, and which data conditions strengthen or weaken performance.

The approach builds on TAIDE-7B/LLaMA 2 with continued pre-training on monolingual Hokkien corpora and instruction fine-tuning on parallel data. The study systematically ablates training conditions, including whether to use only Hokkien Han or all writing systems, whether to extend the tokenizer vocabulary, and whether to add different parallel datasets. It also tests a preprocessing step that standardizes all Hokkien monolingual data into Han characters before continued pre-training, and introduces a GPT-4-based evaluation method with back-translation for Hokkien outputs.

The paper is not an education intervention study in the usual sense, but it does include Hokkien elementary school textbooks among the monolingual corpora and discusses Hokkien language resources in Taiwan. The main findings are that more monolingual Hokkien data generally improves translation, especially when all writing systems are included; vocabulary extension helps mainly for POJ targets and can slightly hurt other directions when data are limited; and standardizing corpora into Han yields small additional gains for HAN-related translation.
