The main contribution is evidence that GPT-4 achieves strong performance on many benchmark tasks, often outperforming GPT-3.5 and prior state-of-the-art systems, including high performance on simulated academic exams and improved language-following and safety behavior after RLHF post-training. The report also emphasizes limitations, including hallucinations, lack of reliable learning from experience, and reduced calibration after post-training. It does not study classroom use, writing instruction, high school students, multilingual learners, students with disabilities, transfer, durability, or implementation moderators in an educational setting; any educational relevance is indirect and benchmark-based rather than efficacy-based.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 scored highly on several academic benchmarks and simulated exams, including AP English Language and Composition (2, roughly 14th-44th percentile), AP English Literature and Composition (2, roughly 8th-22nd percentile), SAT Evidence-Based Reading & Writing (710/800, ~93rd percentile), and GRE Verbal (169/170, ~99th percentile). The paper reports benchmark performance only, not educational use or student learning effects.
finding.measure: Scores/percentiles on simulated and benchmark academic exams (e.g., AP English Language, AP English Literature, SAT EBRW, GRE Verbal)

finding.finding_summary: The report includes literacy-relevant benchmark results, especially on reading and writing exams and tasks such as SAT Evidence-Based Reading & Writing, GRE Verbal, AP English Language and Composition, AP English Literature and Composition, and DROP reading comprehension. GPT-4 outperforms GPT-3.5 on many of these benchmarks, but the paper does not evaluate instructional efficacy or classroom writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Benchmark exam scores in reading comprehension and writing-related assessments

finding.finding_summary: The report describes broader institutional and deployment-related impacts of GPT-4, including model-assisted safety pipelines, red-teaming with domain experts, and improved safety metrics relative to GPT-3.5. It also discusses OpenAI Evals and deployment-time monitoring, but these are engineering and governance artifacts rather than measured policy outcomes.
finding.measure: Safety evaluation metrics, refusal behavior rates, toxic generation rate

paper_profiles.title: Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students’ essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT-3 can improve students’ essay-writing performance when used as a writing assistant. The authors compare essay quality, writing time, authenticity/plagiarism indicators, and content similarity between a control group writing traditionally and an experimental group using ChatGPT-3.

The study recruited 18 second-year master’s students at the University of Split in Croatia (n=9 control, n=9 experimental). Students wrote an 800–1000 word essay in Croatian on a forensic-science topic during a four-hour session. Essays were graded by two teachers using a rubric covering mechanics, style, content, and format; the researchers also measured writing time, plagiarism/authenticity with PlagScan, essay similarity with Jaccard text reuse analysis, and AI-generated-text likelihood with an AI classifier.

Results showed no statistically significant benefit from ChatGPT-3. The control group slightly outperformed the ChatGPT group on overall essay score (2.39 ± 0.71 vs 2.00 ± 0.73), and none of the modeled predictors, including group assignment, significantly affected essay scores. Writing time was similar across groups, and the ChatGPT group showed slightly higher unauthenticity, while overall similarity across essays was low. The authors conclude that, in this small first-use sample, ChatGPT did not improve essay quality and may have contributed to over-reliance or distraction rather than better performance.

finding.finding_summary: In this small experiment (n=18; 9 control, 9 ChatGPT), using ChatGPT-3 did not improve essay writing performance. The control group slightly outperformed the experimental group on the overall essay score (2.39 ± 0.71 vs 2.00 ± 0.73), and the group effect was not statistically significant (P = 0.184).
finding.measure: Essay quality score from rubric-based grading of mechanics, style, content, and format (A-D converted to 4-1)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-3 did not significantly reduce writing time. Mean duration was 172.22 ± 31.59 minutes in the ChatGPT group and 179.11 ± 31.93 minutes in the control group, and writing duration was not a significant predictor of essay score (P = 0.669).
finding.measure: Essay writing time (minutes)

finding.finding_summary: The study found slightly higher text unauthenticity in the ChatGPT group than in the control group (11.87% ± 13.45 vs 9.96% ± 9.81), although pairwise essay similarity was generally low across the sample (Jaccard similarity median 0.002, range 0–0.054). The authors interpret this as showing no improvement in originality and some increased concern about authenticity when ChatGPT was used.
finding.measure: Text unauthenticity / plagiarism indicators and pairwise essay similarity (PlagScan, Jaccard similarity index, AI text classifier)
finding.std_deviation: unauthenticity: control 9.81; experimental 13.45; Jaccard similarity median 0.002

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT, when used with a structured prompt-and-feedback framework, can improve second-language learners’ argumentative essay writing and critical thinking. The authors propose the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW), which integrates the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model and Tan’s framework for argumentative writing with Hattie and Timperley’s feedback model.

The study reports a small experiment with 10 university students from a state university, randomly assigned to an experimental group (CGCAW-guided ChatGPT use) or a control group (unstructured ChatGPT use). Participants wrote a short argumentative essay in 40 minutes on the same prompt about social media. Essays were scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor on criteria such as clarity, logical coherence, evidence use, grammar, and persuasiveness.

Results were mixed across raters. ChatGPT’s scoring suggested the CGCAW group performed somewhat better in clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, while Grammarly and the instructor favored the control group on overall writing quality or thesis/summarization criteria. The authors conclude that CGCAW may help some aspects of argumentative writing and critical thinking, but the framework needs refinement, more training, and longer-term testing before strong efficacy claims can be made.

finding.finding_summary: The experiment found mixed effects on argumentative writing quality for 10 undergraduate second-language learners (n=10). ChatGPT’s evaluation showed the CGCAW group performed slightly better on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence (mean total 74 vs. 72.2), but Grammarly and the course instructor rated the control group higher overall (e.g., Grammarly mean 92.2 vs. 90.6; instructor mean 56 vs. 35).
finding.measure: Argumentative essay scores assessed by ChatGPT, Grammarly, and course instructor; rubric dimensions included clarity, logical coherence, evidence, thesis, reasoning, counterarguments, and summary
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT total SD=7.6 (G1) and 5.5 (G2); ChatGPT evidence SD=1.7 (G1) and 1.2 (G2); coherence SD=1.9 (G1) and 1.5 (G2)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively targets critical thinking as an outcome of using ChatGPT in argumentative writing. Using ChatGPT scores, the CGCAW group showed somewhat better performance in clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use, which the authors interpret as evidence of improved critical thinking processes; however, the instructor and Grammarly results did not consistently support this pattern.
finding.measure: Critical-thinking-aligned qualities embedded in argumentative essays (clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, reasoning, inference/positioning)

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how four secondary-school EFL students in Hong Kong used ChatGPT and other proprietary chatbots while completing the same timed writing task. The central question is not whether the AI improved writing outcomes, but how students constructed prompts over a single session: what prompt content they used, how often they prompted, how they sequenced prompt types, and how these pathways differed across students.

The study used a qualitative multiple-case design based on screen recordings of iPads and the students’ completed blog entries. Students were first-time users of SOTA chatbots for writing, although they had prior experience with other generative AI tools. They were not given instruction on chatbot capabilities or prompt engineering, allowing the authors to observe natural trial-and-error behavior during writing.

The paper identifies six prompt types (e.g., auto-complete, natural-language instruction, question, search-engine style prompts, greeting, and chatbot-suggested follow-up prompts) and shows that students used different combinations and sequences of these prompts to complete the same task. The authors argue that students’ pathways suggest exploratory learning and uneven sophistication in prompting, and they conclude that prompt-engineering education would help EFL students use chatbots more effectively in writing classrooms.

Because this is an exploratory qualitative case study with only four students, it does not support causal or efficacy claims about ChatGPT improving writing performance. Its contribution is descriptive and implementation-focused: it shows what prompt pathways looked like in one classroom context and highlights potential moderators such as prior generative-AI experience, lack of prompt training, and use of multiple chatbots.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines EFL students’ writing-related prompting behavior while composing a blog entry with ChatGPT and other chatbots (n=4 students, 36 coded turns). It does not measure writing quality effects of the AI; instead, it shows students produced varied prompt pathways and completed the writing task using different combinations of auto-complete, natural-language instruction, questions, and search-style prompts.
finding.measure: Prompt content/types and sequencing during a writing task; completed blog entries as contextual artifacts

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret the prompt pathways as evidence that students were learning, through trial-and-error, to engineer more sophisticated prompts and to refine ideas across turns. The paper argues that prompt engineering education could support metacognitive strategy development for using chatbots in writing, but this is an interpretive claim rather than an outcome measured with a scale.
finding.measure: Observed prompt engineering pathways; qualitative indicators of strategy refinement and sequence changes

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses students’ trial-and-error behavior and suggests that they were exploring chatbot capabilities without training, but it does not directly measure motivation, engagement, or persistence with validated instruments. Evidence is limited to qualitative observation that students kept iterating prompts until they finished the task.
finding.measure: Observed persistence/trial-and-error prompting during task completion

paper_profiles.title: Embracing AI in Education: Understanding the Surge in Large Language Model Use by Secondary Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how widely secondary students are using large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, what they are using them for, and how students perceive their usefulness and risks. The motivation is to inform educators and developers about student behavior in an environment where schools often restrict LLM use but students can still access these tools easily.

The authors conducted a survey of 306 middle and high school students across the United States, collected through a survey platform and Google Forms. Students reported whether they had used LLMs, how frequently they used them, which subjects they used them for, how useful they found them, and their perceptions of school policy strictness and ethical concerns. The study is descriptive and cross-sectional rather than experimental, so it does not test an intervention or estimate causal learning effects.

The main findings are that 71% of respondents had used LLMs at least once and usage was consistent across grades 7–12. Students reported using LLMs across multiple subjects, including writing/language arts, history, math, and foreign languages, with 57% of users saying they found them useful for writing text. Students also expressed mixed views: some said LLMs helped simplify complex topics, while others worried about inaccuracy, hallucinations, and overreliance. The paper concludes that LLM use is widespread among secondary students and may exacerbate access gaps, especially for resource-rich students, but it does not provide efficacy evidence for improved writing outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs for writing and language arts assignments, and 57% of LLM users said they found them useful for writing text. However, the paper only reports self-reported perceptions and usage patterns, not writing quality, grades, or other direct literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: Self-reported LLM use for writing/language arts and perceived usefulness for writing text

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs across multiple school subjects, including history and foreign languages, in addition to writing and math. The paper describes subject-specific usage prevalence and student perceptions of usefulness, but it does not evaluate subject learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Self-reported subject areas of LLM use

finding.finding_summary: The survey measured students' reported ethical concern about using LLMs and their views of school policy strictness. Students’ average ethical concern rating was 2.83/5 and their average policy strictness rating was 3.48/5, suggesting usage often persisted despite concern and restriction, but the study did not test motivation or engagement outcomes experimentally.
finding.measure: Self-reported ethical concern and perceived school policy strictness

finding.finding_summary: The paper documents widespread student LLM use despite restrictive school policies and reports differences by state technology index and school sector. It argues that access gaps and policy restrictions may shape who benefits from LLMs, but these are descriptive associations rather than causal institutional effects.
finding.measure: Self-reported school policy strictness; LLM usage by state tech index and school type

paper_profiles.title: Machine-Assisted Grading of Nationwide School-Leaving Essay Exams with LLMs and Statistical NLP
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) and statistical NLP methods can support automated scoring of high-stakes national essay exams in Estonia. The authors focus on the practical problem of grading large volumes of open-ended writing reliably and efficiently, especially when human scoring is time-consuming and shows some inconsistency.

Using two trial-exam datasets from full national cohorts, the study compares scores from several proprietary LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, Gemini) and supervised regression models based on linguistic features against the average of two human raters. The LLMs are used in a zero-shot, rubric-guided setup, with each essay scored separately by rubric dimension; the statistical NLP models use cross-validated regression on hand-engineered features. The paper also includes a small prompt-injection stress test and a separate essay-generation demonstration showing that an LLM can produce essays that score highly under the rubric.

Overall, the study finds that automated scoring can approach human scoring consistency on these essay exams, with some models falling within the human scoring range more often than not and statistical NLP matching or slightly outperforming LLMs on some language-accuracy categories. The authors argue that LLM-assisted grading is feasible for national-scale use in a human-in-the-loop workflow, but emphasize limitations including prompt sensitivity, bias, and the need for clear rubrics and human oversight. The paper is about assessment automation and institutional implementation rather than instructional effects on student learning.

finding.finding_summary: Automated scoring reduced the need for fully manual grading by showing near-human performance on national essay exams, suggesting a viable human-in-the-loop workflow for high-stakes assessment. In the 9th-grade dataset (n=781 essays) and 12th-grade dataset (n=764 essays), LLMs achieved MAE values of 2.66-4.97 on the 0-27 scale, and the paper argues this could reduce assessor workload and speed scoring at national scale.
finding.measure: Mean absolute error against human consensus scores; proportion of predictions within human score range; prompt-injection stress test for robustness
finding.study_size: n=781 and n=764 (main scoring datasets); n=100 (prompt injection test)

finding.finding_summary: The study supports the institutional feasibility of deploying LLM-assisted grading in a national examination system, with the authors concluding that a rubric-driven, human-in-the-loop pipeline is viable for high-stakes assessment. They argue the approach aligns with regulatory requirements and could support national-scale implementation in Estonia’s move toward computer-based exams.
finding.measure: Feasibility of national-scale implementation; comparison to human scoring; discussion of regulatory and operational constraints
finding.study_size: n=1,559 total essays across two cohorts in the broader experiment description; main datasets n=781 and n=764

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates automated scoring of student writing, including content, argumentation, vocabulary, syntax, orthography, punctuation, and structure. LLMs and statistical NLP models generally approximated human raters, with best total-score MAE around 2.66 on the 0-27 scale for GPT-4o in 9th grade and near-human performance in some subcategories such as vocabulary and punctuation.
finding.measure: Essay rubric scores for writing quality, including content, vocabulary, syntax, orthography, punctuation, and structure

paper_profiles.title: Exploring LLM-Generated Feedback for Economics Essays: How Teaching Assistants Evaluate and Envision Its Use
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether LLM-generated feedback can serve as useful suggestions for human graders, focusing on how teaching assistants (TAs) evaluate such feedback and whether they would incorporate it into their workflow. The motivation is practical: feedback on knowledge-intensive essays is time-consuming to write, and the authors ask whether AI can help expedite grading while preserving or improving feedback quality.

The intervention is an LLM-powered feedback engine built for short essay assignments in a foundational college economics course. The system decomposes feedback generation into three steps: identifying relevant essay sentences for each rubric item, judging whether the rubric is met, and generating feedback aligned to instructor-provided high-quality feedback guidelines. The study used GPT-4o with rubric-based prompts, instructor examples, and a Word plugin that displayed AI feedback as in-text comments with highlighted evidence and intermediate outputs.

The population was 5 TAs in an undergraduate ECON101 course at the University of Michigan, across 4 writing assignments and 20 one-hour think-aloud sessions in Fall 2024. Participants first graded essays as usual, then reviewed AI-generated feedback on the same essays and discussed differences, usefulness, and how AI suggestions might fit into their workflow.

Main conclusions are qualitative and implementation-focused. TAs generally thought AI feedback could improve consistency, save time, and provide useful praise, explanations, and guiding questions, especially when the AI highlights relevant text and exposes intermediate reasoning. At the same time, they noted that the system could be too rigid, miss deeper conceptual issues, and depend heavily on well-written rubrics. The paper concludes that AI feedback appears promising as a supplementary tool for human graders, but it does not test student learning outcomes or make causal efficacy claims about effects on writing quality or achievement.

finding.finding_summary: Teaching assistants reported that AI-generated feedback and sentence highlighting could speed up reading, evaluation, and feedback construction. In the 5-TA think-aloud study (20 one-hour sessions), participants said the system would save time by helping them locate relevant evidence faster and by providing ready-to-use comments, especially praise and guiding questions.
finding.measure: TA perceptions of grading speed, time savings, and workflow efficiency during think-aloud sessions

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that AI feedback helped TAs think more carefully about rubric interpretation and compare their own judgments with the system’s outputs, which participants saw as supporting more consistent and reflective grading. This is an implementation and sensemaking finding rather than a student learning outcome, but it directly concerns metacognitive reflection in the TA workflow.
finding.measure: TA reflections on rubric interpretation, consistency, and judgment during think-aloud sessions

paper_profiles.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Persian: A Preliminary Study Focusing on ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper benchmarks several large language models (primarily GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, and OpenChat-3.5) on a suite of Persian NLP tasks. The authors ask how well multilingual LLMs perform on Persian, whether English vs. Persian prompting changes results, and how few-shot prompting and translation to English affect performance.

The study spans classic NLP tasks (sentiment analysis, emotion recognition, named entity recognition, machine translation, and reading comprehension), reasoning tasks (textual entailment and math/logic QA), and knowledge tasks (literature and common-knowledge multiple choice QA). The evaluation uses existing Persian datasets plus two internally created math benchmark sets based on elementary school and 7th/10th-grade entrance exam questions. Experiments compare LLM outputs against task-specific fine-tuned SOTA models, mostly using 200-sample subsets for several test sets.

The main findings are that GPT-4 generally outperforms GPT-3.5 and OpenChat-3.5 across the Persian tasks, but task-specific supervised models still outperform LLMs on many classic NLP tasks. English prompts usually work better than Persian prompts, and translating examples into English improves GPT-3.5 performance on several tasks. Few-shot prompting helps GPT-4 more consistently than GPT-3.5 or OpenChat-3.5. Because this is a benchmarking study rather than an educational intervention, it does not provide causal evidence of efficacy for classroom use; it mainly offers comparative performance evidence about model capability and prompt sensitivity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper benchmarks multiple language tasks that include Persian reading comprehension, translation, sentiment analysis, NER, and textual entailment, but it is not an instructional study of writing support. For academic language tasks, GPT-4 generally performs better than GPT-3.5 and OpenChat-3.5, while task-specific fine-tuned models often remain stronger on classic benchmarks; for example, GPT-4 reaches 0.687 F1 on reading comprehension and 0.712 macro F1 on NER, while the best SOTA NER model reaches 0.988 F1.
finding.measure: Task performance on reading comprehension F1, NER macro F1, translation BLEU, sentiment macro F1, and entailment macro F1
finding.study_size: n=200 subsets for several test tasks; full benchmark sizes vary by dataset

finding.finding_summary: On math-related benchmarks, GPT-4 outperforms GPT-3.5 and OpenChat-3.5, and in the paper’s internally created elementary-school and math-problem sets it achieves the strongest scores among the compared LLMs. GPT-4 reaches 0.740 accuracy on elementary school questions and 0.564 on the math-problems set; GPT-3.5 reaches 0.565 and 0.503 respectively in its best settings. These results are descriptive benchmark comparisons, not evidence of student learning gains.
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice math/logic QA, elementary school questions, and math problems benchmarks
finding.study_size: n=200 subsets for some tasks; elementary school set n=50; math problems set n=179; math/logic QA n=677 in dataset description

finding.finding_summary: The study’s reasoning benchmarks capture model performance on textual entailment and math/logic problem solving, which the authors frame as reasoning ability. GPT-4 performs better than GPT-3.5 and OpenChat-3.5 on these tasks, reaching 0.636 macro F1 on Persian entailment (ParsiNLU) and 0.725 accuracy on math/logic QA. This is evidence about model reasoning performance, not evidence that students’ durable skills improved.
finding.measure: Macro F1 on textual entailment and accuracy on math/logic QA
finding.study_size: n=200 subsets for several tasks; dataset sizes vary

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure classroom productivity directly, but it does study prompt efficiency and task-format sensitivity by comparing zero-shot, one-shot, and three-shot prompting across Persian and English prompts. The authors find that English prompts and translated examples often improve performance, and that GPT-4 benefits more consistently from additional shots than GPT-3.5, suggesting practical implications for prompting workflows.
finding.measure: Performance differences across zero-shot, one-shot, and three-shot prompting; effect of translating samples to English

paper_profiles.title: Detecting AI-Generated Essays in Writing Assessment: Responsible Use and Generalizability Across LLMs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter addresses the problem of how to detect AI-generated essays in writing assessment and how to use such detectors responsibly. It reviews major detection approaches, including supervised text classifiers, watermarking, process-based indicators (such as keystrokes and revision traces), and similarity matching for hybrid human-AI essays. The paper emphasizes that detection is especially difficult in open-ended settings, but more tractable in standardized writing assessments where prompts are fixed and process data may be available.

The empirical component studies cross-LLM generalizability of detectors trained on essays generated in response to two public GRE writing prompts. Using GPT-2 perplexity-derived features and gradient boosting models, the author trains detectors on essays from one GPT-family model and tests them on essays from other GPT-family models, evaluating performance with AUC. The results show strong within-model performance and substantial transfer among several GPT models, but poorer generalization for GPT-o4-mini and GPT-5 unless training data from multiple models are pooled. The chapter concludes that effective detection will require continual retraining and multi-model training data, and that detector use must be cautious because of possible false positives, differential error rates for second-language writers, and challenges with mixed human-AI writing.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines writing assessment, specifically whether detectors can distinguish human-written essays from AI-generated essays. Using two GRE writing prompts and balanced test sets, model-specific detectors achieved high discrimination within the same LLM and often strong cross-model transfer, with AUCs frequently above 0.80 and many above 0.90 among several GPT-family models. This supports the conclusion that writing products in standardized assessment contexts can be classified with high accuracy when detector training data match the generative models being tested.
finding.measure: Detector discrimination performance on essay texts in writing assessment, measured by AUC
finding.study_size: n=700 essays total for model-specific analyses (200 human essays; 200 essays per LLM across 7 LLMs, with 100 human + 100 AI used per model test set and remaining essays used for training)
finding.effect_size: AUC > 0.80 frequently; many > 0.90; exact overall effect size not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.venue: Online Journal of Communication and Media Technologies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the early piloting of CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant designed to provide formative feedback on student writing in K-12 settings. The study asks whether the tool has potential to support writing in diverse subject areas by aligning AI feedback with teacher rubrics, classroom materials, and instructional expectations. It is framed as an exploratory implementation study rather than a causal test of efficacy.

CyberScholar was piloted in four public schools in the United States, including three high schools and one middle school, across English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History. Data came from classroom observations, surveys, and interviews with 121 students and 4 teachers, with 54 students and 3 teachers completing post-surveys and 8 students and 1 teacher interviewed. Teachers and students were trained to use the tool, and the system was customized using retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering so that feedback would reflect teacher-provided rubrics, texts, and assignments.

The findings are qualitative and primarily based on participant perceptions. Students generally viewed the tool positively, describing its feedback as detailed, specific, interactive, aligned with rubric criteria, and useful for revising writing. Some students reported perceived improvements in writing quality, grammar, transitions, and organization, and a subset appreciated the tool’s conversational follow-up feature. At the same time, some participants found the star ratings inconsistent, suggesting implementation and reliability concerns. Overall, the paper concludes that CyberScholar shows promise for formative writing support and may shift teachers’ roles toward guiding AI-mediated feedback, but it does not provide causal evidence of writing gains or durability of effects.

finding.finding_summary: Participants largely perceived CyberScholar as helpful for writing revision, especially for receiving detailed feedback, grammar support, clearer organization, and rubric-aligned guidance. However, the evidence is qualitative and perception-based rather than causal; some students also reported inconsistent ratings when the same paper was resubmitted without changes, which weakens claims of effectiveness.
finding.measure: Student survey comments, classroom observations, and interviews about writing feedback, revision, and perceived writing improvement
finding.study_size: n=121 students; n=54 post-survey respondents; n=8 interviewed students

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the tool increased engagement and made the revision process feel more interactive, supportive, and motivating. Some comments indicate greater willingness to use the tool again and a sense that it helped them feel more capable of improving their writing, but these are subjective perceptions rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Post-survey responses and interview comments on engagement, motivation, and willingness to reuse the tool
finding.study_size: n=121 students; n=54 post-survey respondents; n=8 interviewed students

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that CyberScholar supported metacognition and self-regulation by prompting students to revise drafts, reflect on feedback, and ask follow-up questions. Students described using the tool to identify weaknesses, refine their writing, and compare revised versions, suggesting perceived growth in revision practices and reflective writing processes.
finding.measure: Qualitative evidence from interviews, surveys, and observations regarding revision behavior, reflective feedback use, and follow-up questioning
finding.study_size: n=121 students; n=54 post-survey respondents; n=8 interviewed students

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that students and teachers viewed CyberScholar as fast and convenient, with feedback that could be used quickly during revision cycles. The paper also notes perceived time savings and a potential reduction in teacher workload because the AI could provide aligned formative feedback, though these claims were not quantitatively tested.
finding.measure: Participant perceptions of speed, convenience, and workload implications from surveys and interviews

paper_profiles.title: How Large Language Models Are Changing MOOC Essay Answers: A Comparison of Pre- and Post-LLM Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how the release of ChatGPT and related large language models changed student essay responses in a university-level MOOC on AI ethics. The authors analyze a longitudinal corpus of 56,878 English-language essay submissions from 3,582 course participants spanning November 2020 through October 2024, comparing writing before ChatGPT, during the first year after release, and at least one year after release.

The study does not introduce an intervention; instead, it uses observational text analysis to compare pre- and post-ChatGPT essays. The analyses examine essay length, sentence counts, readability, lexical variety, the prevalence of LLM-associated vocabulary, and topic distributions using word-frequency comparisons and topic modeling. The paper reports substantial post-ChatGPT increases in essay length, sentence count, and readability scores, along with lower type-token ratios and large increases in terms associated with LLMs, AI ethics, and AI governance.

The authors interpret these shifts as consistent with broader LLM influence on student writing and possibly partial reliance on LLMs for generating answers, while explicitly noting that the data cannot prove any specific essay was AI-generated. They find no meaningful change in broader topics via topic modeling, suggesting that prompts and overall discussion themes remained fairly stable even as stylistic and lexical features changed. The paper is mainly about higher-education MOOC writing behavior and does not study K-12 learners, teacher mediation, or prompt training.

finding.finding_summary: Post-ChatGPT essays were longer and somewhat easier to read, but also showed reduced lexical diversity. Compared with pre-ChatGPT essays, mean length increased from 150.5 to 230.1 tokens and sentence count from 6.85 to 9.76 in the later period; Flesch Reading Ease increased from 12.70 to 15.31 and type-token ratio decreased from 0.617 to 0.577 (all p < 0.0001).
finding.measure: Essay length, sentence count, sentence length, Flesch Reading Ease, type-token ratio
finding.std_deviation: Pre: tokens SD=104.3; sentences SD=5.82; sentence length SD=11.56; Flesch SD=4.84; TTR SD=0.091. Post: tokens SD=171.0; sentences SD=7.76; sentence length SD=17.91; Flesch SD=7.72; TTR SD=0.113.

finding.finding_summary: The study found large increases in the prevalence of LLM- and AI-related terminology in essay responses after ChatGPT's release. For example, 'Generative AI' increased 53.53×, 'ChatGPT' appeared post-release where it was absent before, and terms such as 'LLM', 'language model', and 'hallucination' also increased significantly.
finding.measure: Relative prevalence of AI/LLM-related terms in essays

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the observed shifts may indicate greater offloading to LLMs, which could reduce metacognitive effort, but it does not directly measure critical thinking or metacognition. Topic modeling found no meaningful change in broader essay themes, so the durability-related evidence is indirect and interpretive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Indirect textual indicators interpreted as potential LLM reliance; topic models of essay themes

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Writing Research Papers: A New Type of Algorithmic Bias and Uncertainty in Scholarly Work
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and related large language models introduce a new form of context-induced algorithmic bias and uncertainty when used to write scholarly manuscripts. The authors focus on how prompting, user identity cues, institutional affiliation, and limited context can alter AI outputs, potentially reinforcing stereotypes, producing hallucinations, and reducing reproducibility in research writing.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it presents a conceptual argument supported by examples and a systematic review of manuscripts that reportedly used or co-authored generative AI tools. The review identified 104 works using criteria based on ChatGPT/GPT-2/GPT-3/OpenAI mentions, and 79 works retaining the signature phrase "As an AI language model." The authors conclude that generative AI can assist with drafting and literature review, but that its use in scholarly writing may amplify bias, generate inaccurate content, and create a feedback loop if future models are trained on machine-written text.

The context is scholarly publishing and research writing, not K-12 education or student learning. The paper discusses implications for researchers broadly, including non-English speakers and users who may unintentionally reveal demographic or affiliation information in prompts. Its conclusions are primarily normative and theoretical, emphasizing concerns about bias, hallucination, and authorship rather than estimating causal effects of AI writing assistants on outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can speed drafting and act as an autocomplete or literature-review aid, but it does not provide causal evidence that these tools improve productivity. Instead, it emphasizes that uncertain outputs, hallucinations, and prompt-sensitive bias can undermine efficient scholarly writing and require additional human correction.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of manuscript drafting and literature-review assistance

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central claim is that AI-generated or AI-assisted scholarly writing may create harmful effects for academia and knowledge production, including authorship disputes, reproducibility problems, and a positive feedback loop if future models are trained on machine-written papers. The systematic review component reports 104 AI-related scholarly works and 79 with the phrase "As an AI language model," but these are counts rather than effect estimates.
finding.measure: Systematic review counts of AI-authored/co-authored or AI-signature manuscripts; discussion of bias and authorship norms
finding.study_size: n=104 works reviewed; n=79 works with signature phrase

paper_profiles.title: Specialists or Generalists? Multi-Agent and Single-Agent LLMs for Essay Grading
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how two large language model architectures for automated essay scoring compare: a single-agent model versus a multi-agent system that separates grading into content, structure, and language specialists coordinated by a chairman agent. The authors focus on whether architectural decomposition improves essay scoring performance, especially across different essay quality levels, and whether few-shot calibration examples change results.

Using the ASAP 2.0 essay corpus, the study evaluates both architectures in zero-shot and few-shot settings with GPT-5.1. The dataset consists of 24,278 source-based argumentative essays written by U.S. secondary students in grades 6-10; the evaluation uses a stratified test set of 450 essays plus 12 calibration essays for few-shot prompting. Performance is measured against human rubric scores using quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) and exact match accuracy.

The main finding is that few-shot prompting is the dominant factor in performance for both architectures: providing just two examples per score level improves QWK by about 26% for both systems. The multi-agent system performs better at identifying low-quality essays, while the single-agent system is somewhat better on mid-range essays. Both systems struggle with high-quality essays, and the multi-agent system’s veto/capping logic appears to help catch weak essays but also creates conservative under-scoring at the top end. The paper concludes that architectural choice should depend on deployment goals, with multi-agent design better suited for diagnostic screening and single-agent design offering a cheaper general-purpose option.

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluates automated essay scoring performance on writing quality judgments using the ASAP 2.0 corpus. Few-shot prompting substantially improved agreement with human ratings for both architectures (single-agent QWK 0.5664 to 0.7165; multi-agent QWK 0.5917 to 0.7453; n=450 test essays, plus n=12 calibration essays), but the multi-agent system was better on low-quality essays while the single-agent system was better on mid-range essays. Both systems struggled with high-quality essays, indicating mixed performance rather than a uniform advantage.
finding.measure: Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) and exact match accuracy against human essay scores
finding.study_size: n=450 test essays; n=12 calibration essays
finding.effect_size: QWK improvement ≈ 0.1501 (single-agent) and 0.1536 (multi-agent); exact-match improvement 4.89 pp and 9.55 pp

gaps: The sweep is dominated by a small number of recent, mostly generative-AI-oriented examples and does not yet establish the foundational framing of what counts as an AI writing assistant versus adjacent tools (AWE, grammar/style checkers, intelligent tutoring systems) in secondary literacy research.

Operationalization details are missing: there is little evidence about how studies measure writing quality, revision quality, fluency, or related constructs, and no synthesis of common outcome measures or coding schemes.

Population coverage is incomplete: general education high school students are mentioned only indirectly, and there is no clear coverage of multilingual learners, students with disabilities, or subgroup-specific designs beyond speculative claims.

Instructional setting coverage is thin: the sweep does not yet document the range of secondary classroom contexts, teacher-mediated interventions, content-area implementations, or whether studies are ELA-only versus science/social studies.

The evidence base appears to rely heavily on a project description and a 2025 article; it lacks a robust sweep of peer-reviewed high-school studies and older pre-generative AI work that would define the field.

The Semantic Scholar search error suggests the search strategy may not have retrieved enough foundational literature, so the current findings are not sufficient to answer the framing and scope questions comprehensively.

The sweep has examples of generative AI and one intelligent tutoring system, but it does not yet clearly distinguish the major tool categories requested in the thread, especially automated writing evaluation, grammar/style aids, and classic intelligent tutoring tools as separate classes in secondary classrooms.

Coverage of high school literacy outcomes is still thin: the findings mention writing quality and revision broadly, but do not yet map how outcomes are operationalized (e.g., holistic rubric scores, text length, revision types/substantive revisions, fluency measures, accuracy, mechanics, idea development).

The population coverage is incomplete. Multilingual learners are mentioned, but there is no solid coverage of general education samples, students with disabilities as an actual studied group, or clearly documented content-area classroom studies versus ELA-only settings.

The sweep appears to rely heavily on a small number of recent or program-level sources (including project pages) and does not yet surface the likely core empirical high-school studies that would anchor a foundational framing of the field.

There is no clear evidence yet of searches targeting older pre-generative AI secondary writing research, which is important for distinguishing AI writing assistants from long-standing AWE/grammar-check/ITS literatures.

The sweep is too sparse on the core population: high school/secondary classroom-based writing studies are not yet well covered. Results skew to general L2/ESL writing, primary/elementary, or unrelated domains.

Missing baseline/comparison-condition studies that directly examine standard instruction in high school writing: teacher feedback, peer review, conferencing, rubric-based instruction, process writing, and ordinary classroom controls are not yet synthesized.

Alternative non-AI digital supports are undercovered for secondary writing: word processors, spellcheck, grammar check, automated writing evaluation/automated essay scoring, and online writing platforms need direct comparison-condition studies.

The thread asks for baseline levels of literacy growth or writing performance under standard instruction; the sweep currently lacks outcome-focused studies or meta-analyses reporting typical gains/effect sizes for high school students without AI assistants.
The current hits include a systematic review of AWE and a peer feedback article, but not enough classroom trials or reviews that map intervention vs control conditions in secondary schools.

The sweep is still too sparse on the core high-school writing literature: it has only a general AWE review, a peer feedback overview, and several off-topic or very indirect items, but not enough classroom-based secondary-school studies on teacher feedback, conferencing, rubric-based instruction, or traditional process-writing approaches.

Comparison conditions are not yet well covered: missing are clear non-AI comparators such as word processors, spellcheck/grammar tools, online writing platforms, and automated feedback systems tested against standard instruction in high school.

Baseline growth/performance under standard instruction is not yet synthesized: the sweep does not yet surface studies reporting typical gains or outcomes in untreated/control groups or traditional instruction conditions for high school writing/literacy.
Population specificity is weak: several results are not actually high school writing studies, so the evidence base for secondary education remains underrepresented.

The sweep is still dominated by broad conceptual/review pieces and only one clearly relevant school-level writing instruction study appears (e.g., secondary school ELLs with ChatGPT). There is little direct evidence on high school writing implementation during planning, drafting, and revision.
Missing are classroom intervention studies or case studies that specify assignment types, teacher mediation, allowed/restricted use, and how students were trained to use AI writing tools.

The current results do not yet answer the mechanism-of-action side in a grounded way: there is little on immediate feedback, revision opportunities, metacognitive support, cognitive load reduction, or rubric/curriculum alignment in actual high school writing tasks.
Search results appear to skew toward higher education or general K-12 AI commentary rather than high school composition instruction specifically.
Implementation-feature comparisons are missing: feedback specificity, prompt design, teacher oversight, and scaffolding are not yet covered by the extracted studies.

The sweep is still dominated by broad conceptual/review papers and only a small number of directly relevant empirical studies. It does not yet establish how AI writing assistants are actually implemented in high school writing instruction across planning, drafting, and revision.

Evidence on high school/secondary writing classrooms is thin. One likely-relevant study is about secondary school English language learners, but the sweep lacks multiple classroom-based secondary writing studies to compare assignment types, teacher mediation, permitted/restricted use, and rubric/curriculum alignment.

The current results do not sufficiently address mechanism-of-action details such as feedback specificity, prompt design, scaffolding, student training, teacher oversight, and whether these features improve learning outcomes in practice.

The sweep lacks studies focused specifically on writing instruction outcomes or process measures (revision quality, metacognition, cognitive load, engagement) in secondary settings; most found items are general AI-in-education or ChatGPT opportunity/challenge pieces.
